en: Salutations to the illustrious Rāmānuja. Salutations to Śrī. Salutations to Śrīvara.

In the first chapter, it was stated that the "Supreme Brahman"—which is the object of knowledge according to the Vedānta—is distinct from the non-conscious objects within the scope of means of valid cognition such as perception, as well as from the conscious self both when conjoined with and when separated from them; that it is free from even a trace of all that is contrary to human welfare, such as ignorance (avidyā); that it is a single expanse of infinite knowledge and bliss; that it is an ocean of boundless and sublime qualities; that it is the sole cause of the entire universe; and that it is the inner Self.
Immediately following this, the second chapter is commenced in order to demonstrate that the meaning of this [subject] is invulnerable in every conceivable way.
First, having raised the objection that the Vedāntas do not have that [Brahman] as their primary purport because they contradict the Smṛti of Kapila,
that [objection] is now refuted.

"Thus it was stated in the first [chapter]" means that, for the purpose of providing a summary of the meaning of the four sections (pādas) of the first chapter, the reason for the sequential order of the *Īkṣati* and *Ānandamaya* sections is intended by the phrase "beyond the scope of perception and other means of valid cognition. The word "etcetera" (*ādi*) refers to inference. For indeed, through perception, a cause corresponding to the earth and so forth is experienced. Therefore, because the non-intelligent is the first to come to mind, its refutation is undertaken first.

The word *nirasta* (cast out) is used for the purpose of excluding what has been abandoned. The term *ananta* (infinite) expresses the essential nature of the subject (*dharmin*). It is a *bahuvrīhi* compound meaning "one whose ocean of noble qualities is immeasurable. By the word *sāgara*, a "collection" is intended. "The sole cause of the entire world" means the cause even of space and so forth; that is to say, it is both the efficient cause and the material cause. Anticipating the objection that its previously mentioned state of being the opposite of all that is to be abandoned is untenable if it is the cause of the world, he says: "It is the inner self of all."

The word "immediately following" (*anantaram*) refers to the subject matter of the second chapter. For indeed, an objection that has arisen must be resolved. Therefore, by the phrase "is to be considered possible," he introduces the occasion for an objection. By the term "all types," he intends those various modes of introducing objections regarding contradictions found even within each of the four quarters [of the Vedas]. In the first chapter, through the exclusion of non-connection and the exclusion of connection with others, it was established—by examining the purport of the sentences—that the statements contained in the Vedānta have as their sole purpose the fact that Brahman is the single cause.
Now, the meaning is that in the second chapter, the refutation of contradictions with external systems of logic (*bāhyatarka*) is stated.

The subject matter of the section (*pādārtha*) will be explained for the sake of establishing the connection with the second section. Therefore, he states the function of the first topical section (*adhikaraṇa*) with the words, "First, then... The subject matter (*viṣaya*) is the status of being the cause as determined in the first chapter. Doubt arises due to the conflicting views found in the *smṛtis* of Kapila, Manu, and others. Herein lies the inquiry:
in order to make known the connection between the first and second chapters, he briefly states the subject matter of the first chapter.

How is it that the Śruti has a different purport because of its contradiction with Smṛti? For it has been stated: "In case of contradiction, [Smṛti] would be independent [of the Veda]," meaning that Smṛti which contradicts Śruti is not to be respected.
True; [that is so].

In cases such as "one should chant after touching the Audumbarī post," since the determination of the meaning is possible through the text itself, any Smṛti that contradicts it must simply be disregarded. Here, however, because the reality known through the Vedānta is difficult to comprehend, it is impossible to reach a definitive conclusion regarding the meaning when there is a contradiction with a Smṛti composed by a supreme seer (paramarṣi). Therefore, it is not contradictory to establish that the Śruti is not intended to convey that [contradictory] meaning on account of the Smṛti.

What is meant is this: the Agnihotra, Darśa-Pūrṇamāsa, and so forth, which constitute all the means for worldly prosperity (abhyudaya) described in the earlier portions [of the Veda]— (Note: The provided source text appears to be truncated. The translation above reflects the full logical argument presented in the extant portion.)

Can the status of Brahman as the cause of the world be subverted, or not? To that end, do the Vedānta texts have Brahman’s causality as their primary purport, or do they have something else as their purport? To that end, does the contradiction with the Sāṅkhya Smṛti result in the Vedānta texts lacking that purport, or not? To that end, should the Vedānta be supplemented by the Sāṅkhya Smṛti, or rather by the Smṛtis of Manu and others? To that end, is the Sāṅkhya Smṛti based on error, or is it not?

When [the Smṛti] is not based on error, then, because it serves as a supplement (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) to the Vedāntas, there is no contradiction between them; since they [the Vedāntas] have another purpose [than to contradict], the doctrine that Brahman is the cause cannot be shaken.

When, however, it is based on error, then, because it cannot serve as a supplement to them due to that [error], and because they do not have another purpose [than to contradict it] when there is such a contradiction, the doctrine that Brahman is the cause remains unshakable.

The word "how" (*katham*) is used in the sense of censure. In the phrase "for it has been said" (*uktaṃ hi*), the particle *hi* indicates a reason. There is the sūtra: "But that which is in contradiction [with direct perception] should be disregarded; for when there is no [contradiction], there is inference. The meaning is: a statement of Smṛti that contradicts a directly perceived Śruti is to be disregarded—that is, not to be respected. For, provided there is no contradiction with a directly perceived Śruti, there is the inference of a Śruti that serves as the basis for the Smṛti.

"It is true. In that case, it was already stated that because of the contradiction with Śruti, Smṛti is not to be respected; however, the meaning here is that there is a distinction. Regarding "the Audumbarī pillar," etc.: the Śruti says, "One should chant the Udgītha while touching the Audumbarī pillar," whereas the Smṛti says, "The Audumbarī pillar must be entirely covered. Herein lies the intended difference: in cases such as "the Audumbarī pillar," since the direct Śruti is unambiguous, its meaning can be determined by itself, independently of Smṛti.

In that regard, a Smṛti whose meaning is contradictory [to the Vedas] is to be disregarded; for because the Upaniṣadic statements are manifold, their meaning cannot be determined by itself. Indeed, it is only when it has been ascertained that "this is the meaning of the Śruti" that the Smṛti may be rejected on account of its contradiction with it. And since that [meaning of the Śruti] is difficult to ascertain by itself, there is a dependence upon Smṛti for that purpose.
By one who duly accepts the month-long rites, the Jyotiṣṭoma, and other such rituals, as stated in the Śruti, Smṛti, Itihāsa, and Purāṇas: "The Ṛṣi Kapila, the abundant..."

Since it is impossible for those of little learning and dull intellect to determine the meaning of the Vedānta without the support of the Smṛti composed by the Supreme Sage Kapila—who is celebrated as authoritative through such statements as "by him" (ityādi)—and who established the knowledge of supreme beatitude and its means; and since, if one were to accept the literal meaning [of the Upanishads] alone, the entire Sāṅkhya Smṛti authored by that authoritative person would result in being rendered obsolete; therefore, one must necessarily admit that "the very object well-known in the Smṛti is what is to be known from the Vedānta."

Nor should it be argued that, this being the case, there would be the fault of leaving no room for the Smṛtis of Manu and others which declare Brahman to be the sole cause; for those [Smṛtis] find their scope in merely supplementing the ancient portions devoted to the exposition of Dharma. However, since this [present Śruti] is devoted to the exposition of ultimate reality (*tatva*) in its entirety, it would indeed be left without scope if such were not admitted. This very objection is raised [in the Sūtra]: "If it be said that there is the fault of leaving no room for the Smṛti."

"To this, the reply is": "No, because it would entail the fault of leaving no room for other Smṛtis. For other Smṛtis, such as those concerning the Mantras, declare that Brahman alone is the sole cause. As Manu says:
"This was then enveloped in darkness..."
Beginning with these words, [it continues]:

"Then the Blessed One, the Self-Existent, the Unmanifest, who dispels darkness and whose power operates through the great elements and the rest, appeared, manifesting this [universe]. Desiring to emit various creatures from his own body, he meditated and first created the waters; into them he cast his seed.
And also in the Bhagavadgītā:
"I am the source of all the universe, as well as its dissolution," and "I am the origin of all; from me everything proceeds.
And in the Mahābhārata:
"By me was all this created—the entire world, both stationary and moving!"
"And into whom does it merge at the time of dissolution? Tell me that, O Grandfather! Thus questioned, he replied:
"Nārāyaṇa, whose form is the universe, the infinite self, the eternal. Likewise:
"Therefore, O best of the twice-born, the unmanifest (avyakta) consisting of the three qualities (triguṇa) has arisen"; and also:
"O Brahmin, the unmanifest dissolves into the inactive Puruṣa. And the venerable Parāśara said:
"The universe has arisen from Viṣṇu and is situated in Him alone;
He is the author of the sustenance and dissolution of this universe, and the universe is He.
Thus it is said. And Āpastamba says:
"Living beings are all the city of the one who dwells in the cave, who is unslain and free from blemish;
from him all bodies originate, for he is the root, eternal, and constant"— beginning thus, [the text continues].
Thus: if the meaning of the Vedānta statements were to be determined by the Smṛti of Kapila, then a "great" defect—namely, the lack of scope for all these Smṛtis—would result. This is the meaning:

The sentence "The city belongs to the living beings" occurs in the first section of the Adhyātma-khaṇḍa; the sentence "Therefore, the bodies... occurs in the second section. The sentence "The city belongs to the living beings" is cited both to fulfill the expectation arising from the word "therefore" (tasmāt)—namely, "from what?"—and to demonstrate that the word "body" (kāya) refers to the body of the Lord. "City" (pūḥ) means a fortress; here, it means the body.

And when [the vowel *i*] is applied, it becomes "ara. According to this statement, although the Vedānta texts are devoted to establishing a reality that transcends the scope of all other means of knowledge such as perception, and thus require corroboration for the sake of clarifying their meaning for those listeners who have heard little;

Nevertheless, lest there be the contingency of rendering many *smṛtis*—composed by the most authoritative sages and intended to supplement that [Veda] by following its meaning—without scope, the *smṛti* of Kapila, whose subject matter contradicts the *śruti*, must be disregarded. Furthermore, supplementation (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) consists in the clarification of the meaning established by the *śruti*; and that cannot be accomplished by a *smṛti* whose meaning is contradictory.

Nor do these Smṛtis find their scope merely by clarifying the portions of dharma mentioned in the earlier part [of the Veda]; for since they enjoin dharmas as being the worship of the Supreme Person who is the Supreme Brahman, it would be impossible for them to enjoin dharmas that constitute such worship if there were no exposition of the Supreme Person who is the object of worship. For instance: "The Supreme Person..."

Regarding the phrase "having become the ground for esteem" (*sambhāvanābhūmibhūta*): the word *bhūta* here refers to that which is established (*siddha*), because it is intended to convey an already accomplished fact. The meaning is this: if [the text] were concerned with what is to be accomplished (*kārya-paratva*), any contradiction in meaning—whether due to alternative options (*vikalpa*) or differences in the qualifications of the practitioners (*adhikāribheda*)—would be easily resolved. However, if it concerns an established reality (*siddhavastu-paratva*), the meaning of the Veda must be interpreted in accordance with one of the two traditional recensions (*smṛti*); it cannot be interpreted as being in accordance with both. Thus, it is said to be "authoritative" (*āpta*).

"Contrary in meaning to the Śruti" means that its meaning is contrary to the Śruti supported by reasoning (nyāya); this is the sense. "To be disregarded" means that [the Śruti] supported by many Smṛtis which are themselves supported by reasoning propounded by the most authoritative persons is stronger than even a Śruti supported by a single Smṛti whose reasoning is merely stated by an authoritative person. "By one contrary in meaning"—that is, by one whose meaning is contrary to the Śruti supported by a Smṛti consistent with reasoning—the impossibility of corroboration (upabṛṃhaṇa) constitutes the refutation; such is the meaning.

It refutes the charge of being open to objection [by stating] "For instance" and so forth; for it is recorded in the Smṛti that all ritual acts (*karman*) constitute a form of service (*ārādhana*) intended to augment the prior portion [of the sacrifice].

"From whom the activity of all beings proceeds, and by whom all this is pervaded—by worshipping Him through one's own duty, a human being attains perfection. "One should meditate upon the Lord Nārāyaṇa during acts such as bathing and others;
one attains the world of Brahmā and does not return again to this world. (Dakṣa Smṛti)
"O Protector! Those men who have propitiated you through their own actions and by means other than [worldly] ends,
they cross over this entire māyā for the sake of their own liberation."
Thus [it is said].

Nor is it the case that these [Vedic injunctions] possess scope [as independent means of liberation] through the teaching of rituals that achieve worldly or otherworldly results within saṃsāra; for even the nature of those very rituals is solely the propitiation of the Supreme Person. As it has been said:

"Even those who, endowed with faith, worship other deities, they too, O son of Kuntī, worship Me alone, though not according to the prescribed rule. For I am indeed the enjoyer and the Lord of all sacrifices."
"But they do not know me in truth; therefore, they fall. Likewise:
"O Acyuta, you who consist of all the gods, you are eternally worshipped by them;
you alone are the consumer of the *havya* and *kavya* offerings, assuming the forms of both the ancestors and the gods."

As for the claim that—because Kapila is celebrated as an authoritative teacher (āpta) in the statement, "The seer Kapila was born," it is therefore proper to establish the meaning of the Vedānta in accordance with his Smṛti—that is incorrect; for Bṛhaspati is also celebrated in the Śrutis and Smṛtis as an exemplar of those possessing supreme knowledge, and thus there would be the possibility of establishing the meaning of the Śruti according to the Lokāyata system composed by him. || 1 ||

Now, it might be argued: "Since Kapila, through the power of his own yoga, has perceived the true nature of reality, the meaning of the Vedānta should be established in accordance with his tradition. To this, the author reads the following reply: 140.
*Itareṣāṃ cānupalabdheḥ* (And because [the teachings] of others are not found [in the Veda]). II.1.2.

The word "ca" (and) has the sense of "tu" (but), intended to remove the doubt that has been raised. Since the other authorities, such as Manu and others—who have directly realized the true nature of the higher and lower reality through the power of their own yoga—possess words that serve as medicine for the entire world, as established by the Vedic text: "Whatever Manu said is indeed medicine," the perception of Kapila is not found to accord with that [Vedic] truth. Therefore, Kapila’s perception, which contradicts the Śruti, is rooted in error; thus it is established that the aforementioned meaning of the Vedānta cannot be shaken by it.
Thus concludes the section concerning Smṛti (1).

Regarding the phrase "that is false": if the very reason for the rejection of even the Lokāyata system composed by Bṛhaspati is its contradiction with the Śruti, then that same contradiction exists here as well; therefore, the Smṛti of Kapila must also be rejected in its contradictory portions. This has been established in the discussion concerning the rule, "The Audumbarī post is to be entirely covered."

The word "atha" [is used here]. Since Manu and others were intent on other matters, such as the promulgation of Dharma, there was no occasion for them to discuss Yoga. However, Kapila had directly realized the truth of the goal through Yoga; therefore, his Smṛti (traditional teaching) is to be respected—this is the meaning. If it be argued that Kapila's own Smṛti presents [the Pradhāna] in this manner, [we reply]: as for the other sages, since the Pradhāna is not perceived to be the cause of the world, Brahman alone is the cause here. Thus ends the section on Smṛti (Smṛtyadhikaraṇa). 1.1.3.
The section concerning the refutation of Yoga (Yogapratyuktatvādhikaraṇa). || 2.1.2 ||
By this refutation of the *Kāpila* Smṛti, the *Yoga* Smṛti is also answered. What, then, is the further doubt here, for the removal of which there is this extension of reasoning (*nyāyātideśa*)?

[The opponent might argue: "Since the *Yoga* Smṛti also accepts a Lord (*īśvara*), describes the Yoga enjoined in the Vedānta as a means to liberation, and because its author, Hiraṇyagarbha, is authorized to promulgate all the Vedāntas, it is logical that the Vedānta is supplemented by that Smṛti."

"The rebuttal, however, is as follows: because it is a doctrine of the Pradhāna as the cause—which is not of the nature of Brahman; because it accepts only the Lord as the efficient cause; and because it lacks the non-duality with Brahman and the possession of all auspicious qualities such as being the material cause of the universe regarding the Self and the Lord, who are the objects of meditation for Yoga consisting of contemplation (dhyāna) which is defined solely by its object; furthermore, because even the speaker, Hiraṇyagarbha, being a *kṣetrajña*, is subject to occasional subjugation by the qualities of *rajas* and *tamas*, the Smṛti of Yoga is also [unauthoritative]."
"Since it is like an ancient Purāṇa whose root is passion (rajas) and darkness (tamas), its root is error; therefore, it is not reasonable that the Vedānta should be supplemented by it. || 3 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the refutation of Yoga. || 2 ||
"By this," he states the literal meaning of the Sūtra.
By saying "because of the acceptance of Īśvara and the mention of Yoga," he indicates the acceptance of Vedic principles and the acceptance of their practice.
By saying "not having Brahman as its self," he indicates a difference in principle (*tattva*). And by saying "consisting of meditation," he indicates a difference in practice (*anuṣṭhāna*).
2. In the *Smṛti*—or rather (*vā*). • Regarding the cause—*tha*, *da*. Section on the Difference in Characteristics (Vilakṣaṇatvādhikaraṇa) || 2.1.3 ||
Not so, because this [dream experience] has different characteristics; and its being such [as waking experience] is due to the word [of scripture]. (2.1.4)

That is not tenable; for this "world," which consists of the conscious and the unconscious and is perceived through perception and other means as being insentient, impure, non-sovereign, and essentially composed of suffering, is distinct from the Brahman you accept—which is omniscient, the Lord of all, opposed to everything that is to be abandoned, and solely composed of bliss.
The world's distinctness is perceived not only through perception and other means of knowledge; its suchness—that is, its distinctness—is also perceived from scripture:
"Consciousness and unconsciousness," and "In this very way, these elements of being are deposited in the elements of intelligence; the elements of intelligence are deposited in the vital breath."

For by such passages as, "On the same tree, a person is immersed and grieves, deluded by a sense of powerlessness," and "The self, being powerless, is bound because of its state as an enjoyer," the insentience, suffering, and other such qualities of the effect— the world— are indeed indicated.

For whatever is an effect is non-different from its cause, just as jars, necklaces, and the like are non-different from their causes, such as clay and gold. The first inquiry is as before: Is the production of the insentient world from the sentient Brahman possible or not? To that end, is the inference that the cause of the world must possess the same characteristics as the world inconclusive or not?

When [the reason] is not inconclusive, then the doctrine that Brahman is the cause is unshakable, because it is impossible for a non-conscious world to arise from a conscious Brahman. But when it is inconclusive, then the status of Brahman as the cause is unshakable, because the arising of a world distinct in nature from Brahman is possible.

Regarding the word "yat" (which), he explains the sūtra’s term "na" (not). Regarding "asya" (of this), it is that which is to be explained; he explains it as "by means of perception and so forth. The sense is that the word "asya" refers back to [the world] as qualified by the forms established by worldly means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). He explains the term "vilakṣaṇatvāt" (because of being of a different character) as "from what is accepted by you. The fourfold set of qualifiers beginning with "omniscient" is stated as the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) to the fourfold set of qualifiers beginning with "insentience.
1. śvena-tha, pa. 2. [End of fragment].

Therefore, since it is impossible for this world—which is of a different character from Brahman—to be its effect, the Pradhāna, characterized as an effect, must alone be the cause, in accordance with the Sāṅkhya Smṛti.

Furthermore, even though the scripture is independent of anything else and has as its domain objects that transcend the senses, reasoning (*tarka*) must nevertheless be followed; for all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), in whatever specific subject matter they may address, serve as causes for the ascertainment of an object only when assisted by reasoning. Indeed, reasoning is a form of knowledge—synonymous with *ūha*—which consists in the procedure (*itikartavyatā*) of establishing a means of valid cognition regarding a particular object through an investigation into either the nature of the object itself or its causal conditions (*sāmagrī*). And this dependence upon reasoning is common to all means of valid cognition.

But in the case of the Śāstra specifically—which possesses the status of a means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*) dependent upon the cognition of expectancy (*ākāṅkṣā*), proximity (*sannidhi*), and semantic competency (*yogyatā*)—there is a requirement for the assistance of reasoning (*tarka*) everywhere. And it has been said by Manu:

"He who investigates by means of reasoning knows Dharma, and no other. For it is precisely this establishment of the meaning of the Śāstra assisted by reasoning that is intended by the Vedic injunction: "It must be reflected upon" (*mantavya*).
Thus it is said.

Since a scripture that is not of human origin (apauruṣeya) has as its object a reality that is beyond the scope of other means of knowledge, one might argue that reasoning (tarka)—which is rooted in the invariable concomitance (vyāpti) perceived through perception and other means—does not have the meaning established by scripture as its object. To this he says: "And necessarily... [etc.]. This means that although [scripture] is independent of other means of knowledge (*ananyāpekṣasya*), that is, independent of other pramāṇas, reasoning must nevertheless be followed as an auxiliary to those pramāṇas. In certain instances—that is, regarding objects whose meaning is inherently unclear—it [reasoning] is required.

The independence of validity (*prāmāṇya*) from anything else means its lack of dependence on another cognition having the same object; it does not mean its lack of dependence on the *itikartavyatā* (the procedural details), such is the intended meaning. Regarding the word "object" (*artha*): when the non-visual nature of the sky is asserted because of its blue color, that is the establishment of the means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) with respect to a particular object through a determination concerning the nature of the object itself.

By defining the scriptural statement that produces the cognition of the beneficial nature of ritual slaughter (*vaidha-hiṃsā*), it is established that the statement "one shall not kill" (*na hiṃsyāt*) refers to a subject matter distinct from ritual slaughter; this is the determination of the scope of a means of valid knowledge regarding a specific object through the definition of its causal conditions. Furthermore, by defining the production of a flame without [assuming] that perception has the oneness of the flame as its object, the determination is made that its object is merely the essential nature [of the flame].

In the phrase "of the scripture, however" (*śāstrasya tu*), the word "however" (*tu*) indicates a difference regarding the probandum (*sādhyavaiṣamya*). The word "specifically" (*viśeṣeṇa*) indicates a difference regarding the means of proof (*sādhanavaiṣamya*). Dependence upon expectancy, proximity, and semantic competency constitutes the difference regarding the means of proof. By this, the intended meaning is that there is dependence upon reasoning (*tarka*) in all cases, which constitutes the difference regarding the probandum.

Now, it might be argued: "Once it is determined by scripture (*śruti*) that Brahman is the sole cause of the world, it is accepted that consciousness (*caitanya*) persists even in its effect, the world. Just as consciousness is not perceived in a sentient being during states such as deep sleep or fainting, so too in jars and other objects, consciousness exists but is merely unmanifest (*anudbhūta*). It is for this very reason that the distinction between the sentient and the insentient is maintained."

This is not tenable; for the perpetual non-perception of something establishes its very non-existence. For this very reason, even the possession of the power of consciousness (*caitanya-śakti*) has been refuted in their case. Indeed, he who asserts that something has the capacity to produce an effect when that effect is never perceived at any time or place, would be like one who asserts the procreative capacity of barren women in the assemblies of their sons.

Furthermore—once the determination that the Vedāntas establish Brahman as the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world is reached, there follows the determination of the existence of either the power of consciousness (*caitanya-śakti*) in jars and other objects, or of consciousness itself in its unmanifest state; and once that is determined, there follows the determination that the Vedāntas establish Brahman as the material cause of the world. Thus, there is mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*). For indeed, a causal relationship between two dissimilar things cannot even be established.

Furthermore, what is intended by the similarity between the material cause (*prakṛti*) and its modification (*vikāra*), the absence of which you claim makes it impossible to establish that the world has Brahman as its material cause? It cannot be a similarity in all attributes, for in that case the relationship of cause and effect would be untenable. Indeed, one does not observe the persistence of the state of being a lump (*piṇḍatva*) and so forth in the effects of a lump of clay, such as jars and bowls. Or is it similarity through some attribute whatsoever?

Regarding the word "yathā" (just as): the Vedāntins have stated a rebuttal by taking that [case] as a counter-example (pratibandī), since they accept that although consciousness—which is eternal and consists of the manifestation of the nature of the Self—is present even during deep sleep, it is not perceived with extreme clarity.

Anticipating the objection that other disputants—by way of a counter-example (*pratibandī*)—accept that the capacity for the production of consciousness exists even in deep sleep, and thus maintain that the similarity between cause and effect is established because jars and the like possess the capacity for consciousness despite the non-perception of consciousness in them, [the author] says: "For this very reason, regarding consciousness... He states: "For between two dissimilar things... in order to address how the demonstration of Brahman as the material cause depends upon the lack of certainty regarding consciousness in jars and the like.

For a sentence such as "The sacrificial post is the sun" is not capable of conveying an incompatible meaning; the sense is that there is a circular argument (*anyonyāśraya*) because the possibility of establishing Brahman as the material cause depends upon the ascertainment of compatibility.
Therefore, even in the case of clay and Brahman, [the relation] characterized by existence (*sattā*) and so forth is possible.

This is explained as follows: when a thing that serves as a cause is distinguished from other things by a certain intrinsic nature (*svabhāva*), that same intrinsic nature must persist in its effect; this is the "similarity of the effect to the cause. For instance, gold is distinguished from clay and other substances by a certain form, and the persistence of that form is observed in its effects, such as earrings and the like. Brahman, however, has an intrinsic nature consisting of knowledge, bliss, and sovereignty, which are the opposites of all that is to be abandoned (*heya*); whereas the world has an intrinsic nature that is the opposite of those. Therefore, Brahman cannot be the material cause (*upādāna*) of the world.

Furthermore, a causal relationship is not observed even when there is dissimilarity. For example, from a conscious person, unconscious hair, nails, teeth, and body hair are produced; and likewise, from unconscious cow dung, a conscious scorpion is born; and from a conscious spider, an unconscious thread is produced. This is not so; because even in those cases, the causal relationship exists only with respect to the unconscious portions. || 4 ||

Now, it might be argued: even for those things considered to be insentient, there is a connection with consciousness, as it is heard in the Śrutis: "The Earth spoke to him," "The Waters desired," and "Those vital breaths of mine, disputing among themselves for the sake of superiority, went to Brahmā. Even rivers, oceans, mountains, and so forth possess sentience; this is maintained by the Paurāṇikas. Therefore, there is no difference [between them and the self].
6. To this, he recites the following reply:

143. *Abhimānivyapadeśastu viśeṣānugatibhyām* (Sūtra 2.1.5). The word "but" (*tu*) is for the purpose of removing the doubt raised. The deities are those who possess the conceit (*abhimānin*) of being earth and so forth; [as it says], "The Earth spoke to him."

In such passages as these, they are designated by the words "earth" and so forth. Why? Because of both distinction and inclusion. "Distinction" means qualification; that is to say, the word "deity" serves as the qualificand, while "earth" and the others are denoted as its qualifiers. [As it is said:
"Come, I shall merge these three deities..."

—thus, fire and food are qualified by the word "deity" (devatā). This is seen in such passages as, "All the deities indeed were disputing for superiority," and "Those gods, having recognized the highest good in breath. Anugati means entry or following after.
"Fire, having become speech, entered the mouth; the sun, having become the eye, entered the eyes; the wind, having become the breath, entered the nostrils" (Aitareya Upaniṣad, etc.).
By such passages, the entry of fire and the other deities is heard of as being through their presiding over speech and the other faculties.
Regarding the word "but" (*tu*): it is used so that the word *tu* shall not be taken as merely serving to set aside the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*).

Therefore—since the world is of a different nature due to its insentience, and because it is logically untenable for it to be the effect of Brahman—it is established by the Vedāntas, in accordance with Smṛti supported by reasoning, that the world has Pradhāna as its material cause. || 5 ||
This being the case, it is replied:
"But [the soul] is seen [to exist]. (2.1.6)
The position is reversed.

By the word "but" (*tu*), it is indicated that what was stated—that because the world is of a different character from Brahman, it is impossible for Brahman to be its material cause—is incorrect; for we observe the relationship of cause and effect even between two things of different characters. Indeed, it is observed that worms and the like, which are of a different character from honey-bees, arise from them!
[Objection: It was stated that since the relation of cause and effect exists only in the insentient portion, there is similarity (*sālakṣaṇya*) therein!

[Reply: True, it was so stated; however, by that much alone, the "similarity" intended by you between cause and effect is not established. For if similarity were established in any way whatsoever, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that everything arises from everything due to the universal similarity of all things. Therefore, you have accepted that similarity consists in the persistence (*anuvṛtti*) of a form which serves as the cause for the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of one thing from other things.

However, that rule is not observed in the case of the production of worms and the like from honey and so forth; therefore, it is not untenable for the world, though different in character from Brahman, to be the effect of Brahman. For a persistence of common characteristics—which serves as the cause for the exclusion of other things—is not seen in honey, cow dung, worms, scorpions, and the like, in the same way as it is seen in clay and gold, or in jars, crowns, and so on. ||6||

[Objection: Is the similarity between cause and effect in every respect? [Reply: That exists even in our position. [Objection: If it means similarity in all attributes (*sarvadharma-sādṛśya*), then it does not exist even in the case of clay and pots. [Objection: If it means the persistence of a genus (*jāti*) such as "substance-ness" or "consciousness" within a specific category, [Reply: that is merely an external logic (*bāhya-tarka*) because it contradicts numerous Śrutis and Smṛtis which teach that Brahman is the cause; this will be refuted by the Sūtra: "Because reasoning is unestablished" (*tarkāpratiṣṭhānāt*). [Objection: The persistence of consciousness also exists, since the qualified [Brahman] is the cause.

The direct refutation—that "just as the quality of insentience persists in the insentient portion of the effect, so too the quality of sentience persists in the sentient portion"—will be stated in the subsequent sections (*adhikaraṇas*). If it is meant that the effect possesses similarity to the cause in the very form by which the cause is distinguished from other things, then the deviation (*vyabhicāra*) intended in this Sūtra is as follows: the form by which honey is distinguished from other things is its "honey-ness" (*mākṣikatva*); however, that [form] does not exist in beeswax and the like. This is the meaning.
"Just as the production of worms and the like from honey-bees and the like is perfectly logical, so too is the production of the world from Brahman, though it is of a different nature.
(145) "If it be argued that [the effect] is non-existent, we say no, because [the scripture] is a mere negation. (2.1.7)

If it is argued that since Brahman, which is the cause, is different in nature from the world, which is the effect, then—because the cause and the effect would be distinct substances—the world, as the effect, would not exist within the supreme Brahman, its cause; and thus the consequence of the world being produced from what is non-existent (asat) would follow. [To this we reply:
[The world is not produced] from what is non-existent.

This is not so; for in the preceding Sūtra, what was intended was merely the negation of the rule that cause and effect must possess identical characteristics (*sālakṣaṇya*), and not the claim that the effect is a different substance (*dravyāntara*) from the cause. The view that "Brahman, as the cause, transforms itself into the form of the world, which is dissimilar to itself," has not been abandoned. For even in the case of a worm and honey, despite their difference in nature, there is indeed identity of substance (*dravyaikya*), just as in the case of a bracelet and gold. (7)

Here, an objection is raised: **"In that case, [the doctrine] would be inconsistent due to the consequence of [the effect being] non-existent [even after dissolution]. (2-1-8)** The term "in dissolution" (*apītau*) is used for the purpose of demonstrating that creation and so forth are preceded by dissolution.

The phrase "it would be non-existent" (*asaditi*) serves as a reminder, by way of context, of the meaning of the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa* (the section on the origin of the world). By the statement "if," it is implied that the effect is a different substance because of its distinct characteristics; this is the intention of the opponent (*pūrvapakṣin*), who thinks that there would thus follow a theory of the effect being non-existent (*asatkāryavāda*). [The Sūtra replies: "This is not so. Because of the recognition expressed as "this belongs to that," there is indeed a similarity between cause and effect, even though there are internal differences.

If it be argued that this would result in the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*), we say no; for here, the rule of similarity between the two [cause and effect] is merely negated. Otherwise, every Vedāntic statement would become inconsistent, resulting in the propounding of improper meanings.

"Because the world exists within the Supreme Self during both dissolution and creation, the defects of the world would therefore belong to Brahman; thus, the [scriptural] statement would be inconsistent. [Śrībhāṣya 2.1.3]

Because in such passages as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1) and "In the beginning, this was indeed the Self alone" (Aitareya Upaniṣad 1.1.1), we observe that the account of creation and so forth is preceded by an instruction regarding the state of dissolution (pralaya).

If the identity of substance between cause and effect is accepted, then, since the world as an effect merges back into Brahman during dissolution and so forth, Brahman alone would possess the connection with all those respective states; consequently, all the non-spiritual goals (apuruṣārtha) residing in the effect would necessarily attach themselves to Brahman, just as the specific features of an earring reside in gold. As a result, the entire body of Vedāntic scripture would become inconsistent, [contradicting such passages as]:
"He who is all-knowing, all-perceiving," and "Free from evil, free from old age, free from death."

"Neither his activity nor his instrument is perceived; neither one equal to him nor one superior to him is seen"; "One of the two eats the sweet fruit"; "The self, being powerless, is bound by its state as an enjoyer";
"Being deluded, he grieves through lack of sovereignty. Since these mutually contradictory [statements] would apply to a single reality, [there must be a distinction between them].

Now, it might be argued: "Since the Supreme Brahman alone, whose body consists of the conscious and unconscious entities (*cidacidvastu*), exists in the relation of cause and effect, and since defects reside in those conscious and unconscious entities that constitute His body, there is no contingency of such defects applying to the embodied Brahman, whether in the state of effect or the state of cause. [To this we reply: The rule of uniformity based on genus has been refuted; the meaning is that identity of substance (*ekadravyatva*) is not denied. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "of creation etc.," maintenance is intended.

"Like gold" (*suvarṇa iva*): because the analogy of gold, earrings, and so forth is present in the mind, it is said "in that manner" (*tadvat*). Alternatively, the meaning is that [if the world were identical to Brahman], there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of [Brahman] possessing non-final ends (*apuruṣārtha*) and so on, just as the world does. Or else, "tadvat" is a possessive suffix (*matvarthīya-pratyaya*); the meaning is the undesirable consequence that the world would possess final ends (*puruṣārtha*) and so forth [by being identical to Brahman]. "Of mutually contradictory [statements]" means of statements whose meanings are contradictory. 1. *pūrvaśca* — Da; *sarva evāpuruṣārthāḥ* — Ā.

2. All human goals (*puruṣārtha*) are contained within the effects (*kāryagata*). — *da*. 3. Mutually — *na*. 4. 2. *svaiva ta*, *tha*. All indeed — *tha*. 5. And entities — *du*. 6. "In the embodied one" — *da*. That is incorrect; for the relationship of body and embodied (*śarīra-śarīribhāva*) between the world and Brahman is simply impossible, and even if it were possible, defects resulting from the connection with a body would be unavoidable in Brahman. Indeed, it is not possible for the conscious and unconscious entities to constitute the body of Brahman.

For that which is called the "body" (śarīra) is a specific aggregate of the elements such as earth and so forth, serving as the substratum for the sense organs which are the means for experiencing the pleasure and pain that constitute the fruits of karma; it is maintained by the vital breath (prāṇa) which possesses five functions; and this is because such a thing alone is well-known in both worldly usage and the Vedas as being a "body. And as for the Supreme Self—
"Who is free from evil, ageless—
another, not eating, gazes upon [him]."

"Without hands or feet, the Person is a grasper; without eyes, He sees; without ears, He hears"; "for He is without breath and without mind"—from such passages, because there is an absence of both action and the enjoyment of its fruits, because there is an absence of enjoyment dependent on the senses, and because there is an absence of possession of vital breath (prāṇa), neither the sentient nor the insentient constitutes His body.

Furthermore, it is not possible for insentient things—whether in their individual forms such as grass and wood, or in their collective form as subtle elements—to serve as the substratum for the senses and so forth; nor does the subtle element possess the nature of a composite aggregate of earth and the other gross elements. Since this is all impossible for a sentient being whose sole characteristic is consciousness, the possibility of its possessing a body is even less likely.

Regarding the phrase "having the body as its fuel": the intention is that other substances found in a salt-lake (rumā) are seen to attain the state of salt, and it is also said, "and the fifth is that which is conjoined with them."

He states the intrinsic nature of the body: "For the body... This is said to show that when the pervader is absent, the pervaded—the state of being a body—is also absent. By the phrase "the fruit of karma," he indicates the characteristics that pervade the state of being a body. By "pleasure and pain," there is the statement of its being the locus of experience. Its being the means for experiencing the fruits of karma serves to exclude the bodies and senses of those who are liberated. By "having five functions," there is the statement of its being the locus of activity. And [the phrase] "of the Supreme Self... [is included].

By reflecting on the nature of the Supreme Self as intended to be the possessor of a body, he states the impossibility of its being a body. With the words "free from sin" (*apahata-pāpmā*), he indicates the absence of connection with karma; with "not eating" (*anaśnan*), the absence of [karmic] fruit; with "without hands" (*apāṇi*), independence from the sense organs; and with "without breath" (*aprāṇa*), the absence of being a locus for physical activity. Furthermore, regarding the phrase "nor is it possible": those things intended to be bodies possess a nature contrary to the definition of a body;
nor is "being a body" possible in the sense of "being a locus of experience," because the status of being a body is not established in the case of loci of experience such as houses and the like.

If it is argued that "that very thing wherein one currently abides and experiences pleasure and pain is the locus of experience (*bhogāyatana*)," we say no; for there can be no "birth" consisting of entry into another's body, since it is not established that the locus of experiencing pleasure and pain resides within another's body, as the notion of entering a body is unproven. Furthermore, in the case of Īśvara—who possesses by his own nature eternal and unsurpassed bliss—there can be no rule regarding the intellect (*cit*) and the non-intellect (*acit*) serving as the locus for experience.
By this, the claim that anything which is merely a means of enjoyment constitutes a body is refuted.

Now, it might be thought: "That whose nature, existence, and activity are dependent on the will of another is that other's body. Since the nature, existence, and activity of everything are dependent on the will of God, it follows that everything could potentially be the body of God.

That too is not tenable; for among those things commonly recognized as bodies, there is an absence of having their essential nature dependent on the will of a conscious being, since a diseased body lacks activity governed by that will, and a dead body lacks a state of existence dependent upon it. Furthermore, in the case of statues and the like—which possess an essential nature, stability, and activity dependent on the will of a conscious being—the status of being a "body" is not established. Moreover, because a conscious being who is eternal lacks an essential nature dependent on the will of God, the possibility of being His body does not arise.

Nor can it be said that "whatever is governed by one, whatever has one as its sole purpose, and whatever is subsidiary to one—that is the body of that"—because this definition would over-extend to actions and the like.

And [the phrase] "because [it] is not established" refutes the status of being a locus of experience (*bhogāyatanatva*) separately. The previously mentioned refutation applies equally to the status of being a locus of activity (*ceṣṭāśrayatva*) and the status of being a locus of the sense faculties (*indriyāśrayatva*). A "locus of experience" is a specific means of experience; for this very reason, it was stated: "of every mere means of experience."

Regarding the phrase "as a body," he states that there is [the fault of] non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) in the case of statues (*sālabhañjikā*) and the like; over-extension (*ativyāpti*) in the case of the mind (*cetas*); and impossibility (*asaṃbhava*).

By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "in actions and so forth," qualities (*guṇa*) are intended, because of their twofold nature and because of the use of the plural number. Thus, by reflecting on the essential natures of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) and of consciousness and matter (*cid-acit*), the status of consciousness and matter as bodies has been refuted: "The bodiless one among bodies... (*aśarīraṃ śarīreṣu*).

Furthermore, the absence of a body in the Lord is established by such passages as, "Without hands or feet, He is swift and a grasper. Therefore, because the relationship of body and embodied being between the world and Brahman is impossible, and because if such a relationship were possible, defects would necessarily follow in Brahman, there is an inconsistency in the Vedāntic statements regarding the doctrine that Brahman is the cause [of the world]. 8.
To this, the reply is:
"But it is not so, because of the existence of examples" (2.1.9).

There is no such inconsistency; for even though a single entity may undergo two states, there exists an established distinction between virtue and defect, as evidenced by the available analogy. The word "tu" (but) here indicates the utter impossibility of even a trace of connection with anything to be abandoned.

This is what is meant: there is no contradiction whatsoever in the Supreme Brahman—which has the sentient and insentient entities as its body and is their very self—even when it undergoes the two states of cause and effect characterized by contraction and expansion. For contraction and expansion pertain to the sentient and insentient entities that constitute the body of the Supreme Brahman; defects residing in the body do not attach to the Self, nor do the qualities residing in the Self attach to the body. This is just as it is with embodied individual souls (kṣetrajñas), such as gods and humans.

Regarding the phrase "without a body" (*aśarīram*): Now, because the body of the Supreme Being has been negated, [the author] states that it is impossible for anything to be His body. The passage beginning with "without hands" (*apāṇi*) was previously cited to make known the absence of sense organs; now, however, it is intended to make known the absence of a body by way of negating the limbs that serve as the substrata for the sense organs. (8)

Regarding the word "na": although the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) has already been set aside by the word "not" (*na*) alone, the word "but" (*tu*) is used for the purpose of making known the possibility of the relationship between body and embodied one (*śarīra-śarīribhāva*).

The passage beginning with "Just as in the case of a deity" (*yathā deve*) provides an illustration for the impossibility of any connection with that which is to be abandoned (*heyasambandha*). [Regarding contraction and expansion:

"Just as the qualities (*guṇa*), the self (*ātman*), and its body (*tanu*) are established [in varying states], so too it is entirely consistent that the world-body of Brahman is likewise [established]."

Bhāṣya: The states such as childhood, youth, and old age, which pertain to the body of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the body of Brahman, do not attach to the Self (*ātman*). Likewise, qualities pertaining to the Self, such as knowledge and happiness, do not belong to the body. Nevertheless, designations such as "born as a god," "born as a human," and "he himself is a child, a youth, and an old man" are used in their primary sense. Thus, the status of being a god, a human, and so forth, belongs only to the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) when it is associated with the subtle body composed of the elements.
This is stated in the passage beginning with "upon reaching another state" (*tadantara-pratipattau*).
Thus it will be stated—so [it is said].

Furthermore, as for what was said—that the status of the world, consisting of both sentient and insentient entities, whether gross or subtle, as a body with respect to the Supreme Self is untenable—that is merely the manifestation of fallacious reasoning imagined by one's own intellect, arising from a failure to grasp the multitude of Vedāntic statements supported by sound logic. For all the Vedāntas indeed proclaim that everything—gross and subtle, conscious and unconscious—is the body of the Supreme Self.

In the Vājasaneyaka, specifically in the Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa of both the Kāṇva and Mādhyandina recensions, it begins: "He who dwells in the earth... whose body is the earth," and so on, [referring] to all insentient things such as the earth and the rest.

Having separately designated "consciousness" in the passages, "He who dwells in consciousness... whose body is consciousness" and "He who dwells in the self... whose body is the self," it is stated that each of these is the body of the Supreme Self.

10. [Subtlety and grossness. Regarding "subtle elements" (*bhūtasūkṣma*): [it is said] "In the fifth oblation, the waters come to be called 'man'. It is the properties of the waters themselves—such as being a deity—that are intended, not those of the person (*puruṣa*).

This is the correct reasoning (*samyag-nyāya*), that is, reasoning consistent with the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). "Fallacious reasoning" (*kutarka*) is reasoning that contradicts the means of valid knowledge. "Indeed, all... [and so forth].
Desiring to state that the definition [of Brahman] pervades everything, he shows the usage in the Veda of both the conscious and the unconscious as being the body of Brahman.

In the Subāla Upaniṣad, beginning with "He who moves within the earth, whose body is the earth," and so forth, he declares that in exactly the same way, the conscious and the unconscious in all their states constitute the body of the Supreme Self.

"This one, the inner self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the sole god, is Nārāyaṇa"—thus, his being the self with respect to all beings is declared. And they [the traditional authorities] remember:

"The entire world is your body," "That which is water is indeed the body of Viṣṇu," "All that is truly the body of Hari," "All those are his form," "He is meditating upon himself from his own body," and so forth. "From his own body" means from the subtle body consisting of the elements.

Furthermore, in common usage, the word "body" (*śarīra*), unlike words such as "pot" (*ghaṭa*) which are restricted to substances of a single uniform form, is seen to be employed in its primary sense across substances that possess extremely diverse forms—such as worms, insects, moths, snakes, humans, and animals. Therefore, the determination of its basis for application (*pravṛttinimitta*) must be established solely in accordance with all such usages.

Regarding the phrase "I meditate upon that," since the fact that consciousness and unconsciousness constitute the body is not explicitly stated there, [the author] explains it by means of the term "from the subtle elements" (*bhūtasūkṣmāt*). The meaning is that what was introduced in the verse, "This world was then unmanifest darkness," is precisely what is being referred to here as the body.

Regarding the phrase "like a jar, etc.": Just as words such as "jar" are used primarily (*mukhya*) for objects that possess a single uniform form, the word "body" (*śarīra*) is not used in that way; rather, it is used primarily for objects that possess many diverse forms. Therefore, because [the previous definition] lacks universal applicability (*anugatatva*), a definition encompassing even worms, insects, and so forth was stated. The sense is that since even that is not all-inclusive (*avyāptatva*), another universal definition must be accepted. Regarding the term "non-figurative" (*agauṇa*): why is "having two feet" or "humanity" not stated as the definition of a body?

Because the primary usage is observed elsewhere as well. Wherever usage is seen in both common parlance (*loka*) and the Veda, a definition (*lakṣaṇa*) that conforms to that [usage] must be stated; the intention is that one should not state a definition that does not conform [to usage] and then assume a secondary sense (*gauṇatva*) for it elsewhere. The definition of the ground for application (*pravṛttinimitta-lakṣaṇa*)—that which constitutes the denotatum (*vācyabhūta*) and is the cause of the collective power (*samudāyaśakti*)—is both that [ground] and the definition. By means of that...

[Objection: Your definition of "body" as "that which is the cause for the experience of the fruits of karma," and so forth, is characterized by being the occasion for activity (*pravṛtti-nimitta*); it is not consistent with all applications, because it does not extend (*avyāpti*) to the earth and other elements which have been described as being the bodies of the Lord. Furthermore, that definition is non-pervasive (*avyāpta*) regarding the bodies of the Lord's will and the bodies of the liberated souls—understood from such scriptural passages as "He becomes singlefold"—because those do not have the experience of the fruits of karma as their cause. Moreover, the bodies of the Supreme Person's will are not specific aggregates of the elements such as earth and the rest.

This is because of the Smṛti text: "The body of this Supreme Self is not composed of the collection of elements. Therefore, the definition of the body as being "of the nature of a collection of elements" is non-pervasive (avyāpta).

Furthermore, the property of "being sustained by the fivefold vital breaths (prāṇa)" is non-pervasive in the case of immobile bodies; for although vital breath exists in immobile beings, it does not exist in its state of sustaining the body by abiding in five ways. Moreover, in the case of Ahalyā and others whose bodies were made of stone, wood, and so forth due to the force of their karma, the properties of "being the locus of the senses" and "being the cause of pleasure and pain" are non-pervasive.

Therefore: "For whatever conscious being, whatever substance can be entirely controlled and maintained for its own sake, [that substance constitutes] the exclusion (*vyāvṛtti*) of both the etymological ground (*vyutpattinimitta*) and the secondary characteristic (*upalakṣaṇa*). The meaning of the verbal root *gam* is the etymological ground of the word *go* (cow); the possession of odor, which serves as a secondary characteristic of *pṛthivītva* (earthness)—the denotation of the word *pṛthivī* (earth)—is also such a [ground]. Neither of these two is the ground for the actual application (*pravṛttinimitta*) of the word. This is the etymological ground.

Its definition is: being the cause for the experience of the fruits of karma. Regarding the phrase "having five functions": if one intends to refer merely to the existence of the vital breath (*prāṇa*), then there would be the intended fault of non-pervasion (*avyāpti*) with respect to sentient beings and unmanifest entities (*avyakta*) that constitute the body of the Lord. Regarding "being the substratum of the senses": this means being the substratum of the various senses that are capable of generating the activity of cognition; if one intends to refer merely to the existence of the senses, then, as before, the intended fault of non-pervasion applies.

Therefore—because that which conforms [to it] is its defining characteristic (*lakṣaṇa*), whereas that which you have stated does not so conform. By the phrase "of whom" (*yasya*), it is shown that the body is a correlative entity (*sapratiyogika-padārtha*), like a father or son, and not a non-correlative entity (*apratīyogika-padārtha*), like a jar. "That which can be controlled by its own master in every respect," "that which can be sustained for its own master's sake in every respect," and "having the nature of being solely subordinate (*śeṣataika-svarūpa*)"—these are the three defining characteristics of a body.

The word "eka" (one) is used in place of the term "sarvātmanā" (in its entirety). What is intended is "subsistence as long as the substance exists" (*yāvaddravyabhāvitvam*). The word "dravya" (substance) is used for the purpose of excluding action (*kriyā*) and qualities (*guṇa*). [The term] "sva" (own) refers to its own object; here, the word "sva" refers to the body. [It means] that particular body...

Furthermore, its nature consists solely in being subordinate to that [Self]; thus, the definition of a body must be accepted as "that which is the body of that [Self]. The non-perception of control and so forth in diseased bodies and the like is due to the obstruction of the existing power of control itself, just as heat and other qualities are not perceived in fire and such things when their power is obstructed. And a dead body begins to disintegrate at the very moment of separation from consciousness and disintegrates in the subsequent moment.
The conventional usage of the term "body" in that case is based on its having been previously designated as a body and because it is a part of the aggregate [that once constituted] a body.

Since everything is to be governed and sustained for its own sake by the Supreme Person, who is the Self of all, and whose sole nature consists in being subservient to Him; therefore, all that is sentient and insentient is His body.

The passage beginning with "bodiless among bodies" (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.1.1) has as its primary purpose the negation of a body caused by karma; for there is scriptural hearing of His being the body of all as previously described. Furthermore, this will be demonstrated in the subsequent sections by the two sūtras: "In the case of dissolution, [the world would be] inconsistent because of the same contingency as that [of the individual soul]" (2.1.8), and "But not so, because of the existence of examples" (2.1.9).
The point established in the section [of the Brahma-sūtras] beginning with "Because of the designation as something else" (Itaravyapadeśāt) has been recalled. || 9 ||
148. And [he should consider] the defects in his own position. 2-1-10.

Indeed, this [view] is to be resorted to not only because the doctrine of Brahman as the cause is free from defects, but also because the doctrine of Pradhāna as the cause is flawed; therefore, having abandoned that, this alone should be accepted.

The status of the action [is established] with respect to the members of the assembly and so forth, up to that point. The phrase "of a conscious being" (*cetana*) is for the purpose of excluding cognition (*jñāna*). For cognition is not governed by that which is qualified by cognition; rather, it is governed by its own substrate. Therefore, because there is an absence of being governed by a conscious being, there is no inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) in that case. Thus, regarding the other two definitions as well, the excluded cases are stated: the exclusion of the previous terms applies to the phrase "of which the substance can be [perceived] in its entirety. By the word "of a conscious being," light (*prabhā*) is excluded. (9) [Regarding the term] "one's own side" (*svapakṣa*):

The contradiction previously stated— namely, that [the doctrine of] being free from defects and being the material cause of the world is untenable for others— applies equally to you: "O sinless one, since your own position is rife with faults, you should abandon your own view and accept the doctrine of Brahman as the cause."

Indeed, in the theory of primordial matter (*pradhāna*) as the cause, the activity of the world is not logically tenable. For in that system, the activity of the world is based on the superimposition of the attributes of *prakṛti* upon the *puruṣa*, who is changeless and consists solely of the essence of pure consciousness, due to its proximity to *prakṛti*. It must be examined: what is the nature of this "proximity to *prakṛti*" which serves as the cause for the superimposition of the attributes of *prakṛti* upon that which is changeless and of the nature of pure consciousness?
Is it the mere existence of *prakṛti*? Or is it some modification residing in *prakṛti*? Or perhaps some modification residing in the *puruṣa* itself?
It cannot reside in the person (*puruṣa*), because that is not admitted [by you].

Nor is it a modification (*vikāra*) of primordial matter (*prakṛti*); for since that [superimposition] is accepted as being produced by repeated practice (*abhyāsa*), it is impossible for it to be the cause of superimposition.

If mere existence were its proximity, then the consequence would follow that even one who is liberated would undergo superimposition; thus, on your own position, the activity of the world is not tenable. This is the meaning [stated] at the time of refuting the Sāṅkhya position.
This will be elaborated upon by the passage beginning with "Even if [this] were admitted, because of the absence of an object" (abhyupagame 'py arthābhāvāt). || 10 ||
149. Also because reasoning is not firmly established. (2.1.11)

Furthermore, because reasoning is unstable, one must rely solely on the doctrine that Brahman is the cause, which is rooted in scripture; not the doctrine that the Pradhāna is the cause. For the reasonings of the Śākyas, Ulūkyas, Akṣapādas, Kṣapaṇakas, Kapilas, and Patañjalis are mutually contradictory; thus, the instability of reasoning is understood. || 11 ||
By this sūtra, [the objection] has been raised against another [position]. "Because of non-acceptance" means because of being eternally changeless.
The state of being. || 10 ||

150. "If it is argued that the object of inference is otherwise, even so there follows the consequence of no liberation. (2-1-12) Now, having set forth the arguments of the present-day Śākyas and others, if you say: "We shall infer [the truth] in another way—that is, by transcending the doctrine of 'Pradhāna' as the cause, and by means of the refutations demonstrated therein"—if you say this!

Even so, since reasoning is rooted in human intellect, there is the possibility that it may be subject to refutation by a "superior fallacy"—that is, by a reasoning conceived by a person more skilled in sophistry—regarding its very basis, "in the same way" across other places and times. Thus, due to the defect of the instability of reasoning (*tarkāpratiṣṭhāna*), liberation remains difficult to attain. Therefore, regarding objects beyond the senses, scripture alone is the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Reasoning should be employed solely for the purpose of corroborating that [scripture].
And so it has been said:
"The instruction on Dharma given by the seers should be followed with reasoning that does not contradict the Vedic scriptures."
He who investigates by means of reasoning knows Dharma, and no other.

Thus [it is said]. The meaning is: "by that which is not in conflict with the scripture known as the Veda. Therefore, because it contradicts the Veda, the Sāṅkhya Smṛti is "not to be respected" for the purpose of employing reasoning (*tarka*) that serves as a supplement (*upabṛṃhaṇa*) to the Veda by elucidating its meaning. Thus ends the section on "Having Different Characteristics" (Vilakṣaṇatvādhikaraṇa). 3.

"Idānīm" and so forth. The meaning is that just as there is the comprehension of one established logic (*bhūtatarka*) by means of another established logic, so too is the comprehension of one cultivated logic (*bhāvitarka*) by means of another cultivated logic possible. Regarding the term "Vedākhyā," this is for the purpose of excluding [the possibility that] the Sāṅkhya scripture might also be included; for if the words "Veda" and "Śāstra" were in grammatical apposition (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), it would follow that the Sāṅkhya scripture was also intended. As it is said: "The Veda is the eternal eye of the ancestors, gods, and humans. Therefore...
"And it is the established position that the Vedic scripture is immeasurable. "Inconceivable" means being beyond the scope of sublation; "immeasurable" means being beyond the range of proof. || 12 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the difference in characteristics (vilakṣaṇatvādhikaraṇa). || 3 ||

This is the meaning of the Sūtra: otherwise—that is, if it is argued that the Pradhāna must be established through inference in such a way that its refutation by the aforementioned reasonings does not occur—even so, there would be the consequence of non-liberation; for due to the fault of the instability of reasoning (*tarkāpratiṣṭhāna*), liberation would simply not be possible.

Or, if you say: "The Pradhāna is established because of the corroboration of powerful reasoning," even from that, you would not be liberated, because of the sublation by an even more powerful reasoning.
The Section Concerning What Is Not Accepted by the Learned (Śiṣṭāparigrahādhikaraṇa) || 2.1.4 ||

Even regarding that much agreement, since there is no difference in their being rooted in *tarka* (speculative reasoning), and because we observe contradictions concerning the nature of atoms—such as whether they are void or non-void, whether they consist of cognition or an object, whether they are momentary or eternal, whether they are exclusively one-sided or manifold, and whether they are real or unreal—the conclusion is that [theories based on *tarka*] are indeed unstable. This is the refutation. || 13 ||
Topic 5:

The Refutation of the Possibility that the Supreme Brahman is an Enjoyer on Account of Its Connection with a Body. 152. "If it be argued that [Brahman] must be an enjoyer because of its attaining the state of an enjoyer, we say: this would be as in the world. (2.1.14)

The Sāṅkhya again objects: As for what was stated—that because gross and subtle conscious and unconscious entities constitute the "body" of the Supreme Brahman in the form of cause and effect, the distinction between the essential natures of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is established—that distinction is not possible;

for if Brahman possesses a body, it would follow that He is an experiencer (*bhoktṛ*). This is because, just as in the case of the individual soul, it is unavoidable that the Lord (*īśvara*) too, by virtue of possessing a body, would be an experiencer of pleasure and pain resulting from that embodiment.
But surely—

In the sūtra, "If it be argued that there would be the attainment of enjoyment [by the Lord], we say no, because of the difference" (1.2.8), the objection regarding the contingency of the Lord’s own enjoyment has been addressed. Furthermore, in the sūtra, "But not so, because of the existence of examples" (2.3.17), the non-occurrence of qualities such as childhood and youth—which belong to the body—in the embodied self was cited as an example; thereby, the non-attachment of defects belonging to the body (composed of sentient and insentient matter) to the Supreme Self was stated. Here, however, the contingency of being an enjoyer resulting from association with a body is refuted.

The first inquiry is as before. For that purpose, [the question is]: Does Brahman, whose body is the experiencing individual soul (*jīva*), possess a distinctness from the *jīva*—which is its own body—by virtue of having the nature of unsurpassed bliss? Or not? For that purpose, [the question is]: If Brahman possesses a body, does it follow that it is an experiencer of pleasure and pain like the *jīva*? Or not? Is the experience of suffering and so forth caused by the body? Or is it caused by something else? In the scriptural passage, "Indeed, for one who has a body... (*na ha vai saśarīrasya*), does the word "body" (*śarīra*) refer to...
If it is argued that Brahman’s status as an enjoyer would be like that of the individual soul (jīva) because all bodies belong to Him,
and that there is no distinction [between them], then even if duality exists, there can be no status as an enjoyer.

It is not so; for in that case, it has been stated that there is no possibility of experiencing pleasure and pain merely by virtue of being located within the body, since [the Lord] is present in the abode of the heart as the object of meditation. Here, however, it is argued that if Brahman, like the individual soul (jīva), were to possess a body, then the consequence of being an experiencer of pleasure and pain would be unavoidable, just as it is for the soul.

For it is observed that for living beings possessing bodies, even though there is no occurrence of bodily modifications such as childhood or old age, there is still a connection with pleasure and pain caused by the equilibrium or imbalance of the bodily constituents (*dhātu*). And the Śruti says:
"Indeed, for one who possesses a body, there is no removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant; but for one who exists bodiless, the pleasant and the unpleasant do not touch him."
Thus [it is said].

Therefore, [if it is argued]: "Because in the doctrine of Brahman-with-body as the cause, the distinction between the natures of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) is impossible; and because in the doctrine of Brahman-alone as the cause, there is the undesirable consequence that the world would become the locus of all particularities, such as lack of human purpose, like clay or gold; therefore, the doctrine of Pradhāna as the cause alone is superior"—[we reply: Is this [Brahman] intended to mean "mere" [Brahman], or does it refer to a body caused by merit and demerit? Of these, the latter consideration has been undertaken here because it is relevant to the present topic and has come to mind; it is not, however, because it is an uncommon requirement.

When the term "body" (*śarīra*) refers to the body in general, then since the experience of suffering and so forth is necessitated by the state of possessing a body, it would follow that even Brahman experiences such suffering; consequently, there would be no distinction between Brahman and the individual soul (*jīva*), who is the possessor of the body, in terms of possessing unsurpassed bliss. When, however, the word "bodiless" (*aśarīra*) in that passage refers to a body produced by karma, then because the experience of suffering and so forth is not necessitated by the mere state of possessing a body, it is established that Brahman is indeed distinct from the individual soul who possesses a body, as there is no possibility of Brahman experiencing such suffering.

By the word "mere" (*mātra*) in the phrase "merely by existing within the body," the cessation of ownership over the body is excluded. By the expression "in the state of possessing a body" (*saśarīratve*), it is intended that there is ownership of the body, as in the case of the individual soul (*jīva*).

Just as one who has entered another's house for the sake of some business does not incur the benefits or misfortunes associated with being the master of that house merely by being in its vicinity, so too, there is no occurrence of being an enjoyer (bhoktṛtva) necessitated by having a body merely because [the Self] resides in the heart for the purpose of being meditated upon. This was stated in the passage beginning, "If it be argued that there would be the attainment of enjoyment" (*Sambhogaprāptiriti cet*). However, the point here is that the nature of the doubt differs: whereas previously the concern was about the attainment of enjoyment [of sense objects], here the doubt is raised regarding the state of being an enjoyer necessitated by being the owner of the body. This is the meaning.

The difference in the Sūtras, however, is based on the difference in the doorways through which the doubt regarding [the soul's] being an enjoyer arises. By the phrase "even though there is no possibility," the portion already refuted in the statement "but not because of the existence of examples" is restated. With the word "therefore," he states the portion not yet refuted. Here the answer is: "It may be so, as in the world. Indeed, there would be a distinction between the natures of the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara). For the soul's state of being an enjoyer of pleasure and pain, caused by the equilibrium or imbalance of the bodily constituents, is not produced by its possession of a body; rather, it is produced by karma in the form of merit and demerit. "For one who possesses a body... [is not affected by the results of actions].
This also refers to the body produced by karma; as in:
"He becomes one-fold, he becomes three-fold," and "If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers."

"He moves about there, laughing, playing, and rejoicing"—since for one who is liberated from the bondage of karma and has manifested his true nature, even while possessing a body, there is not even a trace of anything that is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*), how much less could there be the possibility of a trace of what is not a human goal for the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who is free from evil, even though He has the entire universe—both in its gross and subtle forms—as His body? For in His case, there is not even a scent of connection with karma. Thus, there is no possibility whatsoever of the occurrence of anything that is not a human goal.

As in the world (*lokavat*): just as in the world, although there is the experience of pleasure and pain caused by the king’s favor or punishment for those who obey or disobey his commands, the ruler—the king—is not [considered] a mere embodied being; nor does the consequence arise that he is the enjoyer of the pleasure and pain resulting from obedience to or transgression of the command. As the *Dramiḍa* commentator said:

"Just as in the world a king, even while residing in a terrible region fraught with many venomous snakes and perilous calamities, is not touched by defects because his body is fanned away [from them] by fans and the like, and he protects the people and the horses he desires, and enjoys pleasures as well"—here [the author] shows the principle to be established. The resolution is made by relying on the meaning that will be explained in the *Muktipāda* (the section on liberation) with the words "Na ha vai" (Indeed, not); it is not, however, resolved right here because the scriptural statement (*śruti*) is intended to be resolved in that context.
"Fans and so forth"—by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the means for warding off various undesirable things are intended.
"Nitarām" [is found in] Ta, Tha; "saśarīrastha" [is found in] Bha; "māno'pi" [is found in] Ta, Tha; "paripipālayiṣati" [is found in] Bhā, Ja;
"karmasaṃbandha" [is found in] Tha; "jagatsaśarīratve'pi" [is found in] Tha; "draviḍa" [is found in] A; "pradeśe'pi" [is found in] Tha, Ta, Tha, Da; "punarapi pālayiṣyati" [is found in] Vā.

"He maintains fragrances and other things that are not to be enjoyed by all people"; likewise, this Lord of the World (lokeśvara), whose chowries are his own wandering powers, is untouched by defects and protects the worlds beginning with the Brahma-world, and he maintains enjoyments that are not to be enjoyed by all people. Thus [it is said].

The transformation of the nature of Brahman is certainly not admitted, as it is [otherwise] declared to be changeless, faultless, and so forth.
