As for the interpretation offered by others—who, having raised the objection that the doctrine of Brahman as the cause entails the absence of the distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed, explain the Sūtra as being intended to establish that distinction through the analogies of the ocean and its foam or waves—for those who accept creation from Brahman as conditioned by *avidyā* (ignorance) which contains within itself the power [of manifestation]: [The Sūtra: "But [the distinction] is like that of water and gold, etc. (Brahma-sūtra 2.1.13). [The commentary: "However, a transformation of the very essence of Brahman is not at all accepted, because of scriptural texts such as 'It is without change' and 'It is without blemish. As for the Sūtra which others have explained as being aimed at demonstrating the distinction—having raised the doubt regarding the lack of distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed in the doctrine of Brahman as the cause—it was interpreted by those who accept creation from Brahman as qualified by *avidyā* wherein the power [of manifestation] is inherent."

That is incorrect; for such an objection and its refutation would be irrelevant, because the experiencer is that which is conditioned by the limiting adjunct (upādhi) of ignorance (avidyā), a power inherent within the cause, while the object of experience is the adjunct itself; indeed, it is impossible for these two distinct entities to undergo a mutual transformation into one another.
Furthermore, even they do not accept a transformation of essential nature (*svarūpapariṇāma*),

because [in the Sūtra] it is stated, "If it be argued that there is no action due to the lack of differentiation, we say no, because of beginninglessness," thereby establishing the beginninglessness of both the knowers of the field (*kṣetrajña*) and the karma residing within them.
And here, the mention of the *cāmara* (fly-whisk) is an elliptical indication (*upalakṣaṇa*) of objects corresponding to the warding off of what is undesirable.

In the theory that Brahman together with the body is the cause, the absence of distinction between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) has been resolved. In the doctrine of Brahman alone as the cause, the aforementioned undesirable consequences regarding the purpose of man (puruṣārtha) and so forth within the world are avoided by not accepting them, just as in the case of clay, gold, and the like.

Regarding the phrase *yat tu*: they themselves have stated that the word "enjoyer" (*bhoktṛ*) refers to the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*). Others, having raised the objection that the object of enjoyment might become the enjoyer and the enjoyer might become the object of enjoyment, have offered a refutation. [The author] refutes that as being improper. By the phrase "contained within the cause," he demonstrates the incoherence of both the objection and its refutation. In the expression "and of the limiting adjunct" (*upādheśca*), the word "limiting adjunct" (*upādhi*) denotes all three: power (*śakti*), ignorance (*avidyā*), and the adjunct (*upādhi*).

Just as the word *avāda* can refer both to discourse in general and to a specific type of discourse, so it is here. Alternatively, by the term *upādhi*, the non-sentient portion is intended. Regarding the phrase "of the two distinct [entities]": although the status of being the enjoyer may belong to Brahman as conditioned (*upahita*) and the status of being the object of enjoyment to the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), nevertheless, the fear that these two—the adjunct and Brahman—are inseparable is raised and then refuted.

"Not action" means that if one accepts the beginninglessness of the knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*) and so forth, then since Brahman as conditioned (*upahita*) is the knower of the field, and the conditioning adjunct (*upādhi*) is accepted as being eternal in its nature as an object of experience (*bhogya*), it follows as a matter of course that there can be no non-distinction between those two which are both accepted as eternal. This is the meaning.

Even if one accepts the transformation of the essential nature (*svarūpa-pariṇāma*), no suspicion whatsoever arises regarding the distinction between the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) and the enjoyed (*bhogya*); for, just as there is a distinction between jars, bowls, bracelets, crowns, and so forth—which are transformations of clay, gold, and the like—the distinction between the enjoyer and the enjoyed is logically established. Furthermore, if there were a transformation of the essential nature, Brahman itself would incur the state of being both enjoyer and enjoyed, and thus there would again be an inconsistency. 14.
Thus ends the section concerning the eater and the offspring (Bhoktrāpatyādhikaraṇa). || 5 ||
The Section on the Origin [of the World] (Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa) || 2.1.6 ||
153. Its non-difference [from Brahman] [is established] on account of the words concerning "origination" and so forth. (2.1.15)

In passages such as "If it be said that [the effect] is non-existent, no, because [the statement] is a mere negation," the fact that Brahman is the cause of the world was established by accepting the non-difference of the world, which is the effect, from Brahman, who is its cause. Now, that very non-difference is being challenged and subsequently resolved.

In this regard, the followers of Kaṇāda (the Vaiśeṣikas) say: "The non-difference of the effect from the cause is not possible, because they are apprehended by distinct cognitions—for indeed, the cognition regarding the objects of the cause and the effect, such as threads and cloth, or a lump of clay and a jar, is not of a single form."

"In such [passages]"—the meaning is "in these sūtras. Does the status of Brahman as the cause of the world hold? Or does it not? Is the non-difference of the world from Brahman, established by scripture, possible if the world is an effect of Brahman? Or are statements such as "beginning with speech" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4) capable of teaching that the effect is merely the cause itself having attained another state? Furthermore, do differences in cognition, terminology, and so forth, arise based on a difference in state, or are they based on a difference in substance?

When differences of cognition and so forth are based on a difference in essential nature (*svarūpa*), then, because the effect would be other than its cause, the world would result in being other than Brahman; consequently, Brahman—which is designated as non-different from that [world]—would not be the cause.

When it is established that distinctions such as those of the intellect (*buddhi*) are based on different states, then, because the effect is non-different from its cause, the non-difference of the world from Brahman is proven; and thus, it is established that Brahman—which is designated as non-different from that [world]—is possible as the cause of the world.
"But here, the horse that is not to be bowed to is the cause of the world, [which arises] from Brahman,
just as [the various forms] arise from a lump of clay, according to such passages as 'beginning with speech' (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.4)."

Also because of the difference in designation: for we do not say, "the threads are the cloth," nor do we say, "the cloth is the threads. Also because of the difference in function: for water is not carried by a lump of clay, nor is a wall constructed by a jar. Also because of the difference in time: the cause exists at an earlier time, and the effect at a later time. And because of the difference in form: the cause has the form of a lump, while the effect has the form of a broad base and a belly.
Likewise, while the clay remains truly existent, it is conventionally expressed that "the jar has been destroyed.
Furthermore, a difference in number is observed: there are many threads, yet the cloth is one.

Furthermore, there would be the futility of the activity of causal factors (*kāraka-vyāpāra*): if the effect were indeed identical to the cause, what would be accomplished by the activity of the causal factors?
If it is argued that "even though the effect exists, the activity of the causal factors must occur for the sake of its utility," then the activity of the causal factors would never cease.
If everything existed at all times, there would be no distinction between the eternal and the non-eternal.

Now, [the opponent] says: "The effect exists even prior [to its production], though it was unmanifest; it is manifested through the operation of causal factors (*kāraka*). Therefore, the operation of causal factors is purposeful, and the distinction between the eternal and the non-eternal is maintained."

Furthermore, if the operation of the causal factors (*kāraka*) were merely manifesting [what already exists], it would follow that the operation of the causal factors intended for a jar would manifest a water-jar (*karaka*) and so forth; for among manifestors such as lamps whose status as manifestors is universally accepted, no restriction regarding the specific object to be manifested is observed. Indeed, a lamp brought forth for the sake of a jar does not fail to manifest a water-jar and other such things. Therefore, the purposefulness of the operation of causal factors consists solely in being the cause for the production of an effect that was previously non-existent.
Consequently, the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) is not established.
Furthermore,
the employment of specific causes does not establish that the effect exists [prior to its production], since that is accounted for simply by the restriction of the causal power.

[Objection: But surely, even for the proponent of the theory of the non-existent effect (*asatkāryavādin*), the operation of causal factors (*kārakavyāpāra*) is not tenable; because the effect is non-existent prior to its production, the operation of the causal factors must pertain to something other than the effect. In that case, since there is no distinction regarding "being other," it would follow as a logical consequence (*prasajyate*) that the production of a jar could occur through the operation of the causal factors residing in the threads! [Reply: Not so; for when a particular cause possesses the capacity to produce a particular effect, the production of that effect is established by means of the operation of the causal factors residing in that very cause.

On this point, they say: the effect is non-different from the cause. For, in the ultimate sense (*paramārthataḥ*), there exists no such entity as an "effect" distinct from the cause; this is because both the entire range of effects and their conventional usage (*vyavahāra*) are based upon ignorance (*avidyā*). Therefore, just as the effects such as jars and bowls—which are perceived in various modifications (*vikāra*)—are not distinct from the causal substance of clay that is perceived therein, [so too is the effect non-different from its cause].

"And it is not restricted. If the pot does not exist in the lump of clay, then—since there is no difference in their both being non-existent—the thread too would be taken up by one desiring to make a pot. But that is not done. Therefore, because the restriction regarding the taking up of a specific cause would otherwise be untenable, the meaning is that the effect must indeed be existent [in the cause]. As for the word "cause": how is there this restriction, namely, "the pot exists only in the lump of clay, not in the threads"?

If it is argued that "only that [effect] is capable of being that [cause]," then it follows that "only that [cause] is capable of producing that [effect]," and thus a restriction to its specific material cause (*upādāna*) is logical—this is the meaning. In this way, the objection consisting in the impossibility of restricting the material cause has been refuted.
"Not so," [he says]; that is, he maintains that the scriptural texts concerning non-difference are not to be taken in their primary sense.

Therefore, regarding the phrase "as" (*yathā*): with reference to the meaning of the passage beginning with "a mere modification of speech" (*vācārambhaṇa*), just as the causal substance of clay alone is real while the modifications perceived therein—which are based merely on worldly usage—are false, so too, distinct from the cause that is Brahman, which is pure Being devoid of distinctions, the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—which is the basis for the usage of "I-consciousness" (*ahaṅkāra*) and so forth—is false; only the cause, Brahman who is pure Being, is real. Therefore, since there is no effect apart from its cause, the effect is non-different from the cause.

Nor should it be argued that "the example is untenable because the unreality of effects such as jars is not established in the same way as [the unreality of] mother-of-pearl-silver and the like," for even in those cases, by means of reasoning, only the substance of clay alone is established as real; everything beyond that is sublated by reasoning.
What, then, is the reasoning here?

It is that the mere substance of clay persists, while that which is distinct from it is excluded. For in the case of a rope-snake and the like, it is observed that the persisting substrate, such as the rope, is real, whereas the excluded elements—such as the snake, the water-hole, or the streak of water—are unreal. Likewise, the persisting substrate, the substance of clay itself, is real; however, the excluded forms, such as the jar and the bowl, are unreal.

Furthermore, since there is no destruction of an existing self and no perception of a non-existent thing such as a hare's horn, it is understood that "the effect is associated with perception and destruction, and is therefore indefinable (anirvacanīya) in terms of being either existent or non-existent. And this indefinability is merely false, like the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell; its indefinability is established by both its appearance and its subsequent sublation.

By this, the reason of "continuity" (anuvartamānatva) is intended to be expressed. The word "thus" (tathā) states the meaning of the phrase "one only, without a second. [Brahman] is the substratum for the empirical usage of the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) and so forth; for their text says: "The first superimposition is 'I'. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), the objects of knowledge (jñeya) are meant. The sense is that the meaning of the term "non-difference from That" (tadananyatva) is the absence of any effect that exists as a reality distinct from Brahman.

Regarding the word "yataḥ": the meaning is that just as when it is stated, "it is momentary like a flame," there is no deficiency in the probandum (*sādhyavaikalya*) because the distinction between individual flames is not perceptible, so it is here as well.

With the words "And what more," and so forth, he states another reason for falsity (*mithyātva*), namely, being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent. By the phrase "of the existent Self," he provides a negative (*vyatirekin*) reason for the effect's being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent. With the words "And it is indefinable" (*anirvacanīyam*), and so forth, he shows that being distinct from both the existent and the non-existent is a positive (*anvayin*) reason for falsity. And by the words "Of that," he demonstrates the indefinability of the similar instance (*sapakṣa*), such as the silver in a mother-of-pearl shell.

Furthermore—does the causal substance, such as clay, produce its effect while remaining entirely unmodified, or does it do so having attained some specific modification? It cannot be the former, because that would entail the consequence that it must produce the effect at all times. Nor can it be the latter; for the attainment of one specific modification must itself be preceded by the attainment of another specific modification, and that too by yet another, leading to an infinite regress.

If it is argued that [the cause] produces an effect only when connected with specific distinctions of place, time, and efficient cause (*nimitta*), we say no; for even a connection with specific factors such as gods and so forth is impossible for that which is either unmodified or has attained another modification, just as before.

Nor should it be argued: "The production of jars, earrings, curds, and so forth from clay, gold, milk, and the like is observed; furthermore, no sublation is seen within the conditions of space, time, and other factors—as is the case with shell-silver and the like. Therefore, for those who rely on perception, the production of an effect from a cause must necessarily be accepted. This is because [the argument] cannot withstand analysis (*vikalpāsahatvāt*). Is it merely the gold and so forth that is the originator (*ārambhaka*) of the svastika and other forms? Or is it the earrings and so forth? Or is it the "gold and so forth" as the substratum (*āśraya*) of the earrings and so forth?
First of all, gold alone cannot be the material cause; for there is no effect distinct from gold, and because it is impossible for something to be its own material cause with respect to itself.

Furthermore, by the words "And what more," etc., the author addresses the difficulty of defining the effect in order to dispel the suspicion of a limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) regarding the reason of "exclusion" (*vyāvartamānatva*). [The phrase] "in the form of an inference" means: "If it were real, it would be easily defined.
[Śrībhāṣya 2.1.6]

If it is argued that a *svastika* (a cross-shaped ornament) is seen as distinct from gold, we say no; it is not distinct from gold, because there is recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*) of it as gold and because no other separate entity is perceived apart from it.

If it is argued that its status as a separate entity is established by means of different cognitions, words, and so forth, we say no; for cognitions, words, and the like, which rely on an unestablished object, have their root in error—just like the cognition and word for "silver in mother-of-pearl"—and thus they cannot prove the existence of a separate entity.
Nor is the *rūcaka* (necklace) the originator of the *svastika* (cross-shaped ornament); for you do not perceive the *rūcaka* in the *svastika*, just as you do not perceive threads in a cloth.
Nor is gold the substratum of the *rūcaka*; for gold is not perceived in the *svastika* in the form that served as the substratum of the *rūcaka*.

Therefore, since it is observed that an effect is unreal when it is distinct from its cause, such as clay and so forth, the entire world, being distinct from Brahman, is false by virtue of being an effect. This unreality of the effect—distinct from Brahman—has been established by relying on the conceptual reality of clay and other materials for the sake of easy comprehension. However, in the ultimate sense, even causes such as clay and gold are false, just like their effects such as jars and earrings, because there is no difference in their both being effects of Brahman.

Anticipating the objection that "all this has that as its self; that is the Truth," [and that] the recognition of gold refers only to the aspect of the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), [the author replies: "In that case, two distinct individuals would be perceived; yet they are not perceived in that way. This means: the opponent maintains that the perception of the cause persists in the effect—just as threads are perceived in a cloth—or that a *rucaka* (necklace) would be perceived in a *svastika* (cross-shaped ornament). However, such is not the case.

Regarding the phrase "due to non-apprehension" (*anupalabdheḥ*): the meaning is that if the cause were qualified by the form of a necklace (*rucaka*), then there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of perceiving gold qualified by the form of a necklace even in a svastika [ornament]. Thus, it is stated here that among mere means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), a means of knowledge supported by reasoning (*tarka*) is more powerful; this constitutes the avoidance of contradiction with perception (*pratyakṣa-virodha*).

"From this" [means]: There is no sublation by perception (*pratyakṣabādha*) because no entity distinct from the cause is perceived. For that very reason, there is no presence of a limiting adjunct (*sopādhikatvam*); the sense is that since [the probandum] is established even in the subject (*pakṣa*), it lacks the status of being a limiting adjunct. "This very thing" [means]: The intent is not upon the reality of clay, but rather solely upon the falsity of everything other than Brahman. 1 *cet* – *da*. 2 *sadbhāvāsādha-* – *vā*. 3 *śabda-buddhyantarādīnām* – *ta*. 4 *tha*. 5 *labhyante* – *vā*. 6 *tatkāryatvena* – *vā*.

The falsity of everything other than Brahman is understood from such scriptural passages as: "There is no diversity whatsoever here; he goes from death to death who perceives here as if there were diversity"; "For where there is duality, as it were, there one sees another"; "But when for him everything has become the Self alone, then by what and whom should one see?"; and "Indra [the Lord] appears in many forms through his powers of illusion (māyā). By these and other such texts, the unreality of that which is distinct from Brahman is established.

Nor should one suspect a contradiction with perception regarding a matter understood through scripture; for, according to the method already stated, it is understood that every effect is illusory (*mithyā*), and perception has only pure existence (*sanmātra*) as its object. Even if there were a contradiction, since scripture—being free from any possible defects and being the final authority—is independent and leaves no room for further inquiry once knowledge has arisen, it is more powerful than perception and the like, even though perception is required for the very existence and nature of the object.
Therefore, everything other than Brahman, which is the cause, is illusory.

Nor should it be suspected that the individual soul (*jīva*) is illusory because the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) is illusory; for the soul is none other than Brahman itself. Indeed, Brahman alone experiences the state of being an individual soul within all bodies, as expressed in such passages as:
"Having entered by means of this living self" (*anena jīvenā'tmanānupraviśya*), "The one God is hidden in all beings," and "The one God has entered in many ways."
And by the scriptures: the intention is that the grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in the statement "All this has that as its self" is for the purpose of sublation.
This is known from such passages as, "This Self is hidden in all beings and does not shine forth," and "There is no other seer but He."

Now, an objection: if indeed Brahman alone experiences the state of being an individual soul (jīva) within all bodies, then there would be a recollection of pleasure and pain across all bodies, just as one says, "I have a pain in my foot" or "I have pleasure in my head. Furthermore, the established distinctions between the individual soul and the Lord, the bound and the liberated, the disciple and the teacher, and knowledge and ignorance, would not exist.

On this point, some who indeed accept the non-duality (*advitīyatva*) of Brahman offer the following resolution: the states of happiness and so forth belonging to the individual souls (*jīvas*), which are reflections of the one Brahman, are "determined" according to their respective limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), just as the smallness, largeness, dirtiness, or clarity of the various reflections of a single face perceived in jewels, swords, mirrors, and the like.
But [it may be objected]:
has it not been stated on the basis of such scriptural texts as "having entered with this living self" (*anena jīvenā'tmanā'nupraviśya*) that the individual souls are not different from Brahman?

This is true from the perspective of ultimate reality (*paramārthataḥ*). However, this systematic arrangement (*vyavasthā*) is stated by relying upon a conceptual distinction (*kālpānika-bheda*). But whose is this conceptualization? It cannot belong to Brahman; for Brahman, whose nature is pure consciousness, is devoid of conceptualization. Nor can it belong to the individual souls (*jīvas*); for that would entail the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*): the state of being a soul is dependent upon conceptualization, yet conceptualization is dependent upon the soul. This is not so; for ignorance (*avidyā*) and the state of being a soul are beginningless (*anādi*), according to the logic of the seed and the sprout.
It has been stated that the distinction between the worldly and the Vedic would be untenable;
this is true from the perspective of ultimate reality—it is indeed true that they do not differ ultimately. However, we [proceed] by relying on a distinction based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*).

Furthermore, since ignorance (*avidyā*)—which is non-substantial and whose nature is solely characterized by impossibility, like the swallowing of a palace—is not a real entity, defects pertaining to real things, such as mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*), do not bring about its impossibility. This is because, although the individual souls (*jīvas*) are in reality non-different from Brahman and are inherently pure, impurity can still occur through limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*), just as a reflection of a face in a sword appears dark. Thus, since the possibility of impurity due to adjuncts is established, the status of ignorance as a conceptual construction (*kālpānika*) is also established, and its being the locus [of the soul] is logically consistent.

Just like the blackness and so forth perceived in a reflection, the impurity residing in the individual soul (*jīva*) is also merely an illusion; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of no liberation. Since the stream of delusion among individual souls is beginningless, its cause need not be sought.
This [objection] is merely the manifestation of a desire for honor and recognition from people who have faith in dualism and who do not know the true nature of non-duality (*advaita*). For instance:

if the individual soul (*jīva*) were the locus of ignorance (*avidyā*) by virtue of its own unimagined, natural form, then it would follow that Brahman alone is the locus of ignorance. If, on the other hand, it were the locus of ignorance through an imagined form distinct from that [natural form], then it would follow that an insentient entity is the locus of ignorance. Indeed, proponents of non-duality do not admit any form apart from those two.

[Śrī Bhāṣya 2.1.6] If it is argued that the status of being the locus of ignorance belongs to the very nature [of Brahman] as qualified by an imagined form (*kalpitākāra*), we say: "That is not so. For the nature of Brahman, which is an undivided single essence (*akhaṇḍaikarasa*), cannot be established as having a qualified form (*viśiṣṭarūpatva*) without ignorance; indeed, it is precisely the form qualified by ignorance that is being defined.

Furthermore, the adoption of the doctrine of the individual soul's ignorance (*jīvājñānavāda*) is indeed for the sake of establishing the systematic order of bondage, liberation, and so forth. Yet that very order is not established even under the view of the soul's ignorance. For liberation is nothing other than the destruction of ignorance. In that case, when one [soul] is liberated through the destruction of ignorance, all others would likewise be liberated.
If you argue that because another [soul] is not yet liberated, ignorance persists [for them], then it follows that not even a single one could be liberated, since ignorance has not been destroyed.

If it is argued that a distinction of ignorance (*avidyā*) is postulated for each individual soul (*jīva*), such that he whose ignorance has not been destroyed will be liberated, while he whose [ignorance] has not been destroyed will remain bound—this is not so. The phrase "for each soul" implies a reliance on a distinction between souls. Is that distinction between souls innate, or is it imagined by ignorance?
It cannot be innate, because such a thing is not admitted; furthermore, the postulation of ignorance would be rendered useless if the distinction were already established.

Now, suppose it is imagined by ignorance (*avidyā*). In that case, regarding this ignorance which fashions the distinction between individual souls (*jīva*): does it belong to Brahman, or to the individual souls? It cannot be the former; for if ignorance were the locus [of the distinction], there would be a state of being "qualified" (*viśiṣṭatva*), meaning that the very form qualified by attributes would be the locus of ignorance—which implies self-dependence (*ātmāśrayaṇa*). Furthermore, and so forth: intending the dilemma of whether ignorance is one or many, the refutation of the position of its being one is given in the phrase "when one [soul] is liberated. Likewise, intending the dilemma of whether ignorance perishes or does not perish even in that case, the refutation of the position of its perishing is provided.
"Of another" refers to the refutation of the position that [the self] is indestructible.

"Per jīva" reiterates the position that there is a plurality of ignorance (*avidyā*). "Will be bound"—that is, it will become bound. "Because it is not accepted"—because it would entail the undesirable consequence of the loss of non-duality (*advaita*).
2 na-i, ta, tha. 0 bhatsyate - a. 1 ṇāvidyā da. naṣṭā - ta, na.
If you say, "It belongs to Brahman," then you have come to my own path!
Now, regarding living beings! Do you forget that this [classification] is intended for the purpose of establishing the distinctions between living beings?

Now, suppose you think that the distinction between individual souls is established by those very ignorances (*avidyā*) which are postulated for the sake of establishing the system of souls being bound or liberated; yet, those [ignorances] are established only when the distinction between souls is established, and the distinction between souls is established only when those [ignorances] are established—this results in the fallacy of mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*).

Furthermore, the analogy of the seed and the sprout does not apply here; for in the case of seeds and sprouts, one distinct seed is the producer of another distinct sprout. But here, those very souls who are postulated by means of the ignorances are themselves the basis upon which those ignorances are established—thus, it is impossible.

Now, if you maintain that the conception of successive individual souls (*jīva*) occurs through ignorances (*avidyā*) residing in each preceding soul—according to the logic of the seed and the sprout—then it follows that souls are transitory, and there would be the undesirable consequences of the acquisition of what was not earned (*akṛtābhyāgama*) and the loss of what was earned (*kṛtavipraṇāśa*). For this very reason, the view that the status of successive souls is fashioned by ignorances residing in the status of each preceding soul within Brahman is also refuted. If a stream of ignorance is admitted, then the "status of soul" imagined by it must also be [admitted as such].
In that case, there would be beginninglessness of the stream, but not an eternal nature; thus, the eternity of the soul until liberation—which is desired—would not be established.

As for what was said—that since ignorance (*avidyā*) consists solely of the impossibility [of being real] due to its non-substantial nature, defects pertaining to real entities such as mutual dependence (*itaretarāśrayatva*) do not apply to it—if that were so, ignorance would have to reside in liberated souls and in the Supreme Brahman. If you argue that because their nature is pure knowledge (*vidyā*), impurity does not attach to them, then is ignorance something that conforms to logical justification? If so, then by the very arguments stated, it could not reside in individual souls (*jīva*) either.

Furthermore: when ignorance (*avidyā*), which has the individual soul (*jīva*) as its locus, is destroyed by the arising of the knowledge of reality (*tattvajñāna*), does the soul perish or not? If it perishes, liberation would consist in the annihilation of one's own nature (*svarūpa*). If it does not perish, there is no liberation even upon the destruction of ignorance, because the state of being an individual soul remains distinct from the nature of Brahman.

As for what was said— that the establishment of distinctions such as purity and impurity is possible, just as the dirtiness or clarity of a face is perceived in a jewel, a sword, a mirror, and so forth—
this must be examined: [are] smallness, dirtiness, and the like...
"They would perish"—this refers to the removal of limiting adjuncts such as a sword. Thus, these are "adjunct-based defects. When? At what time?

Does the reflection, which is the locus of smallness and so forth, persist at that time, or not? If you say it persists, then the meaning is that there would be the conceptualization of successive states of being a living soul (*jīva*). And the phrase "until liberation" indicates that this same refutation applies equally to both positions regarding the conceptualization of attributes and their substrata. [This concerns] the living soul—that is, one characterized by the state of being a living soul.

If [it is argued that ignorance is destroyed], because its nature is pure knowledge (*śuddhavidyā*) and its form is pure cognition (*śuddhajñapti*), then by means of logical arguments such as mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*) and so forth—[we reply: "If not... [then] there is no liberation. The meaning is that because the state of being an individual soul (*jīvatva*), which is the effect of ignorance, persists, there is no liberation. Thus, the refutation has been stated by examining the point of comparison (*dārṣṭāntika*). Since the individual soul, which occupies that position, also remains, the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of non-liberation follows. If [it is argued that ignorance] "perishes," then likewise, due to the destruction of the individual soul, liberation would consist in the annihilation of one's own essential nature (*svarūpa-ucchitti-lakṣaṇa*).

Furthermore: for one in whom there is the appearance of a defect consisting of that which is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*), the removal of that [defect] is the human goal. In this regard, does the appearance of the defect belong to Brahman, who stands in the position of the original object (*bimba*) and is conditioned by limiting adjuncts (*aupādhika*)? Or does it belong to the "individual soul" (*jīva*), who stands in the position of the reflection (*pratibimba*)? Or does it belong to some other entity? In the case of the first two alternatives, this illustration is not applicable; for neither the face nor its reflection is devoid of the appearance of defects such as smallness. Indeed, neither the face nor its reflection possesses consciousness.
Furthermore, there would be the consequence that the knowledge of Brahman pertains to the appearance of defects in Brahman.
The third alternative also is not tenable, because there exists no seer apart from the individual soul (jīva) and Brahman.
Furthermore, it must be investigated: who is the creator of the individual soul, which is itself a construction of ignorance?

It cannot be ignorance (*avidyā*), because it is insentient; nor can it be the individual soul (*jīva*), because the state of being a soul is itself a construction of ignorance—like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell—and because that would entail the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*).

Furthermore, regarding the phrase "of whom": since the appearance of an object for the sake of another person must be rejected—for it is precisely for the sake of rejecting that [appearance] that the Vedānta is commenced—the objection is as follows: because the appearance of defects is impossible in the case of the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, who stand in the relation of the original object (*bimba*) and its reflection (*pratibimba*), the Vedānta need not be commenced for the purpose of rejecting such an appearance. Or, regarding the phrase "of another": this is with reference to the fact that in the illustrative example (*dṛṣṭānta*), there exists a face, its reflection, and a conscious being distinct from both; it is with that intention [that the objection was raised]. [The reply is: "Certainly not."

The reflection of only that which is material and insentient is observed. Therefore, the point is that if one were to accept the relationship of original and reflection between Brahman and the individual soul (jīva), it would follow that both are insentient.

It is being examined. Previously, the impossibility of ignorance having a substratum was stated. Now, the substratum of the error that is the effect of ignorance is being determined. Who is the imaginer (*kalpaka*)? What is the substratum of the error? [The opponent suggests: "The Self is the substratum. [The response is: From the status of being the imaginer, there is establishment; from the status of being the imagined (*kalpyatva*), there is non-establishment. Thus, for its own establishment, it depends upon itself. For only when the substratum of the error regarding the individual soul (*jīva*) is established is the postulation of the individual soul possible. The meaning is that, because the establishment of the individual soul depends on itself—which serves as the substratum of the error regarding its own object—it is self-dependent.
As for the phrase "from the status of being the imagined": if it is argued that Brahman alone is the imaginer, then [it follows that] Brahman is nothing but ignorance.
"Furthermore"—if the ignorance of Brahman is not admitted, does Brahman perceive the individual souls (jīvas) or not?
If it does not perceive them, then such statements as "the manifold creation preceded by seeing" and "the differentiation of names and forms" would be impossible.

If, on the other hand, it does perceive them—since Brahman is an indivisible, uniform essence (akhaṇḍaikarasa), it cannot perceive the jīvas without the existence of ignorance (avidyā); thus, the consequence is that Brahman itself possesses ignorance.
[The Refutation of the Doctrine of the Distinction between Māyā and Avidyā:

For this very reason, even the doctrine of the distinction between *māyā* and *avidyā* is refuted. For, without ignorance (*ajñāna*), even for the Brahman who possesses *māyā*, there could be no state of being a "seer" of the individual souls (*jīva*). Nor is a master of illusion (*māyin*) able to delude others without first seeing them; nor is *māyā* itself the instrument for seeing those others, since its function is merely to delude others once they have been seen.

Now, if you think that the *māyā* of Brahman, by making Him appear as the individual soul (*jīva*), is the cause of the soul's delusion; then, since it makes the absolutely pure, partless, single-flavored, and self-luminous Brahman appear as something else, that *māyā* would be nothing other than *avidyā*, which is synonymous with *māyā*.

Alternatively, if your view is this: "Ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cause of contrary perception; whereas *māyā*, by showing that which is unreal and distinct from Brahman as being unreal itself, is not the cause of a contrary perception of Brahman; therefore, it does not possess the nature of *avidyā*"—[we reply:]...

"Without ignorance" means that the perception of the non-ultimate (aparamārtha) individual soul is not possible without ignorance. "For this very reason" means precisely because the connection with ignorance must be admitted for the purpose of Brahma's creation and so forth preceded by deliberation, and for the purpose of Brahma's perception of the non-ultimate individual soul. Their doctrine is: "Māyā is the cause of another's delusion; ignorance is the cause of one's own delusion. The scriptural text, "But [He is] the Great Lord, the wielder of Māyā," is the basis for this distinction. The phrase "Māyā of Brahma" implies that this is the specific characteristic of this Māyā. "In that case" means: there is no dispute between us regarding the name.

It is not so; for even when the oneness of the moon is being known, ignorance remains the cause of the perception of two moons. Furthermore, if one knows something other than oneself as being merely false, then that [knowledge] does not delude one. Indeed, no one who is not insane would strive to delude someone who already knows a thing to be false!
Brahman:

Now, it may be argued that ignorance (*avidyā*) is the cause of perceiving what is not the supreme human goal (*apuruṣārtha*), whereas *māyā* is not the cause of perceiving what is not the supreme human goal for Brahman; therefore, it is held that *māyā* does not possess the nature of ignorance (*avidyātva*). This is not so; for even though the cognition of two moons (*dvicandra-jñāna*) is not a non-goal (*apuruṣārtha*) because it lacks the quality of being a cause of suffering, its cause is indeed ignorance (*avidyā*). Furthermore, people exert effort toward its removal. Moreover, if *māyā* were not the cause of perceiving what is not the supreme human goal, then—being indestructible—it would be eternal and inseparable from the very nature of Brahman.

If it is argued, "Let it be so; what is the fault?"—the very perception of duality is the fault. For the non-dual scriptures, such as "Where there is, as it were, duality," and "But where for him everything has become the Self alone—who should see whom, and by what?"—would be contradicted.

If it is argued that the Śrutis concerning non-duality have the ultimate reality (paramārtha) as their object, whereas there is no contradiction because Māyā is not the ultimate reality—[we reply: for Brahman, whose sole nature is unlimited bliss, neither the perception of Māyā—which is of a non-ultimate nature—nor its possession thereof, is possible without ignorance (avidyā).

If it is argued that [the Lord acts] for the sake of deluding living beings (*jīvamohana*), what purpose is served by a delusion that lacks a human goal? If it is argued that it is for the sake of play (*krīḍā*), what need has one whose bliss is unlimited for play? If it is argued that in the world, play is observed to be a human goal only for those who possess complete enjoyment, we reply:

this is not tenable here. For indeed, the essence of play does not arise for those who are not insane through a play accomplished by means of play-apparatus that are unreal, which appear as unreal, and which consist of an unreal play and its appearance.
This is because [such things] have *māyā* as their substrate...

Furthermore, the conception of a *jīva* as the locus of ignorance—distinct from Brahman, which is accepted as the locus of *māyā*—is impossible; this is to be understood in the same manner as previously explained. Therefore, for those who maintain that Brahman is non-dual, it must be admitted that Brahman itself, variegated by beginningless ignorance, perceives its own internal multiplicity. Thus, the non-duality of Brahman must necessarily be accepted.

As for the objection that "the distinction between bondage and liberation is not tenable," that is not a valid criticism against the proponent of *brahmājñāna* (Brahman’s ignorance). For, according to this view, it is the one and only Brahman who, being ignorant, is to be liberated through the cessation of its own ignorance; thus, there is no actual state of "bound" or "liberated. Furthermore, the conventionally employed distinctions of "bound," "liberated," "disciple," "teacher," and so forth, are merely conceptual constructs—just like those of one seeing a dream—for all such conceptualizations are possible through the ignorance (*avidyā*) of the single [Brahman], just as in the case of a dreamer.

For indeed, the disciples, teachers, and so forth seen by one person in a dream are merely imagined through that person's ignorance (*avidyā*). Therefore, even the postulation of many ignorances is not logical. The ultimate distinction between bondage and liberation remains exactly as before; this is the meaning of [the refutation] by means of fallacies such as mutual dependence (*anyonyāśraya*).

"Yad iti": the meaning is that this objection is not undesirable. "Because of being conceptual" (*kālpanikatvāt*): just as the various individual arrangements [of the world] are possible through a single ignorance because they are conceptual, so too, since all arrangements are conceptual, the postulation of them is possible through a single ignorance alone—this is the meaning. "Because of the possibility of all conceptualizations": for that which cannot be explained otherwise is what necessitates a postulating agent. Since it can be explained otherwise, it is not logical to postulate a plurality of ignorances—this is the meaning.

"Exactly for this reason": the meaning is that even if [ignorance] has a single locus (*āśrayaka*), the justification for all established distinctions (*sarvavyavasthā*) is possible by whatever reason it is proven; by that very same reason—namely, its conceptual nature (*kālpinikatva*)—it is also not logical to postulate a multiplicity of ignorances (*avidyābahutva*). Regarding the phrase "ultimately real" (*pāramārthikī*) and so forth: the intention is that things which are ultimately real depend upon many causes, whereas for those that are not ultimately real, one cause alone is sufficient. Furthermore, even the proponent of the theory that ignorance belongs to the individual soul (*jīvājñānavādin*) does not accept a distinction between self and other as being ultimately real; however, such a non-ultimate distinction is established through the ignorance of a single [locus].

"And the application [of the reasoning] is as follows: 1) The distinctions of bondage and liberation, as well as the distinctions between self and other, are constructed by one's own ignorance; because they are not ultimately real, they are like the distinctions perceived in a dream. 2) Other bodies as well possess a Self through me alone; because they are bodies, just like this body. 3) Other bodies as well are constructed by my ignorance; because they are bodies, because they are effects, because they are insentient, or because they are constructed, just like this body."

4) That which is under dispute—the collection of sentient beings—is indeed "I," because it possesses sentience; for whatever is not "I" is seen to be insentient, such as a jar. Therefore, the distinction between self and other, and the established order of the bound and the liberated, the teacher and the disciple, and so forth, are all imagined by the ignorance of the One.

Even for the proponent of dualism (*dvaitavādin*), the distinction between the bound and the liberated is difficult to establish. Since past and future kalpas are infinite, even if one person were liberated in each single kalpa, it would be possible for all to attain liberation; thus, the existence of the unliberated would be untenable. If it is argued that because the selves (*ātman*) are infinite, there are indeed those who remain unliberated—what does this "infinitude" mean? If you say it means "incalculability" (*asaṅkhyeyatva*), no; for due to their sheer multiplicity, even if they are incalculable for those of limited knowledge, they would still be numerable for the omniscient Lord (*īśvara*). If even for Him they were impossible to count, His omniscience would not exist. 3.

If it is argued that because the selves (*ātman*) are innumerable, the Lord’s lack of a specific number does not imply an absence of cognition, and thus does not entail a lack of omniscience—[we reply: if there were a difference [between the selves and the Lord], then being devoid of number would not be tenable. The selves possess number; because they are distinct, like beans, mustard seeds, jars, cloths, and so forth. Furthermore, if the selves were distinct, it would follow that they are insentient, non-self, and perishable, just like jars and other such objects; and this would apply to Brahman as well.

And as for the formal argument (*prayoga*): the first and third inferences are directed against the proponent of the doctrine of the ignorance of the living soul (*jīva-ajñāna-vādin*). The second reason is employed against that [proponent] as well as the proponent of difference (*bheda-vādin*). The third contains within it four reasons, each independent of the others. The fourth is a negative inference (*vyatireki-anumāna*). Regarding the term "innumerability" (*asaṅkhyeyatva*), it is intended to exclude the interpretation that the word "infinite" (*ananta*) signifies the absence of limitation in space, time, and so forth.

Infinity would not exist. Infinity means being devoid of limitation. And in the theory of difference (*bhedavāda*), because Brahman is distinct from other entities, it cannot be said that Brahman is in reality devoid of limitation. For the very existence of "other entities" constitutes limitation in reality. Furthermore, for that which is limited in reality, it is illogical to claim it is unlimited in terms of space and time.

Objects such as jars and the like are indeed *vastu*-wise delimited by their distinctness from other objects; for they are observed to be delimited by space and time as well. Likewise, all non-conscious things and Brahman are *vastu*-wise delimited; they are also delimited by space and time. And thus, [it is said]: "Truth, Knowledge, Infinite."

There would be a contradiction with those [scriptural passages] stating that [Brahman] is devoid of limitation in every respect, such as "It is without interior or exterior," and so forth; for [otherwise] birth, destruction, and the like would necessarily follow for both the individual souls (*jīva*) and Brahman. Indeed, it is only through temporal limitation that there can be participation in birth and destruction.

Therefore, the entire universe, from Brahmā down to a blade of grass, is a manifestation of ignorance (avidyā) belonging to the one undivided Brahman. Even the systematic arrangement of the experience of pleasure and pain is possible due to the inherent nature of ignorance, just like the arrangements seen in a dream.

Consequently, there is only one [reality] whose nature is eternally free and self-luminous; by the power of beginningless ignorance, it undergoes illusory transformation (vivarta) into the form of the world. Since, in the ultimate sense, there is nothing apart from Brahman, the world is non-different from it.
To this it is replied: Brahman is indeed without distinctions, consisting solely of self-luminosity, its own true nature obscured by beginningless ignorance.

Just as a jar or the like, the Self is not distinct, because it is non-inert; for whatever is distinct is not non-inert, such as a jar or the like. The Self is not distinct, because it is imperishable; for whatever is distinct is not imperishable, such as a jar or the like. "The state of being another entity" means the possession of another entity, which is to say, limitation by an external object. "And thus" means that the word *ananta* (infinite), when used without a qualifying term, expresses an unrestricted application, namely, the absence of the three kinds of limitation.

Thus, the consequence that the undifferentiated would become differentiated has been stated. Now, he states the consequence that the changeless would become possessed of change—namely, "in its arising" (*utpatti*). This means there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning its changelessness. "It manifests" (*vivartate*) means it becomes the substratum for repeated appearance; it does not, however, undergo transformation (*pariṇamate*). "Its non-difference from that" (*tadananyatvam*) means that the world is not something other than Brahman as its ultimate reality.

The claim that "one perceives an internal diversity" has already been refuted previously on the grounds that, since the nature of light is partless, its concealment—which would consist in the cessation of its manifestation—is impossible; for such concealment would entail the destruction of its very essence, which contradicts all means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and is self-contradictory.

Furthermore, as for what was further stated—that the effect is distinct from its cause and is therefore an illusion (*bhrama*), like silver in a mother-of-pearl shell due to being sublated by reasoning—that is incorrect, because there is no such reasoning (*yukti*).

As for the claim that the persisting cause alone is real, while the non-persisting effects such as jars, bowls, and so forth are unreal—that too has already been refuted previously by such arguments as: "The fact that something seen elsewhere ceases to exist elsewhere does not constitute a sublation [of its reality]."

As for the claim that the effect is false because it is both perceived and subject to destruction—and thus indefinable as being either existent or non-existent—that is incorrect. For the connection with perception and destruction does not establish falsity; rather, it establishes impermanence. Indeed, the reason for its falsity is simply its sublation (bādha) in relation to the same space and time in which it was perceived.

The sublation of that which was perceived as being connected with another place and time by its being connected with yet another place and time establishes merely the non-pervasion [of the object] by those other places and times.

Regarding the phrase "of that which is partless" (*niraṃśasya*): it is not tenable to say that even during concealment (*tirodhāna*) parts devoid of that [concealment] remain; the intention is that this is because it is partless. Regarding the phrase "destruction of its own nature" (*svarūpanāśa*): concealment means the cessation of manifestation. In that case, since an insentient object is distinct from manifestation, its continued existence is logically possible even when manifestation ceases. However, for Brahman, whose sole form is manifestation, concealment in the form of the cessation of manifestation is nothing other than the cessation of its very own nature (*svarūpa*). This is what is meant by "contradictory."

The quality of being devoid of distinctions (*nirviśeṣatva*) is contradicted by statements that establish [the Self] as eternal and so forth. The meaning is that "being an object of the notion of 'I' (*asmat-pratyaya-gocaratva*)" is contradictory to "the nature of consciousness" (*jñaptitva*). It was stated previously—meaning that this was stated by the proponent (*siddhāntin*) in this very treatise. Regarding the phrase "by such [arguments]": the meaning is that these have already been refuted by [pointing out] the presence of limiting conditions (*sopādhikatva*), the fallacy of being mistimed (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭatva*), and contradictions in the verbal expression (*vacanavyāhati*). As for the phrase "that which is spatially...": if non-eternality itself were falsity (*mithyātva*), then the inference of falsity would be proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). If, however, it is something distinct from non-eternality, then there is the presence of limiting conditions and so forth.

[Śrī Bhāṣya 2.1.6] But it is not false. And there is a counter-argument: "An effect such as a jar is real, because it is uncontradicted within its perceived limiting conditions of space, time, and so forth, like the Self."

As for what was stated—that the production of an effect from a cause that is either unmodified or modified is not possible—that is incorrect; for the production of an effect is possible from a cause when it is accompanied by auxiliary factors such as place, time, and so forth. As for the claim that such accompaniment is impossible for both the modified and the unmodified [cause], that is untenable; because it is precisely for the unmodified cause that accompaniment by time and other factors is possible at the outset.

If it is argued that because there is no difference in its being unmodified (*avikṛta*), the conjunction of place, time, and so forth would necessarily follow even prior [to the effect], we say: no. This is because the conjunction of place, time, and so forth, which depends on other causes, does not depend upon this [unmodified cause]. Therefore, it is not the case that anything is lacking in the principle that "a cause, having attained a specific state consisting of the conjunction of place, time, and so forth, produces the effect. Furthermore, the fact that a cause initiates an effect is observed as uncontradicted and cannot be denied in any manner whatsoever.

As for the objection that it is impossible for mere gold (*hemamātra*)—or for the effect such as a necklace (*rucaka*), or for the gold that serves as its substrate—to be the originator (*ārambhakatva*), that is incorrect; for it is possible for mere gold, when endowed with the aforementioned adjuncts (*parikara*), to be the originator. Nor can it be said that no effect is observed apart from the originating gold; for a *svastika* (a specific ornamental design) is seen to be distinct from the gold, and because the existence of a different entity has been established through cognition, a change in terminology, and other such means.

Nor is this an illusion, like that of silver in a mother-of-pearl shell; for there is no sublation observed of that which is perceived during the interval between its production and destruction, nor of its connection with that particular place and time. Furthermore, no reasoning whatsoever is seen that could sublate this perception. Moreover, even at the time when the swastika is perceived, the recognition of the gold—which was not previously perceived—is not contradictory, since the gold persists as the substrate of the swastika.

The proof of the falsity of the phenomenal world (*prapañca*) by means of the scriptures has already been refuted. As for the other objections here, such as the contradiction with perception and so forth, all of those have also been well-stated previously.

As for what was said—that all bodies possess a self by means of a single self—that is incorrect; for it would entail that one and the same person must experience the pleasure and pain produced by all bodies. For in the case of Saubhari and others, [this would be impossible]. The meaning is: it has been stated that gold alone, or merely the effects such as necklaces (*rucaka*), or merely the substance residing in those effects, cannot be the originator [of further things]. "The aforementioned auxiliary conditions" refers to place, time, and so forth.

"And this is not so. This refutes the opponent's (pūrvapakṣin) argument that cognition, verbal expressions, and the like, which lack a well-defined objective basis, are incapable of establishing anything. Regarding the statement "because [the production] is not observed": if impermanence were the property to be proven (*sādhya*), there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhanatva*). Furthermore, the objection regarding sublation (*bādha*) within the accepted conditions (*upādhi*) is also dismissed simply by the non-perception of such [conditions]; this is the intended meaning.

"Refuted" means by the proponent of the final view (*siddhāntin*). "And that which is other" means that what was stated by you—namely, "perception grasps only existence (*sanmātra*); and even when there is a contradiction, scripture is more powerful," and so forth—has already been refuted by this author.

"Of one and the same" expresses a contradiction with the pervasion (*vyāpti*); the sense is that in a body whose nature is admitted to be unitary, the recognition (*pratisandhāna*) of pleasure and so forth is indeed observed. Regarding "Saubhari": [it is used] in the context of the claim that the absence of such recognition is caused by the difference in bodies.
"By the oneness of the Self": the recollection of pleasure and so forth experienced by multiple bodies is observed to belong to a single [Self].

Nor can it be argued that "recollection is absent due to a difference in the referent of the 'I' (ahamartha) because of its being the knower, and not due to a difference in the Self"; for it has been established that "the Self is indeed the knower, and that is precisely the referent of the 'I'. But the egoity (*ahaṅkāra*), which consists of the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*), is not the knower because, being insentient and an instrument, it is like the body, the senses, and so forth."

By means of the properties of being a body, insentience, being an effect, and being imagined, it was asserted that all bodies are imagined by a single ignorance (*avidyā*); however, that too is untenable because there is no such thing as all bodies being imagined by ignorance. Furthermore, that [ignorance] does not exist, since it has been established that what is uncontradicted is real. And as for the assertion that all sentient beings are non-different from one another because insentience is observed in everything other than consciousness—that too is refuted precisely by the demonstration of difference through the distinct distribution of pleasure and pain.

As for that which was established—namely, "I alone am the animator [of all], all things are fashioned by my ignorance, and I alone am the entire collection of conscious beings"—this is the deluded prattle of one who does not understand his own philosophical tenet. For, according to your own view, the Self (*ātman*) is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), distinct from the referents of "I," "you," and so forth.

The meaning is that for certain cognitions of a distinct nature, even when there is a difference of bodies, there is recognition of pleasure and so forth from a previous birth, starting from that point. Regarding "the oneness of the self": if the oneness of the self residing in a single body were being proved, it would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhana*). If, however, the self residing in multiple bodies is the subject, there is sublation by the very means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇabādha*). For the self is indeed inferred from the movements and other signs in another's body; and that inference demonstrates it as being distinct from oneself.
For one's own self indeed manifests directly as "I"; for the self residing in another's body is not directly manifest.

Regarding the term "self": the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*) does not possess the nature of being a knower; rather, that [nature] belongs to the self (*ātman*). Even if [the internal organ] were a knower, there would be no internal distinction [between selves], because for Sanaka and others—who possessed internal organs produced and destroyed in successive prior kalpas—it is possible to have recognition (*pratisandhāna*) of those [past experiences]. Therefore, the absence of recognition is not caused by an internal distinction [between selves].

"That too is improper" means it has been stated that the example is devoid of the property to be proven (*sādhyavikala*). For only if it were established that bodies are imagined through ignorance (*avidyā*) could the fact that the one [Self] is imagined through ignorance be established. But that very thing does not exist, because the body, which serves as the corroborative instance (*sapakṣa*), lacks the quality of being imagined through ignorance. "That too is refuted" means the fallacy of being "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*) has been stated as the refutation.

Regarding the phrase "yat tu" (as for what was said): it was stated that the states of the bound and the liberated are all imagined by a single ignorance (*avidyā*); however, even in that case, the reason—that they are not ultimately real—is unestablished (*asiddha*), and their being "conditioned by an adventitious attribute" (*sopādhikatva*) should also be considered.

Furthermore: For one who asserts that "everything other than the undifferentiated pure consciousness (cinmātra) is false," the effort toward hearing [the scriptures] and so forth for the sake of liberation is fruitless; because it is an effect of ignorance, like the effort to pick up silver in the case of mother-of-pearl appearing as silver. 1) Effort for the sake of liberation is useless; because its result—knowledge—is dependent upon an imagined teacher, like the efforts of Śuka, Prahlāda, Vāmadeva, and others. 2) Knowledge produced by sentences such as "That thou art" (tattvamasi) does not remove bondage; [because it is produced by words, which are themselves effects of ignorance].

Because it is produced by a sentence constructed by ignorance, because it is itself of the nature of ignorance, because it has as its locus a knower constructed by ignorance, or because it is produced by hearing dependent on a teacher who is a construction of ignorance, it is like the knowledge produced by a sentence that removes a bondage in a dream.

Furthermore—Brahman, which is pure consciousness devoid of attributes (*nirviśeṣacinmātra*), is false (*mithyā*), because it is cognizable through knowledge that is an effect of ignorance (*avidyā-kārya-jñāna-gamyatvāt*), or because it is cognizable through knowledge whose locus is superimposed by ignorance (*avidyā-kalpitajñātrāśraya-jñāna-gamyatvāt*), or because it is cognizable through knowledge whose nature is ignorance (*avidyātmaka-jñāna-gamyatvāt*). Whatever is thus [cognizable] is so [false], just like dreams, cities of the Gandharvas, and the like. Nor does Brahman, as pure consciousness devoid of attributes, manifest itself (*svayaṃ prakāśate*) such that it would not depend on another means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

As for that self-luminous knowledge witnessed by the Self (*ātmasākṣika-svaprakāśa-jñāna*) which is observed, it has already been stated previously that this is merely the establishment of a particular object of knowledge (*jñeya-viśeṣa-siddhi-rūpa*) and is seen as residing only in the knower (*jñātṛgata*).
Furthermore, those logical arguments presented to prove its lack of distinction have been refuted by the aforementioned inferences, beginning with "because it is an effect of ignorance."

Furthermore, neither the status of being the witness of ignorance nor the illusory appearance of the world, such as the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*) and so forth, is possible for pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) that is devoid of all distinctions.

By means of a series of reasons, such as "because it is an effect of ignorance," he states this undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭaprasaṅga*). Regarding the phrase "tattvamasyādi": the meaning is that if one resorts to the view that [ignorance] is the root cause, then there would be the undesirable consequence that the knowledge produced by sentences such as "That thou art" (*tat tvam asi*) would not be capable of removing [that ignorance].

For even errors such as being a witness (*sākṣitva*) are observed to reside in a specific knower (*jñātṛ*), not in mere consciousness (*jñapti*). Nor is its "luminosity" (*prakāśatva*), or its self-dependent luminosity, established. For luminosity is seen to be the state of being established (*siddhi-rūpa*) for some person with respect to some particular object; it is precisely on that basis that its self-luminosity is demonstrated even by you yourselves. And luminosity is not possible for that which is "not such"—that is, for the indeterminate (*nirviśeṣa*).

Furthermore, as for the proclamation made within our own circles—that "the effect of the ultimate reality is seen even from that which is not the ultimate reality"—that too is refuted by our own admission: namely, that "all those effects are merely conventionally real, being uncontradicted in their appearance, but in reality they consist of nothing but ignorance. This has already been refuted by us, who have established everywhere that the production of all effects proceeds solely from the ultimately real cause.

Nor can you assert that these inferences contradict the Śruti; for since the Śruti itself is an effect of ignorance and is of the nature of ignorance, it possesses no distinction from the examples already cited.
As for the argument that— although Brahman is accessible through non-ultimate knowledge— it is nonetheless truly real because no subsequent sublation is observed;

That is incorrect; for once it is determined that a cognition is produced by a defective cause, the subsequent non-observation of sublation is irrelevant. For example, even though no subsequent sublation is observed for the cognition produced by the statement "emptiness alone is reality," its object is nonetheless unreal precisely because it is determined to be rooted in a defect. Furthermore, regarding the term *atādṛśasya*—this means "of that which is devoid of attributes," i.e., "devoid of action and agent. If the reading were *tādṛśasya*, the meaning would be: "if one intends such a thing—which appears accompanied by action and agent—to be devoid of attributes, then that [attributelessness] is not established."

Regarding the phrase "yaḥ punar" (as for that which...): previously, it was stated that [an effect] is fruitless because its cause is not ultimately real, like the taking up of mother-of-pearl as silver; however, that is not so, because there is no distinction [in this case], since even from that which is not ultimately real, the ultimately real can arise. The sense is that weakness [of one factor] occurs only when there is a powerful contradiction [with another].

Furthermore: you have asserted that, setting aside direct perception and other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), as well as the collection of scriptural passages in the Veda that refer to the qualified [Brahman], it is the negating passages that possess superior authority. In that case, the former [passages] would be weak because they are positive in form, while the latter would be strong because they are negative in form. And this [position] belongs only to the proponent of universal voidness (*sarvaśūnyavādin*).
[As for example: "There is no diversity whatsoever here," and "Brahman is consciousness and bliss."

Thus, because it negates the entire range of objects as being nothing other than mere consciousness (*vijñānamātra*), and because it is therefore superior to all else, the absence of subsequent sublation is asserted. However, for one who asserts the non-existence even of that [consciousness] by saying "the reality is indeed emptiness" (*śūnyameva tattvam*), a subsequent sublation is observed due to its superiority over that [previous view]. Since no negation is possible beyond universal emptiness, it is precisely in that case that the absence of subsequent sublation is seen. As for the root of error, however, it is common to both perception and the other means of knowledge, as well as to the cognition of universal emptiness born from the Vedāntas.

Therefore—every collection of cognitions resides in a cognizer who is ultimately real, and it is itself ultimately real, consisting in the establishment of a specific object. In that regard, if it is not accepted that some cognition is rooted in a defect (doṣa) and that the defect is ultimately real, and that some [other] cognition is "faultless" and produced by an ultimately real causal complex (*sāmagrī*), then the distinction between true and false objects, as well as worldly transactional practice, will not be established.

For worldly transaction (*lokavyavahāra*), which is indeed conventional and of the nature of non-delusion, is preceded by a manifestation consisting in the establishment of specific objects pertaining to a real knower. However, since it is impossible for that which is devoid of distinctions—the mere existence (*sanmātra*)—and that which is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*), to serve as a cause for such a manifestation, worldly transaction is not possible [in their case].

Furthermore, as for their claim that because an error without a substratum is impossible, the pure Being (*sanmātra*) which is the substratum of all superimpositions must be ultimately real (*pāramārthika*); that too is refuted by the fact that an error can occur even when the substratum is not ultimately real, just as an error is possible even when the defect (*doṣa*), the locus of the defect, the knower (*jñātṛ*), and the knowledge (*jñāna*) are not ultimately real.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) of the word "therefore" (*ataḥ*) is with "it will not be established. Regarding the term "without distinction" (*nirviśeṣa*): because a cognition devoid of distinctions lacks the status of being a knower, it cannot function as a cause by way of being the substratum of an appearance. The meaning is that precisely because it is without distinction, it also cannot function as a cause by way of being a causal factor. The terms "ultimate" (*pāramārthika*) and "non-ultimate" (*apāramārthika*) refer respectively to having the ultimate and the non-ultimate as their objects. In the phrase "of appearance, etc.," the word "etc. (*ādi*) refers to conventional usage (*vyavahāra*).

Now, if you think: "Even though the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is not ultimately real, no error is ever observed [without it]; therefore, the ultimate reality of pure Being (*sanmātra*) must necessarily be accepted"—then, alas! since no error is ever observed even when defects (*doṣa*), the locus of defects, the knower (*jñātṛ*), and knowledge (*jñāna*) are not ultimately real, their ultimate reality must also necessarily be accepted in accordance with observation; there is no distinction whatsoever, other than your zeal for that [Being].

As for the objection that—even on the view of difference—since past kalpas are infinite and all selves have been liberated, there can be no bound self, and thus the distinction between the bound and the liberated is impossible—that is refuted by the infinity of selves. As for the claim that even if selves are distinct, their number must necessarily be finite, like mustard seeds, jars, or cloths—in that case, since jars and so forth are also infinite, the example would be devoid of the probandum.

If it is argued that numerical quantification is observed, as in "ten jars" or "a thousand māṣas," we reply: True; however, that numerical quantification does not belong to the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the jars and so forth. Rather, it belongs to the jars and so forth as they are conditioned by spatial, temporal, and other limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*). We accept such numerical quantification for the selves (*ātman*), yet this does not entail the consequence of universal liberation (*sarvamukti*), because the essential natures of the selves are infinite in number.

"There is no distinction whatsoever. If it is argued that since the substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) is not ultimately real, that too would require another substratum, leading to an infinite regress (*anavasthā*), then [we reply]: even if the defect (*doṣa*) is not ultimately real, there would still be an infinite regress. If you claim that in that case the problem is avoided by the fact that its nature is beginningless (*svarūpānāditva*) or that its stream is beginningless (*pravāhānāditva*), then that [solution] is equal [in both cases]; such is the intention.

Regarding the phrase "by the infinity of the self": just as in the case of black gram (*māṣa*), mustard seeds (*sarṣapa*), and so forth, each individual member of a species is infinite and their collection is also infinite; likewise, the bound souls (*baddha*) are infinite, the liberated souls (*mukta*) are infinite, and all sentient beings (*cetana*) taken together are infinite. Every single one of these selves possesses the number one. Therefore, it is not the mere possession of number that is denied; rather, the meaning is that the limit of the number two is what is denied. This is the illustration.

Because past kalpas are infinite, even if there were only one jar in a single kalpa, the infinity of jars is established; thus, the example lacks the property to be proven (*sādhyavikalatā*). "We accept" [this]. And the authority is the scripture (*śāstra*); and since that scripture establishes them as being infinite, the infinity of sentient beings must be accepted because the reason—consisting of a finite number of entities—is contradicted by the scripture. By the phrase "space, time, etc.," the word "etc. (*ādi*) is intended to include the creator (*kartṛ*).

For it could also be said, "These ten pots were made by this potter. Regarding the phrase "due to infinity": the meaning is that in the absence of limiting adjuncts such as space, the mere nature of the Self is innumerable.

As for the objection—that if there were a plurality of selves, it would follow that they are insentient, non-self, and perishable, just like pots and other objects—that is incorrect; for the difference among things belonging to a single class does not entail that those things belong to a different class. Indeed, the difference among pots and the like does not cause them to become cloth!
[The doubt that mixture in Brahman would undermine its infinity, and its refutation:

As for the objection that—if there were differentiation—Brahman would, by virtue of being a real entity, necessarily be limited by space and time as well, and thus its infinity could not be established—that is incorrect;

In reality, even for things that are limited, an absence of fixed rule is observed regarding the degree of their spatial and temporal limitations; since the determination of the extent of a thing's connection with space and time depends upon other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), there is no contradiction in the fact that Brahman’s connection with all space and time also results from other means of knowledge.

In reality, even from mere delimitation (*pariccheda*), infinity is not established because there is an absence of being devoid of all forms of delimitation. This is not so; for when it is stated, "A pot is not different [from itself] because it possesses pot-ness (*ghaṭatva*); whatever is different is not a pot, just as a cloth," this is a case of the reason being "mistimed" (*kālātyayāpadiṣṭa*). The meaning is that your stated negative-only (*vyatirekin*) arguments are likewise "mistimed."

Limitation (*pariccheda*). By stating "this is not that," it is made known that the opponent's (the *mṛṣāvādī*) intended meaning is that limitation is, in reality, the unfitness for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*). However, the limitation of an entity in another manner, as intended by the proponent (*siddhāntin*), is not accepted by the proponent of falsehood (*mṛṣāvādī*); for this would be the opposite of [his] notion of non-limitation, which contradicts his doctrine of featurelessness (*nirviśeṣatva*).

Therefore, the false proponent, under the misconception that the determination of an object's own nature necessitates the determination of its spatial and temporal limits, has introduced those two [limitations). That is incorrect; for it is observed that a gradation in the form of the effect is based upon a gradation in the form of the cause, just as a gradation in falling is based upon a gradation in weight.
