Consequently, if the determination of an object's nature were to necessitate the determination of its space and time, it would follow that there must be a state of relative deficiency or excess [in those determinations].

And yet, it is not seen as such; therefore, its being the cause of that [limited perception] is untenable. Thus, the meaning is that even though Brahman is in fact limited, its lack of spatial and temporal limitation is logically established. Regarding the phrase "by another means of knowledge," the intention is that the limitation of the object is not the determining factor. By the words "even from mere limitation in reality," he raises the doubt that the scriptural declarations of infinity might be subject to restriction.

If this is argued, then that same point applies equally to you as well, who likewise accept that Brahman is distinct from ignorance (*avidyā*). Therefore, because you accept that the existent Brahman is distinct from ignorance, all the defects resulting from such duality would also accrue to your position due to Brahman being [effectively] differentiated. If, on the other hand, you do not accept its distinction from ignorance, then Brahman would be identical in nature to ignorance itself; consequently, even the defining statement, "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite," would become meaningless for that very reason.

For if difference (*bheda*) were not accepted as a reality, everything would become incoherent due to the absence of distinction between one's own position and the opponent's position, as well as between proof and refutation. Furthermore, [the claim of] infinity is established merely by the absence of spatial and temporal limitation, "but not by the absence of limitation in reality (*vastutaḥ*)," because such a thing is unperceived, being like the horn of a hare.

For the proponent of difference (*bhedavādin*), however, since Brahman possesses all modes of being as the body of all conscious and unconscious entities, no limitation exists either intrinsically or extrinsically.

With the words "If [it were]," etc., he states the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭa*) that follows from the reversal of the proponent of the reductio (*prasañjaka*). [The opponent says: "Truth and knowledge [are Brahman]. [To this, the author replies: It is incorrect to say that "delimitation by an object (*vastu-pariccheda*) is being other than the ultimate reality (*paramārtha*)," for that [delimitation] is precisely sublation (*bādhyatva*). And the result of sublation is cessation at some time, since that [cessation] is included within delimitation by time. Therefore, if "delimitation by an object" were merely being different [from the ultimate], then the consequence of Brahman—which is different from ignorance (*avidyā*)—being delimited by an object would be unavoidable.

Regarding the phrase "the reality of difference": one's own position is faultless and powerful, while the opposing position is flawed and weak; such is the acceptance of difference. If it is argued that difference is not ultimately real, then the opposing position alone would become powerful, and that very [opposing] view would be what is accepted—this is the meaning.

Regarding the phrase "but for those who maintain difference" (*bhedavādinas tu*): the meaning is that in the direct position of the Siddhāntin, the non-limitation of the reality (*vastvapariccheda*) is logically established. This is because Brahman is of all forms. For the limitation of a thing (*vastupariccheda*) consists in the judgment "this is not that. Non-limitation of a thing (*vastvapariccheda*), however, means the fitness for being designated as "this is that," which is the capacity for grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with all things. Indeed, the function of grammatical coreferentiality is the expression of multiple qualifiers culminating in a single qualified object.

And that is because the reality is of such a nature. Alternatively, for Brahman, "non-limitation of reality" means non-limitation by its very nature; this results in the conclusion that it possesses infinite attributes (*guṇānantya*). The term "by itself" (*svataḥ*) excludes objects such as pots and the like, for pots and so forth are indeed limited by themselves. The term "from another" (*parataḥ*) excludes knowledge as a manifested attribute (*dharma-bhūta-jñāna*), for that [knowledge] undergoes contraction dependent upon something else. Thus, the absence of limitation by space and time has been stated.

2. Also in reality—vā. 3. sve—ā, i, vā. 1. The very nature of Brahman is such—na. Only action—tha. Thus, since the effect, which is distinct from the cause, is real, the entire world, which is the effect of Brahman, is indeed other than Brahman.
This being the position reached, [the Sūtra states]:
"Its non-difference [from Brahman] is established on account of the word 'originating-material' (ārambhaṇa) and so forth.

From that—that is, from the supreme cause, Brahman—the non-difference of the world is understood through the word "originating-material" and other such passages that demonstrate it. Those sentences of which the word "originating-material" is the first are called "the word 'originating-material' and so forth."
"Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; the clay alone is real.

"In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only without a second. "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate. It emitted heat. "Having entered with this living self," "All these creatures, my dear, have Being as their root, Being as their abode, Being as their support. All this has that as its essence. That is the Truth. That is the Self. That art thou, Śvetaketu."
These are the [examples]. Other items of this same kind, even those situated in different contexts, are intended here.
For these very statements establish the non-difference of the world, consisting of the conscious and the unconscious, from the Supreme Brahman. To illustrate:
"You have been standing there! Did you not ask for that instruction, by which the unheard becomes heard, the unthought becomes thought, and the unknown becomes known?"

Regarding the passage beginning with *vācārambhaṇa*: in the preceding statement, the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one was proposed as a thesis. A supporting illustration (*dṛṣṭānta*) was then stated for that. Now, fearing that even in the stated illustration the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one would be untenable—since, according to the Vaiśeṣika doctrine, the effect is distinct from the cause—the text establishes its validity with the sentence beginning *vācārambhaṇa*. Therefore, the meaning is that this [illustration] is introduced by the Sūtra. In the phrase *vācārambhaṇam*, *vācā* and *ārambhaṇam* are two separate words.

To show that "vācārambhaṇam" is not a single compound word, [the Sūtra] says "from the word *ārambhaṇa* and others," and not "from *vāk* and others. This is for the purpose of excluding the interpretation that the compound "yeṣāṃ vākyānāṃ tāni" (those of which these are the sentences) is a genitive *tatpuruṣa*.
In the phrase "from the word *śabda* and others," the word "others" (*ādi*) includes such sentences as "Being alone, my dear... (*sadeva somyedam...*) and so forth.

Thus, having kept in mind that the entire world has Brahman as its sole cause and that the effect is non-different from its cause, and once it was asserted that by the knowledge of Brahman—the cause—all things—the effects—would be known, the disciple, not knowing that the entire world has Brahman as its sole cause, asked: "How indeed, O Venerable Sir, can that be an instruction? He raised the objection regarding the impossibility of one thing being known through the knowledge of another. Then, intending to teach that the world has Brahman as its sole cause, [the Teacher] first established the non-difference of the effect from the cause, as proven by common worldly experience.

"O dear one, just as by means of a single lump of clay, everything made of clay would be known"—thus [the scripture] shows. The meaning is that, just as for jars, bowls, and so forth, which are produced from a single lump of clay, there is knowledge of them through the knowledge of that [clay], because their substance is not distinct from it; having raised the objection from the perspective of the Kaṇāda school that the effect is a different substance from the cause, [the scripture] establishes the non-difference of the effect from the cause by means of common worldly experience itself.
"Modification is a mere verbal handle, a name; 'clay' alone is the truth. Here, "ārambhaṇam" means "it is begun," "it is grasped," or "it is touched.
[This is derived] from the rule "kṛtyalyuṭo bahulam" (Pāṇini 3.3.113).

By the words "of the whole," etc., [the author] states the intention of one who asserts that through the knowledge of one thing there is the knowledge of all. By the phrase "of those things produced from a single lump of clay," he explains the term "made of clay" (*mṛnmaya*). By the phrase "therefore, by the knowledge of that," he expresses the intended meaning of the sentence. This is explained as "by the knowledge of that" because it is in accordance with other scriptural passages such as, "In what, indeed... is everything known? and "Verily, my dear, when the Self is known... all this becomes known," and also due to the force of the analogy and the subject of comparison.
For a jar, a bowl, or the like, is not known by means of the existence of a lump of clay; nor indeed is the entire world known through the existence of the Supreme Brahman.

"...is begun. It is incorrect to take the word *ārambhaṇa* as meaning "material cause" (*upādāna*); for, according to the view that the effect is illusory (*māyāmaya*), the effect—which exists merely as a perception—is not "begun by speech," since it is perceived even prior to speech; and according to the view of transformation (*pariṇāma*), the world, which is the effect of Brahman, cannot be a transformation of sound. Furthermore, the *Nighaṇṭu* states: "The root *ā-labh* means touch or injury."

Thus, the suffix *lyuṭ* is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). "By speech" (*vācā*) means by way of verbal activity as the cause; this is the meaning. For activities such as fetching water are indeed preceded by such verbal expressions as, "Fetch water with a jar."

For the sake of establishing that conventional usage (*vyavahāra*), by means of that very same clay substance, there occurs a modification (*vikāra*) characterized by a broad base, belly, and so forth—a specific configuration—as well as a name such as "pot" induced by that [configuration]. For the purpose of accomplishing specific conventional usages such as fetching water, the clay substance itself comes to possess another configuration and another name;

therefore, even a pot and the like are "only clay"—that is, the meaning is that they are known through valid means of cognition (*pramāṇa*) as being merely the substance "clay," and not as a different substance altogether.

Therefore, it is only for that very substance—such as clay or gold—that differences in cognition, distinct words, and so forth, are justified by its merely assuming different configurations (*saṃsthāna*); just as for a single Devadatta, differences in cognition, distinct words, and so forth—such as "child," "youth," and "old man"—as well as specific functional effects, are observed due to his different states.

[Regarding the objection concerning the contradiction between existence and non-existence, characterized by origination and destruction, if the effect is non-different from the cause, and the resolution thereof.]

As for what was said—that because of the conventional usage "the jar is destroyed" while the clay itself remains, the effect is something other than the cause—that is refuted precisely by the admission that origination, destruction, and so forth are merely particular states (*avasthā-viśeṣa*) of the very substance that constitutes the cause. It is logical that those various words and those various effects belong to that very same single substance in its respective states.

[The word] *kārāḥ* [is used]. Because a name (*nāmadheya*) is not something produced from clay, [the term] has been explained as having the sense of "touching" (*sparśa*) in order to establish that both the modification (*vikāra*) and the name are denotable by the word "originating" (*ārambhaṇa*). Regarding the phrase "of the ocean" (*sarirasya*), the intention is that just as the word "ocean" (*sarira*) denotes water, so too the non-difference between the letters *r* and *l* is intended. As for "by the cause" (*hetunā*): the state of being a cause is here in the sense of a purpose (*prayojana*), and not in the sense of an instrument (*sādhana*). Therefore, [it says] "such as a jar."

The intention is as follows: In cases such as "he sits" or "he lies down," even though there is a change of state, we observe the same cognition and different words; whereas in cases such as "a jar" or "a cloth," we observe different cognitions and different words because they are distinct entities. However, in the present case, since the difference is based on a change of state, recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) itself is the direct means of certain knowledge—this is what the Scripture states. [He explains the word *satya* (real/true) by stating] "it is perceived through a means of valid knowledge" (*pramāṇenopalabhyate*). He explains the particle *tu* (but/however) by saying "not... however. If the intended meaning were that modifications (*vikāra*) are unreal, then the use of the particle *tu* would be redundant.

Regarding the phrase "as in the case of one and the same [person]": words such as "child," "youth," and so forth denote the embodied self (*śarīrin*) by means of the body. Since that [self] lacks perishability, other terms such as "consciousness" (*cetana*) and "intellect" (*buddhi*) are based solely upon its various states. By the expression "of that which possesses such-and-such a state," he avoids the objection regarding the diversity of effects. A "state" (*avasthā*) is an impermanent attribute.

The fact that a substance exists in various successive states is dependent upon the operation of causal factors (*kāraka*); this constitutes its meaningfulness [as an effect]. Objections based on the theory of manifestation (*abhivyakti*) are refuted simply by not accepting that theory. Even if the production (*utpatti*) of an effect is accepted, the doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) is not contradicted, because it is precisely the existent that arises.
Thus:
"In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second."

Thus: "This was indeed Being"—meaning that this world, which now appears in manifold forms through the differentiation of names and forms (*nāma-rūpa*), existed in the beginning as one alone; and because it possessed all powers and could not tolerate any other presiding agent, it was non-dual. In this way, its absolute non-difference [from Brahman] has been established. Likewise: "It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate.'"

Thus, by intending its own manifold becoming as the world—which consists of various and diverse stable forms beginning with fire and so forth about to be created—the non-difference of the world, which is the effect designated as "world-creation," from the Supreme Brahman, the ultimate cause, is determined. For the world, which is fit to be designated as "this Being alone" (*sadevedam*), belongs to that very Supreme Brahman denoted by the word *sat*—who is omniscient, whose will is true, and who is faultless—and it is the differentiation of name and form belonging to that very world denoted by the word *sat*.

The syntactical connection (*anvaya*) is as follows: "In this way... non-difference itself has been established. The word "Being" (*sat*) expresses the fitness for connection with the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). By the restriction "Being alone," the possibility of its ever being unreal is excluded. By the phrase "only one," the absence of any division into name and form (*nāmarūpavibhāga*) is stated. By the term "without a second" (*advitīya*), there is a negation of any other presiding agent; such is the meaning. The word "this" (*idam*) found in the sentence "the divided world" is explained [by the commentary]. "Has been established" refers to these words.

The fact that [the passage] has as its sole purpose the stated meaning is understood precisely because it serves to establish the proposition that "by the knowledge of one, all is known. For the exclusion of things of the same class or different classes does not serve the purpose of establishing the proposition. By the words beginning with "in such a manner" (tathā), it is shown that these words have as their sole purpose the stated meaning. Regarding the phrase "fire and so forth": since the creation of fire and the rest is taught immediately after the act of volition (*saṅkalpa*), the word "many" (*bahu*) in the expression "May I be many" refers to multiplicity in the form of fire and the other elements. Thus it is determined.
The intention is that since Brahman, which is the cause itself, is described as becoming manifold through the form of the world, the non-difference of the effect and the cause is established.

By the words beginning with "sacchanda," a specific doubt that must be set aside by the statement regarding the creative resolve (*saṅkalpa*) of the individual creation (*vyaṣṭisṛṣṭi*) is addressed. The intention of the doubt is this: if the word *sat* refers to Brahman, its grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) with the world denoted by the word "this" (*idam*) would be untenable. [The phrase] "of that which is denoted by the word *sat*" is stated with the intention that if the word *sat* were to refer to the world, there would be a contradiction with passages such as "That thought" (*tadaikṣata*). [The phrase] "name and form" is stated with the intention that the unity of the conscious aspect would be untenable.

How can its oneness through being (*bhāva*), its independence from any other presiding agent, and furthermore, its observation consisting of the volition for manifold existence as this world of diverse and stable forms, as well as its creation according to that volition, be logically established? Anticipating this doubt, [the text] says: "That very deity reflected: 'Come now, let me enter these three deities with this living self (*jīva-ātman*) and differentiate name and form';
and of them, [it made each] tripartite."

And so forth. Having pointed out the entire insentient reality with the words, "The three deities," it is stated: "By entering into the individual souls (jīvas) that constitute My own Self, let Me make this [universe] possess various names and forms. The meaning is: "By means of this living soul as My own Self—having entered as the Self—let Me make this [universe] possess various names and forms. Thus, it is declared that the possession of names and forms is brought about by the entry of both one's own Self and the individual soul as the Self.

"Having created that, He entered into it; having entered it, He became the manifest (sat) and the unmanifest (tyat)"— by this other scriptural passage, it is made clear that "the world, together with living beings, has entered into the Supreme Brahman as its very Self."

This very point—that both the conscious and unconscious reality in its causal state and its effected state, in its entirety, whether gross or subtle, constitutes the body of the Supreme Brahman, while the Supreme Brahman constitutes their Self—is established in such texts as the Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa; it has thus been recalled. By this, the previously raised doubt is dispelled.

Since the acid substance (acid-vastu) is Brahman, who exists as the Self within the living being, and because of the scriptural statement regarding the differentiation of name and form (*nāma-rūpa-vyākaraṇa*), it is Brahman alone—having the sentient and insentient substances as its body—that is denoted by the word "world. Thus, the entire passage beginning with "In the beginning, this was indeed Being, one only" is more appropriately explained. Furthermore, all modifications residing in the sentient and insentient substances that constitute the body [of Brahman] are likewise accounted for.

"By way of being the Self" (ātmatayā) means by way of being the controller; this excludes [the Self from being] like space and so forth. "And of the individual soul" (svātmano jīvasya) refers to the meaning of the phrase "by the living self" (jīvenātmanā), in the sense of "having become a lion, they were seized by me. There might be the apprehension that if one says "by the living self consisting of Me," it would be like saying "a pot consists of clay. [The response is: This is made clear by another scriptural passage stating "entered by way of being the Self.

The previously mentioned apprehension—the suspicion that defects inherent in the world might attach to Brahman due to its grammatical coordination (sāmānādhikaraṇya) with the word "this" (idam)—is more appropriately resolved; the intention is that [the relationship] is indeed primary (mukhya).
And because [Brahman] is not a non-human purpose, Brahman’s faultlessness and its status as a mine of auspicious qualities are firmly established.
This very point he will state immediately thereafter: "But [Brahman is] superior, because of the designation of difference. Likewise—
The statement, "All this has that as its self," teaches the identity of the entire universe, both sentient and insentient, with Brahman; and that very same [identity] is expressed in "That thou art."
Thus he concludes.

In this regard, the truth is as follows: Brahman alone, having the sentient and non-sentient entities as its body, is the object denoted by all words at all times, being the substrate of those entities. At one time, it has for its body the sentient and non-sentient entities in a subtle state, from which they cannot yet be designated as separate even in their capacity as its body; that is Brahman in its causal state. At another time, it has for its body the sentient and non-sentient entities in a gross state, fit for the practical usage of distinct names and forms; that is Brahman in its effected state. Thus, the world in its form as an effect is non-different from the supreme Brahman, its cause.

Furthermore, the distinction between qualities and defects based on the established nature of Brahman—the embodied one—and the material and immaterial entities that constitute His body, in both the causal and effected states, has been stated in the passage: "But this is not because of the existence of [worldly] examples. This is established by hundreds of scriptural texts.

However, as for those who describe the non-difference between cause and effect by resorting to the falsity of the effect—for them, the non-difference of cause and effect is not established as real, because the identity of two things that are respectively real and unreal is impossible. If that were the case, it would follow that Brahman is false or that the world is real.

Furthermore, as for those who—while indeed accepting that the effect is ultimately real—maintain that the difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman is merely adventitious (*aupādhika*), whereas their non-difference is natural (*svābhāvika*); yet [who] assert that for the insentient (*acid*) and Brahman both [difference and non-difference] are natural;

for them, since there is no other entity distinct from Brahman and its limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), and because the very nature of Brahman—which is partless and indivisible—undergoes transformation into a form to be discarded due to its connection with the limiting adjunct, [this would result in an unacceptable consequence].

Regarding this point: "Thus [it is said]" means that because a specific effect arises from a specific cause, the relationship between the body and the embodied being (śarīra-śarīribhāva) and so forth is logically established. [The opponent objects: "Since scripture declares the origination and dissolution of both the conscious and the unconscious from Brahman, and since the effect is not different from its cause, and since multiplicity is absent in the causal state, the relationship of body and embodied being would be untenable; consequently, there could be no fixed distinction of essential natures."
Regarding the phrase "ye ca": the qualifiers such as "without parts" (*niravayavatva*) are intended to indicate that no connection with defects can exist in Brahman.

If one were to accept the transformation of power (*śakti-pariṇāma*), then the scriptural texts—which speak of the non-difference between power and Brahman, which establish the distinction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman through their respective states of being subject to karma and being free from sin (*apahatapāpmatva*), and which speak of the transformation of the insentient (*acid-brahmaṇoḥ*) and the non-transformation of Brahman—would all fall into contradiction.
"In the beginning, this was indeed Brahman alone;
being alone, it did not flourish.
Those which are these royal powers among the gods..."
He created from that very form of excellence the *kṣatra*:
Indra, Varuṇa, Soma, Rudra, Parjanya, Yama, Mṛtyu, and Īśāna. "In the beginning, indeed, this was the Self alone; there was nothing else whatsoever blinking.
He thought: 'Let me now create the worlds.'"

"Indeed, Nārāyaṇa alone existed; there was no Brahmā, no Īśāna, no heaven and earth, no stars, no waters, no fire, no Soma, and no sun. Being alone, he did not find delight. While he was absorbed in meditation," and so forth—by such passages, it is understood that "Nārāyaṇa alone is the supreme cause and the Lord of all lords.
For the words *sat*, *brahman*, and *ātman*—occurring in the same context and qualified by the word *Nārāyaṇa* occurring in that same context—lead to the understanding of him alone.

"He is the supreme Great Lord of lords" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.7), and "He is the cause, the lord of the lords of the senses; there is no progenitor of him, nor is there any lord over him" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.9). Thus, the causality of the Lord alone is heard in scripture. Smṛti also [confirms this], as in the Manava-smṛti, which begins with "Then the Blessed Self-existent One," and continues: "Desiring to emit various creatures, he meditated upon his own body."
"He emitted the waters alone, and into them he released his virility.
"Desiring to create, he emitted thousands of persons in two ways. "The world arose from Viṣṇu and remains situated in him alone," and so forth.
Nor can it be said that the Lord is mere Being (sanmātra) alone; for it is admitted that [the individual soul] is a part (aṃśa) of Him, and because it is His subordinate (śeṣa).
Nor can it be said that His possession of infinite auspicious qualities, such as knowledge and bliss, is occasional; for these are inherent and therefore eternal, as stated in the scriptures:
"His supreme power is indeed heard to be manifold, and His knowledge, strength, and action are inherent," and "He who is all-knowing and all-perceiving."
From such passages as these,
hundreds of statements concerning the Lord— such as "Him, the supreme Maheśvara among the lords," and "Neither his equal nor his superior is seen"— would be contradicted.

Furthermore, if the Pure Being (*sanmātra*) were the self of all and possessed parts, then since the Lord (*īśvara*) would be a specific part thereof, the scriptural teachings regarding His being the self of all and possessing parts would be contradicted. For a jar, a bowl, or the like do not possess the nature of the gem-stone itself, nor are they its parts.

If it is argued that "because Pure Being (*sanmātra*) is complete within all its own parts, and because it is also complete within the part that is the Lord (*īśvara*), other things are identical with Him and are His parts," we say: no. For since Pure Being is equally complete even in a jar, it would follow that the Lord is identical with the jar and is a part of it. Furthermore, it is not tenable for Pure Being—which is understood as a property of objects in such cognitions as "the jar exists"—to possess either substantiality (*dravyatva*) or causality. Indeed, existence (*sattva*) is simply the fitness for practical transaction (*vyavahārayogyatā*).

Contradiction consists in the fitness for a particular linguistic usage and the non-existence of that which is unfit for such usage. If one accepts that "only substance is existent," it follows that action and the rest would be non-existent. Even by resorting to the mere straw of a reed (i.e., a desperate argument), it is difficult to establish a single uniform existence across all things, including action and so forth. Furthermore, if everything were non-different from the nature of "Being" (*sat*), then because of the connection with the nature of all things through omniscience, the consequence of a confusion between all virtues and defects has already been stated previously.
Therefore, non-difference is exactly in the manner already described. || 15 ||

Now, it might be argued: "Even when there is only a single entity undergoing a change of state, different cognitions and different words are observed, as in the cases of childhood, youth, and so forth; they are also observed in the case of clay, wood, gold, and the like, even though these are distinct substances. In that regard, how is it determined that in cases such as 'clay' and 'pot,' where cause and effect are involved, the different cognitions and different words are based solely on the difference in state? To this, the answer is as follows:

"And not of pure being alone" (*na ca sanmātrasya*): having raised the dilemma as to whether the persisting "pure being" (*sanmātra*) is a property of an object (*vastudharma*) or a substance (*dravya*), the refutation is given for the position that it is a property. For the position that it is a substance, the refutation is that it would lead to the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that [the substance] itself [would be the cause]. "Grasping at *kāśa* instead of *kuśa*" means grasping *kāśa* in place of *kuśa* while treating it as *kuśa*; the meaning is that it is secondary (*amukhya*). If it is argued that the existence (*sattva*) of action and so forth consists in their relation to a substance, the meaning is that there would be no single unifying cause (*prayojaka*). || 15 ||
154. And because [the self] is perceived when there is an object of experience. (2.1.16)

Furthermore, because the gold—which serves as the cause—is perceived when the effect, such as an earring, exists, the meaning is that there is recognition [of it] as gold, in the form: "This earring is gold. However, clay and other such materials are not perceived in this way within other substances like gold. Therefore, just as in the case of a child or a youth, the very substance that constitutes the cause, having entered into another state, is designated as the "effect."

Furthermore, even for one who maintains that there is a distinct substance, since the occurrence of different states, cognitions, and different designations is already established, it is illogical to postulate an unperceived distinct substance.

Furthermore, this recognition is not based on a genus (*jāti*), because no substance other than the substratum of the genus is perceived. One and the same substance belonging to the gold-genus is seen in both its causal and effected states. Nor can it be argued that, despite a difference in substances, there is a continuity of recognition in the effect due to the persistence of the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*); for if they were distinct substances, it would be impossible for there to be a continuity of recognition in one substance based merely on the persistence of its substratum.

Regarding the phrase "because of recognition": what is intended here is the recognition expressed through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), such as "This earring is gold. This is because for even an advocate of the theory that the effect is non-existent (*asatkāryavādin*) who asserts the persistence of the inherent cause (*samavāyikāraṇa*), a recognition based on grammatical non-coreferentiality (*vaiyadhikaraṇya*) would fail to establish their own position.

By the term "accepted" (*abhyupeta*), it is meant "accepted as being a non-inherent cause (*asamavāyikāraṇa*). For only that which is not established otherwise (*ananyathāsiddha*) serves as a warrant (*kalpaka*). The meaning is that since cognition, distinct words, and so forth are established otherwise, they do not possess the status of a warrant.

"Jāti" (the universal) means "this is that very cow," as in the case of identity. Regarding "jātyāśraya" (the substratum of the universal): for in that case, there is the perception of two distinct individuals; here, however, no other individual is perceived in that manner. Regarding "dravyāntaratve" (if it were a different substance): for when water is contained within a jar, there is no recognition through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) such as "the jar is the water."

If it is argued that in the case of a scorpion arising from cow dung and other such materials, no recognition (*pratisandhāna*) of the cow dung or similar substance is observed—[we reply: No; for even there, there is recognition of the earth-substance (*pṛthivī-dravya*) which constitutes the primary cause. If it is argued that in the case of smoke, which is the effect of fire, no recognition of the fire is observed—[we reply: Let there be no recognition there; nevertheless, there is no fault, because fire is merely the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*). For smoke is produced from moist fuel conjoined with fire.

And because of the identity of odor, smoke is indeed the effect of moist fuel. Therefore, since the perception "this is that very same thing" occurs when the effect exists, it is understood that "differences in cognition, terms, and so forth are based solely on differences in state. Consequently, the effect is non-different from the cause. || 16 ||
And for this reason as well:
"Because of the existence of another. (2.1.17)

Furthermore, because the effect exists within the cause, the effect is non-different from the cause. Indeed, in both common worldly usage and in the Veda, the effect itself is designated as the cause. As in the world, one says: "All this—pots, bowls, and so forth—was previously nothing but clay"; and in the Veda: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone."

156. "If it be argued that [the soul] does not exist because of the designation of its non-existence, we say no; for [its existence] is established by means of another attribute, on account of the supplementary statement and so forth, and from another word. (2.1.18)

As for what was stated—that the existence of the effect in the cause is understood from both worldly experience and the Veda—that is incorrect; because there is a designation of non-existence: "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.19.1) and "In the beginning, this was non-existent" (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.7).

If it is argued that this is not tenable—just as in the world one says, "In the beginning, this was indeed nothing at all," or "All this, such as pots and bowls, did not exist in the forenoon"—we reply: no, for such a designation is made by means of another attribute. That designation of "non-existence" refers to that very same effect-substance at a prior time by means of another attribute—that is, by means of another configuration (saṃsthāna); it does not refer to the kind of non-existence (tucchatva) you intend.

It has been stated that "existence and non-existence are indeed the two properties of a substance. In this context, non-existence is a property distinct from the property of existence. For the world designated by the word "this," existence is its property consisting of name-and-form (*nāmarūpa*), while its non-existence is the subtle state which is the opposite of that. Therefore, for the world endowed with name-and-form, non-existence is the attainment of that opposing subtle condition.
Having rejected the notion of unreality by saying, "But how indeed, gentle one, could it be so?",
[the text continues]: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone."
Thus it has been established;
for it has been very clearly stated: "In the beginning this was indeed unmanifest; it was manifested through name and form. || 18 ||
158. And as in the case of vital breath and so forth. 2.1.20.

And just as the single air, assuming specific functions within the body, takes on different names, forms, and distinct effects such as *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and so forth; in the same way, the one Brahman alone becomes the world in its various stable and moving forms. Thus, it is established that the world is non-different from the Supreme Brahman, the ultimate cause. || 20 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the originative material cause (Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa). 6.
The Section on Designation as Something Else (Itaravyapadeśādhikaraṇa) || 1.2.7 ||

Sūtra 21–23: 159. There is the consequence of defects such as the agency [of Brahman] because of the designation of the other. By those who establish the non-difference of the world from Brahman through such [scriptural passages] as "That thou art" and "This Self is Brahman," [the objection is raised that] defects such as the agency [of Brahman] would follow.
By such passages as these, it has been stated that the individual soul (jīva) is also designated as non-different from Brahman.

To this, the following objection is raised: If the identity of the individual soul (*jīva*) with Brahman is designated by these statements, then defects such as "the non-creation of a world that is beneficial to itself and the creation of a world that is harmful" would follow for Brahman, who is endowed with omniscience, the power of true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*), and so forth. Furthermore, this world is a source of infinite suffering—pertaining to the self, the divine, and the physical—and no intelligent being, when independent, would engage in such a self-disadvantageous undertaking.

"Others," and so forth. Does the status of Brahman as the cause of the world logically hold, or not? If Brahman is the creator of the world, does the defect of performing what is harmful and so on follow, or not? Is the identity understood through grammatical coreferentiality (sāmānādhikaraṇya) in passages such as "That thou art"—characterized by oneness—or is it characterized by the relationship of self and body? Is the consistency of the scriptural texts regarding difference maintained only when identity is understood as the relationship of self and body, or also when it is characterized by oneness?

If the consistency of the scriptural texts concerning difference is maintained even when identity—characterized by the oneness of essential nature—is accepted, then it follows that because the sentences such as "That thou art" would be intent solely upon the oneness of essential nature, the impossibility of Brahman being the cause [of the world] arises due to the resulting defects such as its failure to act for its own benefit. Conversely, if consistency is maintained only through the relationship of self and body, then it is established that because the aforementioned sentences are intent upon the relationship of body and self, there is no occurrence of the defects such as the failure to act for one's own benefit, and thus the possibility of Brahman being the cause [of the world] is secured.

Regarding the term "sārvajñya" (omniscience): the sense is that because [the Lord] is omniscient and possesses true volition (*satyasaṅkalpa*), it is not logically possible for him to be the cause of a world that is harmful [to himself].

As for the scriptural passages declaring a difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and Brahman, they have been abandoned by you yourself—who maintain the non-difference (*ananyatva*) of the world and Brahman—since if there were actual difference, non-difference could not be established.

If it is argued that the scriptural texts concerning difference have as their object difference conditioned by limiting adjuncts (upādhi), while the scriptural texts concerning non-difference have as their object natural non-difference;

In this regard, the following must be addressed: Does Brahman, the cause of the universe, which by its very nature is non-different from the individual soul (*jīva*), know that soul as it is in itself, unconditioned? Or does it not? If it does not know [it], then its omniscience is lost. If it does know [it], then for Brahman—who knows the suffering of the individual soul, which is non-different from itself, as its own suffering—there follows the unavoidable fault of failing to act for its benefit and acting to its detriment. If it is argued that the difference between the individual soul and Brahman is caused by ignorance (*ajñāna*), and that the scriptural texts concerning their non-difference refer to that [ignorance], [the response follows].

In that regard, even under the view that the individual soul (*jīva*) is ignorant, the aforementioned dilemma and its consequences remain as they were. Under the view that Brahman is ignorant, it is impossible for Brahman—which is by nature self-luminous—to be the witness of ignorance or to perform the creation of the world brought about by that ignorance.

If you say, "The light is concealed by ignorance," then since concealment consists in the cessation of light, and since light is the very essence (*svarūpa*) of Brahman, it would follow that the essence itself has ceased to exist. We have already pointed out thousands of defects, such as the destruction of the essence. Therefore, this notion of Brahman being the cause of the world is untenable. (21)

Why? Because of the designation of difference. For the Supreme Brahman is designated as distinct from the inner self (pratyagātman): "He who dwells in the self, yet is within the self; whom the self does not know; whose body is the self; who controls the self from within—he is your self, the inner controller, the immortal"; "Having known the self and the impeller as separate, one becomes beloved by Him and thereby attains immortality"; "The cause of the cause, the lord of the lords of the senses"; "One of the two eats the sweet fruit, while the other looks on without eating"; "Two unborn ones, the conscious and the unconscious, the Lord and the non-Lord."

"Completely embraced by the conscious Self," "mounted upon the conscious Self," "The Illusionist creates this entire universe, and another, bound by illusion, is confined within it," and "The Lord of Pradhāna and Kṣetrajña, the Master of the Guṇas."

"Among the eternal, He is the eternal; among the conscious, He is the one conscious who ordains the desires of the many"; "He who moves within the unmanifest, whose body is the unmanifest, whom the unmanifest does not know"; "He who moves within the imperishable, whose body is the imperishable, whom the imperishable does not know"; "This is the inner Self of all beings, free from evil, divine, the one God, Nārāyaṇa"—by such passages as these. || 22 ||
161. And like a stone and so forth, that [creation] is impossible. (2.1.23)

Regarding stones, wood, clods of earth, grass, and so forth—which are utterly fit for rejection, constant seats of transformation, non-conscious entities, and devoid of all that is blameless, changeless, opposed to everything rejectable, and solely auspicious—it is stated that there is an *arthāpatti* (presumption) based on scripture: "like stone and so forth. Although grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) is equally applicable to words denoting both the conscious and the unconscious, since it is impossible for Brahman and the insentient to have identity of essence, their distinction must be accepted:
"Just as the state of being Brahman is not possible for stones and the like..."
In the same way, it is not possible for a living being who is completely filled by the flood [of karma] to exist here.

Just as it is untenable for there to be identity with the nature of Brahman— which is a unique essence consisting of infinite knowledge and bliss, and which is one with the manifold and infinite great manifestations (*mahāvibhūti*)— so too, for a sentient being who is fit for infinite suffering, who is like a firefly, and who is the opposite of all that is to be discarded as understood from such scriptural passages as "free from sin" (*apahatapāpmā*), it is impossible for him to possess the state of Brahman, which is a mine of countless auspicious qualities and is the antithesis of every form of evil.
This refers to the grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) [of the terms].

This is because of such scriptural passages as "He whose self is the body," since the individual soul (jīva) is the body of Brahman and Brahman exists as its self by being the soul's essence; furthermore, this [interpretation] is not in contradiction with the teaching that Brahman is the substrate (prakāra) of which the individual soul is the mode, but rather it is the very proof of this meaning— as has been demonstrated more than once in passages such as "On account of abiding, so says Kāśakṛtsna."

Therefore, since Brahman in every state has the sentient and insentient entities as its body, the grammatical coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the world and Brahman is established—namely, that "Brahman, whose body consists of subtle sentient and insentient entities, is the cause; that same Brahman, whose body consists of gross sentient and insentient entities, is the effect called the world. Furthermore, this establishes that the world is the effect of Brahman and is non-different from it, and that there is no confusion of the respective natures of the insentient entity, the individual soul (*jīva*), and Brahman—specifically regarding their being subject to transformation, their suffering, and their being a mine of auspicious qualities.

Furthermore, there is no contradiction with any scriptural passage. Regarding the statement, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only," even in the state of non-distinction, it must necessarily be admitted that the individual soul (jīva), conjoined with the insentient (acid), exists in a subtle form as the body of Brahman.

The intention is that this applies to the conscious [Self] as well, just as it does for Brahman, the proponent of knowledge. Regarding the phrase "because of its abiding" (*avasthiteḥ*): the intention is that this sūtra is a supplement to this particular section (*adhikaraṇa*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādibhiḥ*), the author intends to include such passages as "but not because of the existence of examples" (*na tu dṛṣṭāntabhāvāt*) and "for both [recensions] read [the text] differently" (*ubhaye 'pi hi bheda-enam adhīyate*). The sūtra beginning with "both" (*ubhaye 'pi*) also concerns the specific statement that serves as the constituent element for the purpose of making known the difference. In this way, the coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) of the conscious [Self] has been established.

Therefore, with the words "all" (*sarva*) and so forth, he explains the resolution of the grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) between the world and [Brahman], which consists of both consciousness (*cit*) and unconsciousness (*acit*).

Regarding the passage beginning with "the Lord" (*deva*) and so forth: because unity is established in the causal state, the distinction between qualities and defects is not tenable due to the absence of having the conscious and unconscious as His body.
As it is said: "Partiality and cruelty [are not attributed to God] because He is dependent [on other factors]."

Because it is stated in two sūtras—"If it be argued that there is no dissolution because of the non-dissolution of karma, we say no, because of beginninglessness; and this is both logical and observed"—the persistence [of the world] even then exists in a subtle form. Furthermore, "non-dissolution" is logical because of the absence of the differentiation of name and form (*nāma-rūpa*). Therefore, Brahman’s status as the cause is indeed possible.

Furthermore, those who—referring to the state of this very *jīva* when separated from ignorance (*avidyā*)—describe "this distinction," for them all of this would be inconsistent! For in that state, there is no "omniscience," "lordship over all," "being the cause of everything," "being the self of all," "being the controller of all," and so forth. Indeed, it is in this very form that the distinction of the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is established by these scriptural texts; for all of that, according to your own view, is merely imagined through ignorance.

Furthermore, the mutual distinction among things imagined through ignorance during the state of ignorance— such as the distinction between mother-of-pearl and silver— is not what is being established here by the author of the Sūtras in passages such as "But [the difference] is greater because of the mention of difference" (BS 2.1.22).

Rather, in the statement "The inquiry into Brahman ought to be undertaken," the author establishes that Brahman— the cause of the origin and so forth of the world, which was introduced as the object of inquiry— is to be known through the Vedāntas, and he proceeds to resolve any contradictions with Smṛti and reasoning regarding that Brahman.

"In dissolution, there would be the same contingency [as before], hence it is inconsistent," and "nor is it taught. The sense is that one characterized by forms imagined through ignorance cannot be the object of inquiry for one seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*); rather, it is precisely the superiority [of Brahman] over the individual soul (*jīva*) that is established here as the object of inquiry for the seeker of liberation. Regarding the phrase "of what has been introduced": since the knowledge of the non-imagined nature of the soul is what has been introduced, the meaning is that an imagined difference is not being taught. "Vedānta" refers to the subject matter of the first chapter (*samanvaya-adhyāya*), and "Smṛti" refers to the subject matter of the second chapter.

Regarding the phrase "apītāv iti": the two sūtras beginning with "apītau" are not properly connected there [in the previous context]. In this section concerning "apītau," the *pūrvapakṣa* (prima facie) sūtra is connected with its own preceding context, and the *parihāra* (refutation) sūtra is connected with its own *siddhānta* (conclusion) sūtra. As for the two sūtras beginning with "apītau," however—[according to some versions]—"sarvajñatvam tathā" and "na tu dṛṣṭāntabhāvāt. (Note: The parenthetical remarks regarding variant readings—vā., tha, na, ye, da—are included here as they appear in the source text.)

Thus, these two sūtras restate what was established in the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*). For therein, the meaning of the section is precisely that "the relation of cause and effect is possible between two dissimilar things.
And the [sūtra] "If it be said that [the effect] is non-existent, no, because [the denial] is a mere negation" restates what was situated in the previous section. || 23 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the designation of the other. || 7 ||
The Section on the Observation of Withdrawal (Upasaṃhāradarśanādhikaraṇa) || 2.18 ||

162. "If it be argued that [the world] is not [produced from Brahman] because we observe the withdrawal [of effects into their causes], we say no; for [Brahman's transformation] is like milk. (2.1.24)

It has been established that for the Supreme Brahman—who is omniscient and whose will is true—it is not contradictory for Him to possess "the state of being the Self of all" and to be distinct from everything else, insofar as all things, whether sentient or insentient, in their gross and subtle states, constitute His body in every possible way. Now, it is established that for the Supreme Brahman, whose will is true, the capacity to create the manifold world by mere volition is not contradictory.

Now, one might object: since it is observed that those with limited powers depend upon the gathering of a collection of causal factors (*kāraka-kalāpa*), how can it be suspected that there is a contradiction regarding the causality of the all-powerful Brahman if He does not gather such a collection of causal factors?

It is said in reply: because it is observed in the world that even one who possesses the power to produce various specific effects still depends upon the respective instruments (*upakaraṇa*) for them.

Regarding the phrase "of another": the distinction [of the individual soul] from [the Supreme Self] by means of [attributes such as] having true volition (*satyasaṅkalpatva*) has been established. In that context, since it is untenable for mere true volition to be a subordinate attribute, the connection [of this section] arises from the emergence of a doubt as to whether that true volition might have a restricted scope. "Being the self of all" (*sarvātmatvam*) means being the nature of everything. The inquiry is: Is it possible for Brahman to be the cause of the world, or not? And: Does the capacity of an efficient cause to produce an effect necessarily depend upon other auxiliary factors, or not? This is the investigation.

When there is a restriction of dependence, then it is established that for that which is devoid of auxiliary factors (*sahakārin*), causality is impossible; whereas when there is no restriction of dependence, then causality is possible. Thus it is said: the objection that it is improper for Brahman to have mere volition as its sole equipment is a summary of the refutation of the charge that [the world] would not arise.

This is the meaning of the Sūtra: "On account of the observation of the bringing together [of auxiliaries]. Since in the world it is observed that when things are engaged in producing an effect, there is a requirement for the assembly of causal conditions (*sāmagrī*), if it is argued that the creative agency of Brahman alone is not tenable—this doubt being that it is not correct [to say Brahman acts alone]—we reply: this is not right, because just as milk transforms itself into the state of curd through its own nature, so too is that possible for Brahman alone.
"Even when there is capacity, agency does not exist merely through the observation of a causal complex;
this would not apply to the non-dual Brahman, just as curd [arises] from milk.
[This is so] because the Omniscient One is truthful—by the very observation [of reality]. (Da.)

The doubt arises in some of dull intellect that even for the Supreme Brahman, who is endowed with all powers, the status of being a creator is not possible if He is devoid of various instruments; this is now refuted:
"And as in the world, like gods and others" (2.1.25).

Just as the gods and others create in their respective worlds whatever they require by mere volition (saṅkalpa), so too does this Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) create the entire universe by mere volition. It should be understood that the mention of the gods and others—who possess powers known from the Vedas—is introduced as an illustration to facilitate the easy comprehension of the power of Brahman, which is likewise known from the Vedas. || 25 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the observation of the reabsorption [of the world]. || 8 ||
The Section Concerning the Consequence of Totality (Kṛtsnaprasaktyadhikaraṇa) || 2-1-9 ||

164. Either there would be the consequence of [the whole being] entirely involved [in transformation], or else there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts regarding its partlessness. (2.1.26)

In such passages as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," "This, indeed, existed without this [world]," and "In the beginning, the Self alone was all this," it is stated that "in the causal state, Brahman alone, without parts, existed."— [in] the causal state.

Regarding the term "entirety" (*kṛtsna*): it is observed that milk, water, and so forth, which are presented as examples, possess parts; likewise, Brahman would also possess parts. The connection [of this section] arises from the doubt: "If Brahman were partless, there would be the consequence of its being entirely transformed.

Is it possible for Brahman to be the cause of the world? Or not? If it were an effect, would the scriptural teaching of its partlessness be contradicted? Or not? For that purpose, [it must be considered] whether Brahman, in the form of the world...
Thus [it is asked]: for that purpose, is the possession of all powers (sarvaśakti) logical or not?

When it is not logical, then because of the consequence of contradicting the scriptural texts on partlessness (niravayavatva), causality would be impossible. When it is logical, then because there is no contradiction with the scriptural texts on partlessness, causality is possible.

"Beginning with *sadeva*": the immediately following passage, "one only, without a second," is included here by implication. In that context, the meaning of the word "one" (*eka*) is that it is unrestricted and incapable of being divided even in terms of its constituent parts. Regarding the statement "in the beginning this was not anything at all," the meaning is that because the absence of any parts of the world—such as earth and so forth—is declared, its partlessness (*niravayavatva*) is established. Furthermore, in the passage "the Self, verily, this [was]," the word "one" likewise denotes something incapable of division even in terms of its constituent parts.

Regarding the phrase "in such passages as," the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) includes [passages] such as "partless and actionless. "One alone" is the term to be explained; "without parts" (*niravayava*) is the explanation. The sense is that since partlessness is established by the causal statements (*kāraṇavākya*), the absence of a distinction between the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*) is proven in the state of causality. [Objection: "Through the resolve 'May I become many,' Brahman becomes the entire universe; or else, due to contradiction with the statements indicating its partlessness, it cannot be the cause."

It has been stated that Brahman was without parts (*niravayava*) because the distinction between consciousness (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acid*) had been cast aside. Furthermore, it has been stated that that very same undivided, single, and partless Brahman, having formed the resolve "May I become many," became differentiated into the divisions of ether, air, and so forth, as well as the divisions of individual knowers (*kṣetrajña*) beginning with Brahmā and ending with a blade of grass.

This being the case, one must admit that that very Supreme Brahman is the whole, employed as the effect. Now, if it is said that the conscious portion is divided by the distinction of individual souls (*kṣetrajña*), and the unconscious portion is divided by the distinction of ether and so forth, then scriptural passages such as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second," "Brahman alone," and "The Self alone," which speak of the cause-Brahman as being partless, would be contradicted and rendered invalid.

Even if it is accepted that Brahman, whose body consists of the subtle sentient and insentient entities, is the cause; and Brahman, whose body consists of the gross sentient and insentient entities, is the effect—nevertheless, because the body itself must also be admitted as an effect, the aforementioned defect remains unavoidable. Furthermore, the manifold manifestation of that which is partless is untenable, and the persistence of a portion not utilized for the production of the effect is also untenable. Therefore, this appears to be inconsistent. Consequently, the doctrine of Brahman as the cause is not tenable.
Having thus raised an objection, [the author] provides the resolution:
"But on account of scripture, because it has its root in the Word. (2.1.27)

"One, partless, indivisible"—this is the sequence [of the opponent's view]. "This being the case" (*evaṃ sati*) refers to the refutation of the position that the essential nature is one, even though it is not accepted by the proponent of the final doctrine (*siddhāntin*), yet it is presented as a prima facie perception. "'They would be provoked'" means "they would be sublated," since the primary sense [of "provoked"] is untenable here. The meaning is that the word "provocation" (*kopa*), which is the result of sublation (*bādha*), is used figuratively to denote the sublation itself.
"Even if... means that since [the whole] is entirely contained within a single body, it could not exist elsewhere.

"Because it has its root in the Word" (*śabdamūlatvāt*): in such cases as "one should sprinkle with fire," the meaning of the Sūtra is that the subject (*dharmin*) is unfit to be the instrument of sprinkling; however, the transformation of Brahman (though partless) into the form of the world is established solely on the authority of Scripture (*śruti*), because it has its root in the Word—since the causality of the Supreme Brahman is cognizable through Scripture alone—and therefore, an objection against its being the cause based on reasoning is not valid.
[Because it is to be known through the Word alone, the nature of Brahman must be as stated in the Śruti.]
Therefore, it is entirely consistent that the status of being the cause is rooted in all the Śruti texts.
The word "but" (tu) sets aside the aforementioned objection. There is no such inconsistency.

Why? Because of scripture (śruti). Scripture indeed declares that Brahman is partless, and yet it also speaks of a manifold creation. The meaning is that one must accept the meaning of scripture exactly as it is stated.

But surely, even Scripture is not capable of establishing a meaning that is unfit for mutual connection, such as "one should sprinkle with fire. To this he says: "Because it has the Word as its source. Since Brahman is of a nature entirely distinct from all other things by virtue of having the Word alone as its means of valid cognition, its possession of diverse powers is not contradictory; therefore, Brahman cannot be subjected to proof or refutation based on general observation (*sāmānyato dṛṣṭa*). || 27 ||
166. And likewise in the case of the self; for [the world] is indeed manifold. (2.1.28)

Furthermore—when a property belonging to one thing is thus superimposed upon another thing, properties observed in insentient objects such as a jar would necessarily follow even for the sentient and eternal Self, which is of a different nature from them. And that such a consequence does not occur is due to the diversity of the intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) of entities; thus he says: "For they are diverse. Just as heat and other powers are seen to be of a different nature in fire, water, and so forth, which are mutually dissimilar.

In the same way, with regard to the Supreme Brahman, which is of a different nature from what is perceived in the world, there is nothing illogical in the fact that thousands of powers exist within it, though they have not been seen here and there [in the world]. This is established by direct perception [of the scriptures]. Therefore, the statement does not establish its "fitness" (arhatva) [for such powers] through worldly analogy. However, since the subject (dharmin), which is beyond the scope of other means of knowledge, is understood through scripture to be of a distinct nature, the connection of a distinct subject with distinct attributes is not contradictory; this is the meaning. Thus, it is a case of "inference based on general observation" (sāmānyato dṛṣṭam).

In the world, just as one might say, "Fire is not hot because it lacks substantiality," whatever proof or refutation is made based merely on observing the coexistence of something with anything else in some respect due to that general similarity;
as was stated by the venerable Parāśara:
"Of the one who is devoid of qualities, immeasurable, pure, and stainless-souled..."
Having raised an objection based on general observation—asking, "How is Brahman's status as the creator of the world and so forth accepted? [the author replies]:
"The powers of all entities are within the scope of inconceivable knowledge."
For those powers of being, such as creation and the rest, belong to that Brahman.
"O best of those who radiate heat! [This is] just as heat belongs to fire. And the Śruti says:
"What was that forest, and what was that tree, from which they fashioned heaven and earth? O wise ones, inquire with your mind about that upon which he stood while supporting the worlds."
"The forest of Brahman was that tree which existed, from which they fashioned heaven and earth. O wise ones, I declare to you with my mind: Brahman stood supreme, upholding all the worlds.
This objection based on general observation does not apply to the Supreme Brahman, who is distinct from all things; such is the meaning. || 28 ||

Lest the defects observed in the world should apply there as well, Brahman alone—distinct from everything else—must be accepted as the cause. Furthermore, the *pradhāna* is partless (*niravayava*). How, then, can the production of the diverse world beginning with the *mahat* be logically accounted for by that which is partless?

If it is argued that its parts exist in the form of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, then this must be investigated: Is the *pradhāna* a mere collection of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, or is the *pradhāna* something produced (*ārabdha*) by *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*?

In the immediately preceding kalpa, [the claim that] "pradhāna is the primary cause" contradicts their own tenets; it also contradicts the number they themselves have accepted. Furthermore, there is a contradiction regarding the commencement of effects by those [atoms], which are partless.
Moreover, in the case of the theory of a collection, since they are partless, it is impossible for them to initiate a gross substance when they combine without regard for spatial differentiation.

Even in the doctrine that atoms are the cause, the atoms are likewise partless; even if they were to combine with one another without regard for spatial differentiation, they would not be capable of initiating a gross effect. (29)
168. And [the liberated soul] is endowed with all [powers], because of seeing that [Brahman]. (2.1.30)

The supreme deity is of a nature entirely distinct from all other things and is endowed with all powers. Indeed, the Śrutis reveal the supreme deity thus: "His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold; knowledge, strength, and action are His innate nature."
Likewise,

having established that the supreme deity is of a nature entirely distinct from all others by stating, "He is free from evil, ageless, deathless, sorrowless, free from hunger, and free from thirst," it further says,
"He whose desires are true, whose resolves are true."
Thus they establish the yoga of all powers. Likewise:

"Consisting of mind, having the vital breath as its body, whose form is light, whose resolve is true, whose self is space, performing all actions, possessing all desires, possessing all odors, possessing all tastes, pervading all this, without speech, and without need."
And thus it is said: || 30 ||

169. "If it be argued that [the Lord] is not [the agent] because He is devoid of organs, we say: that has already been answered. (2.1.31) Even though Brahman alone is the one who is distinct from everything else and possesses all powers, nevertheless, the phrase "by connection with all powers" implies the intention that the manifestation of His distinct powers—characterized by the fulfillment of His true resolves—is made evident through the effect of His omnipotence. (30)

Regarding the phrase "due to being devoid of instruments": it has been stated that creation occurs by mere volition even in the absence of an entourage [of attendants]. Here, if it is argued that there is a requirement for the apparatus of instruments—given that for Him who is devoid of instruments, as stated in the text "for Him no work nor instrument exists," the commencement of any effect is not possible—[the response follows].

To this, the reply is as stated: "Because it has the Word as its source" and "for [the powers] are diverse. This means that that which has the Word alone as its authority is distinct from all other things; even in the absence of various specific instruments, it is capable of producing those respective effects. Thus says the Śruti: "He sees without eyes, He hears without ears; handless and footless, yet swift and a grasper," and so forth. (31)
Thus ends the section concerning the consequence of the whole [of Brahman being consumed]. || 9 ||
And the section has a purpose. (2.1.10)
Not so, because it possesses a purpose. (2.1.32)

Although the Lord, being one alone prior to creation, distinguished from all others and endowed with the power for all purposes, is capable of creating the manifold world by Himself; nevertheless, the doctrine of God as the cause is not tenable because of the purpose [required] for such a manifold creation, and because the Lord lacks any such purpose.

In the undertaking of those who act with prior intelligence, there are indeed two kinds of purposes: either for one's own sake or for the sake of others. For the Supreme Brahman, whose every desire is by its very nature already attained, there can be no purpose whatsoever in the creation of the world, since that which was unattained is thereby attained. Nor is it for the sake of others; for the state of being "for the sake of others" occurs through the conferring of favor upon others, [and Brahman has no need for such favor].

Furthermore, a compassionate being does not create a world such as this, which is filled with manifold and infinite sufferings like birth, old age, death, and hell; on the contrary, creating out of compassion, he would produce a world consisting solely of happiness. Therefore, due to the absence of any purpose, it is not tenable that Brahman is the cause—thus [ends the objection]. || 32 ||

170.3. "Not for any purpose" (*na prayojaneti*). The connection (*saṃgati*) is clear. The inquiry is whether causality is possible or not. For that purpose, [the questions are]: Is play (*līlā*) the purpose of one who has attained all desires? Or is it not? And do partiality (*vaiṣamya*) and cruelty (*nairghṛṇya*) follow from such play? Or do they not?

When [the world] is produced as a consequence, and when play (*līlā*) is not a motive, then, because a motive in the form of play is impossible, the possibility of being a cause is precluded. But when play is the motive, then, because an activity in the form of play is possible for one who has attained all desires, the possibility of being a cause is established. Thus it is proven. || 32 ||
[Śrībhāṣya 2.1.10] This being the position reached, we reply: "But as in the world, there is mere sport (līlākaivalya). (2.1.33)

For Him who has attained all desires and is perfectly fulfilled, the sole purpose in the creation of this manifold and diverse world—a mixture of consciousness and unconsciousness brought about by His own volition—is mere sport.

As in the world—just as in the world, for a great king who dwells upon this earth consisting of seven islands and possesses complete heroism, vigor, and prowess, balls and other such objects are seen to serve the sole purpose of mere play; in exactly the same way, for the Supreme Brahman, whose creation, maintenance, and destruction of the universe are accomplished by His mere volition, play alone is the motive. Thus, [the objection] is without fault. || 33 ||
172. "Inequality and cruelty [cannot be attributed to the Lord] because He has regard [for merit and demerit]; for thus [the scripture] shows. (2.1.34)

Although it may be possible for the Supreme Person—who is distinct from all other sentient and insentient entities—to create this diverse world of mixed sentient and insentient beings prior to creation, even though He is one and partless due to His possession of inconceivable power; nevertheless, partiality would result from the creation of superior, middling, and inferior beings in the forms of gods, animals, humans, and immobile things. The word "kevala" (merely) is used to exclude [the possibility of] such a contest preceded by a wager, as if it were merely a sport.

The word "only" (*eva*) is used to exclude the possibility that the purpose [of the world's creation] is merely something that has arisen by chance, even though it proceeds with a specific purpose in view;

thus he says, "by His own volition. It is appropriate to describe the undertaking of a ball game and the like as "play" because it lacks the weight of great effort, but this is not the case for the creation of the universe.
This [is stated] for the purpose of dispelling the doubt that [the *pāra*] might be of the nature of a great vehicle (*mahāyāna*). || 33 ||
The term "inequality" (vaiṣamya) has been explained by the term "partiality" (pakṣapāta).
It is just like a king’s play with a ball;
however, in the world, it is like the play of those who are fully satisfied with balls and such.
The purpose of the creation of the perfect Brahman is play (līlā).

The meaning of the Sūtra: [Regarding the objection that Brahman, by creating an unequal world, would possess partiality and cruelty—] there is neither partiality nor cruelty [on the part of Brahman] as he creates an unequal creation, because he is dependent on other factors; for inequality is based upon the karma of the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*). Indeed, the Scripture demonstrates this very point, clearly making it known: "There is neither partiality nor cruelty in the Lord who creates the gods and others, because He creates in accordance with their own karma; thus the Scripture shows."

"Because it causes the experience of extremely terrible suffering, cruelty (*naighṛṇya*) is also unavoidable"—to this, the reply is: "Not so, because [the Lord] is dependent on other factors" (*na sāpekṣatvāt*). Neither partiality (*vaiṣamya*) nor cruelty would follow. Why? Because of His being dependent on other factors—namely, because the unequal creation is dependent upon the karma of the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*), such as the gods and others whom He creates. For the *Śruti* and *Smṛti* indeed show that the connection of the individual souls, such as the gods, with their respective bodies depends upon their own specific karma: "The doer of good becomes good; the doer of evil becomes evil. (Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad 3.2.9)
"One becomes virtuous through virtuous action; one becomes sinful through sinful action.

Likewise, it was stated by the Blessed Parāśara as well: "The cause of the diversity among gods and others is precisely the power of the prior karma of the individual souls (kṣetrajña) being created."

"In the act of creation, he is merely the instrumental cause (nimitta) of the things to be created, since the powers of the objects to be created constitute the primary cause (pradhāna). Indeed, apart from being the mere instrumental cause, he requires nothing else; O best of those who shine, every entity is brought to its state of being an object by its own inherent power."
Thus, by one's own power—that is, by one's own action alone—the state of being a deity or other such entity is attained. || 34 ||

173. "If it be argued that [the distinction between soul and matter] does not exist because there is no differentiation of karma, we say no; for [the world] is beginningless, and this is both logically consistent and observed. (2.1.35)

The phrase "because of the creation of inequality" is supplied [from the context]. God is not dependent upon karma regarding the act of creation; rather, it is only with respect to the element of inequality that He is dependent upon it.

Regarding the term *pradhāna* (primary): "primacy" (*prādhānya*) means being the uncommon cause (*asādhāraṇakāraṇatva*), while "non-primacy" (*aprādhānya*) means being a common cause (*sādhāraṇakāraṇatva*). For example, soil, water, and so forth are common causes for all crops; however, the specific potencies of their respective seeds are the uncommon causes for the production of specific sprouts. Likewise, because God is a common cause, He possesses the status of being merely the instrumental cause (*nimittamātra*). The meaning is that actions (*karman*) possess primacy because they are the uncommon cause of the diverse creation.

If it is argued that because the soul (jīva) is non-distinct from its state of being (bhāva), karma does not exist, [we reply: the beginninglessness of the soul is established by scripture, and thus its non-distinction is also logically consistent.
Prior to creation, there were no such things as "individual souls" (kṣetrajñas). Why? Because of the scriptural teaching of non-differentiation:
"In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone."

[Objection: "If this is so, then since that [distinction] did not exist at that time, that karma does not exist. How then can it be said that 'the inequality of creation depends upon that'? [Reply: No; because the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) and the streams of their karma are beginningless (*anādi*). Even though they are beginningless, their state of non-distinction (*avibhāga*) is possible, because that reality of the individual soul has abandoned name and form (*nāmarūpa*), is incapable of being designated as separate even in its capacity as the body of Brahman, and is extremely subtle (*atisūkṣma*).

If this were not accepted, there would follow the absurdity of encountering the results of actions not committed and the loss of the results of actions committed. Furthermore, their beginninglessness is perceived in such texts as:
"The wise one is neither born nor dies," and in the beginninglessness of the stream of creation.
In such passages as, "Dhātṛ fashioned the sun and the moon as they were before," and so forth.

Since the scripture states only the differentiation of name and form—"In the beginning this was undifferentiated; it was differentiated by name and form"—the beginninglessness of the essential nature of the *kṣetrajñas* (individual souls) is established. Furthermore, in the *Smṛti* it is said: "Know both Prakṛti and Puruṣa to be indeed beginningless.

Therefore, because it is distinct from everything, because it possesses all powers, because its sole motive is divine play (*līlā*), and because it engages in manifold creation in accordance with the karma of the *kṣetrajñas*, Brahman alone is the cause of the world. || 35 ||
He explains the word "also" (*api*) in the phrase "even though that [world] is beginningless.

Regarding the phrase "the arrival of what was not earned," he states the intended meaning of the word "and" (*ca*). For even while the nature [of the world] is beginningless, and indeed while the flow of creation is beginningless, the beginninglessness of the flow of karma is established. Therefore, the passage "the sun and the moon" demonstrates the beginninglessness of the flow of creation. Since this sentence is meaningful in every *kalpa*, the beginninglessness of creation is proven.
