"Therefore" (ataḥ): by stating the matters taught in each respective sūtra in their proper order, he concludes the meaning of the topical section (adhikaraṇa). ||35||
174. And because all dharmas are possible [only] on that basis. (2.1.36)

Since all those categories of properties—both those previously mentioned and those yet to be mentioned—which were cited as deficiencies in the causality of *pradhāna*, atoms, and so forth, are instead established in Brahman as the possessor of causality, it is settled that Brahman alone is the cause of the world. || 36 ||
Thus concludes the section concerning the possession of purpose. || 10 ||
Thus ends the first quarter of the second chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja. || 1 ||

"And because of the production of all dharmas. This sūtra is supplementary to all the preceding topics. "Brahman alone" indicates the syntactical connection with the ablative case; the meaning is that there is a connection with the probandum under discussion in the highest sense. || 36 ||
4. Not non-action; 5. all phenomena [are purposeful]. Thus concludes the section on "Possessing Purpose" (prayojanavattva). || 10 ||
Thus ends the first quarter of the second chapter. || 1 ||
Whatever refutation applies to the theories of Pradhāna, atoms, and so forth as causes,
that does not apply to the theory of Brahman as the cause, because all attributes are logically possible therein.
The Summary of the Topics of the Second Pāda of the Second Chapter in the Śrībhāṣya.
Śrīḥ.
Salutation to Śrī. Salutation to Śrīdhara.

In the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja, the second [section] of the second chapter, the second (logical) quarter: The Section on the Impossibility of Creation (Racanānupapattyadhikaraṇam). || 2-2-1 ||
175. And because the formation [of the world] is impossible, inference [of a creator] is not valid; and because of [the world’s] activity. (2.2.1)

It has been stated: "The Supreme Brahman is the cause of the birth and so forth of the world. Therein, the objections raised by opponents have been refuted. Now, for the sake of protecting our own position (*svapakṣa*), the positions of others (*parapakṣa*) are being rejected; otherwise, some person of dull intellect, unaware that those positions are rooted in fallacious arguments (*yuktyābhāsa*), might—due to the suspicion that they possess authority—experience even a slight deficiency in faith toward the Vedic position. Therefore, the subsequent section (*pāda*) proceeds for the purpose of refuting the positions of others.

In this context—"regarding the cause" (*kāraṇaviṣaye*). "Now" (*idānīm*) means that the refutation of the cause as stated by the opponent's school is being undertaken. By this, the suspicion that the third quarter [of the verse] should have occurred earlier is dispelled; for therein, the rebuttal of the refutations raised by others regarding the effect (*kāryaviṣaye*) is indeed performed. Therefore, establishing one's own position and refuting the opponent's position regarding the cause is logically consistent. *Śrīmate Rāmānujāya namaḥ.*

In this regard, first of all, the doctrine of Kapila is refuted; for, by summarizing such points as the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) accepted in the Veda, the excessive delusion regarding the possibility of including this [doctrine] within the category of the true [Vedic] position is removed.

While in passages such as "Because of seeing, [the Pradhāna] is not [denoted] by the Word" (*īkṣaternāśabdam*), it was merely stated that Vedic statements do not have that [Pradhāna] as their purport; here, however, the actual nature of that position is rejected. Therefore, there is no suspicion of redundancy.
"Indeed! This is the established doctrine of the Sāṃkhyas: 'Root-nature (mūlaprakṛti) is not a modification;

the seven beginning with the Great Principle (mahat) are both natures and modifications; the group of sixteen is only modification; and the Person (puruṣa) is neither nature nor modification. This is the summary of the principles. What is called root-nature consists of the substances sattva, rajas, and tamas, which are composed of pleasure, pain, and delusion; whose effects are lightness/illumination, mobility, and obstruction/heaviness; which are entirely beyond the senses and are defined solely through their effects; which are neither deficient nor excessive, having attained a state of equilibrium."

And that [system]—by the word "and so forth" (ādi) in the phrase "satkāryavāda and so forth"—is intended to mean the acceptance of the twenty-four principles (tattvas), beginning with sattva, rajas, and tamas.

Is the doctrine of Brahman as the cause to be accepted unconditionally, or not? For that purpose, is primordial matter (*pradhāna*) the cause of the world, or not? Is the activity of primordial matter possible through proximity to the Spirit (*puruṣa*), just as the activity of a blind man is possible through proximity to a lame man, or not? Is the capacity for cognition possible for primordial matter through proximity to the Spirit—either by means of the Spirit's reflection falling upon it, like the blind man’s perception of the path through proximity to the lame man, or otherwise—or not?

When the possibility of being a knower exists, then because activity is possible, the doctrine of the Pradhāna as the cause is established; thus, the doctrine of Brahman as the sole cause is not to be accepted. When the possibility of being a knower does not exist, then because activity is impossible, the doctrine of the Pradhāna as the cause is untenable, and it is proven that the doctrine of Brahman as the sole cause must be accepted.
*Bhrama* is a mistaken determination; the meaning is that both of these are included. *Atireka* means excellence (*atiśaya*).

*Lāghava* is the quality that causes fire, wind, and so forth to rise upward or move transversely; by means of activity, it brings about a state of readiness for action in *sattva* and *tamas*, which are themselves inactive. *Upaṣṭambhana* is support or maintenance. [ *Gaurava* is the quality that causes falling. *Āvaraṇa* is non-luminosity. *Atyantātīndriyāṇi* (extremely beyond the senses) means always inferable.]

The phrase "neither deficient nor excessive" is stated for the purpose of explaining the word "equal. Nature (*prakṛti*), which consists of the equilibrium of the [guṇas] *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, is one, non-conscious in itself, intended for the experience and liberation of many conscious beings, eternal, omnipresent, and constantly undergoing transformation; yet it is not a modification of anything else, but rather the ultimate cause itself.

The Great One (mahat) and the others are its transformations (*vikṛti*); furthermore, there are seven others that are both [transformations] and primordial sources (*prakṛti*): the Great One, the ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and the subtle elements (*tanmātra*) of sound, touch, form, taste, and smell. Among these, the ego-sense is threefold—namely, the *vaikārika*, the *taijasa*, and the *bhūtādi*—which correspond respectively to the *sāttvika*, *rājasa*, and *tāmasa* [qualities]. Therein, the *vaikārika* is the *sāttvika* [ego], which is the source of the sense organs and so forth. The *bhūtādi* is the *tāmasa* [ego], which is the cause of the subtle elements that serve as the causes for the gross elements (*mahābhūta*). The *taijasa*, however, is the *rājasa* [ego], which assists both.

The five great elements beginning with space, the five organs of cognition beginning with the ear, the five organs of action beginning with speech, and the mind— these sixteen are exclusively modifications.

The Puruṣa, however, being unchanging, is neither the material cause (prakṛti) of anything nor the modification (vikṛti) of anything. For that very reason, he is devoid of attributes, his essence is pure consciousness, eternal, inactive, all-pervading, and distinct in every body. Because he is changeless and inactive, agency and enjoyership are not possible for him.

Even though reality is thus, the deluded, by the mere proximity of *prakṛti* and *puruṣa*, superimpose the consciousness of the *puruṣa* upon *prakṛti* and the agency of *prakṛti* upon the *puruṣa*—just as the redness of a hibiscus flower is superimposed upon a crystal gem—and they think, "I am the agent, I am the enjoyer. Thus, from ignorance comes bondage (*bhoga*), and from the knowledge of reality comes liberation (*apavarga*). This very point they establish through perception, inference, and scripture. [Śrībhāṣya 2.2.1]

Namely, this inference that "Pradhāna alone is the cause of the world"; since all of their views are refuted by the refutation of that [inference], it is that very [inference] which is now being refuted.

And they describe it thus: the fact that the entire world has a single root must necessarily be accepted; for if one were to accept the production of effects from multiple causes, there would be an infinite regress of causes. For parts such as threads, when conjoined with one another through their six sides which constitute their own portions, produce a whole (*avayavin*). And those [threads] and so forth are produced by their own parts in that same manner.

And those [entities], by means of their own parts existing in that manner—namely, even atoms by means of their own six sides while in conjunction—must be admitted to produce their own effects; otherwise, extension (prathimā) would be impossible. Atoms too, being composed of parts, are produced in the same way by their own parts, and those [parts] likewise by their own parts; thus, there is no finality regarding the causal series anywhere.

Therefore, for the sake of establishing the determination of causes, one substance—which is endowed with the power of various and manifold transformations, which itself never deviates from its own nature, and which is the substratum of infinite states beginning with the Great Principle (mahat)—must be accepted as the cause. And they set forth the reasons for postulating that single cause, the Pradhāna, which consists of the equilibrium of the three qualities (guṇas):

"Because of the finite measure of individual objects, because of their commonality, because of activity proceeding from potentiality, because of the distinction between cause and effect, and because of the non-distinction of the manifold universe."
"The unmanifest is the cause.

This is the meaning: "viśvarūpa" (the universal form) itself is "vaiśvarūpya" (the state of being the universal form); it refers to the entire world consisting of bodies, worlds, and so forth, with their various configurations. And that world, being an effect by virtue of its diverse configuration, has as its cause an unmanifest that possesses a nature similar to it.

Why? Because it is an effect. For indeed, all that is an effect is seen to have its differentiation from a specific cause that is of the same nature as itself (*tatsarūpa*), and its non-differentiation from that very same cause. Just as in the case of effects such as a jar or a crown, there is their differentiation from causes such as clay or gold which are of the same nature as them, and likewise their non-differentiation from those very same causes.

Therefore, since the world—which possesses a manifold form—originates from a primary cause (pradhāna) that is of the same nature as itself, and dissolves back into that very same cause, the world has the primary cause alone as its material cause. The primary cause is indeed the state of equilibrium among the three qualities (guṇas); it is the cause that shares the same nature as the world, because the world consists of pleasure, pain, and delusion, which are themselves composed of the qualities of sattva, rajas, and tamas. Just as for a jar whose essence is clay, the substance of clay alone is the cause; for that [clay] alone possesses the power of activity known as its production, as is observed in experience.

It is understood that causality belongs only to the Unmanifest (avyakta), which consists of the equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas) and is indeed unlimited in terms of space and time; for the differentiated effects—the intellect (mahat), ego (ahaṅkāra), the subtle elements (tanmātras), and so forth—are limited. Furthermore, since the intellect and the rest are limited like jars and other objects, they are not capable of producing the entire universe. Therefore, it is concluded that the world, composed of the three qualities, has as its sole cause the Pradhāna, which is the state of equilibrium of the three qualities.

"Of the effect," etc., is the demonstration of pervasion (*vyāpti*). "Therefore, of the one whose form is the universe," etc., he states the established meaning by the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*). "Therefore, it consists of the three qualities (*triguṇa*). The universe is an effect because it possesses a variegated configuration, like a chariot and so forth. The universe has a cause that is of a similar nature to itself; because it is an effect, whatever is an effect is seen to have a cause of a similar nature, just as a jar and so forth—this is the body of the inference. Here, since the presence of pleasure, pain, and delusion—which consist of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*—is observed in the effect, the cause must necessarily consist of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, possessing the power to produce them.

Since it is untenable for that [cause] to be limited—because being limited would entail the impossibility of its being the cause of everything—and because there would be an infinite regress if that [limited cause] were itself dependent on another cause, it is established by the force of the property of the subject (*pakṣadharmatā*) that the cause must be an unlimited reality.

To this it is replied: "And because the arrangement is impossible, [the Pradhāna] is not an object of inference; and because of [its] activity. "Inference" (*anumāna*) means that which is inferred. Your proposed *pradhāna* is not capable of the arrangement of the diverse world; for, while being insentient, it is not presided over by one who knows its nature. Whatever is thus [insentient and unguided], is so [incapable]; just as mere wood and such materials are in the construction of a chariot, a palace, or the like.

Because it is observed that insentient things such as wood do not initiate an effect unless presided over by the knowledge of that [effect], and because there is the teaching that the commencement of an effect proceeds only when presided over by the knower of that [effect], it is thereby stated that "the Pradhāna is not the cause, as it is not presided over by an intelligent being. By the word "and" (ca), he combines the non-conclusiveness of the positive concomitance (anvaya). For it is not the case that qualities such as whiteness or cowness, though positively concomitant [with their effects], are necessarily pervaded by causality.

Nor should it be argued: "Let it be that qualities such as whiteness, though inherent [in a substance], lack causality; however, for a substance such as gold, which is indeed inherent in its effect, there certainly exists the pervasion of being a cause. Likewise, existence (*sat*) and the other [qualities] are substances that are inherent in their effects and are thus pervaded by causality. For this reason: existence and the others are attributes (*dharma*) of a substance, not the essential nature (*svarūpa*) of the substance itself. Indeed, existence and the others are merely specific modes (*svabhāva-viśeṣa*) belonging to substances such as earth, serving as the causes for properties like lightness or luminosity; they are not [the substance itself].

Like clay, gold, and so forth, they are perceived as substances (dravya) conjoined with effects; furthermore, the established designation for existence (sat) and the other categories is simply "qualities" (guṇas).
176. "If it is argued that [the soul] is like milk or water, even in that case... (2.2.2)

As for what was stated—that the creation of the diverse world is impossible for the Pradhāna if it is not presided over by an intelligent being—that is not so; because its activity is possible, like that of milk and water. For instance, when milk transforms into the state of curd, a succession of transformations beginning with the initial movement is observed to occur spontaneously, without depending on anything else. And just as the transformation of water released from a cloud—which has a single uniform taste—is seen to proceed spontaneously into various tastes, such as those of the coconut, the palm, the mango, the wood-apple, the neem, the tamarind, and so forth; [so too is the case here].

In the same way, for the Pradhāna—which is by nature subject to transformation and remains uncontrolled even during the state of dissolution (pratisarga), persisting through a homogeneous transformation—a manifold transformation occurs during the state of manifestation due to the inequality of the *guṇas*. As it has been said:
"By transformation, like water, according to the specific basis of each individual *guṇa*.
If it is thus argued that the Unmanifest proceeds independently of anything else;

To this, the following reply is given: "In that case also"—meaning, even with regard to milk, water, and so forth, which were cited as examples, activity is not possible without the superintendence of the Intelligent One (Prājña). The intention is that those too were included within the scope of the previous argument.

In the Sūtra, "If it be said that [the Lord does not act] because we see the withdrawal [of effects], we say no, for it is like milk," it was merely stated that "even in the absence of any other observed auxiliary means, its own specific transformation is possible."
It has not been refuted that [the Self] is presided over by the Intelligent One (Prājña), because of such scriptural texts as, "He who dwells in the waters... and so forth. || 2 ||
177. And because there is no establishment of a distinction [between the two], owing to the lack of dependence. (2.2.3)

Furthermore, if [the Pradhāna] were to undergo transformation independently of the superintendence of a Lord whose will is true, there would be the consequence of instability even during the state of dissolution (pratisarga), apart from the period of creation; therefore, the Pradhāna is not the cause when it is not superintended by the Intelligent One (Prājña). If it is superintended by the Intelligent One, then, because of His possession of a true will, the orderly arrangement of the diverse creations of both creation and dissolution is established.

Nor should it be argued that even if [the world] were presided over by the Intelligent One (prājña), it could not be so because there would be no cause for the arrangement of creation and re-creation for Him who has attained all desires, who is perfect, whose bliss is infinitely unsurpassed, who is faultless, and who is stainless; thus [the objection] beginning with "not by the Intelligent One" is refuted. The meaning is that there is no contradiction, as it has been stated that He is independent of any other intelligent agent—such as a staff or a wheel—which might stand in the place of a body external to Himself. || 2 ||

Furthermore, because it would follow that He is merciless in creating inequality, this same objection applies [to your position as well]. For even in the case of a Perfect Being, activity for the sake of "sport" (*līlā*) is possible; since He is omniscient, the cause for specific creation and re-creation—in the form of His perception of primordial matter (*prakṛti*) undergoing specific transformations—is possible. Moreover, the actions of the individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) themselves are what establish the arrangement of unequal creation.

Now, if all these arrangements are established by the very merits and demerits (puṇya-apuṇya) of the individual soul (kṣetrajña), then what is the use of a presiding Lord? Nature (prakṛti) itself, conditioned by the merits and demerits resulting from performed actions, transforms in various ways according to the purposes of the Puruṣa.

This is observed through the arrangement of place and time, just as there is a specific transformation of food and drink that results in pleasure or pain—depending on whether they are tainted by poison and the like, or nourished by a particular medicine.

Therefore, the arrangement of creation and re-creation, the unequal creation of gods and other beings, and the arrangement for liberation are all possible only through the *pradhāna* (primordial matter), which possesses the power of transformation in every way.

You are ignorant of the true nature of meritorious and non-meritorious actions. For the true nature of merit and demerit is to be understood through the scriptures (*śāstra*). And the scripture is the mass of syllables known as the Veda, which is without beginning or end, possesses an uninterrupted tradition of recitation, and is untouched by even the scent of defects such as negligence. Furthermore, it declares: "Meritorious and non-meritorious actions consist in the propitiation of the Supreme Person and its opposite; and the fruits thereof—happiness and suffering—are dependent upon His grace and His restraint. Thus says the venerable Dramiḍācārya.

Of the stainless one—of the faultless one who is not subject to karma; of the untainted one—who is not subject to the *guṇas*. Since the Lord is not subject to karma, he lacks subjection to the *guṇas*; the sense is that the activity of creation and so forth cannot occur by means of a desire that conforms to the *guṇas*.

Regarding the phrase "of the Omniscient One": it is the cause for the arrangement of creation and dissolution; it is the attainment of specific transformations of *prakṛti* as directed by the Lord (*īśvara*). Nor is there a loss of autonomy through this; on the contrary, there is rather a fulfillment of autonomy. For it is only when specific transformations have occurred that the activity of creation and so forth becomes dependent upon His will. The sense is that autonomy consists precisely in acting according to one's own will. As for the "arrangement of place": it refers to the distinction between what is wholesome and unwholesome for one situated in a region devoid of heat or devoid of cold.
"For indeed, with the desire to share the fruit, they seek to gratify the Self by means of ritual acts;
when He is gratified, He is sufficient for the attainment of the fruit—such is the established limit of the scriptures.
And so says the Śruti:

"The center of the universe sustains the universe—the performed sacrifice and the charitable works, the manifold that has been born and that is being born. And likewise, it was said by the Blessed One himself:
"From whom the activity of beings proceeds, and by whom all this is pervaded—by worshipping Him through one's own duty, a human being attains perfection."
Thus:
"Those hateful and cruel ones, the lowest of men in the various worlds, I cast perpetually into inauspicious, demonic wombs alone."

"And thus" [it is said]: That Blessed One, the Supreme Person (*puruṣottama*), who has attained all desires, who is omniscient, the Lord of all, whose resolve is infallible, and who engages in divine play (*līlā*) consistent with His own majesty, having established the twofold nature of karma—distinguishing between these actions as "proper" and those as "improper"—and having generally bestowed upon all individual souls (*kṣetrajña*) the appropriate bodies, senses, and so forth for the undertaking of that karma, as well as the power to govern it, and having revealed the scripture that makes His own command known, [He remains].
And for the sake of withdrawing that [universe], having entered as the inner self (*antarātman*) and remaining as the director (*anumantṛ*), He governs it.

The "state of isolation" (*kaivalya-vyavasthā*) refers to the state of liberation (*mokṣa*). "Sacrifices and works of public utility" (*iṣṭāpūrte*) refers to rites prescribed by the Śruti and Smṛti. "Great variety" (*bāhuvidhya*) arises from the distinctions among deities, fruits, and so forth. "The navel of the world" (*bhuvanasya nābhiḥ*) means that, according to the method of the Śruti—such as "just as the rim of a chariot wheel is fixed upon its spokes"—He is the support of all in the form of the Inner Controller (*antaryāmin*). "He sustains" (*bibharti*) means He accepts [the offerings] as His worship.

The passage from the Bhagavad Gītā beginning with "yataḥ pravṛttiḥ" is intended to demonstrate that sin consists in the transgression of those [injunctions]; since the statement "teṣāṃ satatayuktānām" will be cited later, it has not been included here.

"Bhagavān" means that the meaning of the word *bhagavat* consists in being free from defects and possessing auspicious qualities (*maṅgala-guṇa*). The meaning of the word *puruṣottama* is distinction from those two [qualities]. Attributes such as omniscience are useful for the creation and so forth, which bestow various fruits. "These" means that the arrangement of beginningless merit and demerit is based upon His beginningless sovereignty. "Taking that as its material cause" [means...].

Just as a son, having been born and raised by his parents, instructed, and benefited by them through gifts of wealth, houses, land, and so forth, may either perform sacrifices and other rites with those very same riches and possessions, or may follow after sensual restlessness; in that case, there is no fault on the part of the parents. Nor is the son’s dependence on their sovereignty lost. Such is the intended meaning. Regarding the phrase "having bestowed generally": He gives the body, senses, and all else to everyone. The implication is that any inequality, however, is produced by karma.
"The state of being a permissive witness" (anumantṛtva) means the state of impelling one who has already begun to act.
1. And with a sense of sharing; 2. Thus—ta, da, na; Sarveśvaraḥ—da. 4.

The individual souls (*kṣetrajñas*), however, possessing the power of volition and provided with instruments such as bodies as directed by Him, and supported by Him, themselves undertake actions consisting of merit and demerit according to their own desire. Then, recognizing one who performs meritorious action as "obedient to His command," He causes them to prosper through virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation. But one who transgresses His command, He joins with the opposites thereof. Therefore, objections regarding a deficiency in His sovereignty and other such qualities find no footing.

Compassion (*dayā*), indeed, is defined as the inability to endure the suffering of others, regardless of one's own interest. Yet, even when directed toward one who is intent on transgressing one's own teachings, it does not conduce to virtue; on the contrary, it brings about a lack of manliness (*apuṃstva*). In such a case, restraint alone is the virtue. Otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence that the restraint of enemies and similar acts would not be considered virtues.

By the mere cessation of activity and the renunciation of infinite, unbearable offenses accumulated over beginningless and endless kalpas, He Himself exerts effort for the sake of increasing unsurpassed bliss. As it has been said:
"To those who are ever-devoted and worship Me with love, I grant that yoga of discernment by which they come to Me. And: "Out of compassion for them alone, I dispel the darkness born of ignorance..."
"I destroy [them] while abiding within my own being by means of the radiant lamp of knowledge.
Therefore, *pradhāna* (primordial matter), when not presided over by the Intelligent One (*prājña*), is not the cause. ||3||

Regarding the phrase "placed therein" (*tadāhitā*): the intention is that everything is dependent upon Him because He is the controller by virtue of being the permissive supervisor (*anumantṛ*), because He is the sustainer (*dhāraka*), and because He generally bestows the body, senses, and so forth. Regarding the phrase "Himself" (*svayam eva*): this is because the Blessed Lord is indifferent (*upekṣaka*). The intention is that even this indifference is itself a particular form of His sovereignty (*svātantrya*). By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "sovereignty and so forth," compassion, impartiality toward all, the absence of deficiency, and the lack of connection to fruits for the individual souls (*jīva*) are intended.
His resolve is: "I shall give this fruit to one who performs this action. For one who acts according to that resolve, there is indeed the perfection of sovereignty (*svātantrya*).

The phrase "without regard for self-interest" is intended to exclude the inability to endure the suffering of those dependent on him when their benefactor meets with calamity. The grammatical construction is: "I give [it] preceded by affection. Because the word *satatayuktānām* (of those constantly engaged) uses a past passive participle in the sense of a wish (*āśaṃsā*), the devotee's affection has already been expressed; thus, the word *bhajatām* (of those worshipping) would be redundant. Furthermore, it would result in stating what is not required and omitting what is required. Therefore... [the text continues].

Because there is no possibility of the Lord being subject to a deficiency in His sovereignty, since it is only by means of actions that take the form of His worship that fruits are bestowed; the meaning is that the fact of Brahman alone being the cause is established for the sake of accounting for the orderly arrangement of creation and so forth. || 3 ||

Now, it might be argued: although it has been stated that even "activity" (*parispanda*) is not possible for *prakṛti* unless it is presided over by the Intelligent One (*prājña*), nevertheless, a transformational activity (*pariṇāma-pravṛtti*) is possible for that which is "independent," because such is observed. For instance, grass, water, and so forth, when "consumed" by a cow or similar animal, are seen to transform spontaneously into the form of milk and the like. Therefore, *prakṛti* also transforms itself into the form of the world—"so it must be. To this, he replies:

178. And because [the transformation] does not occur elsewhere, it is not like grass and so forth. (2-2-4) This is not tenable; for since grass and the like do not undergo transformation when not presided over by the Intelligent One (*prājña*), the illustrative example is unestablished. Why is it unestablished? Because [transformation] does not occur elsewhere. For if grass, water, and so forth were to transform into the form of milk even when not used by a cow or the like, or even when discarded, then one could say, "It transforms only when presided over by the Intelligent One. But this is not the case. Therefore, it is the Intelligent One alone who turns what has been consumed by a cow or similar animal into milk.
"If [it is argued that it is] like milk and water, that has already been stated; here it is elaborated in order to demonstrate the fallacy (vyabhicāra) in that very case. || 4 ||

Regarding the word "dhenu" (cow): in order to exclude mere wood and the like, one must accept only the proximity of consciousness (*cit*); however, this does not mean being presided over by a person possessing a specific volition (*saṅkalpa*). For even when a cow has not yet calved, grass and other fodder consumed by her are seen to undergo the transformation into milk and so forth.

The objection that pure consciousness alone (*kevalācinmātra*) cannot serve as an example for transformation has been refuted. By the word "ox" (*anaḍud*), the objection that transformation occurs merely through the proximity of consciousness (*citsaṃnidhimātra*) has been refuted. By the word "the Wise One" (*prājña*), the intention is that the Supreme Self's undergoing transformation through the presiding over a specific conscious being endowed with particular volitions is not accepted [by the opponent]. "Elaborated" (*prapañcita*) means an elaboration in the form of resolving specific doubts raised; that is to say, it is for the purpose of demonstrating the avoidance of fallacious deviation (*vyabhicāra*) regarding that very example of the cloud (*payodṛṣṭānta*). || 4 ||
"Or it is abandoned" [Śrīmadhyamaka 2.2.1].
179. "If it is argued that it is like the case of the man and the stone, even so... [2.2.5].

Now, it might be argued: "Even though the Puruṣa has pure consciousness as its essence and is inactive, and the Pradhāna is likewise devoid of the power of vision, nevertheless, due to the proximity of the Puruṣa, the insentient Pradhāna proceeds [toward creation], because such is observed. For instance, through the proximity of a lame man who lacks the power of locomotion but possesses the power of vision, a blind man—who is aided by that consciousness, lacks the power of vision, yet possesses the power of action—proceeds [to move]. And through the proximity of a magnet, iron proceeds."

Thus, the creation of the world proceeds, brought about by the conjunction of primordial nature (prakṛti) and the spirit (puruṣa). As it has been said: "For the sake of the spirit's perception, and likewise for the sake of the isolation (kaivalya) of primordial nature—the conjunction of both is like that of a lame man and a blind man; from that, creation is produced."
Thus:

for the sake of the Spirit's experience of the Primal Matter and for the sake of its isolation, the Primal Matter proceeds at the beginning of creation due to the proximity of the Spirit— this is the meaning.

To this, the reply is: "Even so"—that is, even in this case, the impossibility of the activity of the Pradhāna remains exactly as it was. For even in the case of a lame man who lacks the power of locomotion, there exist thousands of occasional specific conditions such as the sight of a path or instructions regarding it; and the blind man, being conscious, proceeds by understanding those instructions and so forth. Likewise, even for a magnet, there is the drawing near of iron and other such effects.

But for the Puruṣa, who is devoid of activity, such transformations are not possible. Since he exists merely through proximity, there would follow the consequence of eternal creation due to his eternity; and because he is eternally liberated, there would be an absence of bondage and consequently an absence of liberation. || 5 ||

By the word "enjoyment" (*upabhoga*), the word "perception" (*darśana*) is explained; the sense is that because the primary cause (*pradhāna*) stands as the object with respect to perception, the genitive case is used in the sense of the object (*karman*). Regarding the phrase "the impossibility of activity": this ellipsis (*adhyāhāra*) has been supplied in accordance with the word "inconsistency" (*anupapatti*) found in the preceding and following sūtras. For the eternally changeless *puruṣa*, there is no occasional modification, just as a lame man [undergoes no change] despite the instruction on the path. For *prakṛti*, there is no modification, just as a blind man [undergoes no change] despite his comprehension of that instruction.

Just as in the case of the movement toward a magnet, no modification can arise in the Puruṣa. If it is argued that there is no requirement for movement toward [the Prakṛti] because of its omnipresence (vibhutva), then the consequence would be constant creation; such is the meaning. ||5||
Just as a magnet attracts iron even while remaining inert, so does Pradhāna act toward Puruṣa;
thus, let there be no eternal agency on the part of the Self.
180. And because the status of being the possessor of attributes (aṅgin) is untenable. (Sūtra 2.2.6)

For you yourselves admit that the activity of the world proceeds from the relationship of primary and subordinate factors (aṅgāṅgibhāva) based on the superiority or inferiority of the qualities (guṇas), as you state: "due to the specific nature of each respective substratum of the qualities. However, in the state of dissolution (pratisarga), since the qualities—sattva, rajas, and tamas—exist in a state of equilibrium, there is an absence of mutual excess or deficiency; consequently, the relationship of primary and subordinate factors is untenable, and thus the creation of the world is not possible.
If, even then, you were to admit an inequality [of the qualities], it would follow that creation is eternal.
Therefore, the world is not presided over by an intelligent being (prājña).
Pradhāna is the cause. || 6 ||

181. "And because of the absence of the power of cognition in the case of an inference [of Primordial Matter] in another way" (2-2-7). This refers to a method of refutation distinct from those already mentioned. Furthermore, regarding the inference of *pradhāna* (Primordial Matter) by means of a different mode [of reasoning], there is a contradiction with the specific [nature of the subject] because *pradhāna* lacks the capacity for being a cognizer, as stated in the passage beginning with "of the qualities" (*guṇānām*). Thus, the contradiction with the specific [nature of the subject] has been stated both by way of the undesirable consequence that the inference propounded by the opponent would require the superintendence of an intelligent being (*prājñādhiṣṭhitatva*), and by way of the undesirable consequence that it would result in a state of inequality. 6.

"Otherwise... because of separation. He extends the aforementioned refutation to other types of inference as well: For [the creation of the world] to be possible through volition, there must be the status of being a knower; for only when that exists is the occurrence of activity independent of another controller established. But that [status of being a knower] does not exist [in the case of the Pradhāna]. Therefore, there is the undesirable consequence of eternal creation and so forth.
Furthermore, at the time of dissolution (pralaya), there would be an equilibrium of the qualities (guṇas);
and since it is impossible for a single quality to be the dominant factor (aṅgin), [creation] is impossible.
And if, in that case, the inference of the Pradhāna were otherwise [than through its effects],
then, due to the absence of the power of being a knower, the impossibility of composition and so forth would follow.
Those same faults would arise; therefore, the existence of the Pradhāna is not established by inference in any way whatsoever. || 7 ||
182. Even if [the existence of the object] were admitted, it would be so because of the non-existence of the object itself. (2.2.8)

Even if one accepts the establishment of *pradhāna* through inference, it need not be inferred because there is no purpose for *pradhāna*. Regarding the statement, "For the sake of the Puruṣa’s seeing and for the sake of isolation (*kaivalya*) of the *pradhāna*," this is the purpose of *pradhāna*; however, these two—namely, the experience (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*) of the Puruṣa—are not possible. For the Puruṣa, whose nature is pure consciousness, who is inactive, changeless, and stainless—and therefore by that very fact eternally liberated in essence—neither experience, which consists in the perception of *prakṛti*, nor liberation, which consists in separation from it, is possible.

Since the proximity of *prakṛti* is of such a nature, and because the experience consisting of the perception of pleasure and pain—which are specific transformations of that [proximity]—is possible, liberation will never be achieved, as the proximity of *prakṛti* is eternal. (8)
183. And because of contradictions, [the Sāṃkhya doctrine] is untenable. (2.2.9)

This is the meaning. The sense is that, precisely because [the body] is insentient, it would follow that it must be presided over by the Intelligent One (prājña). This has been stated also for the purpose of demonstrating the undesirable consequence of its remaining in a state of imbalance. || 7 ||

"By means of inference. In response to the question "Of what is this an admission?", the intention is that, due to the proximity of the preceding sūtra, it is *anumiti* (inference) itself that is present in the mind by implication. However, because it is separated by many sūtras, *pravṛtti* (activity) does not constitute a necessary connection (*anubandha*). When there is a doubt regarding the admission of experience and liberation even for that which is eternal and changeless, the following sūtra states: "Because of contradiction. This doctrine of the Sāṅkhyas is indeed contradictory. For instance:

Having accepted the Puruṣa as the enjoyer, the sustainer, the seer, and the witness—on account of Nature’s being for another's sake, its being an object of sight, and its being an object of enjoyment—and having stated that even its liberation (kaivalya) is to be attained through Nature alone acting as the means, they declare that its non-agency and its liberation consist in its very own nature as eternally changeless pure consciousness.

For that very reason, they say that the practice of the means for bondage and liberation belongs to *prakṛti* alone—this is "liberation. They further state that due to the proximity of the Puruṣa, who is thus characterized as changeless and indifferent, *prakṛti* engages in the process of creation and so forth through mutual superimposition (*adhyāsa*), and that this activity is for the purpose of the Puruṣa’s experience and liberation. [This is supported by the Sāṃkhya Kārikā: "Because it is for the sake of another, because of the reversal of the three qualities and so forth, and because of being presided over..."

"The Puruṣa exists because there must be an experiencer and because of the activity directed toward the goal of isolation (kaivalya). Furthermore, from this [apparent] inversion, the witnesshood of this Puruṣa is established, as well as his isolation, neutrality, state of being a seer, and state of non-agency."

Thus, having stated that "the activity of Pradhāna is for the sake of the liberation of the Puruṣa," they say this: "Therefore, indeed, no one is bound, nor is anyone liberated, nor does anyone transmigrate; rather, it is Prakṛti, which has various supports, that transmigrates, is bound, and is liberated."
Thus:

"Therefore, through union with that [Puruṣa], the insentient *liṅga* (the subtle body) appears as if it were sentient; and likewise, although the Guṇas are the actual agents, the indifferent Puruṣa appears as if he were the agent. This is for the sake of the Puruṣa’s perception and for the sake of the isolation (*kaivalya*) of the Pradhāna."
The union of both is like that of the lame man and the blind man; from that union, creation arises.

Witnesshood, the state of being a seer, the state of being an enjoyer, and so forth, are not possible for that which is eternally changeless, non-agent, indifferent, and whose sole nature is absolute isolation (*kaivalya*). For such a being, even the delusion rooted in superimposition (*adhyāsa*) is impossible; for both superimposition and delusion are modifications (*vikāra*). Furthermore, these two cannot belong to *prakṛti*, because they are attributes of consciousness (*cetana*).

Superimposition (adhyāsa), indeed, consists in the attribution of the qualities of one thing to another by a conscious being. And this [superimposition] is a property of consciousness and is a modification (vikāra). Now, superimposition and the like cannot occur in the Puruṣa merely through its proximity to Prakṛti, precisely because the Puruṣa is changeless (nirvikāra). If they were to occur, they would follow as being eternal. Furthermore, the fact that mere proximity is ineffective has been established in the section beginning with "Not so, on account of the difference of nature" (na vilakṣaṇatvāt).
If it is Primordial Nature (prakṛti) alone that transmigrates, is bound, and is liberated, how can it be said that "she is beneficial to the eternally liberated Puruṣa"? For they say:

"By various means, she who is possessed of qualities acts for the sake of the Puruṣa, who is devoid of qualities and receives no benefit; thus she moves about for his purpose, though her efforts are ultimately fruitless."

Thus it is said: "In the same way, Nature (prakṛti) ceases at that very moment from that Puruṣa by whom she has been seen according to her true nature. And they say: "Just as a dancer, having exhibited herself on the stage, desists from her dance."
In the same way, Prakṛti ceases from the Puruṣa once she has manifested herself to him.
"It is my conviction that there is nothing more subtle than primordial nature (prakṛti).

Once she has been seen [by the Puruṣa], thinking 'I have been seen,' she does not present herself for sight again. Sometimes she is seen, yet she does not superimpose [herself upon him]. Furthermore, she does not perceive her own self, because she is insentient (acetana). Nor does she superimpose the Puruṣa’s perception of his own self as being her own perception, because she herself is insentient. And for the Puruṣa, there is no possibility of modification consisting of the act of seeing.
Now, if it is argued that "perception is merely proximity," it has already been stated that because proximity is eternal, there would follow the consequence of eternal perception.
Furthermore, even a temporary proximity distinct from the essential nature is not possible for that which is eternally changeless.

If you argue that the cause of liberation is simply the very presence [of the Lord]—that is, His being perceived—then the cause of bondage must also be that same thing; consequently, both bondage and liberation would exist eternally.
Furthermore:

If it is argued that "seeing things as they are not" (ayathādarśana) is the cause of bondage, while "seeing the true nature of things as they are" (yathāvatsvarūpadarśana) is the cause of liberation—[we reply: since both kinds of seeing do not exceed the nature of mere proximity (saṃnidhāna), both would necessarily occur at all times. If proximity were non-eternal, its cause would have to be sought, and for that cause as well, [another cause], leading to an infinite regress (anavasthā). Now, if—desiring to avoid this fault—it is claimed that proximity is simply the existence of the essential nature itself (svarūpasadbhāva); then, because the essential nature is eternal, bondage and liberation would likewise be eternal.
Therefore, because of such contradictions as these, the doctrine of the Sāṃkhyas is inconsistent.

As for those who claim that Brahman— which is immutable, eternal, devoid of distinctions, and pure self-luminous consciousness— is the witness of ignorance and thus partakes in unreal bondage and liberation, their position is indeed inconsistent because of the impossibility of its beginning;
for even according to their own stated logic, the superimposition of being the witness of ignorance [is untenable].

However, there is this distinction: "The Sāṅkhyas desire a plurality of puruṣas for the sake of establishing the fixed order of birth, death, and so forth; but they do not even accept that [plurality] here"—thus, there is all the more inconsistency.

With the words beginning with "atha," [the author] states the refutation regarding whether proximity (*sannidhi*) is non-different from the essential nature (*svarūpa*) or different from it. With the words beginning with "ye'pi," he states that once this position of the Sāṅkhya has been refuted, there is no room for the proponents of Māyā (*māyāvādins*). By the phrase "by the aforementioned method," the meaning is that the superimposition (*adhyāsa*) of the experience of ignorance (*avidyā*) is impossible upon that which is changeless (*nirvikāra*).
By the phrase "this much, however," he indicates an additional refutation.
As for the disparity mentioned—based on the distinction between the ultimate reality and non-ultimate reality of *prakṛti*—[it is as follows]:

That is incorrect; for whether [the distinction] is ultimately real (*pāramārthika*) or not ultimately real (*apāramārthika*), it is untenable for the eternal, changeless, and pure consciousness—which is of the nature of a single essence of light—to be a witness (*sākṣin*) distinct from itself. Moreover, if it were not ultimately real, it would be even more inconsistent, since one would have to admit that it is an object of perception (*dṛśya*) and subject to sublation (*bādhya*).

Even in the doctrine of "difference based on limiting adjuncts" (*aupādhika-bheda-vāda*), the inconsistency has already been stated previously: because it is impossible for Brahman, which possesses the limiting adjuncts, to have this very nature [of being distinct], and thus the connection with the adjuncts is untenable. || 9 ||
Thus concludes the section on the impossibility of the arrangement [of the world]. || 1 ||
The Topic of the Great and the Long. 2.2.2.
Refutation of the Theory of Atomic Causality as Maintained by Logicians: 184. Or [the production of the large and long is] like [the production of] the short and the spherical. (2.2.10)

The term "inconsistent" (*asamañjasam*) carries over [from the previous sūtra]. The word "or" (*vā*) has the sense of "and. From the two—the minute (*hrasva*) and the spherical (*parimaṇḍala*)—that is, from the dyad (*dvyaṇuka*) and the atom (*paramāṇu*), [the world arises] like the production of the triad (*tryaṇuka*); and everything else accepted by them is inconsistent. The meaning is that, just like the doctrine of the world's production from atoms through the sequence beginning with the dyad, everything else [they accept] is likewise inconsistent.

Nor should it be argued that the difference between a mustard seed and a mountain is due to the smallness or greatness of their parts; for if even an atom possessed infinite parts, then because of the equality of having infinite parts, the difference between the mustard seed and the mountain would not be established. Since one must necessarily admit a limit to the reduction of parts, and since atoms lack any distinction of spatial location (*pradeśabheda*), no dimension greater than that of a single atom could arise; thus, the very existence of the mustard seed and the mountain remains unproven.
If you ask, "What shall we do?"—then let the Vedic position be adopted.

As for the explanation offered by others—that this sūtra is intended solely to refute the objections raised against the doctrine that Brahman is the cause—that is both irrelevant and redundant. For, having already refuted the defects alleged by opponents against the doctrine of Brahman as the cause in the preceding section (pāda), it is precisely in this section that the rejection of rival positions is undertaken. Furthermore, the possibility of the world’s origination from the conscious Brahman was already elaborated upon in the very sūtra, "Not so, on account of the difference of nature" (*na vilakṣaṇatvāt*). Therefore, [the objection] is... [incomplete].

"Nor," and so forth. In order to establish the disparity between a mustard seed and a mountain, one must accept that atoms are partless (*niravayava*). Otherwise, because there would be an equality in the infinity of parts, the disparity between those two could not be established; this is the meaning. Regarding "of atoms": if they were partless, then even when a thousand atoms conjoin, their dimension would not exceed that of a single atom, and thus the subjects called "mustard seed" and "mountain" would not be established. Therefore, one must accept that atoms possess parts (*sāṃśatva*); this is the meaning.

Thus, partlessness was asserted for the sake of establishing the property (dharma) called "disparity," while possession of parts was asserted for the sake of establishing the subjects (dharmin) known as "mustard seed" and "mountain."

"What shall we do? means: if [the cause] possesses parts (*sāvayavatva*), the inequality (*vaiṣamya*) is not established; if it lacks parts (*niravayavatva*), the subject (*dharmin*) is not established—therefore, what should be relied upon? Regarding the passage beginning with "Vedic" (*vaidika*): let that object which is accessible solely through scripture (*śāstra*) and is beyond the scope of logical sublation (*yuktibādha*) be accepted. For in that case, there is no production of the vast from the small; rather, it is taught that the small is the effect of the vast Brahman, which is tenfold greater—and that [teaching] is not within the scope of logical sublation. This is the meaning.
Just as from two circles there arises the production of something large, long, minute, or short, so too everything else accepted by that [opponent] is inconsistent;
such is the meaning of the Sūtra. || 10 ||
"What else here is inconsistent? To this, he says: "185. In either case, there is no karma; therefore, its absence [follows]. (2.2.11)

For according to the theory that atoms are the cause [of the world], the origin of the universe is held to proceed through the sequence of dyads and so forth, preceded by conjunctions produced by action inherent in the atoms. In this regard, it is accepted that "the initial action inherent in the atoms which serve as the cause for the production of the entire universe is brought about by the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*)," as stated in the principle: "The upward flaming of fire, the horizontal movement of air, and the initial actions of atoms and the mind are caused by the unseen force. Now, is this action inherent in the atom caused by an unseen force residing in itself, or is it caused by an unseen force residing in the self?

In either case, it is not possible; for the *adṛṣṭa* (unseen force) produced by the performance of merit and demerit by the *kṣetrajña* (the knower of the field) cannot reside in the atoms. Even if such residence were possible, it would entail the consequence that [action] would be produced eternally. Furthermore, it is not possible for *adṛṣṭa* residing in the self to be the cause for the production of action residing in the atoms.

In this context, by the statement "just as from two short spherical [atoms] there is the production of the large, the long, the minute, and the short," the employment of two causes and the employment of two effects are clearly stated. The meaning is that the production of a triad (tryaṇuka) from a dyad (dvyaṇuka) is like the production of a dyad from an atom (paramāṇu). || 10 ||
"And [the argument] regarding that which resides in the self" means that it is because they belong to different loci (*vyadhikaraṇatva*).

Now, if the production of action in atoms occurs due to conjunction with the self through *adṛṣṭa*, then, because that stream of *adṛṣṭa* is eternal, there would follow the consequence of an eternal creation.

Now, it may be argued: "The unseen (adṛṣṭa) is capable of producing a fruit only in dependence upon its maturation (vipāka). Some unseen forces mature at that very moment; some in another birth; and some in another eon. Therefore, because they depend upon maturation, there is no contingency of their producing [the fruit] at all times."

This is not so; for it is unproven that the various unseen forces (*adṛṣṭa*) produced by manifold actions performed at different times by infinite "selves" without prior convention could ripen simultaneously in a single form at one time. For this very reason, neither a simultaneous universal dissolution nor the persistence [of the world] for two *parārdhas* without such ripening is tenable.

Nor is it the case that action arises in atoms due to the conjunction of the Lord’s will with a specific unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*), because an inferential Lord has not been established, as was demonstrated in the [sūtra] "Because He has the scripture as His source" (*śāstrayonitvāt*). Therefore, the origination of the world does not have action residing in atoms as its antecedent. || 11 ||

186. "And because of the admission of inherence (samavāya), due to its similarity [to other relations], there would be an infinite regress. (2-2-12) Furthermore, it is inconsistent because of the admission of inherence (*samavāya*). [The opponent claims: "The ripening (*vipāka*) is from the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*). [The Sūtra says: "And not so. The word "conjunction" (*saṃyoga*) refers indirectly to a general relation; the meaning is: "from the conjunction of the Self with that which possesses the unseen merit/demerit. Regarding the phrase "by means of inference" (*ānumānika*): even if God (*īśvara*) were established, since His eternal will is admitted by the opponent, the consequence of an eternal creation would follow. Because this is clear by the method previously stated, it is not mentioned here. (11)

Why? Because of the lack of finality due to parity. Since inherence (*samavāya*), like the whole (*avayavin*), the genus (*jāti*), and the quality (*guṇa*), would require another supporting factor due to parity, and that further supporting factor would likewise require another, there is an infinite regress (*anavasthiti*); thus, it is indeed inconsistent. 187. And because it exists eternally [as a cause]. (2.2.13)
Because inherence is a relation, and if the relation were eternal, then since its relatum— the world— would also exist eternally, [the doctrine] would be inconsistent. 13.

Because of this admission, the opposites of the intended permanence, subtlety, partlessness, and so forth—namely, impermanence, grossness, and possession of parts—would necessarily follow; for we observe that jars and other things possessing color and other qualities are impermanent and are produced from other such causes. Indeed, an unperceived object being postulated in accordance with what is observed cannot be established in a way that contradicts one's own intended specific characteristics. For you yourself postulate that atoms possess color and other qualities in accordance with what is observed. Therefore, this [position] is also inconsistent. || 14 ||
This is not accepted;
now, wishing to avoid this fault, he states [the following] regarding the possession of color and other qualities by atoms:
189. And because there is a fault in either case, [the opponent's position is untenable]. (2.2.15)

Not only is there a fault in the admission that atoms possess qualities such as color (*rūpa*), etc., but even if they were devoid of color and so forth, the earth and other elements would be devoid of color and so forth, because the qualities of an effect are preceded by the qualities of their causes. If, on the other hand, one admits that they possess color and so forth in order to avoid that [consequence], then the previously mentioned fault remains. Thus, since there is a fault in both cases, the theory is inconsistent. (15)
190. And because of non-possessiveness, there is absolute lack of concern. (2.2.16)

Although the position of Kapila has been abandoned because it contradicts scripture and logic, there is still some acceptance of it by Vaidikas who maintain the theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*). However, since this position of Kaṇāda is not accepted in any respect and is logically untenable, those seeking the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) must disregard it entirely. 16.
Thus concludes the section concerning the "large" and the "long. 2.
The Topic of the Aggregate as the Locus (Samudāyādhikaraṇa). || 2-2-3 ||
191. Some [hold that] the aggregate is caused by both [the self and the elements]; however, there is no attainment of that [aggregate]. (2.2.17)
The Vaiśeṣikas, who maintain the theory of atoms as the cause [of the world], have been refuted.

As for the Buddhists, since they accept that the world has atoms as its cause, it will now be stated that even according to their view, the origination of the world and its conventional usage and so forth are not tenable.

They are of four kinds: some accept external objects consisting of the primary elements (bhūta) and their derivatives (bhautika), such as aggregates of atoms of earth, water, fire, and air, as well as internal objects consisting of mind (citta) and mental factors (caitta), all established through perception and inference. Others, however, assert that all external objects, such as earth and the rest, are to be inferred from consciousness (vijñāna). Still others maintain that consciousness alone, devoid of objects, is ultimately real (paramārthasat), while the external object is merely... [an imagined nature].

Regarding the term "paramāṇu" (atom): the connection [of this section] is that the Buddhist position is refuted by virtue of its presence in the intellect, due to the similarity in their acceptance of the fourfold nature of atoms as being exclusively of one kind. In the Ārhata doctrine, there is an inconclusiveness (*anaikāntya*) regarding permanence, impermanence, and so forth; for they indeed accept that atoms are of a single uniform nature. Regarding the word "te" (them): the meaning is that since the Vaibhāṣikas and Sautrāntikas have introduced the discussion by accepting the theory of atoms as the cause, the Yogācāras and Mādhyamikas are also refuted because of their commonality as Buddhists.

Are atoms momentary and the initiators of the world, or not? Is it possible for those [atoms], being momentary, to be the cause of aggregation? Is the ignorance consisting of the notion of stability and so forth with respect to what is unstable and so forth capable of establishing that atoms are the cause of the aggregation of earth and the other elements, or not?

By asserting that all things are momentary, they claim that "the aggregate is rooted in atoms"; thus, these three [schools] describe the entity accepted by themselves as being momentary. They do not admit, even in its own right, anything such as a self (ātman) or space (ākāśa) apart from the aforementioned elements, their derivatives, mind, and mental factors. Others, however, maintain the emptiness of everything.
Among those, first, the proponents of the existence of external objects are refuted. They maintain this view:
"The atoms of earth have the nature of form, taste, touch, and smell."
The watery elements have the nature of color, taste, and touch;

the fiery elements have the nature of color and touch; and the airy elements have the nature of touch. These [elements]—earth, fire, and air—combine together. From these elements, namely earth and the others, there arise the aggregates consisting of the body, the sense organs, and their objects. Within that [aggregate], it is the continuum of consciousness itself, abiding as the internal subject and mounted upon the conceit of being a grasper, that persists as the "self. It is from this alone that all worldly transaction proceeds.

To this, it is replied: "Even if the aggregate were caused by both, there would still be no attainment of that [result]. This means that even if the aggregate consists of both types of causes—the aggregate composed of the elements such as earth which have atoms as their cause, and the aggregate consisting of bodies, senses, and objects which has earth and the other elements as its cause—its attainment is not possible; that is to say, the production of the aggregate that constitutes the world is not logically tenable.

Since you admit that atoms and the primary elements such as earth are momentary, atoms and the elements are subject to destruction at every moment. At what time do they function in combination? Or when are they combined? When do they become objects of consciousness? And when do they become the locus for worldly transactions such as rejection and acquisition? Who is the "conscious self," and which object does it touch? Which conscious self perceives which object at what time? Or where is the perceived object located?

When does one grasp [an object]? For that which is touched has perished; that which is touched has perished. Likewise, the feeler and what is felt have perished. And how could one who is different from the one who touched experience it? And how could one who is different from the one who cognized grasp the object known by another? Even if there were a unity of the continuum (*santāna*), since it is not admitted that the members of the continuum (*santānin*) are in reality distinct entities from the continuum itself, linguistic usage and the like based upon them are not tenable.
Furthermore, it was established previously that the self is precisely the referent of the "I" (*ahamartha*), and that it is indeed a knower. || 17 ||

192. If it is argued that [the existence of the world] is established because of mutual conditionality, we say "no," because this does not provide a cause for the state of being a composite whole. (2.2.18)

If it is argued that the state of being an aggregate and so forth is established because knowledge (*vidyā*) and the other factors act as mutual causes for one another—[we reply: they do not "exert activity" (*vyāpriyante*). "Activity" means motion. The word "what" (*kiṃ*) is used in a derogatory sense. It "touches the object"—that is, it makes [the self] connected with the sense organ. The meaning is that the activity of the sense organs, as well as cognition, rejection, acquisition, and so forth, would be impossible. The sense is: when? Never at all. Regarding the phrase "of the continua" (*santānānām*): since the continuum is not admitted to be a distinct entity due to its stability and its nature as a persisting succession, this is the meaning.
"It is only the referent of 'I' [that is the self]"—the intention is that it is improper for consciousness to be the self. || 17 ||

The word *pratyaya* signifies a cause. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*) in the phrase "the state of being an aggregate and so forth," the status of being an object of consciousness and the state of being the locus of worldly transaction are intended.
If it is argued that the world arises from ignorance and the rest because they serve as mutual causes, even so, this [ignorance] lacks causality with respect to the state of being an aggregate.

This is what is meant: although all phenomena are momentary, nevertheless, all of this is established through ignorance (*avidyā*). Ignorance, indeed, is a perverted cognition whose object is such things as permanence in what is actually momentary. Through that [ignorance], the formative forces (*saṃskāra*)—namely, attachment, aversion, and so forth—are produced. From those, consciousness (*vijñāna*), which consists of the manifestation of the mind, arises; and from that, the "name" (*nāman*) factors—the mind and mental concomitants (*citta-caitta*)—arise; and from those, the material substances such as earth and the rest arise.

From that arises the group of six sense faculties known as the *ṣaḍāyatana*; from that arises the body known as contact (*sparśa*); from that arise sensation (*vedanā*) and the others; and from those, once again, ignorance (*avidyā*) and the rest as previously described. Thus, this beginningless cycle of the twelve links, rooted in one another, revolves like a wheel. Furthermore, all of this is not possible without the collection of the primary elements (*bhūta*) and their derivatives (*bhautika*), such as earth and the rest. Therefore, the existence of the composite whole and so forth is established.
To this, the reply is: "No, because they are not the cause of the state of being a composite.

This is not tenable, because these [factors], beginning with ignorance (*avidyā*), are not the cause for the state of being a composite of the elements (*bhūta*) and elemental derivatives (*bhautika*), such as earth and so forth. Indeed, ignorance—which consists of the cognition of permanence and so forth regarding what is impermanent—and the attachment, aversion, and other passions caused by it, do not function as the cause for the aggregation of a distinct entity that is momentary.
For the cognition of silver in mother-of-pearl does not become the cause for the aggregation of the object, namely the mother-of-pearl itself.

Furthermore, for one who perceives stability in what is momentary, that very person has already perished; so whose passion and other afflictions arise? For those who do not accept a stable, single substance as the substratum of the formative forces (*saṃskāra*), even the persistence of those formative forces cannot be logically conceived. (18)
193. And because the subsequent arises upon the cessation of the preceding. (2.2.19)

Furthermore, on the view of momentariness, the production of the world is not tenable; because at the time of the arising of the subsequent moment, the preceding moment has already perished, it cannot logically serve as the cause for that subsequent moment.
If non-existence were a cause, everything would arise at all times.

Now, if it is argued that "causality consists precisely in existing in the immediately preceding moment," then in that case, a single moment of a jar would become the cause of everything that exists in the three worlds—cows, buffaloes, horses, walls, stones, and so forth—that occurs at all subsequent times. Or, if it is maintained that only what belongs to the same class and exists in the preceding moment is a cause, even so, a single jar existing in the preceding moment would be the cause of all jars existing in subsequent moments throughout every location.
Now, if you think that "one [momentary thing] is the cause of one [other]," even so, it is not known which one is the cause of which one. Or, if you say:
"The momentary jar existing in a certain place is the cause of the subsequent jar-moment belonging to that very same place"—do you maintain that the place is permanent?

Furthermore, because an object conjoined with the eye and other sense organs does not persist at the time of the arising of cognition, it is impossible for any object to be the objective referent (*viṣaya*) of cognition. || 19 ||

Regarding the term "mother-of-pearl": the meaning is that when an illusion of silver and so forth occurs in relation to mother-of-pearl and the like, it does not become two pieces of mother-of-pearl joined together. || 18 ||
194. If it were non-existent [at the time of production], there would be a contradiction of the thesis; otherwise, there would be simultaneity. (2.2.20)

If you say that an effect arises even when a cause is absent, then it has already been stated that everything would arise everywhere and at all times. Not only would there be a contradiction regarding production, but your own proposition would also be undermined;

for your proposition is that "the four conditions—the dominant, the co-operative, the objective, and the immediately preceding—are the causes for the arising of consciousness," wherein the dominant condition (*adhipati*) is the sense faculty.

Now, [if it is argued that] for the sake of not contradicting the proposition, one maintains that while the moment of the jar remains, another moment of the jar arises! If that were the case, there would follow the simultaneous perception of both the cause and the effect—the two moments of the jar; yet they are not perceived in such a manner. Furthermore, the proposition of momentariness would thus be abandoned.
If you say, "Momentariness remains established," then it would follow that there is simultaneity between the contact of the sense organ and the cognition. || 20 ||
The cooperative cause (*sahakārī*) is light and so forth. The objective support (*ālambana*) is the object (*viṣaya*).
The immediately preceding condition (*samanantarapratyaya*) is that which is immediate—
The preceding moment is the condition (*pratyaya*).

And so it is said: if the preceding moment were to persist into the succeeding moment, there would be the twofold fault of the consequence of simultaneous perception and the loss of momentariness; such is the meaning.
"If [it were] momentary... means: if the subsequent moment were to exist at the time of the preceding moment. "It would follow" means:

consequently, there would be the undesirable consequence (prasaṅga) that the relationship of cause and effect does not exist. Furthermore, simultaneous perception is established by the nature of things; [this pertains to] cause and effect—
The consequence of simultaneity is intended merely as an illustration;
such is the meaning. || 20 ||

Furthermore, regarding objects, there would be the undesirable consequence of simultaneity between the momentary pot that serves as the cause and the momentary pot that is the effect. (Sūtra 2.2.19). "There is no attainment of cessation through deliberation (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) or cessation not through deliberation (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*), because there is no interruption. (Sūtra 2.2.21). Thus, first of all, the arising of what is non-existent has been refuted. Now it is stated that the destruction of what is existent without leaving a trace (*niranvaya-vināśa*) is also untenable.

The meaning is that for those who maintain the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*), two types of destruction are not possible: first, that gross destruction which consists in the final term of a similar continuum (*sadṛśasantāna*) and is perceptible immediately following the impact of a hammer or other causes; and second, that subtle, non-perceptible destruction occurring at every moment within a similar continuum, which is a total cessation without residue (*niranvaya-vināśa*) designated by the terms "cessation through deliberation" (*pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*) and "cessation not through deliberation" (*apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha*).
Why? Because there is no interruption (*avicchedāt*); that is, because a total cessation without residue is impossible for that which exists. And this impossibility is as follows:

By us, who establish that the so-called production and destruction of an existent thing is merely the attainment of another state, while the substance possessing those states is one and the same and permanent—by us, this non-difference of the effect from the cause was demonstrated in the section titled "Tadananyatvam" (Non-difference from That).

If it is argued that because the lamp of nirvāṇa is seen to perish without leaving a trace (niranvaya), destruction elsewhere is also inferred to be without a trace—this is not so; for since it is certain from the observation of the persistence of substances such as clay in jars, bowls, and the like, that "destruction is merely the attainment of another state by an existing substance," it is more logical to assume in the case of the lamp and similar things as well that there is simply the attainment of another state, even though this is not perceived due to its having reached a subtle condition. || 21 ||

"Non-difference from that" means here [in this context]: because no other entity is perceived, and because the differences in cognition, terminology, and so forth are otherwise accounted for. Regarding the phrase "of the extinguished [pot]": since the persistence of the clay is established by uncontradicted recognition, it is not right to deny it. For it is logical to infer the unseen from the seen, but not to deny what is seen. || 21 ||
196. "And because there is a fault in both ways. (2.2.22)

It has been stated that for those who maintain the doctrine of momentariness (*kṣaṇikatvavādin*), neither the arising from a void (*tuccha*) nor the subsequent lapse into voidness of what has arisen is possible. Furthermore, there is a fault in accepting either of these two modes: if there were arising from a void, the effect would itself be of the nature of a void. For whatever arises from something is seen to be of the nature of that [cause]; just as a jar, a crown, or the like, produced from clay or gold, is seen to be of the nature of clay or gold.

Furthermore, you do not accept that the world is of a void nature, nor is it perceived as such. If there were the destruction of an existing thing without any residue (*niranvaya-vināśa*), then after a single moment, the entire world would necessarily lapse into a state of voidness. If the world were to arise subsequently from that void, it would possess the very "nature of being void" mentioned immediately above. Therefore, because of the defect in both cases, the two modes of origination and cessation asserted by you are untenable. (22)
197. And [the same applies] to space, because there is no distinction. (2.2.23)
"And it is not perceived" means that it is not perceived as something non-existent (*tuccha*).

In the *Śrībhāṣya* (2.2.4), in order to establish the stability of external and internal objects, the non-existence (*tuccharūpatā*) of both *pratisaṅkhyā-nirodha* and *apratisaṅkhyā-nirodha* is refuted. In connection with that, the non-existence of space (*ākāśa*), which the Buddhists enumerate as non-existent along with those two, is also rejected.

Furthermore, it is not logical for space (*ākāśa*) to be indefinable (*nirupākhyatā*), because it is accepted as being of the nature of an existent entity (*bhāvarūpa*), just like earth and the other elements; for there is no difference in that space, too, is established by uncontradicted cognition (*abādhitapratīti*). Indeed, space is perceived as the locus of the flight of hawks and the like, in such cognitions as, "A hawk flies here," or "A vulture flies here."

Nor can it be said that "space is merely the absence of earth and the other elements," because this position cannot withstand logical analysis (*vikalpāsahatvāt*). Is space the prior absence (*prāgabhāva*) of earth and so forth, their posterior absence (*pradhvaṃsābhāva*), their mutual absence (*itaretarābhāva*), or their absolute absence (*atyantābhāva*)? In every case, the cognition of space would be untenable.
If prior absence and posterior absence were space, then as long as earth and the other elements exist, the cognition of space would be impossible, and the world would be devoid of space.

Even if mutual non-existence (*itaretarābhāva*) were space (*ākāśa*), since mutual non-existence resides within each respective object, there would be no cognition of space in the intervals between them.
Furthermore, absolute non-existence (*atyantābhāva*) is not possible for earth and the other elements.

Regarding the phrase "by way of that incidental discussion" (*tatprasaṅgena*): the meaning is that the connection [to the next topic] is by way of an incidental discussion, because it is not useful for refuting momentariness (*kṣaṇikatva*). Regarding the phrase "along with those two": the meaning is that it is included in the enumeration together with them, according to the statement: "Space and the two types of cessation are unconditioned (*asaṃskṛta*) and eternal."

Regarding the phrase "śyenādi" (the hawk, etc.): the meaning is that what is perceived here as the substratum for the hawk’s flight is not the absence of light; for it is impossible for that which is perceived as the substratum for both light and darkness—as in the cognitions "there is light here" and "there is darkness here"—to be of the nature of the absence of light.
Smiling.

"And it cannot be [said]... means that it is impossible to maintain that the meaning of the word "space" (*ākāśa*) is merely an opening (*avakāśa*) consisting of the absence of dense matter. As for the phrase "but absolute non-existence" (*atyantābhāvas tu*): the sense is that absolute non-existence is impossible for all things, because while some things that are yet to arise possess prior non-existence (*prāgabhāva*), and some things that have already arisen possess destruction (*dhvaṃsa*).
