Furthermore, because it has been established that non-existence (abhāva) is a particular state of an existing entity, even though space (ākāśa) is of the nature of non-existence, it is not devoid of all description (nirupākhya). Moreover, since the space within the cosmic egg possesses form through the process of quintuplication (pañcīkaraṇa), as demonstrated by the instruction on triplication (trivṛtkaraṇa), there is no contradiction in its being perceptible to the eye. || 23 ||
198. And on account of remembrance. (2.2.24)

What was previously introduced is now established as the very stability of the object. Recollection (*anusmaraṇa*) is knowledge having as its object a thing previously experienced; it is synonymous with recognition (*pratyabhijñāna*). "This is that very same [thing]"—in this way, the entire range of objects experienced in past time is recognized. Nor can you maintain that this delusion of oneness is based on similarity—as in the case of a flame and the like—because you do not admit the existence of a single cognizer who could be subject to such delusion.

No! Another person does not connect the identity or similarity of what was experienced by one with what was experienced by oneself. Therefore, those who claim that the delusion of identity is based on the experience of similarity residing in objects existing at different times must necessarily admit the unity of the knower. Furthermore, we do not perceive any means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that establishes difference even among objects of knowledge such as jars, as we do in the case of flames and the like; whereby we might imagine that recognition (*pratyabhijñā*) is based on similarity.

Furthermore, it is said in the Veda: "The momentariness of a jar and other such things is established by means of perception and inference. Perception, first of all, has as its object that which is present; it makes known its own object by excluding it from what is not present, just as blue is distinguished from yellow. In this way, the present thing is understood to be a distinct entity from the past and the future. This is so even though [the object] is visible. By this, it is understood that its inferability is also accepted. || 23 ||

The designation by the word ‘anusmṛti’ (recollection) is due to its similarity to memory, as in the case of [the appearance of] flames and so forth. There is also an inference from origination: because it performs causal efficiency and because it exists, a jar and such things are momentary. Whatever...

That which is non-momentary, such as a rabbit’s horn and the like, is incapable of performing a purposeful action and is therefore non-existent. Likewise, one might argue that the preceding moments of existence of a jar are perishable because they possess the existence of a jar-moment, just like the final moment of existence of the jar; however, this [argument] has already been refuted previously through [the demonstration of] the impossibility of the causal relation (*kāryakāraṇabhāva*) and other reasons.

Furthermore—perception reveals the exclusion of the present from the non-present; it does not, however, make known that the present is a different entity [from itself], but rather merely its connection with the present time. And by that much, its status as a different entity is not established, because it is possible for that very same thing to be connected with another time.

As for the two reasons stated for momentariness—namely, "because of existence" and "because of causal efficiency"—these are contradictory because they prove the opposite of what is intended. For one could indeed say: "Because of existence or because of causal efficiency, a jar and the like are enduring; whereas that which is non-enduring is non-existent and lacks causal efficiency, like a rabbit's horn. Furthermore, causal efficiency would actually establish non-momentariness itself. For it has been stated that causal efficiency is impossible for things that perish in a moment, due to the impossibility of their performing an operation.

The meaning is: because of the absence of the persistence of the causal complex for destruction (*vināśasāmagrī*). [Regarding the phrase "the final moment of the jar": the moments of the jar prior to the final moment of the jar are perishable, because they are moments of the jar, just like the final moment of the jar. Since there is no difference between the moment of the jar and its existence (*sattva*), it is conventionally designated as "existence."

"Refuted" means that the inference, which is contrary to reason, is sublated by the perception of recognition supported by reasoning. "Of that very [thing]" means that just as the connection of a thing with blueness and lotus-ness does not establish it as a different entity, so too the connection with two times is possible.

"‘Tad’ and so forth. Because pervasion exists even through the contrary [of the intended meaning], the sense is that it is a prover even of the opposite. ‘Because of contradiction’ (savāditi) means that it has been stated to be a *prakaraṇasama* (an inconclusive reason whose counter-argument is equally strong). ‘Because of the impossibility of operation’ (*vyāpārāsambhavāt*): neither the state of being a cause nor the state of being a substratum for an operation is possible; because it perishes in the very moment immediately following its production. Therefore, it does not produce the intended effect—this is the meaning. ‘A contradictory reason (*viruddha*) is one that proves the opposite of what is desired’—such is its definition."

Likewise, since the final moment of the jar is observed not to perish through a cause, other moments of the jar as well must have their destruction dependent upon causes; thus, until the occurrence of a cause such as a mallet, they simply persist.

Nor should it be argued that mallets and the like are not causes of destruction, but rather causes for the production of a dissimilar continuum such as potsherds, and that therefore "destruction" is merely the attainment of the state of being potsherds; for this has already been established. Even if one accepts that destruction is distinct from the production of potsherds, it is logical that the mallet and other such things are indeed the cause of destruction, because of their immediate succession. 199. Not [from non-existence], because it is not observed. (2-2-25)

Thus, first, the objections common to both the Vaibhāṣikas and the Sautrāntikas—who maintain the existence of external objects—have been stated. Regarding that which was said—that because an object associated [with consciousness] does not persist at the time of the arising of cognition, it is impossible for any object to be the objective domain of cognition—the Sautrāntika offers this rebuttal:

At the time of cognition, there is no non-existence of the object; rather, "not being an object of cognition" is the reason [for its non-perception]. Indeed, being the cause of the arising of cognition is precisely what constitutes being an object of cognition. Nor does this entail the consequence that the eyes and other sense organs would be objects of cognition; for we accept that only that which is the cause of cognition by imparting its own form (ākāra) is an object of cognition. Even though an object perishes after having imparted its own form to the cognition, it is inferred through the form of blue or other qualities residing in the cognition.

Nor can the form of each subsequent cognition be established by means of each preceding cognition; for if that were so, it would follow that in a stream of cognitions of blue, a cognition of yellow could never arise. Therefore, the diversity of cognitions is produced solely by the object.

To this, it is replied: "Not from a non-existent [object], because it has not been observed. This form of blue and so forth which is perceived in cognition cannot be the form of an object that has perished and is thus non-existent.
Why? Because it has not been observed. Indeed, when the substratum (the object) has perished, its attribute cannot be transferred to another thing.

It is observed that even reflections and the like belong only to something stable; moreover, this does not apply to a mere property (dharma) alone. Therefore, the variety of cognitions is produced by the variety of objects, and it occurs precisely because the object persists at the time of the cognition. || 25 ||
Furthermore, he states a common objection:
"200. And in this way, even for those who are indifferent, [the result] would be accomplished. (2-2-26)

If one thus accepts that things are momentary, arising and perishing without cause, then even for those who are indifferent—that is, for those who do not exert effort—there would be the accomplishment of all aims. For it is through effort and the like that the attainment of the desired or the avoidance of the undesired is achieved. However, if there is destruction at every moment, then among all entities, neither the preceding object nor any quality inherent in it, such as a latent impression (*saṃskāra*) or knowledge (*vidyā*), persists into the subsequent moment. Consequently, there would be nothing whatsoever to be accomplished by means of effort and the like.

This being the case, since all accomplishments would be established without a cause, even for those who remain indifferent, results pertaining to this world and the next, as well as liberation, would be achieved. || 26 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the aggregate (samudāyādhikaraṇa). || 3 ||

"Reflections and so forth": by the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the casting of the shadow of a hibiscus flower onto a crystal is intended. "In that case too": the meaning is that not only is the reflection of a mere attribute (*dharma*) observed, but rather the reflection of the substrate itself (*dharmin*) is observed. || 25 ||

The specific [cause] beginning with *saṃskāra* is that which serves as the cause for heaven and so forth; the specific [cause] beginning with *vidyā* is that which serves as the cause for liberation. || 26 ||
Topic: Perception (Upalabdhi). Sūtras 27–29.
201. "Non-existence [of external objects] is not [possible], because of perception" (2-2-27).
The Yogācāras, who maintain that only consciousness exists, offer this rebuttal.

As for what was stated—that the diversity of cognition is caused by the diversity of objects—that is not tenable; for it is the cognitions themselves, possessing forms (*sākāra*), that are diverse in their own right, just like the objects. And this diversity of intrinsic nature is accounted for solely through the force of mental impressions (*vāsanā*). Mental impression is simply a continuous stream of distinct cognitions. Thus, the cognition having the form of a jar is the producer of the cognition having the form of potsherds, and the producer of such [a subsequent cognition] is the preceding cognition of the jar.
And the stream of cognitions of that very kind, which precedes the production of such [a cognition], is what is called "latent impression" (vāsanā).

Regarding the phrase "not non-existence": Is the arising of the world possible within the doctrine of cognition devoid of objects? Or not? Is that position rooted in sound reasoning? Or not? Is the form [of the object], such as a jar, a form of cognition? Or rather, is it the form of an external object? What is meant by the "uniqueness" (*asādhāraṇya*) of an object—is it its similarity (*sārūpya*) to that specific object? Or is it its relation (*sambandha*) to that object? Does a form of cognition appear that is conducive to the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) of an object, distinct from the form of the jar and so forth? Or does it not?

When no other form appears, and when the uniqueness of the object is characterized by its similarity to the object, then—because the doctrine of consciousness-only (*vijñaptimātra*) is rooted in correct reasoning—the possibility of the world's arising exists therein, [consisting of] the form of a jar and so forth, and the form of consciousness itself. When another form appears that is conducive to the conventional usage of this or that object, and when the uniqueness of the object is characterized by its connection [to that form];

In that case, since the form of the jar and so forth lacks the nature of being a form of cognition, the Yogācāra position is devoid of logical justification; thus, according to their view, the production of the world is impossible. [This concludes the relationship between the means and the end regarding the prima facie and final positions. As for the phrase "the form of the jar": the meaning is that within a continuum of heterogeneous cognitions, the final cognition possesses the power to produce a heterogeneous [result]. The sense is: just as even when an external object is admitted, a heterogeneous jar and so forth produces a heterogeneous potsherd and so forth, so it is here.
How is it said that the form of external things, such as mustard seeds or mountains, belongs to internal cognition alone?

It is thus: even the capacity of an object for practical activity (*vyavahāra-yogyatva*) depends upon the illumination of cognition; otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) of no distinction between what is known by oneself and what is known by another. Furthermore, since this cognition is manifesting, its possession of a form (*sākāratva*) must necessarily be accepted, because that which is formless cannot be manifest. And this single form being perceived belongs to cognition alone. Moreover, its appearance as if external is caused by error (*bhrama*).
Furthermore, because of the rule that cognition and its object are necessarily perceived together (*sahopalambhaniyama*), the object is not distinct from cognition.

Moreover, even by those who accept an external object, it must be admitted that in cognitions such as those of a jar or a cloth, the cognition’s specific exclusivity to each respective object—and its conformity to the form of that object—is impossible without the presence of a similarity to that object. Therefore, a form identical to the object must necessarily be accepted within the cognition itself. Since all worldly transactions are established by this alone, the postulation of an object distinct from that [cognition] lacks any basis in valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Consequently, consciousness alone is reality; there is no external object.

This being the case, we reply: "There is no non-existence [of the object], because it is perceived. It is not possible to assert the non-existence of an object distinct from cognition. Why? Because of perception—because cognition is perceived as that which brings about in the knowing self (*ātman*) the capacity for practical engagement (*vyavahāra*) with specific objects. For in this very way all worldly people understand: "I know the jar."

Regarding the phrase "of cognition and its object": the point is that, just as in the cognition of two moons, because the second moon is necessarily perceived simultaneously with [the first] moon, it is non-different from the [first] moon; such is the sense.

The meaning is as follows: [the phrase] "And what more," etc., signifies that consciousness alone is reality. This is because the diversity [of appearances] is established through the force of the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) of cognitions themselves; because the final cognition, like an object, possesses the power to produce a dissimilar [effect]; because cognitions manifest only by having a form, and since two forms are not perceived, it is cognition itself that assumes those various forms; because of the rule of simultaneous perception (*sahopalambha-niyama*); and even if external objects were admitted, the fact that a cognition's specific relation to each respective object is based on its similarity to that object, and since all worldly transactions are established by that much alone. Thus, consciousness-only is the ultimate truth.

Regarding the phrase "by means of the form of the knower": by this, the reason "because manifestation is impossible for that which is formless" is refuted; for the meaning has been stated that "blue and so forth are not the form of cognition; rather, the very suitability of cognition for the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) of those respective objects such as blue is its form."

They are perceived as such—by means of the meaning of the verbal root *jñā* (to know), which is transitive and possesses an agent, appearing directly before the eyes of all the world. Thus, while ostensibly proving that "consciousness alone is the ultimate reality," they deceive the entire world. This has been explained in great detail in the refutation of those Buddhists who are cleverly disguised under the cloak of Vedic doctrine, along with their supporting arguments.

As for the claim that "because of the rule of simultaneous apprehension, there is no difference between the blue object and the cognition thereof"—that is self-contradictory; for co-existence (sāhitya) is caused by a difference in objects. To say, "of a cognition whose sole nature is the fitness for the linguistic usage of those objects, there is a rule of simultaneous apprehension with them, and therefore it proves non-distinction," is laughable.

Since cognitions perish without leaving a trace (*niranvaya-vināśin*), they lack a persisting and stable substratum; therefore, mental impressions (*vāsanā*) are difficult to establish. How can a subsequent cognition, which has not yet arisen, be impressed by a preceding cognition that has already perished? Consequently, even the diversity of cognitions is produced solely by the diversity of objects.

The specific character (*asādhāraṇya*) of cognition—which is directly perceived as having the nature of producing the fitness for the practical usage (*vyavahāra*) regarding this or that object—is dependent upon its relation to those respective objects. And this relation is characterized by conjunction (*saṃyoga*). For cognition, too, is indeed a substance (*dravya*); it has been stated that just as the substance of light, which is a quality (*guṇa*) of a lamp, possesses substantiality, so too there is no contradiction in the substantiality of cognition, which is a quality of the self (*ātman*). Therefore, there is no absence of external objects. || 27 ||

202. And on account of difference in nature, [the waking state] is not like dreams and so forth (sūtra 2.2.28). Because of the difference in nature from dream-cognition, it is not tenable to assert that waking cognitions are devoid of objects. For dream-cognitions are produced by sense organs impaired by defects such as sleep and are sublated; waking cognitions, however, are the opposite of those, and thus they cannot be equated with them.

Furthermore, if all cognitions were devoid of objects, even the object you seek to establish would not be established; for inference, being without a support, would likewise be devoid of an object. If that [inference] possessed an object, then the property of being a cognition would lack exclusivity (anaikāntya), and thus the absence of objects would be even more thoroughly unestablished. || 28 ||
203. There is no existence [of the effect], because it is not perceived. (2.2.29)
The existence of a solitary cognition devoid of an object is not possible;

why? Because it is never perceived anywhere. Indeed, there is no perception "anywhere" of a cognition that is without an agent or without an object. Furthermore, even in cases such as dream-cognition, there is no absence of an object, as was established in the investigation of manifestation (*khyāti*). 29.
Thus ends the section on apprehension (upalabdhyadhikaraṇa). 4.

"In some cases" means that in deep sleep there is only the manifestation of the substratum (dharmin) alone; the intention is that there is no manifestation of knowledge as a quality (dharma). || 29 ||
Just as in the case of dreams and the like, the falsity of waking cognition is not tenable;
it is established precisely by its dissimilarity [to dreams] through its freedom from defects.
Furthermore, the existence of a cognition devoid of an object is not found at all,
because a cognition separated from both action and agent is unperceived.
Thus ends the section on perception (upalabdhyadhikaraṇa). 4.
• Perception [of it] anywhere—this is the section concerning the impossibility in every respect. 204. And because it is impossible in every way. (2.2.30)

Here, the Mādhyamika, the proponent of universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnya*), objects: "Indeed, the doctrine of emptiness alone is the pinnacle of the Sugata’s teaching. Moments of existence such as momentariness and so forth were taught by means of the acceptance of objects and other methods, in accordance with the fitness of the disciples' intellects."

"Consciousness, all external objects, and even [the self] do not exist; emptiness alone is reality, and liberation is simply the attainment of non-existence"—this is the Buddha's intention. And that indeed is logical, because emptiness is established by itself, being neither caused nor producible. For a cause must be sought only for that which already exists. And that which exists is not produced from either existence or non-existence. To begin with, the production of anything from existence is never observed; for a jar or the like does not arise unless the lump of clay and so forth have first been destroyed.

Nor is production from non-existence possible. For if a jar or the like were produced from non-existence when the lump of clay and so forth have perished, it would itself consist of non-existence. Likewise, production neither from itself nor from another is possible: if it were produced from itself, there would be the fallacy of self-dependence (*ātmāśraya*) and a lack of purpose; if it were produced from another, then because "otherness" is indistinguishable, there would be the undesirable consequence that everything could be produced from everything.

"In every way" means: Is the doctrine of universal emptiness (*sarva-śūnyavāda*) stated by the Mādhyamika possible or not? Is every effect of the nature of existence (*bhāva-rūpa*) or of the nature of non-existence (*abhāva-rūpa*)? Is it the case that for all effects, only existence is the cause, or rather non-existence? Is non-existence a distinct entity of the nature of absence, or is it a separate category called "the void" (*tuccha*)?

When "non-existence" (*abhāva*) is a separate entity (*arthāntara*) that is merely void (*tuccha*), then non-existence alone would be the cause of all effects; since the effect itself would thus consist of non-existence, the doctrine of emptiness (*śūnyavāda*) would be established. When "non-existence" is another form of existence (*bhāvāntara*), then existence alone would be the cause of all effects; since the effect itself would be of the nature of existence, the doctrine of universal emptiness would be untenable. Regarding the term "without a cause" (*ahetu*): the proof of emptiness arises precisely from the absence of a cause for what exists; it does not depend on some other proving cause—this is the meaning.
"Not indeed" means that it arises precisely from destruction. As for the absence of purpose: because it already exists by itself, there is no dependence on production.
Furthermore, the doctrine of universal emptiness cannot be established according to your own position,
because it is entirely untenable and contradicts the means of valid cognition and other criteria.
1. Universal emptiness (sarvaśūnyatva) – ā, i, ga, va. • na – tha. 3. It is not tenable – ga, da.

Because of the very absence of birth, there is also the absence of destruction. Therefore, emptiness alone is the reality. Consequently, birth, destruction, existence, non-existence, and so forth, are mere illusion.

Nor can it be argued that, because an error without a substratum is impossible, some ultimate reality must be accepted as the substratum of the error; for just as an error arises even when the defect, the locus of the defect, and the knowerhood are not ultimately real, so too an error is possible even when the substratum is not ultimately real. Therefore, emptiness alone is the reality.
This being the position, it is replied: "And because [the void] is untenable in every way. Because it is untenable in every way, the universal void (*sarva-śūnyatva*) intended by you is not possible.

Do you assert that "everything exists," or that "it does not exist," or otherwise? In no case is the emptiness (*tucchatva*) you intend possible, for in the world, the words "existence" and "non-existence," as well as the cognitions corresponding to them, have been shown to refer only to existing things in their various specific states.

Therefore, by one who asserts that "everything is empty," just as by one who asserts that "everything exists," what is actually asserted is merely the fact that everything which exists possesses a particular state; thus, the "insubstantiality" (tucchatā) favored by you is not established from any source whatsoever.

Furthermore, having apprehended emptiness through some means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), one who desires to prove that emptiness must necessarily accept the "truth" of that very means of cognition. If that [means] were "untrue," then everything would be true, and the total emptiness of everything would be entirely untenable. || 30 ||
Thus ends the section on the impossibility [of the opponent's view] in every respect. 5.

By the word "in every way" (sarvathā), the impossibility of conceptualizing the means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) and the impossibility of conceptualizing the objects of valid cognition (prameya) are intended.

What is it that you, sir, are conceptualizing as the object of knowledge (*prameya*)? Is it otherwise? That is to say: is it by way of having the nature of both, or by way of not having the nature of either? If it were of the nature of both or of the nature of neither, it would simply be a case of falling into another state (*avasthāntarāpatti*); for, according to worldly consensus or the manner of the opponent's own admission, existence and non-existence are merely specific states. Indeed, for a proponent of emptiness (*śūnyavādin*), the practical discourse of proof and refutation is not possible apart from these two modes.

Pot-ness is existent with respect to itself, but non-existent with respect to the shards; thus, it possesses a dual nature. A pot is not non-existent with respect to itself, yet it is non-existent with respect to the shards. Therefore, even the nature of experience is merely a particular state.

The phrase "Furthermore" (kiñca) states the impossibility of a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). The word "means of valid cognition" is also intended to imply "valid cognition" (*pramiti*) itself. Is everything—both the valid cognition and its cause—real, or is it unreal? If it is real, then there is no universal emptiness (*sarvaśūnyatva*). If it is unreal, then [the conclusion follows] all the more so; such is the meaning. || 30 ||
Thus ends the section on the impossibility [of the opponent's position] in every respect. 5.
The section on the impossibility [of multiple natures] in one [entity]. (2.2.6)
205. Because [the two] cannot coexist in one [substratum]. (2.2.31)
The Buddhists have already been refuted; now the Jaina position is rejected, as they also assert that atoms and the like are the cause of the world.

They indeed believe as follows: this world consists of living beings (*jīva*) and non-living things (*ajīva*), and it is without a Lord (*nirīśvara*). Furthermore, it consists of six substances (*ṣaḍ-dravya*). These substances are known as: 1) *jīva*, 2) *dharma*, 3) *adharma*, 4) *pudgala*, 5) *kāla*, and 6) *ākāśa*. 1) Among these, *jīvas* are of three kinds: bound (*baddha*), those who have attained perfection through yoga (*yogasiddha*), and liberated (*mukta*). 2) That which is called *dharma* is a specific substance that pervades the universe and serves as the cause of motion for those possessing movement. 3) And *adharma* is that which serves as the cause of stability.

Regarding the word "refuted": for the Vaiśeṣikas and Buddhists, who maintain the doctrine that atoms are the cause [of the world], the refutation of their respective positions—the absolute [nature of atoms] and the fourfold classification of atoms—is appropriate. Following the Buddhists, the refutation of the Ājīvika doctrine follows.

Is the doctrine of the absolute cause that is Brahman to be refuted, or not? Is the Jaina doctrine based on sound reasoning, or not? Is it possible for a single entity to possess multiple natures, such as existence and non-existence, difference and non-difference, permanence and impermanence, and so forth, or not? Can the possession of multiple natures by a single entity be established through its modes (*paryāya*) and its essential nature (*svabhāva*), or not?

If it were possible [to establish this], then, because a single entity could possess multiple natures, the Jaina doctrine—being rooted in sound reasoning—would render the theory of Brahman as the cause unconvincing. However, when it is not possible, then, due to the impossibility of a single entity having multiple natures and because the Jaina doctrine is rooted in fallacious reasoning, the theory of Brahman as the cause becomes most worthy of faith.

4) Because of its omnipresence (*sāmyāt*), it is all-pervading (*vyāpī*). Furthermore, what is called "matter" (*pudgala*) is a substance (*dravya*) possessing color, smell, taste, and touch. It is of two kinds: in the form of atoms (*paramāṇu*) and in the form of their aggregates (*tatsaṅghāta*), such as wind, fire, water, earth, bodies, worlds, and so forth. 5) Time (*kāla*), however, is a specific kind of substance in the form of an atom, which is the cause for the conventional usage of "it was," "it is," and "it will be. 6) Space (*ākāśa*) also is one and consists of infinite spatial units (*anantapradeśa*).

And among those, substances distinct from atoms are subsumed under the term "five astikāyas": namely, the jīvāstikāya, the dharmāstikāya, the adharmāstikāya, the pudgalāstikāya, and the ākāśāstikāya. The word "astikāya" is applied to a substance that exists in multiple spatial locations.
They also provide another summary that is useful for the liberation of living beings: "Living beings, non-living things, influx, bondage, dissociation, restraint, and liberation."

Thus, by means of this summary of liberation (*mokṣasaṅgraha*), the means to liberation is also included. And that [means] consists of right knowledge (*samyag-jñāna*), right vision (*darśana*), and right conduct (*cāritra*). Among these, the soul (*jīva*) possesses the qualities of knowledge, vision, bliss, and energy. The non-soul (*ajīva*) is the entire collection of objects to be experienced by the soul. Influx (*āsrava*) consists of the sense organs and so forth, which serve as the instruments for that experience. Bondage (*bandha*) is eightfold: the four destructive karmas (*ghāti-karma*) and the four non-destructive karmas (*aghāti-karma*). Among these, the former is the cause of the obstruction of the soul's qualities—the cause of states such as immobility, meaning the cause of non-activity.

"And the means to liberation. Although the means to liberation is indeed already expressed by the word "restraint" (*saṃvara*) alone—as in the statement, "Influx (*āsrava*) is the cause of existence; restraint is the cause of liberation"—nevertheless, this [separate mention] should be understood as being stated for the purpose of including other means besides the specific cause of liberation intended by the term "restraint. Regarding the phrase "the enjoyment thereof": "Influx is bondage through karma."

The statement of Jinadatta, "Nirjarā is liberation from that [karma]," should be understood as being according to the perspective of another school of thought (*matāntara*). The destructive karmas (*ghātikarmāṇi*) are fourfold: knowledge-obscuring (*jñānāvaraṇīya*), perception-obscuring (*darśanāvaraṇīya*), deluding (*mohanīya*), and obstructive (*āntarāyika*). The non-destructive karmas (*aghātikarmāṇi*) are fourfold: feeling-producing (*vedanīya*), name-determining (*nāmika*), lineage-determining (*gotrika*), and life-span-determining (*āyuṣka*). Among these, the knowledge-obscuring karma consists of the misconception: "Right knowledge is not a means to liberation."

*Darśanāvaraṇīya* (the obscuring of perception) is the knowledge [that arises] from the thought: "Liberation does not result from the practice of [right] perception. *Mohanīya* (deluding karma) is the failure to ascertain the specific distinctions among the many conflicting paths to liberation shown by the Tīrthaṅkaras. *Āntarāyika* (obstructive karma) is the cognition that creates obstacles for those engaged in the path to liberation. These are called the *ghāti-karmas* (destructive karmas) because they destroy spiritual excellence (*śreyaḥ*). 1.

The destroyer of the innate qualities of knowledge, vision, vigor, and bliss is *apara* (the other [karma]). Furthermore, it is the cause of the body, its configuration, the ego-identification with it, its maintenance, and the resulting pleasure, pain, and equanimity. *Nirjarā* is the means to liberation (*mokṣa*), consisting of austerity (*tapas*) as understood from the teachings of the Arhat. *Saṃvara* is the restraint of the senses, taking the form of meditative concentration (*samādhi*). *Mokṣa*, however, is the manifestation of the innate nature of the self for one whose afflictions such as the *rajas* (passion) and others have ceased.

Furthermore, the atoms that serve as the causes of earth and the other elements are not of four kinds, as held by the Vaiśeṣikas and others; rather, they possess a single nature. The distinctions such as earth and so forth are produced by transformation (*pariṇāma*). And they maintain that the entire range of entities is indeterminate (*anaikāntika*) with respect to existence and non-existence, permanence and impermanence, difference and non-difference, and so on—namely:

"in some sense it exists" (*syād asti*), "in some sense it does not exist" (*syān nāsti*), "in some sense it both exists and does not exist" (*syād asti ca nāsti ca*), "in some sense it neither exists nor does not exist and is inexpressible" (*syān nāsti ca syād avaktavyam*), "in some sense it exists and is inexpressible" (*syād asti cāvaktavyam ca*), "in some sense it does not exist and is inexpressible" (*syān nāsti cāvaktavyam ca*), and "in some sense it both exists and does not exist and is inexpressible" (*syād asti ca nāsti cāvaktavyam ca*).

Thus, because the method of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgīnaya*) applies everywhere, it is established that the entire collection of entities consists of substance and modes (*dravya-paryāya*). Consequently, they demonstrate that everything is characterized by unity, permanence, and so forth from the perspective of substance, while the opposite is true from the perspective of modes. Furthermore, since modes are specific states of a substance and possess the nature of both existence and non-existence, everything—such as being and non-being—is logically consistent.
Tejas (heat-energy) is the cause of the transformation of the body into its specific form through slight thickening, like the process of cooking.
Vedanīya (feeling-producing karma)— which is nominal and resides within the seed of the three dhātus— is [the cause] once that potency has been established in that seed.

*Kalala* is the specific activity that initiates the nature of the Buddha-soul. *Gotrika* is the capacity for the transformation of the combined semen and blood into the form of a body. *Āyuṣka* refers to the combined semen and blood, so called because it "proclaims" (*kāyati*) or "indicates" (*kathayati*) the lifespan through its production. *Aghāti* means non-obstructive, due to the absence of any quality that destroys merit (*śreyas*). *Tapaḥ* refers to practices such as climbing heated stones and the like. *Saṃvara* is the means to liberation consisting of the restraints (*gupti*), careful conduct (*samiti*), and so forth, because it "shuts off" (*saṃvṛṇoti*) the activity of the senses.

"Manifestation of the nature of the self" means that some maintain liberation (*mokṣa*) to be the abiding in the world-space (*lokākāśa*) for one whose afflictions have entirely ceased. Others declare that liberation is the constant upward movement of one who is freed from the bondage of the categories of merit and demerit (*dharmādharmāstikāya*), like a parrot released from its cage, or like a gourd fruit whose mud has been washed away by immersion in water.

*Paryāya* means "state. The meaning is that because specific states consist of both existence and non-existence, the existence (*sattva*) and other qualities of the substance (*dravya*) are logically established.
To this, it is replied: "Because [these qualities] cannot coexist in one [substance]. (NS 3.2.30)
This is not tenable;

why? Because of the impossibility of [contradictory attributes] in one [entity]. For in a single substance, contradictory properties such as existence and non-existence cannot coexist simultaneously, like shadow and light.

What is meant by this is that since the substance and its specific states—which are denoted by words expressing particular attributes—are distinct categories of reality, the coexistence of contradictory qualities within a single entity is impossible.

For instance: it is impossible for that which is qualified at one time by a particular state such as existence to be simultaneously qualified by its opposite, such as non-existence. Furthermore, impermanence consists in a substance being the locus of specific modifications known as arising and destruction; how then could permanence, which is the opposite of that, inhere in it? Moreover, difference consists in being the substratum of contradictory attributes.

And how could its opposite, non-difference, co-inhere in that [entity], given that the simultaneous existence of both horsehood and buffalo-hood in a single thing is impossible? This point was already elaborated upon during the refutation of the proponent of difference-and-non-difference (*bhedābheda-vādin*) under the aphorism "But that [Brahman is the cause] because of the coordination [of all things with it]" (*tattu samanvayāt*).

Since time is perceived solely as a qualifier of objects, its separate existence, non-existence, and so forth need not be asserted; nor do they need to be refuted. The conventional usage "time exists" or "time does not exist" is equivalent to the conventional usage regarding the existence or non-existence of genus (*jāti*) and other categories for those who employ such conventions. For it has already been stated that genus and the like are perceived only as qualifiers of substances.

"But how [is it so]?"—this refers to the statement by the Vedic scholars (*śrotriya*) that "Brahman alone, being the self of all, is one. By this, the refutation of the atomicity of time is established as the result. The postulation of multiple times is improper; for there is the cognition, "multiple objects exist at one time," through which the existence of time is understood as a qualifier of substances. Therefore, the doubt regarding its non-existence has no room to arise—this is the meaning. [The text reads: "...existence and so forth... (du, 0 kathaṃ - da).

It has been stated that the Supreme Person (Puruṣottama) is omniscient, omnipotent, and possesses true resolve, because He is the body of all conscious and unconscious entities. Furthermore, it has been explained that there is an absolute difference between the body and the embodied one, as well as between their respective attributes.

Moreover, since the six categories of substances—beginning with the soul—lack the nature of being a single substance and its modifications, it is difficult to establish unity and plurality within them by treating them as a single substance in terms of their substantial and modal aspects.
Now, if it should be argued: "These six substances exist in such a way through their own modifications and their own individual selves," [the response follows].

Even so, there is a contradiction with the tenet that "everything is non-conclusive" (sarvamanaikāntika), because of the absence of mutual identity [between the universal and the particular]. Therefore, this Jaina doctrine is not tenable. In the theory that atoms are the cause without being presided over by a Lord (īśvara), the previously mentioned defects remain exactly as they were. || 31 ||
206. And thus there would be incompleteness of the Self. (Sūtra 2.2.32)

If this is your position, it follows that the self would be incomplete. For your established doctrine is that "the jīva consists of innumerable spatial units (pradeśas) and is equal in size to the body. In that case, [in a body such as] that of an elephant, etc.,...

"Of all sentient beings" means that while there is a mutual difference among bodies and a difference between bodies and Brahman, there is oneness of the embodied one, who is Brahman. The qualifying attributes such as "omniscience" are intended to dispel the doubt regarding the impossibility of a single being being the controller of all conscious and unconscious entities. By the phrase "of the body and the embodied," he establishes that the defects of the body do not touch the embodied one. ||31||

The word "bhavat" (becoming) explains the word "evam" (thus) found in the Sūtra. The meaning is that the sense of the word "evam" is the mode of accepting that [object] as present in the intellect. "Countless locations" means a location devoid of a single form or number; the meaning is that its locations are indefinite. [Regarding "hastyādi": when [the self] enters the body of an ant from the body of an elephant and so forth, if it were limited to the size of that body while leaving aside the portion that does not fit, there would be incompleteness of the self.
This applies when one residing in an elephant's body enters the body of a goat.]

Thus, for the self (*ātman*) which is [previously] established [in a large body], when it enters a body such as that of an ant, which is of a smaller dimension, the consequence of incompleteness follows—that is, the consequence of being non-pervasive due to its occupation of a limited space—follows; this is the meaning. || 32 ||

Now, if it is argued that the contradiction [between the eternal nature of the Self and its changing states] is avoided by saying that the Self possesses the properties of contraction and expansion, such that it undergoes different states designated by the term ‘paryāya’ (successive modifications), to this he replies: 207. Nor is there non-contradiction even through successive modifications, because of [the resulting] transformation and other defects. (2.2.33)

Nor can the contradiction be resolved even by the admission of different states consisting of contraction and expansion; for that would entail defects such as modification and the resulting impermanence, leading to the undesirable consequence [of Brahman] being equivalent to objects like a jar. 208. And because of the persistence of the final state, and because both are eternal, there is no distinction. (2.2.34)

The final size of the soul, which occurs in the state of liberation, remains fixed because there is no subsequent assumption of another body; and since both that [final] size and the self in the state of liberation are eternal, that very size must be the soul's natural dimension. Consequently, there would be no difference from that [final state] even previously. Therefore, the claim that the soul has the size of the body is untenable; thus, this doctrine of the Ārhats is indeed inconsistent. (Sūtra 34). This concludes the section on "The Impossibility in One."

[The meaning is that] if there were entry [into the body], it would follow that the individual soul (jīva) would suffer incompleteness (*akātsnya*) in the form of deficiency compared to its previous state. || 32 || The specific state is characterized as being of the nature of contraction and expansion. By this, there is the exclusion of growth, decay, and so forth, as found in trees and the like. "Modification" (*vikāra*) refers to origination and destruction. "Impermanence" (*anityatva*) means existing for only a limited duration of time. || 33 ||
Even when there is a conjunction with another state of existence, contradiction is not established;
for if the Self were subject to modification, it would be equal to a jar or other such objects.
Since both the liberated soul and the size of that liberated soul are eternal, the individual self (jīva) does not possess the dimensions of the body.
Thus ends the section [6] on the impossibility [of multiple attributes] in one [substratum].
3. And not [in] the final state. 4.
Of that which is situated—i.e., because of its equality, etc.—vā. 2. In the body—vā. 7. Understood as a state—bhā.
3. It follows [as a consequence]—Bhāṣya, Śrī Madhyama 2.2.7].
Section on Paśupati || 2-2-7 || 209. On account of the lack of consistency in the case of the Lord (pati). 2-2-35.
It has been stated that the systems of Kapila, Kaṇāda, Sugata, and the Arhats are to be disregarded by those seeking the supreme good, because they are inconsistent and fall outside the Veda.
Now, it is stated that the system of Paśupati is likewise to be disregarded because it contradicts the Veda and is inconsistent.

The followers of that doctrine are of four kinds: 1. the *Kāpālas*, 2. the *Kālamukhas*, 3. the *Pāśupatas*, and 4. the *Śaivas*. All of these postulate a system of principles (*tattva-prakriyā*) contrary to the Vedas, as well as various means for attaining worldly prosperity and the ultimate liberation (*niḥśreyasa*) here and hereafter. They maintain a distinction between the efficient cause (*nimitta-kāraṇa*) and the material cause (*upādāna-kāraṇa*), and they declare Paśupati to be the efficient cause. Likewise, they prescribe the wearing of six seals (*mudrikā-ṣaṭka-dhāraṇā*) and so forth as a means to liberation. As the Kāpālas say: [The text continues with their specific doctrines.]
One who knows the six mudrās and the dance, and is skilled in the supreme mudrā, attains nirvāṇa by meditating on oneself seated upon the bhaga-throne.
The necklace, the breast-ornament, the earrings, the crest-jewel, the sacred ash, and the sacrificial thread—these are declared to be the six mudrās.
"Indeed, one whose body is sealed by these is not born here again.
Such is the passage beginning with these words.

Likewise, the Kālāmukhas [practice] such things as eating from skull-bowls, bathing in the ashes of corpses, consuming those ashes, carrying a staff, placing jars of liquor, and worshipping deities supported therein.
The means for achieving all goals pertaining to this world and the next— thus they declare:
"A bracelet of rudrākṣa on the hand and a single matted lock on the head."
"The skull-bowl and bathing with ashes," and so forth, are well known in the Śaiva Āgamas.
Likewise, through certain specific rites, even those of different castes attain the status of Brahmins and reach the highest stage of life (uttamāśrama).
And they say: "By the mere act of entering initiation, one becomes a Brāhmaṇa in an instant;
by undertaking the vow of the skull, a human being becomes an ascetic (yati)."

This conceptualization, this meditation, and this practice are contrary to the Vedas. Indeed, the Vedas declare that Nārāyaṇa alone is the Supreme Brahman, the efficient cause and the material cause of the universe:
"Nārāyaṇa is the Supreme Brahman; Nārāyaṇa is the supreme reality."
"Nārāyaṇa is the supreme light, the self; Nārāyaṇa is the highest.
"He thought: 'May I become many, may I procreate.'"
"He desired: 'May I be many, may I procreate';

He made Himself by Himself"—such are the passages [of the Upaniṣads]. Furthermore, they declare that meditation, which consists precisely in the knowledge of the Supreme Person who is the Supreme Brahman, is the means to liberation; for all the Vedāntas are in agreement on this point through such texts as: "I know this great Person, resplendent like the sun, beyond the darkness," and "Knowing Him alone, one becomes immortal here; there is no other path for the journey."

They state that the ritual action which constitutes the *itikartavyatā* (the manner of performance) consists precisely of sacrifices and the like connected to the castes (*varṇa*) and stages of life (*āśrama*) ordained by the Veda—as in such passages as: "Brahmins seek to know this very Self through the study of the Vedas, through sacrifice, through giving, through austerity, and through fasting... desiring this world alone, wandering mendicants go forth into homelessness. Furthermore, they argue that words such as Prajāpati, Śiva, Indra, Ākāśa, and Prāṇa—which are heard in certain injunctions concerning meditation (*upāsanā*) and the like—are established as referring to Nārāyaṇa by the *Nārāyaṇānuvāka*, which is dedicated solely to propounding the supreme reality.

This has been established in the [sūtra]: "But the teaching is according to the perspective of the scripture, as in the case of Vāmadeva. Likewise, [the phrase] "Indeed, the Vedas... expresses the difference between the Vedic position and that of the Pāśupatas; the sense is that all the branches [of the Veda] have attained unity through the principle of the cognition of all recensions (*sarvaśākhā-pratyaya*).

"Kevala" and so forth: Just as the sentence "He offers with the *juhū*" has as its sole purport the fact that the *juhū* is an instrument for the oblation (*homa*), and thus has no intention (*tātparya*) regarding the determination of the specific substance [to be used]; and just as the sentence "He whose *juhū* is made of *parṇa-wood*" has as its purport the determination of that specific substance, whereby the sentence "He offers with the *juhū*" becomes consistent with that meaning—so too, because sentences such as "Śambhu is to be meditated upon in the midst of the sky" are intended as injunctions for meditation (*upāsanā-vidhi*), they do not have the purport of determining the specific nature of the object of meditation (*upāsya-viśeṣa-nirṇaya*).
"Nārāyaṇa-anu" and so forth; [this refers to] the wandering mendicants desiring the world, beginning with: "In the beginning, Nārāyaṇa alone existed; neither Brahmā nor Īśāna existed. etc.

The words "Being alone, he would not find delight," which refer to the Creator Nārāyaṇa as spoken by the Breath at the beginning of creation, are established as being identical with those common terms— such as *sat*, *brahman*, and *ātman*— found in the same context in passages like, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone. These terms thus establish that very same entity.

This was established in the aphorism, "From which [proceeds] the birth, etc., of this [world]. Therefore, because it teaches the practice of meditating upon principles that contradict the Vedas, the system of Paśupati is indeed to be disregarded. || 35 ||
210. And because the substratum is untenable. (2-2-36)

For those outside the Veda, the conception of an Ishvara who is a mere instrumental cause arises from inference; however, that being the case, the Vedic mantras (*anuvāka*)—since they do not have as their primary purpose injunctions for meditation and the like—do indeed have as their primary purpose the determination of the specific object of meditation. Therefore, it must be accepted that sentences such as "Śambhu is the ether" and so forth have meanings that are consistent with that [determination]. Regarding the passage "One indeed... (*eko ha vā*): among the words *sa*, *brahman*, *ātman*, and so on, each preceding one is a general term, while each succeeding one is a specific term.

Thus, with respect to the word *Nārāyaṇa*, terms such as *Śambhu* and *Śiva* are general terms. Therefore, just as in the case of the injunction "one should sacrifice with an animal," where—according to the principle that "it is a goat because of the wording of the mantra"—the term is restricted to a specific [animal], it is logical that words such as *Sat*, *Brahman*, and *Ātman* culminate in the specific form of Nārāyaṇa; this is the meaning. Regarding the phrase "it has been established": since this very meaning was intended in passages such as "from which indeed these [beings arise]," it means that the author of the Sūtras also intended it in that way.
This meaning has been indicated by the commentary on the Sūtra beginning with "janmādi" and ending with "aparasmāt puṃsaḥ. || 35 ||

[The word] *adhīti* [means] "having studied. When it is desired to know whether a human statement has its source in a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*), it must have as its source either the Veda (*śruti*) or inference (*anumāna*) regarding matters beyond the reach of the senses. Among these, the view that it has the Veda as its source is rejected by demonstrating that it teaches the superiority and inferiority of things in a manner contrary to the Veda; thus, there follow three sūtras intended to refute the view that it has inference as its source. [The phrase] "of those who maintain the Vedas" [is used]. And because it is logically untenable—creation of the world by a bodiless Lord who is himself bodiless is not established, because, like a potter, the necessity of a supporting substrate is absent, which leads to contradiction.

Like a potter and others, [the Lord] must exercise superintendence by means of an essence. However, it is not possible for Paśupati, who is merely the efficient cause (*nimitta*), to exercise superintendence over *pradhāna* in the manner that a potter and others superintend clay and other materials; for he is bodiless (*aśarīra*). Indeed, the power of superintendence is observed only in those who possess bodies, such as potters and the like.
Nor should the possession of a body be admitted for the Lord; for whether that body were composed of parts and thus eternal or non-eternal, [it would lead to further difficulties].
Because a defect has been stated in the [sūtra] "Because [Brahman] has the Śāstra as its source" (Śāstrayonitvāt). || 36 ||
211. If it be argued that [the soul] is like an instrument, we say no, because of enjoyment and so forth. (2.2.37)

If it is argued that just as the soul (*jīva*), though bodiless, is seen to preside over the instruments such as the body, so too the Supreme Lord (*maheśvara*), though bodiless, can appropriately preside over *pradhāna*—we say no; because of [the necessity of] experience and so forth. For that presiding is caused by unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*) consisting of merit and demerit, for the sake of experiencing the fruits of karma in the form of merit and demerit. Similarly, it would follow that Paśupati also possesses merit and demerit in the form of *adṛṣṭa*, and thus all the experiences of their fruits and so on would result [for him]. Therefore, "presiding is not possible. (Sūtra 37)
212. Either it would have an end, or it would lack omniscience. (2.2.38)

The word "vā" has the sense of "and. [If it were so], like Paśupati, there would be the possession of unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), and like the individual soul (*jīva*), there would be finitude—namely, being the locus of creation, dissolution, and so forth—as well as non-omniscience; therefore, this view is indeed not to be respected.
As it is said: "On account of contradiction, it would be independent [of scripture]" (*Pūrva Mīmāṃsā Sūtra* 1.3.3).

Although it has been established by such statements that anything contrary to the Veda is to be disregarded, the Sūtra "On account of the lack of consistency in [the doctrine of] the Lord" (Patyurasāmañjasyāt) is commenced again for the purpose of demonstrating that the Pāśupata system is indeed contrary to the Veda. Even though certain features of the Pāśupata and Śaiva systems appear to be non-contradictory to the Veda, they are entirely inconsistent because their root lies in the postulation of a distinction between material cause and efficient cause—which contradicts the Veda—and the inversion of the relationship between the higher and lower principles (*parāvara-tattva*). Therefore, it is said: "on account of the lack of consistency. (38)
Nevertheless;
thus ends the section concerning animals and birds. 7.
The Section on the Non-Arising of What Has Already Arisen (Utpannasambhavādhikaraṇa) || 2-2-8 ||
213. Because of the impossibility of arising. (2.2.39)

On account of its similarity to the *Kapila* and other Tantras, the lack of authority (*aprāmāṇya*) is suspected even in the *Pañcarātra Tantra*, which teaches the means for attaining supreme liberation as declared by the Blessed One; that suspicion is here refuted.
In this regard, the following objection is raised:
"From Vāsudeva, who is the supreme cause and the Supreme Brahman, the individual soul named Saṅkarṣaṇa is born."

"From Saṅkarṣaṇa, the mind known as Pradyumna is born; from that, the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra) known as Aniruddha is born"—this is the meaning of the two *pūrvapakṣa* (prima facie) sūtras, introduced by the word "āśaṅkya" (having raised a doubt). "It is refuted"—this is the meaning of the two *siddhānta* (conclusive) sūtras. This is the division. [The inquiry is: Is the Pañcarātra authoritative in some respects like the Sāṅkhya and other systems, or is it authoritative in its entirety? Does it have any contradiction with the Śruti in some places, or is there no contradiction anywhere? And here, is the birth of the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth intended to be taught, or not?

Are the terms *saṅkarṣaṇa*, *pradyumna*, and so forth mentioned as qualifiers for the terms *jīva* and the rest? Or not? Alternatively, are the terms *jīva* and the rest mentioned as qualifiers for the terms *saṅkarṣaṇa* and the rest?

If words such as *saṅkarṣaṇa* were qualifiers of words such as *jīva*, then the origination of the individual soul (*jīva*) and so forth would be intended; however, because this would entail a contradiction with the Śruti, only that portion which is non-contradictory would possess authority, and thus only a single part of it would be acceptable. Conversely, if words such as *jīva* were qualifiers of words such as *saṅkarṣaṇa*, then since the origination of the individual soul and so forth would not be intended, there would be no contradiction with the Śruti anywhere; therefore, because it possesses authority in its entirety, its acceptability in its entirety by those seeking the supreme good (*niḥśreyasa*) would be established.

[Sūtra-meaning: Because birth—in the sense of a transformation (*vikāra*)—is impossible (*asambhava*), that is, because it is untenable for living beings (*jīvas*) who are established by scripture as being changeless (*nirvikāra*), the *Pāñcarātra-tantra*, which teaches a birth consisting of a change in essential nature (*svarūpānyathābhāva*), is not authoritative.
Furthermore, the doctrine of the birth of the living beings and so forth is seen in the *Pāñcarātra*;
however, due to its contradiction with the scriptural teaching on the impossibility of birth, it is inconsistent.
Thus indeed is the system of the Bhāgavatas. Herein, the birth of the individual soul (*jīva*) appears to be contrary to the Śruti. For the Śrutis declare the beginninglessness of the soul:
"The wise one is neither born nor does he die."
And so forth. || 39 ||
214. And the instrument does not belong to the agent. (2.2.40)
The production of the instrument, the mind (*manas*), from the agent, the individual soul (*jīva*)—as in the statement "from *Saṅkarṣaṇa* [is born] that which is called *Pradyumna*"—is not possible;
for [the scripture states]: "From this [Self] are born the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the mind (*manas*), and all the sense organs."

Thus, since there is scriptural testimony for the origin of even the mind from Brahman alone, the authority of this system [of logic] is also rejected because it propounds a meaning contrary to the Śruti. || 40 ||
This being the case, we reply:

"Or, even if [the Lord] exists as consciousness and so forth, there is no negation of that. By the word "or" (*vā*), the position is reversed. "Consciousness and so forth" refers to the *Pañcarātra* text beginning with "The Supreme Brahman, the ultimate cause," and so on. (Sūtra 2.2.41)

Regarding the phrase "from the word *vā*": the intention is that this is like [the sūtras] "Or rather, because the agent is common" (*api vā kartṛsāmānyāt*) and "Or rather, it is one, because the connection, form, injunction, and name are not different" (*ekaṃ vā saṃyogarūpacodanākhyāviśeṣāt*). As for the expression "and the beginning of consciousness" (*vijñānaṃ cādi*): from the root *ad* (to eat), with the suffix *ṇini* used in the sense of necessity, the form *ādi* is derived. By this, the entire agent is the individual soul (*jīva*), and the instrument is the mind; indeed, the mind is not born [from the soul].
For the birth of the mind is proclaimed as being from the individual soul, which is Saṅkarṣaṇa.
However, because Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others are determined to be the Supreme Self,
and because they are incarnations [who assume] the conceit of being individual souls (jīva), their authority is not denied.

Consciousness and the rest [are the forms]. Even though Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha are of the nature of the Supreme Brahman, the authority of the scripture intended to explain them is not negated.

What is meant is this: this objection—that "the origination of the individual soul (jīva) is stated as contradictory"—is raised by those who do not understand the Bhāgavata system. For their system is as follows: "The Supreme Brahman itself, known as Vāsudeva, who is affectionate toward those who take refuge in Him, manifests Himself in fourfold form by His own will in order to become the object of refuge for those who depend on Him. As it is said in the Pauṣkara-saṃhitā:

"Where the fourfold self (cāturātmya) is worshipped as that which is to be performed, that is indeed the Āgama [taught] by Brāhmaṇas through their own traditional designations passed down in succession. And regarding that worship of the fourfold self, it is stated in the *Sātvatasaṃhitā* that it is the worship of the Supreme Brahman known as Vāsudeva:
... [text continues] ... Thus, this worship of the fourfold self is the worship of the Supreme Brahman called Vāsudeva, as declared in the *Sātvatasaṃhitā*.
"For the Brahmins who perform sacrifices to the true Brahman known as Vāsudeva,
this great Brahmopaniṣad is the supreme scripture that bestows discernment."

The causality [of the Lord] is established precisely through His role as the destroyer of the world, based on the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the mantra, "He whose nature is consciousness," and from the statement, "The Blessed Vāsudeva is the supreme *prakṛti*. Thus, having established that Vāsudeva is of the nature of knowledge and the ultimate cause, the Blessed Vāsudeva is recalled by such terms as "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), according to the passages: "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite," "From that indeed... He was born," and "From which indeed..."

And in order to illuminate the unanimous consensus of the Vedānta texts—which establish that Brahman, whose nature is consciousness (*jñāna*), is the supreme cause—the term has been explained as "consciousness (*vijñāna*) and the primordial source (*ādi*).

Regarding the phrase "this has been stated": the meaning of the sentence of the Sūtra beginning with "Saṅkarṣaṇa" and so forth has been declared. Now, who are Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others? How is their state of being the Supreme Brahman established? Likewise, how is the origination from Brahman [of these] possible? Or how is the authority of the scripture [to be maintained]? On this point:

The statement beginning with ‘*kartavyatvena*’ (as something to be performed) is the etymological definition of the word ‘*āgama*’. By their own names—that is, by their respective names accompanied by the word ‘*namaḥ*’ (salutation)—the scripture possesses the quality of being an *āgama*, because it presents the object of worship through a traditional sequence; such is the meaning of the verse. By the phrase ‘the fourfold nature (*cāturātmya*) is worshipped,’ it is shown that the fourfold form beginning with Saṅkarṣaṇa is the object of refuge. Thus ends [the discussion of] ‘the fourfold nature.’

Since it is observed that the scripture devoted to the worship of the fourfold self (*cāturātmya*) is in fact devoted to the worship of the Supreme Brahman known as Vāsudeva, it is established that this fourfold nature belongs to Vāsudeva.

Indeed, that Supreme Brahman called Vāsudeva—whose body consists of the complete six divine attributes (*ṣāḍguṇya*), who is distinguished by the divisions of the subtle (*sūkṣma*), the expanded (*vyūha*), and the manifest (*vibhava*) forms, and who is worshipped by devotees according to their respective capacities through action preceded by knowledge—is fully attained.

They say: "Having attained the *vyūha* through the worship of the *vibhava*, and through the worship of the *vyūha*, the subtle *paraṃ brahma* known as Vāsudeva is attained. For the *vibhava* refers to the group of manifestations such as Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others. The *vyūha* consists of the fourfold form of Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha. The subtle one, however, is the *paraṃ brahma* known as Vāsudeva, whose body is composed solely of the [transcendent] *guṇas*. As it is stated in the *Pauṣkara*: "From this scripture, the supreme, imperishable *brahma* known as Vāsudeva is properly attained through action preceded by knowledge."

And so forth. Therefore, since even Saṅkarṣaṇa and the others are forms assumed by the Supreme Brahman itself through its own will, there is no denial of the authority of the scriptures that describe them; for they speak of a birth in the form of assuming a body by His own will, caused by His affection for those who have taken refuge in Him—a birth established by the Śruti text: "Though being unborn, He is born in many ways. Thus, the authority of the scriptures that describe this is not refuted.

In this context, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha are the presiding deities over the principles (tattvas) of the individual soul (jīva), mind (manas), and ego (ahaṅkāra). It is not contradictory that these very deities are designated by the terms "individual soul" and so forth, just as Brahman is designated by terms such as "ether" (ākāśa) and "breath" (prāṇa). 41.
216. And because of contradiction. (2-2-42)
Indeed, the production of the individual soul (*jīva*) is contradictory even within that very system. As it is stated in the *Paramasaṃhitā*:
"Inert, for the sake of another, eternal, and constantly changing;
composed of the three qualities (*triguṇa*), the field (*kṣetra*) of those who act—this is said to be the nature of *prakṛti*."
"The relationship between that [prakṛti] and the person (puruṣa) is by way of pervasion;
it is determined to be beginningless and endless from the perspective of ultimate reality.

Thus, because the eternity of the individual soul (jīva) is stated in all the *saṃhitās*, the production of the soul's essential nature is indeed prohibited in the *Pañcarātra-tantra*. However, the worldly and Vedic conventions regarding birth, death, and so forth, as they apply to the soul, are established accordingly.
Likewise,

this will be stated in the section beginning with "The Self does not originate, because of scripture" (BrSū 2.3.18). Therefore, since the origination of the individual soul is likewise refuted there, the suspicion regarding its lack of authority based on the doctrine of the soul's origination is "cast far away."

"And because of contradiction" (*vipratiṣedhāt*). When the individual souls (*jīva*) and others are the subjects qualified by the terms "Saṅkarṣaṇa" and so forth, favorable indicative marks (*liṅga*) have been stated. Now, when the individual souls are the subjects qualified by the terms "Saṅkarṣaṇa" and so forth, unfavorable indicative marks are being stated. "Contradiction" (*vipratiṣedha*) means a specific negation (*viśeṣeṇa pratiṣedhaḥ*), or alternatively, a manifold negation (*vividha-pratiṣedhaḥ*). Just as in the expression "one who has understood through a conflict of scriptural texts" (*śrutivipratipannā*), the meaning is that she has understood specifically through hearing from us; so it is here.

Just as the word "contradiction" (*vipratiṣedha*) is used in the phrase "it is contradicted by those treatises," so too this [word] is intended to mean negation (*niṣedha*), that is, contradiction (*vyāghāta*). By the words "in all cases," the meaning of the prefix *vi-* is intended to be expressed. "It will be stated" means that it will be explained that origination and destruction consist in the expansion and contraction of knowledge caused by the conjunction of the body with the substratum of the cause and so forth. And as for this objection raised by some—

Regarding the claim that "Śāṇḍilya, finding no finality in the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs (aṅgas), studied the Pañcarātra scripture," and the assertion that "the Tantra is contrary to the Vedas because of the statement that 'no fulfillment of the human goal was obtained within the Vedas along with their auxiliary limbs,'" this too is merely a manifestation of faith on the part of those who have not smelled the words of the Vedas and have not grasped the collection of logical arguments that supplement them. For example:

It has been stated that the passage, "Day after day they speak untruth, those who offer the Agnihotra before sunrise," is a deprecation of the pre-sunrise offering for the purpose of praising the post-sunrise offering; and likewise, in the introduction to the Bhūmavidyā, after Nārada has begun by saying, "O Venerable One, I have studied the Ṛgveda, the Yajurveda, the Sāmaveda, and the Atharvaṇa as the fourth, and the Itihāsa-Purāṇa as the fifth," and so forth,
having enumerated all the branches of knowledge, [he continues].

"Therefore, O Blessed One, I am merely a knower of mantras, not a knower of the Self"—this statement regarding the non-attainment of "knowledge of the Self" in all sciences other than the Bhūmavidyā is made for the purpose of praising the Bhūmavidyā that is about to be taught.

Alternatively, this declaration by Nārada is due to his failure to attain that supreme reality which is propounded in the Vedas along with their auxiliary branches (vedāṅgas). This is understood from the subsequent mention of the supreme Brahman known as Vāsudeva, who is to be known through the Vedānta, in the case of Śāṇḍilya as well.

Likewise, because the meaning of the Vedas is difficult to comprehend, the commencement of this treatise for the sake of easy understanding is stated in the *Paramasaṃhitā*: "O Blessed One, the Vedas have been studied by me along with their limbs (*aṅga*) and sub-limbs (*upāṅga*), in full detail; and the auxiliary sciences (*aṅga*), including the dialogues (*vākovākya*), have also been heard by me. Yet, despite all these, I do not perceive anywhere the path to the highest good (*śreyas*)—without which doubt—I by which perfection shall be attained."
Thus:
"The Lord Hari, the wise one, having extracted the essence from the Vedāntas,
condensed [this work] at his ease out of compassion for his devotees."
And thus it is said.

Therefore, that Blessed One—Vāsudeva, known as the Supreme Brahman, the sole physician whose Veda is the Veda alone; an ocean of infinite, noble qualities such as knowledge and bliss, which consist solely of auspiciousness opposed to everything to be abandoned; whose will is ever true; [establishes] his devotees—who abide according to the system of the four castes and four stages of life and are oriented toward the human goals known as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa.

"Likewise"—the meaning is: "in accordance with what has been stated. "By doubt" (*saṃśayena*): doubt is of the form, "Is there a contradiction between the heard meanings in the Vedic recensions (*śākhās*) that have not been studied, or not? Alternatively, it is of the form, "I do not know which among the understood matters is the most beneficial (*śreyas*)."

"In the Vedāntas," etc. [This refers to] the *Mokṣadharma*: "In which Anuvākas, Niṣads, and Upaniṣads do those whose nature is truth proclaim the Truth within the truthful Sāmans? Regarding the subject of the *Ekāyana* branch, there is the statement of the Supreme Lord (Pārameśvara): "O Sage, this great [branch] is the root of the vast Veda-tree; the *Ṛg* and other Vedas are its trunk, and likewise, they are its branches. Such passages are to be observed.

Therefore—because the meaning of Vedānta is difficult to comprehend—the epithets such as "the Blessed One" (*bhagavān*) and so forth are intended to exclude the possibility of doubt regarding delusion, deception, and the like. By the word "Blessed One" (*bhagavat*), what is intended is the state of being exclusively composed of auspicious qualities while being the opposite of all that is to be abandoned (*heyapratyanīka*). The use of the word "only" (*eka*) in the phrase "Veda-only" (*vedaika*) is made with the intention of refuting the inference that "He is subject to defects because He is a person," by means of the sublation of the very means of knowledge that apprehends the subject (*dharmigrāhakapramāṇabādha*).

The phrase "nikhilahēya" (devoid of all that is to be discarded) expresses the meaning established by the authority of the designation "Bhagavat. The phrase "satyasaṅkalpa" (of true resolve) is a qualification consistent with the systematic arrangement to be described hereafter. The word "bhaktān" (devotees) is based on the statement: "Having attained a state of purity through devotion, I know Janārdana from the scripture."

Having observed that the Great Ocean of boundless compassion, virtuous conduct, affection, and magnanimity, having ascertained the Vedas—namely the divisions of Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan—which are divided into infinite branches and consist of the forms of knowledge (vidyā), explanatory passages (arthavāda), and mantras; and having realized that these are difficult to fathom for all gods and men other than Himself, He Himself composed the Pañcarātra scripture which reveals the true nature of their meaning. This is beyond reproach.
Having begun thus and established the system of the *Pañcarātra* scriptures through an extensive treatise, [it says]:

"This [work] has been extracted from the vast narrative of the *Bhārata*, which consists of a hundred thousand [verses], by churning it with the churning-stick of the intellect, like clarified butter from curd; just as fresh butter is [extracted] from curd, and just as the Brahmin is [the foremost] among bipeds."
"The Āraṇyaka is like nectar extracted from the Vedas and from medicinal herbs. "This Great Upaniṣad is endowed with the four Vedas;

it is designated as Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Kṛtānta, and Pañcarātra. "This is the highest good, this is Brahman, this is the unsurpassed benefit. "It is honored by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as by the Atharva-Aṅgirasas."

"This instruction alone shall indeed be the authority. By the two terms "Sāṅkhya" and "Yoga," the Yoga of Knowledge and the Yoga of Action are respectively denoted, as it has been said: "By the Yoga of Knowledge for the Sāṅkhyas, and by the Yoga of Action for the Yogis.
Furthermore, in the Bhīṣma Parvan:
"By Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, and Śūdras who have fulfilled their characteristics..."
Mādhava is to be honored, served, and worshipped.
"Having resorted to the Sātvata rule, which was sung by Saṅkarṣaṇa.

How could Bādarāyaṇa, speaking thus—a foremost knower of the Vedas—declare the lack of authority of the Sātvata scripture, which is devoted to propounding the worship and meditation upon Vāsudeva, who is the Supreme Brahman to be known through the Vedānta?
But surely it has been asked:
"Sāṅkhya, Yoga, Pañcarātra, the Vedas, and likewise Pāśupata—
O Sage, do these have a single foundation or separate foundations?"

By such statements, it is indicated that even the Sāṃkhya and other systems deserve respect; however, in the *Śārīraka*, the Sāṃkhya and others are refuted. Therefore, this system (*tantra*) is also equal to them!
To this it is said: no; for even there, [the author] introduces this very same logic set forth in the *Śārīraka*.

Regarding the question, "Are these [systems] based on a single foundation or on separate foundations?", the meaning is as follows: Do Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pāśupata, Veda, and Pañcarātra aim to propound a single reality, or do they aim to propound separate realities? If they aim to propound a single reality, what is that one reality? But if they aim to propound separate realities, then—since they would be intent on propounding mutually contradictory meanings regarding the [single] entity—[there would be a contradiction].
And because conceptual construction is impossible, only one means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) must be accepted; what is that one?—thus [is the question].
Speaking this reply to him:
"O royal sage, know that these are various systems of knowledge;
Kapila is indeed the proponent of Sāṃkhya."
Beginning with these words, having established that the Sāṃkhya, Yoga, and Pāśupata systems are of human origin because they were composed by Kapila, Hiraṇyagarbha, and Paśupati respectively,
he stated that the Vedic teacher named Apāntaratamas is [the source] of the Vedas, thereby declaring their non-human (apauruṣeya) origin; and then he said,
"Nārāyaṇa himself is the speaker of the entire Pañcarātra," and "Nārāyaṇa himself is the speaker of the Pañcarātra-tantra."

Regarding the phrase "yataḥ" and so forth: the meaning is that he introduces the logical principle that while the Sāṃkhya and other systems possess authority in those parts not contradicted by the Vedas, the Śrī Pāñcarātra possesses authority in its entirety because it is entirely non-contradictory.

"What are these? [This question arises as follows: if the intent is to establish a single reality (*ekatatva*), there is a desire to know the specific object of knowledge (*prameya*); if the intent is to establish distinct realities (*pṛthaktatva*), there is a desire to know the specific means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). In such cases as "One takes the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice," "One does not take the *ṣoḍaśin* cup at the *atirātra* sacrifice," "One offers after sunrise," "One offers before sunrise," "One should sacrifice with rice," and "One should sacrifice with barley," an option (*vikalpa*) is possible in practice, depending on the difference in qualified persons (*adhikārin*), the difference in time (*kāla*), or the difference in result (*phala*).

The meaning is that, since conceptual construction (*vikalpa*) is impossible regarding an established entity (*siddhavastu*), there would be a contradiction [if multiple means of knowledge were applied], and thus there would be only one single means of knowledge. Regarding the phrase "these are cognitions": have you asked about the respective intentions of those various authors? Or have you asked about the status of the object? The meaning is that if one asks about their respective intentions, the doctrines are indeed established separately.
