Also, in the *Śārīraka* [Brahmasūtra]—[the text continues with: *na* ... *praṇītatvena*—*da*. 2 *yathā*—*du*. 6 *tamā*—*da*.

Regarding the statement [in the *Śrībhāṣya* 2.2.8], "Thus speaking," the intention is as follows: since human-authored *tantras* propound mutually contradictory matters, and because they assert things contrary to the reality known through the Veda—which, being authorless (*apauruṣeya*), is free from even the slightest trace of defects such as error—it is difficult for them to possess validity regarding the reality as it truly exists. Furthermore, that which is known through the Veda is Nārāyaṇa, who is the Supreme Brahman.

Therefore, the reality of this [Supreme Being], who is taught as Pradhāna, Puruṣa, Paśupati, and so forth in their respective systems, must be accepted as being essentially Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme Brahman known through the Vedāntas. Thus it has been said:
"O best of kings! In all these systems of knowledge, the Lord Nārāyaṇa is seen as the final goal, according to scripture and according to reason."

Thus: "Reflecting upon the reality taught in various scriptures according to tradition and according to reason" means that for one who reflects on the objects taught in those respective scriptures as supported by logic, it is seen that "Nārāyaṇa alone is the ultimate ground (niṣṭhā) of every entity. The meaning is that for one who contemplates the Brahman-nature of everything—by means of such texts as "All this is indeed Brahman" and "The universe is Nārāyaṇa"—regarding those principles propounded in various systems [of thought] which do not have Brahman as their essence, it is perceived that Nārāyaṇa alone is the ultimate ground.

Therefore, since Nārāyaṇa—who is the supreme Brahman known through the Vedānta—is himself the speaker of the entire Pañcarātra, and since that Tantra is the exposition of His essential nature and the means of worshipping Him, no one can attribute to it the same status as other systems (tantras). Thus, it is said therein: "In this way, Sāṅkhya, Yoga, the Vedas, and the Āraṇyakas are mutually related as limbs; yet the Pañcarātra is declared [to be their soul]."

Thus: Sāṅkhya and Yoga constitute "Sāṅkhyayoga"; the Vedas and the Āraṇyakas constitute "Vedāraṇyaka. These are mutual auxiliaries; because they are unified by their intent to propound a single system, they are called "the one Pañcarātra."
"Thus he speaks"—with these words, he states the result [of the previous argument].
By the phrase "because they do not have Brahman as their essence," he states the nature of the reflective awareness (*parāmarśa*) of the reality supported by logic.

The expression "the Pañcarātra is one" expresses unity through implication (*ārtha*), because it ends in the singular number. Alternatively, by the phrase "become unified" (*ekībhūtāni*), the meaning resulting from the relationship of primary and subordinate parts (*aṅgāṅgibhāva*) is stated. "The Pañcarātra is one" is the explanation of the single word *eka*.
The authoritative sources are the Vedas and the Āraṇyakas. He says: [the text] refers to these. They are endowed with their auxiliary limbs (aṅgas).

This is what is meant: having accepted the twenty-five principles (tattvas) taught in Sāṃkhya, the yoga consisting of restraints (yama), observances (niyama), and so forth as taught in Yoga, and the essential forms of rituals prescribed in the Vedas, [these texts] declare that the principles have Brahman as their essence, that yoga is a mode of meditating upon Brahman, and that rituals are a form of worshiping Him; thus the Āraṇyakas establish the true nature of Brahman.
This very point has been clarified by the Supreme Brahman, Nārāyaṇa himself, in the Pañcarātra Tantra—thus [it is said].

In the *Śārīraka* [Brahma-sūtras], it is only the non-Brahman nature of the principles taught by the Sāṃkhya that is refuted, not their essential form; the same applies to Yoga and Pāśupata. Furthermore, in these systems, the Lord's status as a mere efficient cause (*nimittakāraṇa*), the conception of a supreme principle contrary to reality, and conduct excluded from the Vedas are refuted; however, the essential form of Yoga and the essential form of Pāśupati are not refuted. Therefore: "Sāṃkhya, Yoga, Pañcarātra, the Vedas, and likewise Pāśupata—these are authoritative regarding the Self and should not be attacked with logical arguments."

Thus, it is said: "Only those specific essential natures (svarūpa) expressed by this or that [teacher] should be accepted; not everything taught by the Jinas and Sugatas should be rejected," because this has the same meaning as the statement: "According to the scriptures and according to reason, the Lord Nārāyaṇa is the ultimate goal. || 42 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the impossibility of origination. || 8 ||
(The Section on the Pañcarātra).
Thus ends the second quarter of the second chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja. || 2 ||

"According to the rule" (yathānyāyam): it is not merely a reference to those respective scriptures; for here, a reference to the *nyāya* (logical principle) is also stated. If the statement "Sāṃkhya, Yoga," etc., were interpreted otherwise, then this statement—which declares the authority [of these systems] even regarding parts that contradict the Veda—would become non-authoritative according to the *nyāya*: "In case of contradiction, however, it should be disregarded" (*virodhe tvanapekṣaṃ syāt*). This is because the Sāṃkhya system propounds that the killing of the animal dedicated to Agni and Soma (*agnīṣomīya*) and other such acts are unrighteous (*adharma*). The phrase "because of having the same purpose" (*aikārthyāt*) provides the reason for the point already stated. || 42 ||
2. Nor from a creator; 3. consciousness and so forth; 4. contradiction—thus ends the section on the impossibility of origination (Utpattyasambhavādhikaraṇa). || 8 ||
Thus ends the second quarter of the second chapter.
The Third Pāda of the Second Adhyāya in the Śrībhāṣya.
MT: 11
Salutations to the illustrious Rāmānuja. Salutations to Śrī. Salutations to Śrīdhara.

In the Śrī Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya, in the second chapter on Non-contradiction (Avirodhādhyāya), the third section (pāda) concerning the ether (viyat): 217. "The ether [is not produced], because it is not mentioned [in the scriptures]. (2.3.1)

It has been stated that the systems outside the Veda, such as Sāṅkhya and others, are inconsistent because they are rooted in fallacious reasoning and involve contradictions. Now, in order to demonstrate that our own position is free from even the slightest scent of defects such as contradiction, the manner in which the world—composed of sentient and insentient beings—is an effect of Brahman is clarified.

Regarding the phrase "from Sāṃkhya and so forth": this is the meaning. In the first quarter (pāda) of the second chapter, the objections raised by opponents concerning the cause were refuted. Now, in the third [quarter], the objections raised by opponents concerning the effect are being refuted. Therefore, the third quarter is connected with the first. If it is argued that the second [quarter] must come last because its purpose is the rejection of the positions of others, [we reply: the refutation of objections regarding the cause and the rejection of the positions of others are both logically consistent [with the first quarter].

The connection [of this section] is as follows: it is appropriate that the refutation of the defects stated by the opponent regarding the subject matter of the effect (kārya) should follow immediately. With this meaning in mind, [the author says] "as being the effect of Brahman. [Regarding the phrase] "consisting of the sentient and the insentient": therein, a doubt is raised as to whether the ether (viyat) is produced from those two entities—the sentient and the insentient—or not.
Thus [ends the introduction].

What is logical? That space (*viyat*) is not produced. Why? Because it is not heard [in scripture]. For there is the possibility of hearing [the mention] of that which is possible; however, for that which is impossible—such as the production of space or a sky-flower—the status of being denotable by a word is not possible. Indeed, the production of space—which is partless and all-pervading—cannot be established, just as it cannot be of the Self (*ātman*).

And for this very reason, because of the impossibility of [the soul] being produced, in the Chāndogya Upaniṣad, within the context of creation, the origin of fire and the other elements alone is recorded:
"It thought: 'May I be many, may I procreate. It created fire."
Thus it is said in the Taittirīya, the Atharvaṇa, and other texts:
"From this very Self, space was produced"; and "From this [Self] are born breath, mind, and all the senses;
[and] space, wind, light, water."
The production of ether heard in such passages as these is sublated by reason of its contradiction with the actual state of things. || 1 ||
This being the case, it is replied: "But it exists. (2-3-2)

However, there is indeed the origination of space (*ākāśa*). For the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) concerns objects that transcend the senses; it is indeed capable of establishing the origination of space, even though that is not apprehended by other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*). Nor can an inference of non-origination—based on reasons such as its being partless (*niravayavatva*), which would contradict the Veda—successfully arise regarding a matter established by the Veda. Furthermore, it will be stated later that the non-origination of the Self (*ātman*) is not caused by its being partless. || 2 ||
He raises an objection again:

"Because of the impossibility of a secondary sense and because of the word [itself]. (2-3-3). Regarding the statement, "From that very Self, space was produced," he states the reason intended by the word "but" (*tu*)—namely, the Śruti. In the subsequent sūtra, which aims to establish an alternative interpretation of this sūtra, the use of the feminine gender in the term "gauṇī" (secondary) indicates that the Śruti is intended as the proving authority. And it is not capable of arising...; here, the fallacy of "missing the proper time" (*kālātyayāpadeśa*) is intended. || 2 ||

"Therefore" [is said]. Since figurative application (*gauṇavṛtti*) is a property of words, and because it also possesses the feminine gender ending there, the direct Vedic statement (*śruti*) is the primary qualifier. And because by that direct statement it is declared that "from the Self, space was produced," it is certain that the origination of that space exists.
There may be a multitude of scriptural passages concerning origination [of the world], because the emergence of space is impossible,
and because of the connection with the primacy of fire, as well as from the scriptural statement regarding its own immortality.

It is therefore appropriate to consider that the scriptural passage concerning the origin of ether, such as "From that [Self], ether was produced," is figurative; for the statement "It created fire" indicates that,
for the desirous-to-create Brahman, fire is produced first, and thus the priority of the production of fire serves to negate the production of ether.
Because of the impossibility [of that being the case],
and because of the statement, "The wind and the intermediate space— this is the immortal," and because of the designation of the ether as "immortal. (Sūtra 3)
If it is asked: "How can the single word 'sambhūta' be figurative with respect to space (ākāśa) and primary with respect to fire and so forth?"—[the answer is:
"And it may be so for a single [word], as in the case of the word 'Brahman'. (2.3.4)

Therefore, because the term "originated" (*sambhūta*) cannot be taken in its primary sense with respect to space (*ākāśa*) in the passage, "From that very Self, indeed, space originated," the word "originated," which is used figuratively there,

must certainly be taken in its primary sense when it is applied in subsequent passages such as "from air, fire. This is just like the word "Brahman"— just as the word "Brahman" [is used figuratively in one context and primarily in another].

The intention is that the comprehension of specific scriptural passages occurs by virtue of the subject matter at hand. Regarding the phrase "the production of fire" (*teja utpatti*): it is not possible for the production of ether (*viyat*) to occur after the production of fire and the subsequent elements; nor is it possible for it to occur before, because fire is the first [element mentioned]. Thus is the meaning. In the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*), since the two reasons relate to the intermediate points to be established, the two words "impossibility" (*asaṃbhava*) and "word" (*śabda*) are presented within a single sūtra. Therefore, a division of the sūtras is not appropriate. || 3 ||

It may be so. One should consider such usages as "Brahman is austerity" (*tapasā brahma*) and "Austerity is Brahman" (*tapaḥ brahma*). The examples "Food is Brahman" (*annam brahma*) and "Bliss is Brahman" (*ānandaḥ brahma*) are not cited because they lack the status of being either primary or secondary [designations]. Indeed, the application of the word "Brahman" to food and the like occurs only when the notion of Brahman is superimposed upon them.
In the passage, "From that, this Brahman, name, form, and food are born," the term is used figuratively with respect to the *pradhāna* (the primary cause); yet, within that very same context:

Just as the expression "Brahman is built up by austerity; from that food is born" is used primarily with reference to Brahman, so it is here. And in the case of a secondary application (anuṣaṅga), there is indeed a repetition of the designation, just as there is a repetition of hearing [the word]; this is the meaning. || 4 ||
221. He avoids [the objection] by stating: "There is a loss of the thesis because there is no distinction. (2-3-5)

According to the *Chāndogya* Śruti, it is not appropriate to assume that other Śrutis which speak of the origination of ether (*viyat*) are figurative; for the origination of ether is indeed accepted by the *Chāndogya* Śruti itself through the passage beginning with "By which [Brahman] the unheard becomes heard," since there is the promise of the "cognition of all" through the cognition of Brahman. Indeed, the non-contradiction of that promise occurs precisely because ether, as an effect of Brahman, is non-different from it. || 5 ||
222. From words [the suffix *cha* is applied]. (Pāṇini 4.2.92)
Furthermore, the origination of space is understood from the Chāndogya Upaniṣad;
for prior to creation, there is the statement establishing oneness: "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only, without a second."

And from such scriptural passages as, "All this has that as its self" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.8.7), there is the cognition of non-difference [of the world] from Brahman by virtue of its being an effect. Nor [is it the case that Brahman is not the cause], for [the scripture says]: "It emitted heat" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.3).
Thus, the scriptural statement regarding the origin of fire precludes the origin of ether;
however, the mere non-mention of the origin of ether is not sufficient to negate the origin of ether as established by another scriptural passage. 6.

The phrase "of this nature" (*aitadātmyam*) is employed because its purpose is to convey the meaning that "the entire world, which is an effect, has as its self the Brahman which is its cause. The word "self" (*ātman*) refers to the Inner Ruler (*antaryāmin*). By the word "this" (*etad*), the state of being the cause previously introduced is intended. The meaning is: he who is the self of the world in its causal state is indeed the self of the world even in its effected state. By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*), passages such as "All these, my dear, have Being as their root" and "All this, verily, is Brahman" are intended.

"Nor [is it so]" means that the statement regarding the origin of the pot does not preclude the origin of the cloth; such is the meaning. Regarding "of fire": for only the origin of fire is heard in scripture, not the non-origin of other things. Therefore, priority is not heard. It is improper to assume what is unheard on the basis of what is heard; rather, it is proper to assume what is unheard on the basis of what is heard. || 6 ||
223. But as far as there is modification, there is division, as in the case of the world. (2.3.7)

The word "tu" (but) has the sense of "and. By such statements as "All this has that as its self," the non-differentiation of that ether from Brahman—its very origin—is indeed stated. It is like the worldly case: just as in the world, after stating "All these are the sons of Devadatta," by specifying the origin of some among them from him, the origin of all of them is effectively stated; so it is here. This being the case,
"The wind and the intermediate space—this is the immortal," this refers to the intention that they endure for a long time, like the gods. || 7 ||
224. By this, Mātariśvan is explained. (2.3.8)

By this very same reasoning, the origin of Mātariśvan—that is, Vāyu—has also been explained. The separate mention of ether (viyat) and Mātariśvan in the sūtra is for the purpose of referring back to Mātariśvan in the subsequent statement: "Fire [is born] from that, for so it says. || 8 ||

"Being a modification" (*vikāratva*) means "being an effect" (*kāryatva*). By the word "etcetera" (*ādi*) in the phrase "by these and so forth," the determination of oneness (*ekatvāvadhāraṇa*) and other such [reasons] are intended to be included. And "this being the case" means that if the meaning were not restricted, there would be the undesirable consequence (*prasaṅga*) that even air (*vāyu*) would not be produced; this is the sense. (7) "For the sake of reference" (*parāmarśārtham*): although it could have been stated in a single sūtra, the separate formulation of the sūtras is for the purpose of referring back to them later; thus is the meaning. *Yoga* refers to the sūtra. (8)
By the Śruti statement, "All this has that as its self," the state of being a modification of everything is established;
thus, the origination of all things from Brahman occurs just as in the world.
Likewise, from the statement "from space,
air," it is certain that the destruction of the effects of Brahman has been explained by the word "air."
225. But the non-existence of that which exists is impossible, because it is not logically tenable. (2.3.9)

The word "tu" (but) has the sense of restriction. "Impossibility" means non-origination; it is impossible for anything other than the existent Brahman itself to originate, because such a thing is logically untenable.

This is what is meant: the demonstration of the origin of ether (*viyat*) and wind (*mātariśvan*) is for the sake of illustration. However, regarding the impossibility of the origin of that which exists—the supreme cause, the highest Brahman itself—there is no "non-origination" possible for the entire phenomenal world (*prapañca*) distinct from it, such as the unmanifest (*avyakta*), the great principle (*mahat*), the ego (*ahaṅkāra*), the subtle elements (*tanmātra*), the sense organs, ether, wind, and so forth; for this world has been understood to be an effect through the promise of the knowledge of all by means of the knowledge of one, and other such statements. Thus, [the claim of its] non-origination is not tenable. || 9 ||
Thus ends the section concerning ether (viyad-adhikaraṇa). || 1 ||
The Section on Light (Tejo’dhikaraṇa) || 2.3.2 ||

226. *Tejo'tastathā hyāha* (2-3-10). [The meaning: The creation of air and so forth proceeds from Brahman alone, which has fire (*tejas*) and the other elements as its body, and not from fire and the others alone.]
It has been stated that everything other than Brahman is an effect of Brahman.
Now, it is considered whether the production of remote effects arises solely from their respective immediate causes, or rather from Brahman in those specific forms.
What is the correct view? That they arise solely from those respective entities.
Why? Because it is like fire; therefore, it arises from air itself. For [the scripture] says: "From air, fire. || 10 ||

Regarding the phrase "it is being considered": Is the production of the principles (tattvas) beginning with Mahat from their own respective prior causes alone, or rather from Brahman in those various forms? Furthermore, in passages such as "from space, air," do the words "space" and so forth refer merely to space and the rest, or do they refer to Brahman existing in those states? And in passages such as "the fire thought," does the indicative mark of reflection (abhidhyāna) lead us to understand that the words for fire and the rest refer to Brahman existing in those states, or not?

Is there a figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā*) when [the word] has that state as its ultimate referent? Or not? Does a fault such as contradiction with linguistic usage (*vyutpatti-virodha*) arise when Brahman is denoted by means of a non-literal function (*avasāna-vṛtti*)? Or not? When [such a fault] does arise, then—since denotation of Brahman is impossible through a non-final [literal] sense and because this results in the necessity of figurative indication (*lakṣaṇā-prasaṅga*)—the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of "meditation" (*abhidhyāna*) would lack the power to convey that [the passage] refers to Brahman. Consequently, the words would refer only to ether and so forth, and thus [the result] would be merely ether and the like. 227. *Āpaḥ* (Water). Sūtra 2.3.11.
Water also, therefore, is produced from fire alone; for it says: "From fire, water" and "He created that water. || 11 ||
The earth arises from water;
"from water [came] the earth," and "they created food."
Thus indeed he said. 12.

The production of air and so forth occurs [from Brahman] when there is no defect such as the breakdown of etymological derivation (*vyutpatti*). At that time, since there is the possibility of denoting Brahman through non-terminating [application], there is no occasion for the fault of secondary indication (*lakṣaṇā*); because the indicative marks of pervasion (*abhivyāpti*) found in words such as "fire" (*tejas*) lead to the understanding that they refer to Brahman, words such as "ether" (*ākāśa*) also refer to Brahman in its respective state. Thus, it is established that the production of air and so forth is from Brahman itself in its state as ether. || 12 ||
One might raise the objection: "Since water was created by fire (*tejas*), how can it be determined by the Śruti that 'these [waters] are the work of Brahmā'?
(The *Tejo’dhikaraṇa*).
[Objection: But how is the earth denoted by the word "food" (*anna*)? To this, he says: 229. "On account of the context, the form, and other words. (2.3.13)

Since this section concerns the creation of the great elements (*mahābhūta*), it is understood that "earth" alone is denoted by the word "food" (*anna*). This is because everything edible is a modification of earth; thus, the term for the effect is used for the cause. Likewise, in the subsequent portion of the passage where the forms of the elements are described—"That which is the red form of fire is the form of heat (*tejas*); that which is white is of water; that which is black is of food"—it is understood that what is denoted by the word "food" is of the same nature as water and heat. Furthermore, there is another scriptural statement in the same context: "From fire [comes] water; from water, earth."
Thus it is heard in scripture. Therefore, the earth alone is denoted by the word "food" (anna), and from water alone the earth is born.
Fire and the others cited [in the text] are for the sake of illustration;
the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest are likewise [born] from their own immediate antecedents.
Thus they arise, in accordance with their respective scriptural declarations and without contradiction:

"From this [Self] is born the vital breath, the mind, and all the senses; space, air, light, water, and the earth which supports all. "From that, indeed, are born name, form, and food. "From that very Self, space was produced. "It created fire."
These and other such [arguments] are consistent even though Brahman is the cause only through a traditional succession (paramparayā). || 13 ||
The heading—this is the introduction. Regarding the phrase "of that which is to be eaten" (adanīyasya): the meaning is that the term for the effect is applied metaphorically to the cause. || 13 ||
"The [gods] created food"—by this, the creation of the earth is stated;
for from words such as "food" and "bearer," there arises the form of the domain of the elements.
In this regard—[the opponent might argue] that [the Supreme Person is not the cause], because [the texts] are supplementary to other statements.
This being the position reached, we reply:

**"But from the meditation on Him alone [proceeds the creation], on account of His characteristic marks; He [is the cause]. (2.3.14)** By the word "but" (*tu*), the previous position is set aside. Even for the effects such as the Great Principle (*mahat*) and the rest, that same Supreme Person is the cause, having as His body each respective subsequent entity.

Why? Because of that characteristic mark, which consists in the form of reflection upon that [Brahman]. "Reflection" refers to the volition, "May I become many. From the scriptural hearing of such reflection in the form of a volition for one's own manifold becoming—namely, "That fire reflected:
'May I be many, may I procreate,' and 'Those waters reflected:
May we be many, may we procreate'"—it is understood that even for the causes such as Mahat, Ahaṃkāra, and Ākāśa, their creation of their own effects is preceded by a similar kind of reflection.

And such a vision is possible only for the Supreme Brahman itself, which has those various things as its body. Moreover, the Supreme Brahman’s state of being the Self of all by virtue of having all things as its body is heard in the Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa:
"He who dwells in the earth," "He who dwells in the waters," "He who dwells in fire," "He who dwells in air," "He who dwells in space," and so forth.
And in the Subāla Upaniṣad:
Beginning with "He whose body is the earth," it continues:
"He whose body is the ego," "He whose body is the intellect," and "He whose body is the unmanifest."
And so forth. || 14 ||
As for what was stated—

that the creation of the vital breaths and so forth from Brahman, as heard in passages such as "From this [Brahman] is born the vital breath, mind, and all the sense organs," is possible even through a succession— here it is replied:
231. But on the contrary, the sequence [of dissolution] is established from this [same principle] by way of inversion. (1.3.15)

The word "tu" (but) serves the purpose of restriction. That sequence—in which all effects follow immediately after Brahman in reverse order from the unmanifest, mahat, ego, ether, and so forth—is perceived in passages such as, "From this [Brahman] is born breath," and so on. And that sequence is established only by the production of each respective effect directly from Brahman in its corresponding form. For if the causality were only through a succession, the scriptural teaching of immediate succession would be contradicted. Therefore, even the passage beginning with "From this is born" supports the direct origination of everything from Brahman. || 15 ||

It is understood not only through the creation preceded by *īkṣā* (contemplation), but also from scripture (*śrauta*); this is the meaning. Regarding the term "Subāla": in order to establish that even the principles beginning with *mahat* were created preceded by *īkṣā*, [the author] states that their causes as well have the Supreme Person as their body. || 14 ||

"Unmanifest" (avyaktā) means by reversing the order stated by others. "And that" (sa ca): in the passage "from this [it] is born," the immediate succession of Brahmā is established by the natural force of the text. Thus, since the sequence consisting of immediate succession from Brahmā is understood through the natural force of the sentence, the meaning is that the production of those various effects proceeds from Brahmā alone. "Support" (uttambhanam) means an indicator. This was stated with the intention of showing the grammatical connection (anvaya) in such passages as "from this the vital breath is born" and "from this the mind is born. || 15 ||
Because there is no contradiction regarding the immediate or successive order of the acts of immediate retribution,
the creation and so forth from those respective bodies is indeed possible for Brahmā.
[Śrībhāṣya 2.3.2] 232.
"If it be argued that between [the senses and the self] come cognition and mind in sequence because of their respective indicators, we say no, because there is no distinction. (2.3.15)

Because they are the means for cognition, the sense organs are called "cognition" (*vijñāna*). As it has been stated in the passage beginning with "From this [Self] is born," it is taught that everything is the immediate effect of Brahman. Therefore, by this statement, the direct origination of everything from Brahman—which was understood through the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of the creative reflection (*abhidhyāna*)—is being "established. That, however, is not tenable; [The full argument continues: For if the sense organs were indeed the effects of Brahman, then the statement "From this [Self] is born... the breath, the mind, and all the sense organs" would be redundant, as their origin from the Self had already been established by the preceding statement "From this [Self] is born... the vital breaths. Furthermore, if the sense organs were the effects of Brahman, then the subsequent statement "From him [the Self] are born the fire, the waters, and the earth" would be superfluous, since the origin of all things from Brahman had already been declared. Moreover, the sense organs are perceived as distinct from the Self, just as the body is; therefore, they cannot be identical with the Self. Consequently, the sense organs are not the effects of Brahman. Thus, the claim that the direct origination of everything from Brahman is established by this passage is untenable.

Because this sentence is intended to convey a specific sequence, a sequence is perceived here for all [the elements] as well. First, regarding ether (*kha*) and the others, the sequence is established by another scriptural passage (*śruti*), and it is likewise perceived here. From the indicative mark (*liṅga*) of their being mentioned together, it is understood that *vijñāna* (cognition) and *manas* (mind) also arise in sequence between the elements (*bhūta*) and the vital breath (*prāṇa*). Therefore, if it is argued that this sentence does not serve as a supporting factor (*uttambhaka*) for the possibility of everything arising directly from Brahman alone—

"That is not so; because there is no distinction. Since by the statement "from this [Brahman] is born the vital breath" (*etasmāj jāyate prāṇaḥ*), there is no distinction made regarding consciousness (*vijñāna*), the mind (*manas*), and the elements beginning with space (*khādi*); because the relationship of direct origination denoted by the phrase "is born from this" applies equally to all things from the vital breath down to the earth (*prāṇādi-pṛthivyanta*), that [relationship] alone is what is to be enjoined, not the sequence.

"In this case as well" means that this is not only the case in other scriptural passages (*śrutyantara*). "Together with them," etc., implies the principle of the first among equals (*agryaprāyanyāya*).

The phrase "because there is no distinction" (*aviśeṣāt*) means because there is no distinction in the syntactic connection (*anvaya*) understood from the sentence. The meaning is that this relationship—consisting in the possibility [of dissolution] directly from this [earth], as expressed by the sentence beginning with "from this"—is common to all elements from the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) up to the earth.

Furthermore, because it would contradict the sequence established in another scriptural passage, this [text] does not intend to prescribe a specific order; for [another text] begins with, "The earth dissolves into water," and so forth.

Because another sequence is perceived by the concluding statement, "He becomes one with the Supreme Deity beyond darkness," therefore the origin of all effects proceeds from the Supreme Brahman alone, whose body is the unmanifest (avyakta) and so forth. Furthermore, words such as "light" (tejas) and others denote Brahman itself, which constitutes their very essence. || 16 ||

But if all words were thus denotative of Brahman, would not the designation of various specific objects by their respective words—which is established through linguistic convention—be obstructed? To this he replies: 233. "The designation [of objects] as moving and non-moving would be figurative, because it occurs when that [Brahman] exists. (2.3.17)

The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of removing the doubt that has been raised. The designation by various specific names based on all moving and stationary beings is "figurative" (*bhākta*); the meaning is that it applies only to a portion of the denotable object. This is because Brahman, who is the substratum (*prakārī*) of all things, is not an object of means of valid cognition such as perception—which grasp only the modes (*prakāra*)—and thus the substratum is not cognized prior to hearing the Vedāntas.
[Regarding the phrase] "in another Śruti": for *prāṇa* is indeed an effect of air; it arose immediately after itself [i.e., after air], and did not arise before the elements. || 16 ||

Regarding the word "nanu": where there is the expressive power (*vācakatva-śakti*) of a word, there is linguistic convention (*vyutpatti*). Therefore, because there is no linguistic convention regarding Brahman as being denotable by words, it follows that words lack the power to denote it—this is the meaning.

Regarding the phrase "samasta" (entirety): explaining the section on the reason (*hetu*), he connects it to the meaning of the sentence. The absence of linguistic convention is due to the fact that the final determination of a word's meaning is contingent upon the cognition of a qualified object (*prakāri-pratīti*); in common worldly usage, those various words are designated as "breaking [the whole] into parts" (*bhaṅktvā bhaktvā*) with respect to only one part of the denotable object (*vācyaikadeśa*).

Alternatively, one might suspect that the designation of Brahman by words such as "fire" (*tejas*) and so forth—being established as denoting merely those respective objects—would be figurative (*bhākta*), that is, non-primary; anticipating this objection, it is said: "But [the designation] has its basis in the moving and the unmoving. The designation based on the moving and the unmoving—that is, the word denoting them—is not figurative with respect to Brahman, but is indeed primary. Why? Because all words possess their status as denoters of Brahman through the infusion of the nature of Brahman, for it is understood thus from the Śruti concerning the differentiation of names and forms (*nāma-rūpa-vyākaraṇa*). (1.1.7)
Thus ends the section concerning light (tejo'dhikaraṇa). || 2 ||
The Topic of the Self (Ātmādhikaraṇa) || 2-3-3 ||
234. The Self is not [the body], because it is eternal according to those [scriptures]. (2.3.18)
The origin of the entire world, beginning with space, has been stated to proceed from the supreme Brahman.
Now, a doubt arises as to whether the individual soul (jīva) also has an origin, or not.

What is logical? That [the soul] exists. Why? Because the proposition that "by the knowledge of one, there is the knowledge of all" is thus established, and because prior to creation, there is the determination of oneness. Furthermore, there are scriptural passages declaring the origination of the individual soul (*jīva*), just as in the case of ether and the rest:
"From whom the origin of the world proceeds... by water he emitted living beings upon the earth," and "Prajāpati created the creatures."
"O gentle one, all these creatures have Being as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support"; and "from which indeed these beings are born.
Since the origin of the conscious world is thus stated, the origin of the individual soul (jīva) is also understood [to follow].

Nor should it be argued that because Brahman is eternal and because statements such as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) lead to the understanding that the individual soul (jīva) is Brahman, the individual soul must therefore be eternal;
for [the scriptures declare] "All this has that as its self" (aitadātmyam idaṃ sarvam) and "All this, indeed, is Brahman" (sarvaṃ khalvidaṃ brahma).

By such statements as these, since even ether and the rest are understood to be Brahman, it follows that they too must be eternal; therefore, the individual soul (jīva) also arises, just like ether and the other elements.
This being the case, it is replied: "The Self [is not produced], because of scripture. The Self is not produced. Why? Because of scripture:
"The wise one is neither born nor does he die," and "The two, the Knower and the Unknower, are both unborn."
By such passages as these, the denial of the soul's origination is indeed heard. Furthermore, the eternity of the Self is understood from those very scriptures, such as:
"The eternal among the eternals, the conscious among the conscious, the one who fulfills the desires of the many";
and "Unborn, eternal, everlasting is this ancient one; he is not slain when the body is slain," and so forth. Therefore, the Self does not originate.

How, then, is the proposition that "by one cognition all cognitions [are known]" established? It is established in this way: because the individual soul (*jīva*) is also an effect, and because there is no difference between cause and effect. If that is so, then would it not follow that the soul must be subject to origination, like space and the other elements?

It is said: "No. For what is called "being an effect" is indeed the attainment of another state by a single substance; that certainly exists for the individual soul (*jīva*) as well. However, this is the distinction: the kind of transformation (*anyathābhāva*) that belongs to non-conscious entities such as space (*viyat*) and so forth does not belong to the soul. The soul's transformation consists in the contraction and expansion of knowledge (*jñāna*); whereas for space and the like, it consists in a change in essential nature (*svarūpa*). It is this kind of origination, characterized by a change in essential nature, that is denied in the case of the soul.

(An Analysis of the Three Principles) This is what is meant: having established that the objects of experience (*bhogya*), the experiencer (*bhoktṛ*), and the controller (*niyantṛ*) possess distinct natures; having denied origination and other such qualities to the experiencer by refuting them as belonging to the objects of experience and establishing his eternity; and having denied to the controller both the origination and other qualities belonging to the objects of experience and the state of being the locus of what is not the goal of man (*apuruṣārtha*) belonging to the experiencer—[the text establishes] his eternity, his faultlessness, his omniscience at all times, his possession of true resolve, his sovereignty over the lords of the senses, and his lordship over the universe.
Having thus established that in all states both the conscious and the unconscious constitute the body with respect to Him, it has been demonstrated that He is their Self.

Regarding the phrase "for being an effect" (*kāryatvaṃ hi*): the definition of an effect is that which follows both the conscious (*cit*) and the unconscious (*acit*). In response to the doubt—"The soul's status as an effect and the non-acceptance of its origination, like that of ether and so forth, are contradictory"—[the author] says: "because it is established [as such] with respect to the object of enjoyment. The meaning is that origination and other such properties residing in the object of enjoyment are denied in relation to the enjoyer, but not those that are unique to the enjoyer himself. By the words "Lord of the lords of the organs" (*karaṇādhipādhipa*) and so forth, the scriptural texts are recalled. The phrase "in the states of creation and dissolution" expresses the meaning of the supporting scripture. [Śrī Bhāṣya 2.3.3]

Therefore, Brahman always exists as having the sentient and insentient entities (*cidacidvastu*) as its body, being the substrate (*tatprakāra*) of them. At certain times, it remains with the sentient and insentient entities as its body in a subtle state, which is incapable of being designated as distinct from itself; that is Brahman in its causal state (*kāraṇāvastha*). And at other times, it has the sentient and insentient entities as its body in a gross state, wherein name and form are manifested; that is [Brahman] in its effected state (*kāryāvastha*).

In that regard, when that which exists in the state of cause attains the state of effect, the non-conscious portion (*acid-aṃśa*), which was devoid of sound and other qualities in its causal state, undergoes a modification consisting of a change in its essential nature by becoming possessed of sound and other qualities for the sake of being an object of enjoyment. And as for the conscious portion (*cid-aṃśa*), it undergoes a modification consisting of the expansion of knowledge corresponding to that [enjoyment], for the sake of being the enjoyer of specific fruits of karma. In the aspect of the Controller (*niyantṛ-aṃśa*), which is qualified by both these modes, there occurs a modification consisting of the state of being qualified by both of those.

Modification (*vikāra*), which consists in the attainment of another state (*avasthāntarāpatti*) by the causal state, is common to both the two modes and the possessor of those modes. For this very reason, with reference to the modification consisting in the attainment of another state of a single [cause],
the text first proposes the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one— expressed as "by which the unheard becomes heard"— and then provides the analogies of clay and so forth.
This has been illustrated by the passage beginning with, "Just as, my dear, by one [clay]," and so forth.

Intending to refer to the connection with and separation from various bodies that cause such contraction and expansion of knowledge, [the texts] speak of the birth and death of the individual soul (jīva),
stating: "Prajāpati created the creatures."

Such are the scriptural passages. Those which deny origination and proclaim eternity— such as "It is neither born nor does it die"— are intended to show that, unlike the insentient portion [of reality], there is no change in its essential nature (svarūpa).

And scriptural passages such as "He is the eternal among the eternals" intend to convey the absence of both kinds of undesirable modifications: those consisting in a change of essential nature, and those consisting in the contraction or expansion of knowledge.
"‘This very Great Self is ageless, deathless, immortal, Brahman’; ‘The eternal among the eternals’—such scriptural passages have the Supreme as their object.

Likewise, the determination of the oneness of Brahman, who is always qualified by the sentient and insentient entities, prior to creation, is established because of the absence of the differentiation of name and form."

"For indeed it was undifferentiated; it was differentiated by name and form"—thus [the scripture] speaks of plurality and unity through the presence and absence of the distinction between name and form.

1) Those who say that the state of being an individual soul (*jīvatva*) is conditioned by the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*) of ignorance (*avidyā*); 2) those who say it is produced by an ultimate limiting adjunct; and 3) those who say that Brahman, whose nature is pure existence (*sanmātra*), exists itself in three forms—as the enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*), the enjoyed (*bhogya*), and the controller (*niyantṛ*)—all of these [agree] regarding the power of ignorance, the power of the limiting adjunct, and [the roles of] the enjoyer, the enjoyed, and the controller.

Regarding the phrase "unwanted transformation" (*aniṣṭavikāra*): by the word "unwanted," those desired transformations mentioned in such passages as "He desired: 'May I become many'" are excluded. As for the word "thus" (*evam*): if Brahman is always qualified by the sentient and the insentient, how can there be a definitive statement of oneness? To this question, the meaning is that the scripture declares both plurality and unity through the distinction between name and form and the absence thereof.
• Or sometimes it dies. * Intending a modification; da. And they say—na. Threefold—i. • Of the power of ignorance—tha.
' They say—a. [Śrī Mādhyama 2-3-3]

And although the powers (*śakti*) persist at the time of dissolution, they establish the determination of their unity at that time precisely because of the absence of the differentiation of name and form (*nāma-rūpa-vibhāga*). [The Sūtras state:
"Inequality and cruelty [do not apply to the Lord] because He has regard for [other factors]" (Brahmasūtra 2.1.34);

and "If it be argued that [the world] cannot exist because of the non-differentiation of karma, we say no, because [samsara] is beginningless; and this is both logical and observed" (Brahmasūtra 2.1.35).
And because, by these two sūtras, the beginninglessness of the distinction between souls and the stream of their karma is admitted.
The Topic on Knowledge (Jñādhikaraṇa). 2.3.4.
235. "The knower [is the Self] for this very reason. (2.3.19)

It has been stated that the individual soul (*jīva*) is not produced, unlike ether and other elements. In connection with that, the true nature of the soul is now being examined: Is the nature of the self merely pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), as maintained by the Sugatas (Buddhists) and Kapila (Sāṃkhya)? Or is its nature insentient (*acitsvabhāva*), like a stone, possessing consciousness as a merely adventitious quality (*āgantuka*), as maintained by Kaṇabhuj (the Vaiśeṣika)? Or is the very state of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) its essential nature? Thus [is the inquiry].

Regarding the word "ether" (*viyat*): since there is no description of the manner in which the nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) is an effect, it has no direct connection with the [preceding] section (*pāda*). Therefore, the meaning is that the connection is by way of a contextual transition (*prasaṅga*) to the four subsequent sections (*adhikaraṇa*) that are about to be discussed.

What is the case? Is the individual soul (*jīva*) one whose body is pure consciousness (*caitanyamātra-vapuḥ*), or is it of an insentient nature (*jaḍa-svarūpa*) with consciousness as a adventitious quality (*āgantuka-caitanya*), or is it by its own nature a knower (*svataḥ-jñātṛ*)? Is there consistency with all the scriptures if the soul has the nature of pure knowledge (*jñāna-mātra-vapuḥ*)—whether as being of the very essence of knowledge (*jñāna-svarūpatva*) or as having knowledge as its attribute (*tad-dharmakatva*)? Or is there consistency if it is of an insentient nature with adventitious consciousness? Or is there consistency if its sole nature is that of being a knower by itself? If being a knower were its essential nature (*svarūpatva*), would it not follow that it would be perceived everywhere? Or not?

For that purpose, is the individual soul (*jīva*) all-pervading, or is it atomic? If it were atomic, would the apprehension and non-apprehension of distant objects be possible or not? Is the relationship between a fixed property and its substratum (*dharmadharmibhāva*) logically tenable or not for two things of the same class?

When [the soul's being the knower] is not logically tenable—due to the impossibility of perceiving distant objects, the consequence that it would be perceived everywhere because of its omnipresence, and the lack of consistency with all scriptural texts if being a knower were its very nature—then one of the two alternative positions must be accepted. When, however, it is logically tenable—due to the possibility of both perceiving and not perceiving distant objects once its atomicity is established, and because there is no consequence of it being perceived everywhere—it is established that the Self has the nature of being a knower, in full consistency with all scriptural texts.

"Pure consciousness alone" (*cinmātram*) is an expression emphasizing the abstract state; it means "the nature of being knowledge" (*jñānatva*). By the suffix *-mātra*, the exclusion of being a knower (*jñātṛtva*) and so forth is intended. Furthermore, there is the relationship of being the correlate of manifestation for the Supreme.
This is an expression emphasizing the abstract state:
"the nature of being a knower" (*jñātṛtva*)—of oneself.
*Svarūpa* means its innate form.
*Jñātṛtva* means the state of being the "I" (*ahaṃtva*).
The *ātman* is consciousness; it is indeed a knower, characterized by knowledge that is inseparable from it. Therefore—
Because it has been stated, "This person indeed knows," it is certain that the Self is the knower whose very nature is knowledge and who is pure consciousness;
for the Śruti says, "Seeing, he rejoices, being a mass of consciousness," and so forth.

2. Is it the adventitious (āgantuka) [nature]—as in the readings *i*, *gha*, or *vā*? What is logical? It is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*). Why? Because of such scriptural testimony (*śruti*). For, in the Antaryāmi Brāhmaṇa: [it is stated thus].
In place of the Mādhyandina recension’s passage, "He who dwells in the self," the Kāṇva recension reads, "He who dwells in consciousness. Likewise, [it continues]:

"Consciousness performs the sacrifice; it also performs ritual acts"—thus, consciousness alone is heard in scripture to be the very nature of the self as the agent. Furthermore, in the Smṛtis, in passages such as "In the ultimate sense, its nature is knowledge and it is absolutely pure," the fact that the self has the nature of knowledge is perceived.

But another [teacher] says: if the nature of the individual soul (*jīvātman*) were admitted to be inherently both "knowledge" (*jñānatva*) and "knowership" (*jñātṛtva*), it would follow that, being omnipresent, it would be perceived everywhere at all times; furthermore, the sense organs would be rendered useless, since consciousness is not perceived even though the self exists during deep sleep, fainting, and so forth, whereas we observe the arising of knowledge when the causal complex (*sāmagrī*) is present for one who is awake. Therefore, knowledge is not its essential nature (*svarūpa*), nor is knowership; rather, consciousness is merely adventitious (*āgantuka*).

Furthermore, the omnipresence of the self must necessarily be accepted, because effects are perceived everywhere and because it is admitted that the self is present everywhere. Since the production of effects can occur through the movement of the body alone, there is no evidence for postulating [a separate] motion [of the self]. Scripture also shows the absence of cognition at the time of deep sleep: "Verily, in this state, he does not know himself as 'I am this,' nor indeed these beings. Likewise, it shows the absence of cognition in the state of liberation.

Regarding the statement, "There is no consciousness after death," the usage [of the term] "consisting of the nature of knowledge" (*jñānasvarūpa*) and so forth is figurative (*lākṣaṇika*), because knowledge is a quality unique to that [Self].

This being the case, we reply: "He is indeed the Knower" (*jña eva*). This Self is indeed the Knower; its very nature is that of a cognizer, not mere consciousness (*jñāna-mātra*), nor is it insentient by nature. Why? Precisely for this reason, meaning on account of Scripture itself (*śruteḥ*). The phrase "on account of Scripture" (*śruteḥ*) refers back to the Scripture under discussion in the passage, "The Self [is] not [the body], because of Scripture. Likewise, in the *Chāndogya Upaniṣad*, within the discourse of Prajāpati, regarding the description of the nature of the liberated and unliberated Self: ... [text continues] ... Thus, the Self is established as the Knower. Furthermore, in the *Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad*, in the dialogue between Yājñavalkya and Maitreyī, it is stated: "Verily, my dear, the Self is to be seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon. When the Self is seen, heard, reflected upon, and meditated upon, all this is known" (BṛU 2.4.5). Here, the Self is designated as the agent of the act of knowing (*jñāna-kriyā-kartṛ*). Therefore, the Self is the Knower. Moreover, in the *Kaṭha Upaniṣad*: "The wise one, who knows Him as the Knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*)," and so forth. Thus, the Self is the Knower. Furthermore, in the *Praśna Upaniṣad*: "From whom speech, along with the mind, turns away unable to reach Him—He is the imperishable Brahman, He is the supreme goal" (PrU 4.8). Here, the fact that speech and the mind turn away from Him indicates that He is the Knower, for the mind and speech are the instruments of cognition. Therefore, the Self is the Knower. Also, in the *Muṇḍaka Upaniṣad*: "He who is the seer, the toucher, the hearer, the smeller, the taster, the thinker, the knower, the doer—the one within the city of nine gates" (MuU 3.1.7). Here, the Self is described as the Knower. Consequently, the Self is the Knower. Moreover, in the *Māṇḍūkya Upaniṣad*: "The one who is conscious in waking, the dreamer in dreams, and the blissful in deep sleep—He is the Self" (MāU 5). Here, the Self is designated as the Knower. Therefore, the Self is the Knower. And finally, in the *Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad*: "The Knower of the field (*kṣetrajña*), the Great Lord, the Ruler of all beings" (ŚveU 6.16). Here, the Self is called the Knower of the field. Thus, the Self is the Knower. For these reasons, the Self is indeed the Knower. Its nature is that of a cognizer, not mere consciousness, nor is it insentient. This is established. End of section. (Note: The ellipsis represents the portion of the original text provided in the prompt where the specific citation from the *Chāndogya* was cut off.)
Thus [it is said]:
"By what, my dear, should one know the knower?
and "This person surely knows."
Likewise:
"For this indeed is the seer, the hearer, the smeller, the taster, the thinker, the knower, the agent—the Puruṣa, the self of consciousness";
and, "In this very way, these sixteen parts belong to this all-seeing one."
Thus [ends the section]. || 19 ||

As for what was stated—that if the state of being a knower were inherent, it would follow that for such an all-pervading entity, there would be perception [of it] everywhere at all times—it is replied to this: "236. Of its departure, movement, and return" (2.3.20).
This self is not all-pervading; rather, it is atomic.
Why? Because of the scriptural texts concerning its departure, going, and returning. First, its departure is heard in scripture:
"By that light, this self departs, either through the eye, or through the crown of the head, or through other [parts of the body]."
"From the regions of the body,
[the texts] have as their subject the liberated self: 'Another inner self consists of consciousness,' 'There is no loss of the consciousness of the knower,' and so forth."
It should be joined. || 19 ||
Thus [it is said]. Departure also is taught:

"Whoever indeed depart from this world, they all go to the moon. Return also is taught: "From that world, they return again to this world for the sake of action. For if [the soul] were omnipresent, these processes—departure and so forth—would not be possible. || 20 ||
And by its own nature, [it is the cause] of the two subsequent ones. (2-3-21)
The word ‘ca’ (and) is used for emphasis. Although “departure” consists in the form of separation from the body, [it is nevertheless...]
But going and coming are not possible in any way whatsoever; therefore,
although they might somehow be possible for a permanent self, [they are not possible for the soul].
I shall attain [this] by my very self. || 21 ||
238. "If it be argued that [the soul] is not atomic because of the scriptural statement [to the contrary], we say no, because of the context of the other. (2.3.22)

"‘He who consists of consciousness among the vital breaths,’ ‘whoever they may be’—the word ‘going’ (gati) follows immediately after the word ‘departure’ (utkrānti); the sense is that it refers to the movement occurring subsequent to departure. In this Sūtra, the implication of the scriptural statement (śrutyarthāpatti) is demonstrated. || 20 ||

By the word "somehow" (*kathaṃcit*), a lack of intrinsic appropriateness (*asvārasya*) is indicated even in that case; for since both minuteness (*aṇutva*) and motion (*gati*) must be postulated, the opponent has pointed out the fault of excessive conceptualization (*kalpanā-gaurava*). In that regard, since motion is established by scripture (*śruti*), it is not something to be postulated. || 21 ||
Since going and coming are accomplished by the self alone,
the doubt that the self's atomicity is established here is simply not tenable.

If it is argued that the Self is not minute because the Śruti declares "the Self is great," we reply that such scriptural statements refer to the Supreme Self; thus, it is certain that the individual soul (jīva) is minute.
If this is argued, [we reply:
even with regard to the self that is already established—as indicated by the word "also" (ca) following the introduction of the individual soul (jīva)—it is said: "of the self that is also abiding."

If it is argued that the individual soul (*jīva*) is not minute because of the scriptural statement regarding its greatness, "This great, unborn Self," we say no; for there is reference to another—since in that context, the reference is to the Wise One (*prājña*), who is other than the *jīva*. Although the *jīva* was introduced at the beginning, nevertheless...
"The Self, which is known and awakened,"—thus the Supreme is taught in the middle [of the passage]; this greatness belongs to that [Supreme], not to the individual soul (jīva). || 22 ||
239. And [the suffix *ka* is applied] by virtue of its own specific word-form and by measure. (Pāṇini 5.2.37)

The word "aṇu" itself is heard directly [in scripture]: "This subtle (aṇu) Self is to be known by the mind, into which the fivefold vital breath has entered. Having extracted the measure—that is, the standard of measurement—by extracting an object similar to an atom, the scripture declares that the living self (jīva) possesses that same measure.
"The individual soul (jīva) is to be known as a part of a hundredth part of the tip of a hair, further divided into a hundred parts."
And it is said: "Even one as small as the tip of an awl is seen. Therefore, this self is indeed atomic (aṇu).
Now, it might be argued: if the self were atomic, a sensation pervading the entire body would not be possible; regarding this, he states a refutation according to another school of thought:
240. There is no contradiction, as in the case of sandalwood. (2-3-24)

Just as a drop of yellow sandalwood paste, though residing in only one part of the body, produces a refreshing sensation pervading the entire body; so too the self, though residing in only one part of the body, experiences a sensation that pervades the whole body. || 24 ||

241. "If it be argued that [the difference in experience] is due to a difference in location, we say no, because that is not admitted. (2-3-25) If it is argued that the particular state [of experience] resulting from drops of yellow sandalwood paste and the like is due to their being located in a specific part of the body, whereas such a thing does not exist for the Self—[we reply: No; for even in the case of the Self, its abiding in a specific part of the body is admitted. Indeed, the abiding of the Self in the region of the heart is taught [in scripture];
for pain is the experience of suffering, and this is also an illustration of the experience of pleasure.

"He experiences feeling" (*vedanāmanubhavati*) is like the expression "he cooks the cooking of rice" (*odanapākaṃ pacati*); or rather, it means "he experiences suffering" (*duḥkhamanubhavati*). || 24 ||
Even though the self is atomic, its experience of happiness throughout the entire body is logical, just as the fragrance of sandalwood, though located in one spot, pervades the whole.
If it is argued that sandalwood becomes fragrant due to a specific quality (vaiśeṣya) while remaining in its own state, we say no; for the Self, too, is said to abide within its own heart.
"For this Self is in the heart; there are one hundred and one channels there. Likewise:
"Which is the Self?"

Having introduced the subject with the words, "This one who consists of consciousness among the vital breaths, the light within the heart," the example of sandalwood is presented in order to demonstrate that the Self resides in a particular location; it is not, however, because sandalwood itself requires a particular location [to manifest its fragrance]. || 25 ||
Regarding the manner in which that which exists in one part performs an action pervading the entire body, he states his own view: 242. "Or [it is] due to its quality, like light" (2.3.26).

The word "or" (*vā*) is intended to exclude other opinions. The Self (*ātman*), having pervaded the entire body by means of its own attribute, knowledge (*jñāna*), remains there; it is like light (*āloka*). Just as the light of jewels, the sun, and so forth—which reside in a single location—is seen to pervade many locations, in the same way, the knowledge of the Self residing in the heart exists pervading the entire body.

It has been established in the first sūtra that the operation of knowledge—which is like the radiance of the knower—outside its own locus is possible, just as in the case of the radiance of a gem. || 26 ||

But has it not been stated that "the Self is merely knowledge"? How then can it be said that knowledge possesses qualities distinct from its own nature? To this, he says: 243. "The distinction [of the Self from knowledge] is like that of fragrance; and thus it shows. (2.3.27)

Just as there is a distinction between the earth and its quality, smell, which is perceived as belonging to it, so too is the distinction between the Self and cognition established; for cognition, though perceived as a quality of the knower in the form "I know," is distinct from the Self. And the Śruti demonstrates this:
"This person indeed knows. (27)
244. Because of the separate instruction [of the two]. (2.3.28)

The intention is that another explanation is offered with the view that consciousness is taught as distinct from the knower by its own specific term (*svaśabdenaiva*). Regarding the word "prabhā" (light): even for a quality that is inseparably established (*ayutasiddha*), there can be existence in another location. || 26 ||

Regarding the word "separately" (*pṛthak*): just as in the previous sūtra [the term] "fragrant flower" denotes a qualified entity, so too by means of a word expressing a qualifier, cognition—being perceived as "I know"—would indeed be separate from the knower.
However, just as fragrance belongs to the earth which possesses fragrance, so it is according to the sacred tradition (*śruti*).
For it is said in the Śruti, "The knower is not [known] by the act of knowing," and because knowledge is spoken of as distinct from the Self, knowledge must therefore be separate from it.
"For there is no loss of consciousness for the knower.
As it has been said:
"He who, dwelling in consciousness," and "Consciousness performs the sacrifice."
In passages such as "The nature of knowledge is absolutely stainless," the Self is designated as being nothing other than knowledge; to this, [the Sūtra] replies: 245.
But that designation [of the Self as knowledge] is due to its having that [knowledge] as its essential quality, as in the case of the Intelligent One (Prājña). II.3.29.

The word "but" (tu) sets aside the objection. Because its essence consists of that quality—that is, because its essence consists of the quality of consciousness—there is the designation of the Self as "consciousness. Consciousness alone is its essential quality. Just as bliss is the essential quality of the Prājña [the state of deep sleep], and thus the Prājña is designated by the word "bliss"—as in the passages, "If this bliss did not exist in this space," and "He understood that bliss is Brahman"—for indeed, bliss is the essential quality of the Prājña.
"That is the one bliss of Brahman";
"Knowing the bliss of Brahman, he fears nothing from anywhere";
"Brahman is truth, knowledge, and infinite"—thus the designation by the word "knowledge" (jñāna) refers to the wise one, the one possessed of higher intellect.
In passages such as "together with the wise Brahman" and "He who is all-knowing," it is understood that for the Intelligent One (Prājña), knowledge is His essential attribute. || 29 ||
246. And because it has been cultivated as long as the self exists, there is no fault in seeing that [self]. (2.3.30)

Since consciousness (*vijñāna*) is a property that persists as long as the self exists (*yāvad-ātmabhāvin*), there is no fault in designating it by that term. Likewise, for example, things such as a cow (*khaṇḍādi*) are seen to be designated as "cow" by means of words denoting properties like "cowness" (*gotva*), which persist as long as the thing's own nature (*svarūpa*) exists; the meaning is that these properties are those whose existence is defined by the thing's own nature. By the word "and" (*ca*), [the author] combines the point that, just like cognition, there is also no fault in designating the self as "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), because it is self-luminous (*svaprakāśatvena*). || 30 ||

Regarding what was stated—that because there is an absence of cognition during deep sleep and similar states, cognition does not possess the property of being intrinsically connected to its own nature—the author replies:
"But [cognition] belongs to that which exists, because it is capable of manifestation, like masculinity and so forth. (2.3.31)

The word "tu" (but) is for the purpose of removing the raised doubt. Since this knowledge—which exists even during states such as deep sleep—is manifested during states such as waking, its status as an attribute inherent to one's essential nature (*svarūpānubandhidharma*) is established, just like masculinity and so forth. For example, although the specific faculty of masculinity exists in a man during childhood, it is unmanifest; yet, when it becomes manifest in youth, that possession of it by the man does not become merely occasional. Indeed, the fact that the body consists of seven constituents (*saptadhātumayatva*) is inherent to its essential nature.

This is because of the description of the body's true nature as "that body consisting of seven constituents, three impurities, two origins, and four kinds of food. It has already been stated previously that the referent of the "I" (ahamartha) shines forth even in states such as deep sleep. That this existing consciousness has objects as its domain is perceived during waking and other such states. Furthermore, these attributes of the Self, such as being a knower, [are present] "in waking and so forth"; by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the state of dreaming is intended. By the word "masculinity," the constituent element (dhātu) is indicated; it is understood that by the word "and so forth" (ādi), the female is also included as an illustration.

Regarding the phrase "masculinity, etc.": it is meant that the apprehension of knowledge is dependent upon its connection with an object. This illustration refers merely to the manifestation of that which exists but is unmanifest at a certain time. Since its fitness for connection with an object and its fitness for manifestation exist even then, there is no loss of its self-luminosity (*svayaṃprakāśatva*).

Regarding the phrase "of that... [is] perceived": the meaning is that the connections with objects and the apprehension occur during the waking state and so forth. Regarding the phrase "these two": although these belong to the Self (*ātman*) which is always present, they belong specifically to this—namely, to knowledge itself, which is an attribute (*dharma*).
Because it is logical that there is a manifestation [of the object],
due to its connection with the sense organs—
[this is the section concerning knowledge (*jñādhikaraṇa*)].
This has already been established. Therefore, the very nature of the individual self (jīvātman) is that of being a knower. And this self is of atomic dimension (aṇu-parimāṇa). [As for the objection:
"After death, there is no consciousness."

Thus, it is not said that there is an absence of knowledge for the liberated one; rather, what is meant is that for the liberated one, that perception of birth, destruction, and so forth— which in the state of transmigratory existence is conditioned by conformity to the elements, as expressed in the passage, "having arisen from these elements, one perishes after them"— does not exist.
"The seer sees neither death, nor disease, nor even suffering.
The seer indeed sees everything; he attains everything in every way. "Not remembering this body into which he was born..."
Because this is consistent with such scriptural passages as, "Beholding these desires with the mind, he rejoices," and so forth. || 31 ||
Now, regarding the doctrine that the self is consciousness, he states the refutation of its being omnipresent:
248. "Otherwise, there would follow the consequence of either perpetual perception or perpetual non-perception, or else the necessity of restricting it to one or the other. (2.3.32)

Otherwise—in the case of the doctrine that [the Self] is omnipresent, and in the case of the doctrine that it is mere consciousness—there would be the consequence of its being eternally perceived or unperceived; and if it were the object of the notion of "I," there would follow the consequence of its being insentient and so forth. "Not after death" means that the delusion consisting of the identification of the body with the Self does not exist. || 31 ||

"Sampratīti" [means]: this is the refutation of the doctrine that the self is consciousness (*jñānātmavāda*) under the view of its omnipresence (*vibhutva*); and there is also the refutation of the doctrine that the self is insentient (*jaḍātmavāda*) under the view of its omnipresence; both are intended by the Sūtra and will be explained. Among these, this is the refutation regarding the first position.
If the self were omnipresent and its cognition were eternal, there would necessarily be either constant perception,
constant non-perception, or a restriction to one or the other.
Either both would always follow, or there would be a restriction to one of the two— either perception alone would be eternal,
or non-perception alone.

This is what is meant: regarding the perception and non-perception of the self as they occur in the world, this conscious self would have to be the omnipresent cause of either perception alone or non-perception alone. If it were the cause of both, then both would necessarily result at all times and in all places. If it were the cause of perception alone, there would never be non-perception of anything, anywhere, at any time. Conversely, if it were the cause of non-perception alone, there would never be perception of anything, anywhere, at any time.

Because the self (ātman) resides within our very body, its perception occurs only there and not elsewhere; thus, the established rule is maintained. Even if perception were dependent upon the instruments (karaṇas), since all selves are omnipresent and therefore always conjoined with all instruments, the aforementioned defect remains the same, as there would be no restriction regarding the location of perception. || 32 ||
Thus ends the section concerning knowledge (jñādhikaraṇa). 4.

The phrase "this has been said" means that three refutations are stated with the intention of addressing three alternative positions (*vikalpa*). Regarding the expression "in the world, for instance": the self is perceived in some places; it is not perceived in places such as the banks of the Ganges. Thus, one alternative position (*śiras*) is that both existing perception and non-perception would be the cause [of its existence]. Or, [another position is] "only perception" [is the cause]. Here too, the phrase "would be the cause" carries over from the previous context. In this way, three alternative positions are intended.

The meaning is: is the nature [of the thing] apprehension alone? Or is it non-apprehension alone? Or is it both? The employment of the word "reason" (*hetu*) is for the purpose of indicating independence from any other reason.
By saying "for us," he states that the aforementioned refutation does not touch upon his own position.

"Dependent on the instruments" refers to the refutation [of the opponent's view] regarding the position that the self is insentient (*jaḍa*) and all-pervading (*vibhu*). "Of the unseen merit and so forth as well" means that because bodies—which are the causes for the performance of various actions—are common to all selves, there would be no restriction regarding the unseen merit (*adṛṣṭa*). The meaning is that the aforementioned fault is equal [to the opponent's own position]. The intention is that, having raised the alternatives—whether the instruments and so forth are the cause of perception, or of non-perception, or of both—the refutation is clear, just as before. || 32 ||
The Section on the Agent (Kartradhikaraṇa) || 2-3-5 || 249. The agent [exists], because the scriptures would otherwise be purposeless. (Sūtra 2-3-33)

It has been stated that this self is the knower and that it is of atomic dimension. Now, it is considered whether that very [self] is the agent, or whether, while being itself non-agent, it merely superimposes upon itself the agency of the insentient *guṇas*. What is appropriate here? That "the self is indeed non-agent."

Why? Because in the scriptures on the supreme self (*adhyātma-śāstra*), it is heard that the Self is indeed non-agent (*akartṛ*) and that agency belongs only to the *guṇas*. For instance, in the *Kaṭhavallī*, after negating birth, old age, death, and all such states as being attributes of *prakṛti* through the passage beginning "It is not born, it does not die," even the agency of the individual soul (*jīva*) in actions such as killing is negated.

Regarding the word "this" (*ayam*): since agency (*kartṛtva*) follows from being a knower (*jñātṛtva*), the sense is that the connection here [in the text] is established because agency is defined immediately after defining the knowledge that is conducive to agency.

Is the Self alone the agent, or is it primordial matter (*pradhāna*)? Is the meaningfulness of the scriptures concerning the *Jyotiṣṭoma* sacrifice and other rites contingent upon the agency of the Self, or upon the agency of primordial matter? And regarding the denial of agency: is such denial possible if the Self possesses agency, or not?
"If the slayer thinks he slays, or if the slain thinks he is slain, both of them do not understand; this one neither slays nor is slain. (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.19)
Thus: "Knowing himself to be the slayer, he does not know the Self"—this is the meaning. And so the Blessed One says:
the very nature of the individual soul (*jīva*) is non-agency; the conceit of agency, however, is delusion—thus it is stated:
"All actions in every way are performed by the qualities of *prakṛti*."
"His self deluded by egoism thinks, 'I am the doer.
"When the seer perceives no agent other than the qualities," "In the agency of cause and effect, Nature (prakṛti) is said to be the cause;
the Spirit (puruṣa) is said to be the cause in the experiencing of pleasure and pain."
And thus it is said: therefore, the state of being the enjoyer belongs only to the Puruṣa, whereas the state of being the agent belongs only to Prakṛti.
This being the case, we reply: "The Self alone is the agent, because otherwise the scriptures would be purposeless. The Self alone is the agent, not the qualities.
Why? Because otherwise the scriptures would be purposeless. For the scriptures...
"One who desires heaven should sacrifice"; "One who seeks liberation should meditate upon Brahman."

Passages such as these enjoin the very enjoyer of fruits such as heaven and liberation to act as the agent. For if an insentient entity were the agent, no "other" could be enjoined. Furthermore, there is "instruction" (śāsana); that is, scripture (*śāstra*). And instruction is the act of instigating.

When the scriptures have purpose only if the primary cause (pradhāna) is the agent, and if the negation of the self's agency is not possible, then the primary cause must be the agent. When the scriptures have purpose only if the self alone is the agent, and the negation of agency has a valid object, then the self alone must be the agent.

In the phrase "hantum," the word "hantu" is in the accusative case ending in -u, as in the expression "setum jantum. Its meaning is "the slayer. The word "ātmānam" (himself) must be supplied [as the object]. Thus, because all agency in action is denied in the corroborative passage (*upabṛṃhaṇa-vākya*), the act of killing mentioned in the verse "if he should be the slayer" is intended as a mere illustration (*upalakṣaṇa*).

Because it is the subject matter of the scriptures (*śāstrārthatvāt*)—that is, for the sake of making the scriptures meaningful; [the scriptures serve as] the cause by way of being their purpose. And because they instruct (*śāsanāt*); for the scriptures function as motivators by means of generating understanding. Furthermore, the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) is insentient and cannot be made to understand. Therefore, the meaningfulness of the scriptures can only exist if the sentient enjoyer (*bhoktṛ*) alone is the agent. As it has been said: "The fruit of the scripture belongs to the performer."
Thus [it is said].

As for what was stated—beginning with "If the killer thinks... and so forth—that the non-agency of the Self in the act of killing is heard in the Śruti, that is said because, due to the eternity of the Self, there is no possibility of its being killed.

As for the statement that "the agency belongs to the *guṇas* alone," as taught in the passage beginning with "Actions are performed by the *guṇas* of *prakṛti*," this is said because—by distinguishing between what is already established and what is not—the agency of the Self in worldly activities is caused by its association with the *guṇas* of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, and is not inherent to its own nature. Accordingly, it is stated in that very same place: "The cause of its births in good and evil wombs is attachment to the *guṇas*. Likewise, in that same context, agency is attributed to the Self while still acknowledging [its true nature].
"In that case, he who, due to his unrefined intellect, perceives the self alone as the agent— that person of dull wit does not see. Thus it is said.
