"The locus, as well as the agent, the various instruments, the diverse and distinct efforts, and destiny as the fifth—when the agency of the self depends upon these factors beginning with the locus and ending with destiny, he who considers the self alone to be the agent does not see. (33) This is the meaning: he does not perceive correctly.

Since agency belongs only to the enjoyer, and enjoyment belongs only to the conscious being, and since the scripture functions as an instigator by means of generating knowledge—given that the generation of knowledge is impossible for that which is insentient—the meaning is that the conscious being is the agent. "As it has been said" means: in the inquiry into action (*karmavicāra*). "It is said" means: it is stated that this [Self] possesses no agency in killing. "Of the qualities alone" is a restatement of the meaning as it appears in that scriptural statement. "By the discrimination between what is obtained and what is not obtained" means: by the determination of positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

Worldly activity—activity during the state of transmigratory existence. The meaning is that his agency regarding worldly activities is produced by the conjunction of *sattva*, *rajas*, and *tamas*, as established through positive and negative concomitance (*anvaya-vyatireka*).

"Kevalam" means devoid of a substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*) and so forth. The term "substratum" is used to dispel the misconception that even the statement beginning with "in that very [place]" is intended to negate the agency (*kartṛtva*) of the Self. "Substratum" refers to the body. By the word "activity" (*ceṣṭā*), the five-fold vital breath (*pañcavṛtti-prāṇa*) is indicated. The phrase ending with "when there is dependence" provides the explanation for the words "this being so. (33)
250. Because of the teaching regarding appropriation and because of the teaching regarding the abode. (2.3.34)
Having introduced the subject with "Just as a great king," [the text continues]:

"In this very way, having taken hold of these vital breaths (prāṇas), he moves about within his own body according to his desire. Thus, the agency in both the taking up and the relinquishing of the vital breaths is taught. || 34 ||

251. And because of the designation [of consciousness] as the agent in action; if it be argued that this is not so because there would be a reversal of the grammatical designation. (Sūtra 2.3.35). Because of the designation of the agent in worldly and Vedic actions, such as "Consciousness performs the sacrifice and also performs ritual acts," [consciousness] is the agent.

If it is argued that the word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*) does not designate the Self, but rather the internal organ, the intellect (*buddhi*), then in that case there would be a reversal of the grammatical designation. Since the intellect is an instrument, there would have to be a designation using the instrumental case, as in "by means of consciousness" (*vijñānena*). (35)

"Having grasped" refers to appropriation (upādāna). "It revolves" refers to the dwelling-place (vihāra). The meaning is that agency is attributed to it in the impelling of the sense-faculties and the impelling of the body. || 34 ||

"‘He extends the sacrifice, he extends the ritual acts’—thus the agency of worldly and Vedic actions has been stated. Regarding the phrase ‘by means of consciousness’: the point is that even in that case, if [agency] were merely metaphorical, the same fault would apply. || 35 ||
252. There is a restriction regarding the theory of apprehension. (NS 2.1.36)
The defect in the case of the Self being a non-agent is stated as follows:

just as, by the argument beginning with "If the Self were all-pervading, there would be the consequence of constant perception or non-perception," an irregularity in perception was asserted; similarly, if the Self were a non-agent and Primordial Matter (prakṛti) were the agent, then because that [Matter] is common to all Puruṣas, all actions would result in experience for everyone, or else they would not result in experience for anyone at all.

Since the all-pervasiveness of the selves is admitted, their proximity as well is indistinguishable for all. For this very reason, a restriction regarding the internal organs and so forth is also untenable; that upon which the systematic arrangement would depend [is equally present to all]. || 36 ||
253. Because of the reversal of capacity. [2.3.37]

If the intellect (*buddhi*) were the agent, since it is impossible for one who is the agent to be a separate experiencer, the power of experiencing would also belong to that [intellect] alone; thus, the self’s power of experiencing would be lost. Furthermore, since experiencing would then belong to the intellect alone, there would be no evidence for the existence of a self. And yet, it is said: "The person exists because there is the state of being an experiencer."
For such indeed is their admission. || 37 ||

There is also a restriction regarding the internal organs and so forth: whatever action one who possesses a particular internal organ performs, that must be experienced by him through that very same internal organ. || 36 ||
254. And because of the absence of meditative concentration (samādhi). || 2-3-38 ||

If the intellect (*buddhi*) were the agent, then it would also be the agent in the meditative absorption (*samādhi*) that serves as the means to liberation. And that meditative absorption consists in the form, "I am other than *prakṛti*. Now, *prakṛti* is not capable of being the one who meditates in the thought, "I am other than *prakṛti*. Therefore, for this reason as well, the Self alone is the agent. (38)
Now, an objection is raised: "If the agency of the Self is admitted, then its state of non-agency would never cease! To this, he replies: "And as the carpenter [is both], in both ways" (2.3.39).

Even though the Self is endowed with instruments such as speech and so forth, it acts only when it desires, and does not act when it does not desire; just as a carpenter, despite the presence of tools such as an axe, acts or refrains from acting according to his own will. However, if the insentient intellect were the agent, then because there would be no cause for regulating its desire for experience and so forth, it would necessarily be an agent at all times. (39)
Thus ends the section concerning the agent (kartradhikaraṇa). 5.

"And not from primordial nature (prakṛti). Because primordial nature is insentient, the meditative absorption (samādhi) is not possible; furthermore, because it is of the nature of "I am other than primordial nature," it is not possible—this is the meaning. || 38, 39 ||
Since even meditative absorption (samādhi), which serves as the means to liberation, is impossible [for them],
agency belongs to the self alone, as expressed in such passages as "other than primordial matter" (prakṛter anya).
And thus, there is no non-cessation of agency.
For even when tools such as an axe are present, this [individual soul] acts like a carpenter;
this is the section concerning dependence on another (Parāyattādhikaraṇa). 2.3.6.
256. But [the Self] is from the Highest, because of the scriptural statement to that effect. (2.3.40)
Is this agency of the individual soul (jīva) independent, or is it dependent upon the Supreme Self?

What is the prima facie view? That [the soul's agency] is independent. For if it were dependent upon the Supreme Self, the scriptural injunctions and prohibitions would result in being purposeless. Indeed, only one who is capable of initiating activity or desisting from it by means of his own intellect becomes a person to be enjoined (*niyojya*). Therefore, since its agency is independent, this is the position reached. To this, it is replied: "But [it is] from the Supreme, because of the scriptural statement of that. The word "but" sets aside the previous position. That agency of this individual soul (*jīva*) arises solely from the Supreme, that is, the Supreme Self, as the cause.
Why? From scripture:
"He has entered within as the ruler of people, the Self of all";
"He who dwells in the self, yet is within the self, whom the self does not know, whose body is the self, who rules the self from within—he is your self, the inner controller, the immortal."

[Śrībhāṣya 2.3.6]: "And I am seated within the heart of all; from Me come memory, knowledge, and their loss. "The Lord, O Arjuna, dwells in the heart-region of all beings, causing all beings to revolve by His power of illusion (māyā), as if they were mounted on a machine."
Thus [ends the verse]. 40.

But has it not been argued that, if this were so, the scriptures of injunctions and prohibitions would result in being purposeless? To this, he replies: 257. But [the Lord's grace] depends on the effort performed, because otherwise the enjoined and the prohibited would be rendered meaningless, and for other reasons as well. (2.3.41)

In all actions, depending upon the effort made by the person—namely, exertion—the Inner Controller, the Supreme Self, impels him by granting His permission. The meaning is that his activity is not possible without the permission of the Supreme Self.

Whence is this [known]? From the fact that prescribed and prohibited acts would otherwise be rendered meaningless, and so forth. By the word "and so forth" (ādi), favoring, punishment, and the like are included. For example, when wealth is common to two people, the transfer of ownership to another cannot take place without the consent of one of them; yet, even so, if the other's consent is given, the fruit of that act belongs to him alone, as it was performed by his own [will].

When it exists, then it is dependent on itself; when it does not exist, then it is dependent on the Supreme Self—thus it is established. The word "tat" (that) is the term to be explained; "kartṛtvam" (agency) is the explanation. || 40 ||

By the phrase "depending on the effort," the indifference of the Supreme toward the other [the individual soul] at the stage of the initial impulse is shown. For "encouraging one who has already begun" is indeed "consent. Regarding the term "Supreme Self": subsequent activity is possible only through the granting of this consent; this is the meaning. "Prescribed and prohibited" refers to injunctions and prohibitions. "Restraint and favor" refers to anger and grace. By the word "and so forth" (*ādi*), the bestowing of their respective fruits is intended. ...
For the sake of the accomplishment of prohibitions and injunctions, He [the Supreme Self], depending on the effort of the individual soul...
And he causes that [action] to proceed; for agency indeed depends upon another.
"It is established in the exposition of the Sāṅkhya system that even for one who has the power to turn others away from evil deeds, the state of being a consenter does not entail cruelty."

But if this is so, then the following would not be tenable: "It is He alone who causes him to perform good deeds whom He wishes to lead upward from these worlds; it is He alone who causes him to perform evil deeds whom He wishes to lead downward"—that is, "by the desire to lead upward and the desire to lead downward, He Himself causes one to perform both good and evil actions."

It is said: This is not common to all. However, for one who proceeds with the firm resolve to be exceedingly favorable toward the Supreme Person, the Blessed Lord, bestowing grace upon him, personally generates an inclination toward His own means of attainment—toward actions that are indeed most auspicious. And for one who proceeds with the firm resolve to be exceedingly antagonistic, [the Lord], restraining him, generates an inclination toward those actions that obstruct the attainment of Himself and lead to downward states of existence. As it was said by the Blessed Lord Himself:
"I am the source of all; from me everything proceeds."
"Thus mortals worship me, the wise, endowed with devotion. Starting from this point, [the Lord says]:
"To those who are ever-steadfast and who worship me with love, I grant that yoga of wisdom by which they come to me. Out of compassion for them alone, I dispel the darkness born of ignorance..."
"I destroy [the seed] residing within the self by means of the radiant lamp of knowledge. Likewise:
"They say that the world is unreal, without foundation, and without a Lord."
After stating this and so forth, up to the end of the passage: "Those who hate Me in their own bodies and in the bodies of others, being envious," [the Lord says:]
"Those hateful, cruel, and inauspicious lowest of men in the cycle of existences, I hurl perpetually into demonic wombs alone"—
thus it has been said.
Thus ends the section concerning dependence on another (Parāyattādhikaraṇa).
The Section on Parts (Aṃśādhikaraṇa) || 2.3.7 ||

258. [The individual soul] is a part [of Brahman], because of the various designations [of their relationship], and also because some record that it possesses the nature of a servant, a gambler, and so forth. (2.3.41)

It has been stated that the agency of the individual soul (jīva) is dependent upon the Supreme Person. Now, a doubt arises as to whether this jīva is absolutely different from the Supreme, or whether it is the Supreme Brahman itself, or whether it is Brahman limited by adjuncts (upādhi), or whether it is a part of Brahman; for this doubt arises from conflicting scriptural statements.

Regarding the phrase "of the individual soul" (*jīvasya*): it has been stated that the individual soul (*jīva*), which by its own intellect is capable of initiating activity or cessation, is impelled by the Supreme through the granting of permission, depending upon the effort already performed [by the soul]. If that were so, there would be an absolute difference between the individual soul and the Supreme, like that between a king and his servant. Therefore, the connection [of this section] arises from the doubt that the scriptural texts concerning non-difference must be figurative, like the statement "the king himself is the entire world."

Regarding the phrase "a portion of Brahman" (*brahmāṃśa*): does this mean a portion that is a part of the substantive (*viśeṣya*), or a portion that is a qualifying attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*) of the qualified? Such an alternative is implied here, and it will be discussed later. Is the individual soul (*jīva*) absolutely different from the Supreme Self (*paramātman*)? Or is it the ignorant Supreme Self itself? Or is it divided by a difference based on limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*)? Or is it different and non-different by its own nature? Or is it a portion of the Supreme Self by way of being its qualification? To determine this, one must consider: in which position is the primary significance of all the Śruti texts concerning difference and non-difference logically established, and in which is it not?

When that [logical] possibility exists in other alternative positions (*pakṣa*), then any one of those positions should be accepted. When that possibility exists in its being a part (*aṃśatva*) by way of being a qualifier (*viśeṣaṇatayā*), then that very [position] is to be accepted. Regarding the word "scripture" (*śruti*): since even the disagreement among disputants is rooted in the disagreement regarding scripture, that [scriptural disagreement] alone is stated here as the reason.

Objection: Is it not the case that this very point has already been determined in the sūtras, "The non-difference from That [is established] on account of the words concerning the beginning [of an effect], etc. and "But there is more [to the soul] because of the mention of difference"? Reply: True; however, that very point is now specifically determined by resolving the conflict between the scriptural texts regarding multiplicity and unity, through the demonstration that the individual soul (jīva) is a part (aṃśa) of Brahman. For as long as the fact that the individual soul is a part of Brahman is not determined, the soul's non-difference from Brahman and Brahman's superiority over it cannot be firmly established.
What, then, is the conclusion reached? That they are absolutely distinct.
Why? Because [the scripture says]:
"The two, the Knower and the Unknower, the Lord and the Non-Lord."

Because of the specification of difference by such passages as these; whereas the scriptural texts concerning the non-difference of the two [Brahmans] are figurative, since they convey a contradictory meaning, like the statement, "one should sprinkle with fire."
Or rather, the individual soul (jīva) is simply Brahman itself in a state of delusion.
Why? Because of the [scriptural statement]: "That thou art."

This is because of the teaching on the identity of Brahman and the Self in such passages as "This Self is Brahman. As for those [scriptural texts] that speak of plurality, since they merely restate matters established by perception and other means of knowledge, they are shown—by other Śruti passages which teach non-duality in a way not otherwise established—to be included within ignorance (*avidyā*), just like perception and the rest.

Alternatively, the individual soul (*jīva*) is Brahman itself as delimited by beginningless adjuncts (*upādhi*). Why? Precisely because of the teaching regarding the identity of Brahman and the Self. Nor can it be said that "this adjunct is imagined through delusion," for that would render the distinction between bondage, liberation, and so forth, untenable.
This being the position reached, it is replied: "It is a part of Brahman."

Why? Because of designation as manifold (*nānā*) and because of designation otherwise—that is, as one. Designation in both ways is observed. To begin with, designation as manifold is seen through [the distinctions of] creator and created, ruler and ruled, omniscience and non-omniscience, independence and dependence, purity and impurity, being a mine of auspicious qualities and the opposite thereof, lordship and being a subordinate, and so forth. And "otherwise" means that there is also designation by way of non-difference.
Indeed! 10.

Whether one considers "That thou art" or "This Self is Brahman," the meaning is that the individual soul (jīva) is indeed Brahman; for in the case of non-duality (advaita), the sixfold marks of purport are possible, whereas duality is otherwise established.
He binds [the argument]. Furthermore, the impossibility of establishing the categories of means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) and objects of valid cognition (*prameya*) is implied.
"In this way" (*evam*): the word "also" (*api*) from the Sūtra indicates that the intended meaning is difference (*bheda*).

This is seen through such passages as these. Furthermore, even the state of being fishermen, slaves, and gamblers is taught by some: the followers of the Atharva Veda recite, "Brahman is the fishermen, Brahman is the slaves, Brahman is the gamblers. Thus, the state of Brahman being those who are fishermen, slaves, and so forth is also taught. Consequently, the meaning is that non-difference is designated because [Brahman] pervades all living beings. Therefore, in order to establish the primary validity of both designations, this individual soul must be accepted as a "part" (aṃśa) of Brahman.

Nor can the designations of difference be established otherwise (anyathāsiddhatva) merely because their objects are well-known through perception and other means; for the individual soul's being created by Brahman, being governed by Him, being His body, being subservient to Him, being supported by Him, being protected by Him, being withdrawn by Him, being His worshipper, and its partaking in the human goals (puruṣārtha)—namely virtue, wealth, pleasure, and liberation which are obtainable through His grace—as well as the resulting difference between the individual soul and Brahman, are not within the scope of perception and the like, and are therefore "not established otherwise" (ananyathāsiddha).

Therefore, the [scriptural] passages concerning the creation of the world and so forth do not have as their primary purpose the teaching of a false object by way of restating distinctions already established by other means of valid cognition.

Nor is there—in Brahman, whose nature is undivided, unitary, and pure consciousness—any failure to realize its own identity with that [Brahman], nor the creation of ether and the rest preceded by the resolve to become manifold, nor entry into those [beings] in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*), nor the manifestation of diverse names and forms, nor the experience of pleasure and pain caused by the perception of infinite objects, nor the state of being the inner ruler (*antaryāmitva*) by remaining there as the non-enjoyer while governing them, nor the realization by the self, having become the individual soul, of its identity with the causal Brahman.

It is taught that one who composes a treatise for the sake of liberation from saṃsāra and its instruction must proceed with circumspection; for otherwise, there would be the consequence of it being nothing but the ravings of a madman.

Regarding the phrase "tataśca" (and therefore): in the case of a coordination (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) involving a superior [entity], there might be a suspicion that the non-difference is merely figurative (*aupacārika*). Here, however, the coordination with inferior [entities] such as fishermen (*dāśa*) and gamblers (*kitava*) serves to illuminate the reality (*tāttvikatva*) of the non-difference; this is the meaning.

The positive sense of the statement is that "Brahmā should wander about. For the teaching of an object that is not within the scope of other means of valid cognition (pramāṇa) is intended for the purpose of enlightening another. Therefore, by speaking of that which is beyond the scope of other means of valid cognition, the Veda enlightens [the listener] by saying, "Understand it thus. Consequently, by teaching a delusion that is not ultimately real, it is as if the Veda were saying, "Brahmā should wander about"; and that is not appropriate—this is the meaning. "That being so" (tathā sati) refers to this.

The meaning is that by the Veda, which is engaged in enlivening the world through the cessation of delusion, it is contradicted to produce another greater delusion. "By one who acts, one must be deluded" means that because of the state of acting, one must be deluded; the final sense is that it is not taught that "Brahman is deluded as if it were acting. Siddhāntin: [The word] "bhoktṛtva" (the state of being an enjoyer) [is used]. i, na. [These are manuscript variants.]

1. Or, it is the state of being that [nature] of the self. 2. The status of being an instrument (karaṇa-bhāva). 3. Or, it is a portion of Brahman (brahmāṃśa). 4. Established otherwise (anyathāsiddha). 5. Or, the absence of difference from that (tadbhedābhāva).
6. Alternative establishment (anyathāsiddhi). 7. Or, the absence of non-that (atadabhāva) in the self. 8. Of selves (ātmanām). 9. It is said (ucyate). 10. Ga manuscript.

The view that "the individual soul (jīva) is Brahman delimited by limiting adjuncts (upādhi)" is also not tenable, precisely because it contradicts the previously mentioned designations such as "being governed" (niyāmyatva). For it is not the case that for a single person like Devadatta, the relationship between ruler and ruled is established merely through different limiting adjuncts such as his house and so forth. Therefore, in order to justify both these designations, one must accept that "this jīva is a part (aṃśa) of Brahman. 42.
259. On account of the color of the mantra. (2.3.43)

And from the wording of the mantra, "One foot of Him is all beings; His three feet are the immortal in heaven," the individual soul (*jīva*) is a part (*aṃśa*) of Brahman. For the word "foot" (*pāda*) signifies a part. In the phrase "all beings," the plural number is used in the mantra because of the multiplicity of individual souls. In the Sūtra as well, the singular number in the word "part" (*aṃśaḥ*) intends to refer to the genus (*jāti*). Even in the Sūtra, "The Self [is not produced], on account of scripture" (*nātmā śruteḥ*), the singular number intends to refer to the genus. [As it is said: "He is the eternal among the eternals, the conscious among the conscious, the one who fulfills the desires of many."
—From such scriptural passages as these, because the difference from the Lord, as well as the multiplicity and eternity of the selves, are being declared.

"Upādhi" means a real limiting adjunct (*satyopādhi*). Regarding the phrase "from the wording of the mantra": in the previous sūtra, the state of being a part (*aṃśatva*) was inferred through the presumptive implication (*arthāpatti*) of the scriptural meaning consisting in the establishment of the primacy of the dual designation. Here, however, it is said that the state of being a part is explicitly stated. Regarding the phrase "denoting a part," etc.: the scripture "The eternal among eternals... is a qualified injunction (*viśiṣṭavidhi*), similar to "That which belongs to Agni, [consisting of] one cake on eight potsherds"; for its qualities are to be enjoined, since there is no separation from the purpose of the injunction.

Thus, when the plurality of eternal selves is established by valid means of knowledge, even though they are all of one form by virtue of having the nature of consciousness, their distinguishing characteristics are perceived only by those capable of knowing the true nature of the self. Furthermore, immediately following this, he will state that "there is no confusion because there is no continuity [of the self]. (43)
260. It is also recorded in tradition: 2-3-44.

"Such as this [is He] in the world of the living, the eternal one who has become the individual soul"—thus it is remembered that the individual soul (jīva) is a portion of Puruṣottama. And for this reason, this [soul] is a portion. 44.

Even if the individual soul (*jīva*) is a part [of Brahman], one might suspect that because the soul is a single portion of Brahman, the defects residing in the soul belong to Brahman itself; anticipating this objection, the Sūtra says: "But the Supreme is not so, like light and other things" (2.3.45).

The word "tu" (but) sets aside the objection. The individual soul (*jīva*) is a part of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), like light and so forth, according to the maxim: "If it were not [so], they would have been taught by another. By the phrase "even though there is identity of nature," it is shown that the supreme non-dualistic statements regarding the soul have the purpose of indicating its specific form. "It is understood" means that difference is perceived through both inwardness (*pratyaktva*) and outwardness (*parāktva*). || 43 || 44 ||
It is also stated in the Smṛti: "A portion of My very self is the world of living beings.

Thus, [the soul] is said to be a portion of Vāsudeva; yet, although it is a portion of Brahman, the soul's status as a living being remains, for its nature as a soul does not cease even when it is a portion of the Supreme.
But the intrinsic nature of light and so forth does not exist in the middle or elsewhere as it does [at its source].

Śrībhāṣya 2.3.7]: For example, from luminous sources such as fire or the sun, there arises a "portion" which is light consisting of form (*bhārūpaḥ prakāśaḥ*); or, for instance, in the case of entities qualified by "cowness" and so forth—such as cows, horses, white, black, and the like—the qualifiers, such as "cowness," are their portions; or again, just as for an embodied being such as a god or a human, the body is a portion—in the same way [the individual soul is a portion of Brahman].

Indeed, being a part (*aṃśatva*) consists in being a portion of a single entity. For a single qualified entity (*viśiṣṭa-vastu*), the qualifier (*viśeṣaṇa*) is precisely a part. Thus, discerning people designate [this] regarding a qualified entity as: "this is the qualifying part," and "this is the qualified part. Even though there is a relationship of part and whole between the qualifier and the qualified, a difference in their intrinsic natures (*svabhāva*) is observed; in the same way, the relationship of part and whole and the distinction in intrinsic nature between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*)—as qualifier and qualified—are logically established.
This is what is meant by the statement: "The Supreme is not like this."

The individual soul (*jīva*) is not of the same nature as the Supreme (*para*). For just as light is of a different nature than its radiance, so too the Supreme—the possessor of parts—is a distinct entity from the individual soul, which stands in the place of the radiance; this is the meaning.
[This is the distinction between the scopes of the designations of difference and non-difference.]

Thus, designations of difference proceed by relying on the distinction in essential nature (*svabhāva-vailakṣaṇya*) produced by the relationship of qualifier and qualified between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*). However, designations of non-difference are established in their primary sense by relying on the fact that qualifiers which cannot exist independently terminate in the qualified.

The phrase "gavāśva" (cow and horse) is included by the word "etc. (*ādi*). Alternatively, as in the case of "dehinaḥ" (embodied beings): the intention is that by one who asserts the relationship of part and whole (*aṃśāṃśitva*) between two substances that exist as inseparable qualifiers (*apṛthaksiddha-viśeṣaṇa*), the relationship of part and whole is thereby stated to exist even between the two substances of the body and the self. Regarding the phrase "of the qualifier and the qualified": the meaning is that a difference in essential nature (*svabhāva*) is observed, such as density and compactness versus sparseness and expansion.

In such passages as "That thou art" (*tattvamasi*) and "This Self is Brahman" (*ayam ātmā brahma*), the words "thou" (*tvam*) and "this Self" (*ayam ātmā*)— just like the words "that" (*tat*) and "Brahman" (*brahma*)— denote the same single object because they signify Brahman as having the individual soul as its body; this point has already been explained at length.
262. And they remember [it]. 2-3-46.
Thus, Parāśara and others record the relationship of part and whole between the world and Brahman in terms of light and its possessor, power and its possessor, and body and soul:

"Just as the radiance of a fire situated in one place spreads far and wide, so does this entire world constitute the power of the Supreme Brahman. Whatever is created by whatever being, O twice-born one!"

"Upon the manifestation of that which is to be created, all of that is indeed the body of Hari," and so forth. By the inclusion of the word "and" (ca), it is stated that the Śrutis also—through such passages as "He whose self is the body"—declare the relationship of part and whole (aṃśāṃśitva) by way of the relation between self and body. || 46 ||

"Jyotiṣmān," "tejas," "tejasvī," and so forth; even words such as "you" (tvam) and "this self" (ayam ātmā) have meanings equivalent to those of the word *tat* and the word *brahman*. The portion beginning with "that" (*tat*) and ending with "also" (*api*) constitutes the statement of the proposition (*pratijñā*). "Having the individual soul as its body" (*jīvaśarīraka*) is stated as the reason (*hetu*). Regarding the phrase "it has been explained": the meaning is that everything intended by the Sūtra, which was to be stated here, has already been previously explained.

"And they remember" (smaranti ca). In the sūtra "It is also remembered" (api smaryate), the mention of Smṛti was stated merely regarding the state of being a part; in this sūtra, however, the mention of Smṛti is stated even regarding the state of being a part that consists of a specific attribute of a particular portion—this is the distinction. Regarding the word "and" (ca): since both scriptural (Śruti) and Smṛti statements were to be mentioned, the Smṛti statement is explicitly stated in the sūtra because it provides a greater degree of clarification by way of presenting an illustrative example. || 46 ||
"Just as the radiance of a fire situated in one place spreads abroad,
so too is this [world] the power (śakti) of the Supreme Brahman," according to the Smṛti.

Even the word [of the Veda]—thus, since being a part of Brahman, being impelled by Brahman, and being ignorant are common to all, how is it that in the scriptures there is permission for some to study the Vedas and perform their rites, while for others there is a prohibition thereof; and for some there is permission to see and touch [the sacred objects], while for others there is a prohibition? Anticipating this objection, he says: **263. Permission and prohibition arise from connection with a body, as in the case of light and so forth.** (2.3.47)

Even though all beings are of one and the same nature by virtue of being portions of Brahman and possessing knowledge and so forth, the rules of acceptance and avoidance are nevertheless appropriate based on their connection with bodies that are pure or impure—such as those of Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and others. This is like the case of fire and other things: although fire is of one nature as fire, it is accepted from the house of a learned Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*), but avoided from a cremation ground and the like; and likewise, food and such are accepted from a *śrotriya* and others, but avoided from one who has been accused of a crime (*abhiśasta*) and the like. || 47 ||
264. And because there is no continuity [of the soul], there is no confusion [of actions and their results]. (2.3.48)

Even though the individual souls (*jīvas*) are of a single nature by virtue of being portions (*aṃśas*) of Brahman and so forth, there is no confusion of experiences because they are distinct from one another and, due to their atomic size (*aṇutva*), are separate in each body.

"In the state of being a portion" refers to the subject matter of this current section; "in the state of being impelled by Brahman" refers to the subject matter of the preceding section; and "in the state of being a knower" refers to the subject matter of the section prior to that. || 47 ||

Regarding the term *asantateḥ*: *santati* means "continuous extension" (*samantāt tatiḥ*), that is, omnipresence (*vibhutvam*). Its absence is *asantati*, which is atomicity (*aṇutvam*). Furthermore, the reason indicated by the conjunction of the word "and" (*ca*) is "because of mutual distinction.

Even though the individual souls (*jīvas*) are portions of Brahman, the distinction between their inclusion and exclusion [in specific states] is logical, due to the difference in their bodies and conditions, just as in the case of fire and other such things.
Furthermore, because it is distinct in every body and because of its atomic nature,
the experience of pleasure and pain therein is determined by the best of sages to be individual. (Brahmapurāṇa)
264) 1. And in the case of being a knower—ta, tha, ca, da. Even though there is the nature of form—da.
* Seeing—60.

7. With the intention that all defects—such as the confusion of the experiences of enjoyment (*bhoga-vyatikara*) between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*), and among the individual souls themselves—exist both in the theory of the deluded Brahman-as-soul (*bhrānta-brahma-jīva-vāda*) and in the theory of the conditioned Brahman-as-soul (*upahita-brahma-jīva-vāda*), the absence of such confusion of enjoyment is stated in his own position (*svapakṣa*). || 48 ||

But surely, even in the doctrine that the individual soul (*jīva*) is an illusory manifestation of Brahman, the regulation of experiences and so forth are possible due to the distinctions created by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) produced by ignorance (*avidyā*); therefore, he says: "And that very [Brahman] is the appearance. (2.3.49)

For that whose essential nature is nothing but the undivided, single-flavored manifestation, it is *ābhāsa* alone that serves as the cause for establishing the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) preceded by the concealment of its own nature. It has already been established that for that whose sole nature is manifestation, the concealment of manifestation is indeed the destruction of manifestation. Alternatively, there is the reading "ābhāsā eva" (only manifestations).
In that case, the manifestations are the causes; and by virtue of the word "ca" (and), [the following is included].
"Having known the Self and the Impeller as distinct," "The two, the Knower and the Unknower," and "Of these two,
one eats the sweet pippala fruit."

Furthermore, there is a contradiction with such scriptural passages as these. For, even if one accepts the distinction of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) imagined by ignorance (*avidyā*), since the nature of the Self as conditioned by all those adjuncts is admitted to be one, the confusion of experiences remains exactly as it was. (49)

Regarding the word "erroneous" (*bhrānta*): the meaning is that the impossibility of establishing the distribution of experiences (*bhoga-vyavasthā*) in the opponent's position is intended. That impossibility arises because there is no distinction in the locus (*āśraya-bheda*) of ignorance (*avidyā*) and the rest. Some argue: "In the Sūtra, *'nānātmāno vyavasthātaḥ'*, does 'establishment' (*vyavasthā*) refer to a difference in the intrinsic nature (*svarūpa-bheda*) of pleasure and so forth, or to a difference in their locus? It cannot be the first, because it would not entail a difference in locus. Nor can it be the second, because the reason (*hetu*) would be indistinguishable from the probandum (*sādhya*). This is not correct.

This is because the intended meaning is that the established state consists in the absence of reconnection (*pratisandhāna*). When there is an absence of an obstructing factor, reconnection is pervaded by the identity of the self. The meaning is that even in the absence of an obstructing factor, because reconnection does not occur, the identity of the self is negated. || 48 ||
"In that very state" means that even concealment and so forth are not logically possible; and even if they were possible, the established order would not be tenable—this is the meaning. || 49 ||
It is certain that all luminous appearances would become causes;
however, this is so only when one postulates the concealment (*tirodhāna*) and other states of the individual soul (*jīva*) within its non-difference from Brahman.

Even in the theory that the individual soul (*jīva*) is Brahman as conditioned by ultimate adjuncts (*upādhi*), one might suspect that the systematic order [of experiences] will be maintained through the power of beginningless unseen merit and demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), which serve as the cause for the distinction between those adjuncts; anticipating this objection, he says:
"266. Because there is no restriction regarding the unseen [merit and demerit]. (2-3-50)

Even though the unseen force (*adṛṣṭa*), which serves as the cause for the succession of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi-paramparā*), has Brahman’s own nature as its substratum, there is no restriction [of its effects] because of the absence of a governing cause; furthermore, it is impossible for the nature of Brahman to be partitioned by the limiting adjuncts and the unseen forces through their mere connection with it. || 50 ||
There would indeed be no fixed rule;

267. "And it is the same even in the case of intention and so forth" (2-3-51). Even in the case of intention and other factors that serve as causes for the unseen (*adṛṣṭa*), there is precisely no fixed rule, for the very reason already stated. 51.

268. "If it be argued that [the distinction] is due to the difference in locations, we say no, because [all locations] are included within [Brahman]. (2-3-52) Even though the nature of Brahman is one alone, it is connected with various kinds of limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) which are incapable of being cut or divided; nevertheless, it may be argued that the regulation of experience is indeed possible on account of the difference in those locations of Brahman that are connected with the limiting adjuncts. If this is the objection:

"That is not so"; because the limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) move from place to place, and because all locations are included within all adjuncts, the confusion (*vyatikara*) remains exactly as it was. Even if there were a connection [of suffering] with specific distinct locations, since every location belongs to Brahman, the suffering associated with each particular location would belong to Brahman alone. As previously stated: "Otherwise, there would be the consequence of either constant perception or constant non-perception, or else a restriction to one or the other; [but] there is no such restriction, just as in the case of perception."

By these two sūtras, the fault of those who follow the Vedas and who maintain that the individual soul (jīva) is omnipresent has been stated. However, here, by means of the sūtras beginning with "And [the soul] is merely a reflection" (ābhāsa eva ca), the fault of those who rely on the Vedas and who maintain the oneness of the Self (ātmaikatvavādin) is being stated. || 51 || Thus ends the section concerning the part (aṃśādhikaraṇa). || 7 ||
Thus ends the third quarter of the second chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja.

Regarding the phrase "of the adjuncts" (upādhīnām), it refers to the mutual exchange of experiences among the individual souls (jīvas). By the phrase "through the distinction of locations" (pradeśabhedena), the meaning is that the experiences and so forth of these [souls] would belong to Brahmā. In this way, the confusion between the individual soul (jīva) and the Lord (īśvara) is stated. || 52 ||

If the individual soul (*jīva*) were the portion [of Brahman] conditioned by ignorance (*avidyā*), there would be a restriction [of its nature]; for here, the unconditioned [Brahman] does not enter into the movement of the limiting adjunct (*upādhi*), nor is it included within it.
The Fourth Pāda of the Second Adhyāya in the Śrībhāṣya: An Indication of the Subject Matter of the Adhikaraṇas.
Śrīḥ!

Salutations to the venerable Rāmānuja. Salutations to Śrī. Salutations to Śrīdhara. This concludes the fourth section, the Prāṇapāda, of the second chapter (the Avirodhādhyāya) in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad-Rāmānuja. 24.
Section on the Origination of the Vital Breaths (Prāṇa). Sūtra 2.4.1:
"In the same way, the vital breaths. 2.4.1.

When it has been stated that everything other than Brahman, such as the ether and so forth, arises as an effect, the notion of "arising" characterized by a change in essential nature—even regarding the individual soul (jīva) as an effect—has been refuted. In connection with that, the true nature of the individual soul has been "purified."

"Brahman" refers to the subject matter that defines the status of being a knower and so forth; it is connected here by way of context. Therefore, the meaning is that its connection to the preceding section is through its relation to the chapter (pāda). The connection [of this specific section] is as follows: immediately after the definition of the origin of the individual soul (jīva), the manner of the origin of the individual soul's instruments (upakaraṇas) is now clarified. This is the connection.

The established conclusion (*siddhānta*) is reached through definitive assertions, propositions, and so forth; it is not the case that this section of the treatise is not to be commenced. This is because the scriptural statement, "The vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*) are indeed the seers (*ṛṣayaḥ*)," has not yet been fully resolved. For this very reason, having in mind the principle of the established conclusion previously mentioned, the author of the Sūtras did not compose a separate sūtra for that [previous point], but rather composed a sūtra specifically to resolve the scriptural passage concerning the vital breaths.

"Indeed, that Supreme Brahman is the one by whom the vital breaths were established even before creation! Now follows the manner of the origin and so forth of the senses— the instruments of the individual soul— and of the vital breath."
It is purified.
In this regard, it is considered: Is the status of being an effect belonging to the sense organs like that of the individual soul (jīva), or like that of ether and the other elements?

What is logical? The proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) says: "Just like the individual soul (*jīva*)," namely, "so too are the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*). The vital breaths are the sense organs (*indriyāṇi*). Just as the individual soul is not produced, so too the sense organs are not produced. Why? Because of scripture (*śruti*). Just as the non-production of the individual soul is understood from scripture, so too the non-production of the vital breaths is understood from scripture alone. By the statement "so too are the vital breaths," the authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) is being indicated.
What, then, is the scriptural authority (śruti) for this?

"In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent (asat). Regarding that, they ask: 'What existed then? The sages (ṛṣis), verily, were that existence in the beginning. Regarding that, they ask: 'Who are those sages? The vital breaths (prāṇas), verily, are the sages.

Thus, the existence of the sense organs prior to the origin of the world is heard in scripture. Because the word "prāṇa" is used in the plural, it is determined that these are indeed the sense organs.

Nor can the theories regarding the origination of the sense organs be assimilated like the theory of the origination of the Self, because we do not find scriptural texts prohibiting the origination of the Self, nor do we find texts asserting its eternity.
Even in such passages as "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent," it is the Supreme Self alone that is indicated by the word "prāṇa," as in the text:
"All these beings, verily, enter into prāṇa alone and emerge from prāṇa."
Thus, since the word "prāṇa" is well-known to refer even to the Supreme Self;
and the word "ṛṣi," as in "The prāṇas indeed are the ṛṣis," is applicable only to that Omniscient One, and not to the insentient sense organs. || 1 ||

If it be asked how the plural scriptural statement, "The sages are the vital breaths" (*ṛṣayaḥ, prāṇāḥ*), is to be understood, the Sūtra replies: 270. On account of the impossibility of a secondary sense, and because of the prior scriptural mention [of the singular]. (2.4.2)

"But not in the case of the insentient sense organs. Since the immediately preceding sūtra was intended merely to resolve the issue of the plural number, [the author] himself has stated everything intended by the Sūtrakāra—that the entire collection of other arguments for the established doctrine (siddhānta) is established by implication—as his own intention. || 1 ||

The scriptural mention of the plural number is figurative; for it is impossible for that same Supreme Self to possess multiple entities, precisely because scripture declares that He alone existed prior to creation. || 2 ||
271. Or [the word is eternal] because speech is preceded by that [cognition]. (2.4.3)

For this reason as well, the word "prāṇa" denotes the Supreme Self. This is because the creation of the elements such as ether—which are the "beings" (bhūta) that constitute the objects of speech, namely names distinct from the Supreme Self—is preceded by [the existence of] speech. The meaning of the passage, "In the beginning, this was indeed unevolved; it was evolved through name and form," is that at that time those [senses] such as speech did not exist, because there was an absence of things possessing name and form, and because there was an absence of the functions of the sense organs like speech. || 3 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the origin of the vital breaths (Prāṇa). || 1 ||
The Topic of the Seven Courses of Existence (Saptagaty-adhikaraṇa). 2.4.2.
272. And because the seven states of existence are specifically distinguished. (2.4.4)
Regarding those sense organs, a doubt arises from conflicting scriptural statements:
are there exactly seven, or are there eleven? This is what is being considered. What is the prima facie position? That there are seven.

Why? Because of their movement and because they are specifically distinguished. First, regarding movement: the movement consisting of the wandering through the worlds together with the living being who is being born and dying is heard of as belonging to the seven alone, in the text:

"These seven worlds exist, in which move the prāṇas, hidden in the cave, seven by seven. The repetition [of "seven"] is intended to indicate a plurality of persons. Furthermore, those moving prāṇas are distinguished by their own nature.

Regarding the word "seven": are there only seven sense organs (*indriya*), or are there eleven? Does the mention of the movement [of seven] imply that the number of sense organs is seven? Or not? For that purpose, even in the absence of a mention of their movement, is it possible for the hands and so forth to be sense organs? Or not? Is the scriptural statement, "These ten are in the person," etc., not an authority for the fact that there are eleven sense organs? Or is it?

"When the five [senses] stand still together with the mind, and the intellect does not stir—that they call the supreme goal. Here, the "supreme goal" refers to the departure for the sake of liberation, leaving behind the movement within the body. Thus, because the movement of only seven is heard of in relation to birth and death along with the individual soul (jīva), and because they are specifically qualified as "the senses" (jñānāni) in the state of yoga, it is understood that the individual soul possesses exactly seven instruments: hearing, touch, sight, taste, smell, intellect, and mind.
But as for those others which function as the perceivers of objects—
namely, "the eight graspers" and "there are seven vital breaths in the head, and two in the lower part"?

In such passages up to the fourteenth, in the statements establishing the vital breaths (*prāṇas*), the sense organs known as speech, hands, feet, anus, genitals, ego-sense (*ahaṅkāra*), and mind are understood; however, because there is no scriptural mention of their departing along with the individual soul (*jīva*), the designation "vital breath" applied to them is merely figurative, based solely on their providing very slight assistance to the soul. || 4 ||
This being the position reached, we reply: "But the hands and so forth [are not so], for [the self] remains [in the body]; therefore it is not thus. (2.4.5)

It is not only seven faculties; rather, there are eleven, including the hands and so forth—this is the meaning. "The supreme goal" (paramā gatiḥ) means yoga, because its nature consists in proceeding toward the purpose of liberation. "Cognitions" (jñānāni)—by the etymological derivation "that by which something is known"—means the sense-faculties (indriyāṇi). "The others" means together with the previous seven. || 4 ||

"While the body exists," [the hands and so forth exist] because they are instruments for the living being's enjoyment, and because their functions are distinct. For indeed, a distinction in function is observed in the case of the hands and so forth, just as it is in the case of the ears and other senses—namely, grasping and so on. Therefore, they certainly do exist. Thus, the meaning is that one should not think in this way, namely, that "the hands and so forth do not exist."

The mind itself is designated by the terms *buddhi*, *ahaṃkāra*, and *citta* due to the distinctions in its functions of determination (*adhyavasāya*), self-conceit (*abhimāna*), and reflection (*cintā*).
Thus, there are eleven sense-faculties; hence it is said:
"These ten are the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) in a person, with the self (*ātman*) as the eleventh."
Thus, by the word "ātman," the mind is denoted.
"The ten and one senses, and the five objects of the senses" (Bhagavad Gītā).
"They say the senses are taijasa, while the ten deities are vaikārika."

The number of sense organs established by such scriptural and traditional texts as "And here, the mind is the eleventh" is fixed. Claims for a higher number are intended to refer to the different modifications (vṛtti) of the mind. As for designations of a lower number, they are employed in various instances based on specific functions intended to be expressed, such as the act of moving. || 5 ||
Thus ends the seventy-second topic. 2.
The Section on the Atomicity of the Vital Breath (Prāṇa) || 2.4.3 ||
And [they] are atomic. (2-4-6)
Since it is heard that "all these are indeed equal, all are infinite," the omnipresence of the vital breaths (prāṇas) follows—
this being the position reached, the following is stated in reply:

Since their limited size is established by the scriptural hearing of "departing" and so forth—based on the statement, "When the principal breath departs, all the breaths depart along with it"—and since they are subtle (aṇu) because departing and other such acts are not perceived by bystanders, [the inquiry arises]:

Are the sense organs all-pervading (sarvagata), or are they of atomic dimension (aṇuparimāṇaka)? Is the hearing of their infinity for the sake of meditation (upāsanā), or not? Does the hearing of their departure lead one to understand their atomicity, or not?

In the absence of any evidence for atomicity (*aṇutva*), since the scriptural hearing of their infinity would lack the purpose of being for meditative worship (*upāsanā*), they are all-pervading (*sarvagata*). However, if the hearing of their departure (*utkrānti*) establishes atomicity, then because the scriptural hearing of their infinity is for the purpose of meditation, they are atomic in form. (*[And] "atomic" [is said]. Here, the intended atomicity is established as qualified; it is not absolute minuteness like the essential nature of the individual soul (*jīvātman*). For in that regard, absolute minuteness has already been stated by the passage beginning with "on the tip of a hair," and thus such an admission [of absolute minuteness] is made there. The atomicity mentioned here—*) *Note: The text provided contains a fragmentary commentary on the Sūtra "And [they are] atomic" (Brahma-sūtra 2.3.19–22). The translation reflects the logical structure of the argument regarding the size of the individual souls.*
Having reflected upon the difficulty of construing the sentences in the *Śrutaprakāśikā*, the intended meaning has been accepted here according to my own understanding.
[Because of the statement:
"These very senses are atomic, for their departure and so forth are heard in scripture; indeed, these are described as being infinite for the purpose of meditation."

Because they are finite, and the vital breaths (prāṇas) are atomic. As for the scriptural statement regarding their infinity—namely, "Now, he who meditates on them as infinite"—this is because meditation is being enjoined; it intends to refer to the multiplicity of the effects that serve as attributes of the vital breaths to be meditated upon. || 6 ||
275. And [the word] *śreṣṭha* [is used]. 2-4-7.

Regarding the "Principal Breath" (*mukhya-prāṇa*), which is determined to be the most excellent as the cause of the body's maintenance in the dialogue of the vital breaths (*prāṇasaṃvāda*): one might suspect that it is not produced, because of the scriptural hearing of its existence through its own function of breathing at the time of the great dissolution (*mahāpralaya*)—in the passage, "That One breathed, windless, by its own power" (*ānīd avātaṃ svadhayā tad ekaṃ*)—and because the hearing of its birth in the passage, "From this it is born," is logically consistent with the hearing of the birth of the individual soul (*jīva*). However, this suspicion is set aside because it contradicts the determination of oneness prior to creation and other such [scriptural] passages.

Because of the scriptural statement, "From this [Being] is born Prāṇa," which declares an origin equal to that of earth and the other elements, and because there is no denial of its origination, it is said that the preeminent Prāṇa is indeed born. However, the passage "Breathless it breathed" does not refer to the preeminent Prāṇa as such; rather, it declares the existence of the one supreme Brahman alone, since the term "breathless" is heard in reference to that very same [Brahman].
Although the reasoning is identical to that of the preceding [sūtra], the formulation of a separate rule is for the sake of the subsequent consideration. || 7 ||
Thus concludes the section concerning the minuteness of the vital breaths (prāṇas). || 3 ||
The section concerning the activity of air (vāyu). 2.4.4.
276. Or rather, [the vital breath] is not a function of air, because it is taught separately. (2.4.8)

Regarding this "best vital breath" (śreṣṭhaḥ prāṇaḥ), is it merely the air that is the second among the great elements (mahābhūta)? Or is it the activity consisting of its vibration? Or is it the air itself having attained some particular state?—in this doubt, the prima facie view (pūrva-pakṣa) is that it is simply air; for it is said, "That which is prāṇa is air."

Because of this designation; or rather, because the status of being "prāṇa" is not established for air in general, whereas the term "prāṇa" is well-known to refer to the activity of air such as inhalation and exhalation, it is that very activity [which is meant].
[The description of the latter half of the Sūtra as representing the established conclusion:
This being the position reached, it is stated: "Neither mere air, nor its activity. "Why? Because of the separate instruction"; for [the scripture says]:
"From this [Brahman] are born the vital breath (prāṇa), the mind, and all the sense organs; as well as space and air."

"Not indeed so. Is the chief vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*) merely air (*vāyu-mātra*), or is it the function of air (*vāyu-kriyā*), or is it air in a particular state (*avasthā-viśeṣa-prāpta*)? Among the views based on scripture, worldly consensus, separate instruction, the nature of reality, and common renown, which position is consistent? If there is consistency in the view that it is merely air or the view that it is the function of air, then one of those two would be established. If there is consistency in the view that it is air in a particular state, then that alone is the final conclusion. Therefore [it says]: "Air from space" (*khaṃ vāyuḥ*).

Thus, because it is taught as distinct from those very [elements], the vital breath (*prāṇa*) is not merely the activity of air. For the activity of fire and the other elements is never taught as a separate substance alongside them. The statement, "That which is the *prāṇa* is air," is for the purpose of making known that the *prāṇa* is simply air having reached a different state, and not that it is a different entity altogether like fire and the others. Furthermore, even in the case of inhalation and exhalation, the conventional usage of the word "prāṇa" refers to a substance possessing activity—as in "the *prāṇa* vibrates"—and not to activity alone. (Sūtra 8)

Is this *prāṇa* a modification of air, being a distinct element like fire? No; [the Sūtra] says: 277. "But it is like the eye and so forth, because of its being taught along with them, and for other reasons. (2.4.9)

This [prāṇa] is not a specific element (*bhūtaviśeṣa*), but rather a specific instrument of the living being (*jīvopakaraṇaviśeṣa*), like the eye and other organs. And that status as an instrument is understood from its association with the sense organs, which are themselves specific instruments, as well as from [scriptural] injunctions and so forth. This prāṇa is enjoined together with the eyes and other organs; for if it were of the same class as them, its being enjoined along with them would be appropriate, as seen in the "Dialogue of the Vital Breaths" (*prāṇasaṃvāda*) and similar passages.

The meaning is that because of this separate instruction, [the vital breath] is not merely air. By the phrase "from that very [source]," the status of being an action is rejected. Regarding the words "together with them," etc.: if it were argued that actions such as fire and so forth are taught separately because this is a section concerning the production of substances, then they would have been taught as substances; but that is not the case. Therefore, since an action cannot be taught separately because it lacks substantiality, the meaning is that the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which is taught separately, is not the action of air. || 8 ||

"What is this? [The answer is: "Prāṇa is air (vāyu) that has attained a particular state (avasthāviśeṣa)," as it has been stated. For there might be the doubt: "And the attainment of another state must occur only through the abandonment of its state as air, just as in the case of fire and so forth. [The author addresses this with] "In the dialogues on Prāṇa, etc. The intention is that there are many traditional teachings (śiṣṭayaḥ) along with various scriptural divisions (śrutibhedena), and there are also many specific designations. Alternatively, the plural number is used to indicate that the assistance provided is equal to that of the instruments (karaṇa), which will be explained in the immediately following sūtra. [The phrase] "for if they were of the same class" is said with reference to the principle of "that which is most prominent" (agryaprāyanyāya).
This distinction of states [of air] would not constitute a different element,
because of its being taught by the learned along with the sense organs in the dialogues concerning Prāṇa and so forth.
Among the organs included by the word "prāṇa," this [specific one] is designated by distinction; it is grasped by the word "etcetera" (ādi).
"Now, indeed, that which is this chief prāṇa..."
Because of the specific designation [of the Self] in such passages as, "This which is the middle breath," and so forth. || 9 ||

If it is argued: "Since this [nāḍī] is also an instrument like the eye and other organs, it too must perform a specific service for the individual soul (jīva) just like them; however, such a service is not perceived. Therefore, the nāḍī cannot be an instrument like the eye and so forth," to that he says: 278. "And because it is not an instrument, there is no fault; for scripture shows it to be so. (2.4.10)

Because it is "without action" (*akaraṇatvāt*)—action being *kriyā*; that is, because it is "devoid of activity. Furthermore, the defect which is raised—that this vital breath (*prāṇa*) is devoid of any specific activity in the form of service toward the living self (*jīva*)—does not exist. For the Śruti demonstrates activity in the form of specific service, such as the sustaining of the body and the senses:
"When he has departed, this body appears as if most wretched; he is indeed the best among you."

Because this has been stated, and because after demonstrating that the body and the sense organs remain even when speech and the other [organs] depart, it is declared that upon the departure of the *prāṇa*, the body and the senses become flaccid; therefore, this *prāṇa*, existing in fivefold forms as *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *vyāna*, *udāna*, and *samāna*, assists the individual soul (*jīva*) by sustaining the body and the senses, and thus possesses the status of an instrument (*karaṇa*), like the eye and other such organs. || 10 ||

[Objection: But if this is so—due to the difference in names and the difference in functions—would not the *prāṇa*, *apāna*, and so forth, be distinct principles (*tattvāntara*)? To this, he says: **279. Having five functions, it is designated like the mind.** (2.4.11) Just as, despite the difference in functions such as desire and the like, and despite the difference in their effects, desire and the rest are not distinct principles from the mind—because of the scriptural statement: "Desire, resolve, doubt, faith, lack of faith, steadfastness, lack of steadfastness, shame, intelligence, fear—all this is truly the mind"—so too, [it is said]: "Prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, samāna—all this is truly prāṇa."
From this statement, it is understood that the apāna and the others are also merely specific functions of the prāṇa itself, and not separate principles. || 11 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the activity of the vital air (vāyu). 4.
The Section on the Greatest and the Smallest (Śreṣṭhāṇutvādhikaraṇa) || 2.4.5 ||
280. And [the soul] is atomic (aṇu). 2.4.12.

This [individual self] is atomic, because, as before, there are scriptural statements regarding its departure and so forth, such as: "When he departs, the vital breath (prāṇa) departs after him," and so on. However, a further doubt arises from the passage:
"He is equal to these three worlds; he is equal to this entire universe."
"Everything is established in the vital breath," and "All this is indeed enveloped by the vital breath"—
from such scriptural declarations [it follows that the vital breath] is "of great dimension."

The rebuttal, however, is as follows: since its limited size is established by scriptural statements concerning its departure from the body and so forth, the doctrine of its omnipresence is justified by the fact that the existence of the entire class of living beings depends upon the vital breaths. Thus [ends section 12].
Thus ends the section concerning the excellence of atomicity. 5.

"And [is it] atomic?"—that is, is this prāṇa all-pervading or is it atomic? Does the designation of infinity in the phrase "What have I to do with these three worlds? imply its omnipresence? Or not? Does it indicate that [the term] is figurative? Or not?

When the scriptural mention of "departure" (utkrānti) does not lead one to understand infinity, then [the self] is all-pervading, because the designation of infinity indicates omnipresence. When it leads one to understand a figurative sense, then [the self] is atomic, because the statement of infinity is understood as being secondary.

The statements beginning with "Equal to these three" (*sama ebhis tribhiḥ*) are not recited in a fixed sequence in any single place. Although the prima facie argument (*pūrvapakṣa*) is the same as in the previous section, the refutation (*parihāra*) is also similar to that of the preceding *adhikaraṇa*. Since the status of the world prior to its creation has been established through the determination of oneness (*ekatvāvadhāraṇa*) and other means, and because the passage concerning the "non-existent" (*asat*) has been shown to have Brahman as its ultimate purport, the contradiction regarding the scriptural mention of infinitude in passages such as "And [the souls] are atomic" (*aṇavaś ca*) was resolved by interpreting it as being for the purpose of comparison (*upamānārtha*). Such a resolution is not possible here; therefore, this is a separate *adhikaraṇa*.

Section on Light and the Other [Elements] (Jyotirādyadhikaraṇa). 281. But light and the other [elements] have as their presiding deities those [gods] mentioned in scripture, because they are accompanied by the vital breath, as is known from the sacred word. Sūtra 2.4.13.

The origin, extent, and measure of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) along with their presiding deities have been stated. Furthermore, the fact that those vital breaths are presided over by deities such as Fire (*agni*) was already established in the context of the previous discussion by the sūtra:

"But there is designation based on presiding deities because of distinction and following" (*abhimāni-vyapadeśastu viśeṣānugatibhyām*). Moreover, it is well known in the world that the individual soul (*jīva*) is the presiding controller of these [breaths], which are the instruments for its own experience.
And this is established by such scriptural passages as: "In this very way, having taken hold of these vital breaths (prāṇas), he moves about at will within his own body.

Regarding this matter—the presiding over the vital breaths by the individual soul (jīva) and the deities such as Fire—is this control dependent on themselves, or is it dependent on the Supreme Self?—such is the doubt.

*Īyattā* means number; *parimāṇa* means the individual measurement of those things that have been numbered. Regarding the question of whether the soul’s and the presiding deities such as Agni’s control over the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) is independent or dependent upon the Supreme Self: Is the perception of their independence in that regard correct, or is it rooted in delusion? If it is correct, there is independence; if it is rooted in delusion, there is dependence on the Supreme Self. However, in the case of light and so forth, [the power] arises from the will of the Supreme Self through the soul.
The substratum of the sense organs and so forth is understood from sound alone.

Since [the senses] are independent and thus self-dependent—[as argued in the phrase] "the description of their own purpose"—this being the position reached, it is said: "The presiding over light and so forth. This means that together with the possessor of breath—the individual soul (jīva)—there is the presiding over the objects of breath by the lights and so forth—the deities such as Fire and others. This occurs because of the mention of Him; that is, because of the mention of the "Supreme Self" (paramātman). "Mention" (āmanana) means thinking with direct orientation. The meaning is that it occurs solely through the volition (saṅkalpa) of the Supreme Self.

Whence is this known? From scripture (*śabda*). For it is established by the scriptures that the sense organs, along with their presiding deities, and the individual soul (*jīvātman*) are dependent upon the contemplation of the Supreme Person (*paramapuruṣa*) in their respective functions. As in the *Antaryāmi-brāhmaṇa* and other texts:

"He who dwells in fire, yet is within fire, whom fire does not know, whose body is fire, who controls fire from within—he is the inner controller (*antaryāmin*), the Self, the Immortal. And: "He who dwells in air... and so forth.
"He who dwells in the sun," "He who dwells in the self," and "He who dwells in the eye."
And so forth. As it is said:
"Out of fear of Him the wind blows; out of fear of Him the sun rises."
"Out of fear of him, fire and Indra, and death as the fifth, run about.
Likewise:
"Under the governance of this Imperishable, O Gārgī, the sun and the moon stand held apart."
And so forth. || 13 ||
And because that [Self] is eternal. (2.4.14)

Since the fact that all [beings] are presided over by the Supreme Self is eternal—and because it is necessarily bound to their very nature—their being presided over by Him through His will alone is unavoidable. By such passages as, "Having created that, He entered into it; having entered it, He became the manifest (sat) and the unmanifest (tyat)," the entry of the Supreme Person into all sentient and insentient things as their controller is heard to be inseparable from His own nature.
And it is also recorded:
"Pervading this entire universe, I remain with but a single portion.
Thus ends the section [concerning] the presiding over light and so forth. || 6 ||

By the phrase "and so forth," the word "etcetera" (ādi) is intended to include such statements as, "He alone rules this world eternally. Since the essential nature of deities such as Agni is established by itself, it is not said that their presiding over the senses and other faculties depends on another; rather, the meaning is that even their very existence is dependent upon the Supreme Self—how much more so, then, is their presiding over the senses and other faculties dependent upon the Supreme Self? Regarding the word "pervading" (viṣṭabhya): because of the statement, "having pervaded the entire world without distinction," it is established that the world’s connection [to Him] is dependent upon the Blessed Lord. || 14 ||
Thus concludes the section concerning the presiding over light and the other elements. || 6 ||
Since the world of existing things is eternally presided over by a supreme self,
its governance must therefore arise from an unavoidable volition.
The section concerning the sense organs (indriyādhikaraṇa). || 2.4.7 ||
283. "Those [organs] are the senses (indriyāṇi)," because they are designated as such, with the exception of the Best (the mind). (Sūtra 2.4.15)
In this doubt— whether all those designated by the word "prāṇa" are the senses, or only those distinct from the chief prāṇa—
the conclusion is that all of them are indeed the senses, because they are denoted by the word "prāṇa" and because they are instruments (karaṇas).

This being the position, it is replied: the sense organs (*indriya*) are indeed the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) other than the preeminent one (*śreṣṭha*). Why? Because the designation "sense organ" is applied specifically to those vital breaths other than the preeminent one. For, in such passages as "The sense organs are eleven, and five are the objects of the sense organs," the word "sense organ" is applied precisely to the eyes and so forth, together with the mind (*manas*). (Sūtra 1.1.15)
284. And because of the difference from the scripture concerning distinction. (2.4.16)

Regarding the statement "these are the sense organs" (indriyāṇi): Are all vital breaths (prāṇas) sense organs, or only those distinct from the principal vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa)? Does the word "prāṇa" apply to the ears and so forth, as well as to the principal vital breath, by virtue of a single basis, or by virtue of different bases? If it is by virtue of a single basis, then all vital breaths are sense organs; if it is by virtue of different bases, then only those distinct from the principal vital breath are sense organs. || 15 ||
Even though all [the senses] are instruments, they are designated as "senses" (*indriya*) only when distinct from the Best (*śreṣṭha*); for that Best One does not become a sense.
Because its arising is declared to be distinct from the sense-faculties together with the mind,
and because the activity of the vital breath (prāṇa) is specifically perceived during deep sleep.
Not from the gods—da.
But the sense organs—śra.
"From this [Being] is born the vital breath (prāṇa), the mind (manas), and all the sense organs."

In such passages as these, because the vital breath (prāṇa) is heard of separately from the senses, it is understood that the status of being a sense organ belongs only to those things distinct from the vital breath. Although the mind (manas) is also heard of separately, its inclusion within the other senses is stated elsewhere, as in the passage: "The senses, with the mind as the sixth," and so forth.

Furthermore, the superiority of the principal vital breath (*prāṇa*) over the eyes and other organs is perceived. For during deep sleep, the activity of the *prāṇa* is observed, whereas the activity of the eyes and other organs is not observed. Moreover, the function of the eyes, speech, and so forth—along with the mind—is to serve as the instruments for knowledge and action; the function of the *prāṇa*, however, is the sustenance of the body and the senses.

However, because their maintenance is dependent upon the vital breath (*prāṇa*), the designation of the word ‘*prāṇa*’ is applied to the sense organs. And so says the Śruti: “They all became his very form; therefore they are designated by this name. “They became his form” means “they became his body”; the meaning is that they came to have their activity dependent upon him. Thus ends the section on the sense organs (Indriyādhikaraṇa). || 16 || || 7 ||
In the phrase "‘bhedaśruteriti’ ityādi,” the word “ādi” (and so forth) is intended to include such passages as: “The ten organs and the five objects of the senses.”

"In deep sleep," and so forth. This means that in deep sleep there is a difference regarding the perception of mental modifications (*vṛtti*), a difference regarding the effects consisting in the maintenance of the body and the senses, and a difference regarding the grounds for the application of the term "prāṇa. The application of the word "prāṇa" to the eyes and other organs is figurative (*lākṣaṇika*); however, its application to the principal *prāṇa* is primary (*mukhya*). It is appropriate to treat this as a single sūtra—beginning with "and because of the scriptural statement of difference and because of the difference"—since the scripture itself, supported by these differences, serves as the reason.

For when there is a difference in cause, a difference in the Sūtras is logically established; since a distinction can be indicated by the maxim of "the cow and the bull," once a distinctness is proven through another defining characteristic, the scriptural statement of difference becomes firmly established. || 16 ||

285. But the fashioning of names and forms belongs to Him who makes the triplication, because of the scriptural teaching. (2.4.17)

It was stated previously that the collective creation of the elements, senses, and so forth, as well as the agency of individual souls, proceeds from the Supreme Brahman; furthermore, it was subsequently recalled for the sake of confirmation that the souls' presiding over their own senses is dependent upon the Supreme.

"Previously"—in the third quarter (*pāda*). "Immediately after"—in this quarter, even before the preceding section (*adhikaraṇa*). Regarding the word *sthira* (firm): by determining that even the gods have their activity dependent on another, the agency of living beings (*jīvas*) as being dependent on another becomes firm. The meaning is that for that purpose, that very [dependence] was recalled as an illustration. Starting from the third quarter, there has been one section (*peṭikā*) prior to this; therein was the description of the creation of the collective totality (*samaṣṭi*) of the elements and the sense organs.

Now, the topical connection (*peṭikā-saṅgati*) is that this section concerns the description of the individual creation (*vyaṣṭi-sṛṣṭi*). Since the individual is of the nature of an instrument for the individual soul (*jīva*), the description of its creation constitutes the connection with the chapter (*pāda-saṅgati*). An intermediate connection (*avāntara-saṅgati*) arises from the doubt: "In the preceding section, it was stated that the collective creation (*samaṣṭi-sṛṣṭi*) has the Supreme Self as its agent; however, the individual creation is perceived as having the individual soul as its agent. Furthermore, the connection between the description of the individual creation and the description of the collective creation mentioned in the previous chapter is established. As for the other various sections (*adhikaraṇas*), they have been described by way of what follows from the subject at hand (*prasaktānuprasakti*); this has been explicitly stated.
