Now this so-called "differentiated creation" (*prapañca-vyaṣṭi-sṛṣṭi*), consisting of the manifestation of names and forms (*nāmarūpa-vyākaraṇa*): is it the work of Hiraṇyagarbha alone, who is the collective individual soul (*samaṣṭi-jīva*)? Or is it the work of the Supreme Brahman, who has the subtle elements such as fire (*tejas*) and so forth as His body—just as He is the creator of water and the rest—having Hiraṇyagarbha as His body? This is what is now being considered. What is the correct view? That it belongs to the collective individual soul. Why?

Rather, [the Self enters] in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*), which is its own part, according to the scriptural statement: "By this living self (*jīva*). Now, one might object: in this case, the use of the first person in the phrase "I shall manifest" (*vyākaravāṇi*) would be like saying, "Having entered the enemy's army by means of a spy, I shall count it," where the verb "to enter" (*praviśati*) has its action residing in the agent; thus, it would be figurative (*lākṣaṇika*). This is not so. In that case, there is a figurative usage because of the difference in essential nature between the king and his spy. Here, however, since the individual soul is also an essential part of the Self, its entry is in that very form. Furthermore, since the manifestation (*vyākaraṇa*) is of the Self itself, there is no occasion for it to be considered figurative.

Nor is this instrumental case characterized by association (*sahayoga*); for when a case ending denoting a *kāraka* (grammatical participant) is possible, it is improper to employ a case ending based on a mere accompanying word (*upapada*).

Nor is the instrumental used here in the sense of the instrument (*karaṇa*); for in the acts of entering and manifesting whose agent is Brahman, the individual soul lacks the status of being the most effective means (*sādhakatama*).

Nor can it be said that the agency of the individual soul (jīva) terminates merely in entering [the body], while the differentiation of names and forms (nāma-rūpa-vyākaraṇa) belongs to Brahman alone; for by the suffix *tvā*, a common agent is perceived. Although the jīva is a part of [Brahman] and not distinct from its essential nature, the reference as "by this living self" (*anena jīvena*) is made as "the other" (*parātvena*) in order to distinguish it from the supreme nature. Therefore, this differentiation of names and forms has Hiraṇyagarbha as its agent.

Regarding the phrase "the action resides in the agent" (*kartṛsthakriya*): by the intention that "the action resides in the agent of the grammatical operation" (*vyākaraṇakartṛsthakriya*), the meaning is "having a common agent" (*samānakartṛka*). Regarding the word *praviśati*: here, it is not intended that the verbal root (*dhātu*) is figurative (*lākṣaṇika*), but rather that the suffix following it is; for, due to the qualification "the action resides in the agent," the sense of "the [agentive] form ending in *lyap*" (*lyabantapraviśati*) is obtained.

"It is not so": because, in reality, the individual soul (*jīva*) is a part of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), its agency belongs to the Supreme Self alone. Therefore, this constitutes the primary category (*mukhyakoṭi*); such is the meaning.

And [the word] "not with" (*na ca saha*). Having raised the objection that "if the third case ending were intended to convey meanings other than conjunction, such as accompaniment, then agency would belong to the Supreme Self alone," this was stated: A *kāraka-vibhakti* is a case ending prescribed by rules such as "the third case is used for the agent and the instrument" independently of any other word. An *upapada-vibhakti* is a case ending prescribed in connection with the co-occurrence of another word. Regarding the phrase "because it is improper": "impropriety" is intended because [the latter] involves a delayed application due to its dependence on the co-occurrence of another word.
1. [Objection: Agency belongs to the Supreme Person—this has been stated.

Therefore, it is precisely for this reason that in the Smṛtis, within the context of creation, the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*) is proclaimed as having the four-faced Brahmā (*caturmukha*) as its agent: "He created the names and forms of beings, and the expansion of their activities, from the very words of the Veda; thus he brought about [the world] of gods and others."
— and so forth.

This being the position reached, it is replied: "But the fashioning of names and forms. The word "but" sets aside the previous view. "The fashioning of names and forms" means the differentiation of name and form (*nāma-rūpa-vyākaraṇa*). That belongs to the Supreme Brahman alone; for it is that very [Brahman] which is taught as the differentiator of names and forms. Indeed, it is precisely while performing the tripartition (*trivṛt-karaṇa*) that the differentiation of names and forms is taught: "That divinity thought: 'Well, let me enter into these three divinities with this living self (*jīva-ātman*')..."

This is because we perceive a common agent in the passage: "I shall evolve name-and-form... I shall make each of these tripartite. However, this tripartition cannot belong to the four-faced Brahmā residing within the cosmic egg; for it is by means of the tripartite fire and food that the egg itself is produced. Moreover, the birth of the four-faced one within the egg is recorded in Smṛti:
"In that egg was born Brahmā, the grandfather of all the worlds."

Thus, it is understood that the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) belongs to the Supreme Brahman alone, and the differentiation of names and forms (*nāma-rūpa-vyākaraṇa*), which has the same agent, also belongs to Him alone. How, then, is the phrase "by this living self" (*anena jīvena*) to be reconciled?

It is through grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*) as "by the self, [which is] the living self"; that is, the Supreme Brahman itself, having the living self as its body, is the "living self."
It is designated by means of sound (śabda), as for example:
"That fire thought," and "That created the waters."

"By means of those things made tripartite" means that the process of triplication (trivṛtkaraṇa) was for the purpose of creating the cosmic egg. [As it is said: "Those waters reflected; they created food."

Thus, that which has fire and so forth as its body is designated as the Supreme Brahman itself. Therefore, the differentiation of names and forms is the work of the Supreme Brahman alone, whose body is Hiraṇyagarbha—the collective totality of individual souls (jīvasamaṣṭi).

And thus, in the passage "Having entered, let me evolve name and form," both the verb "entering" and the first-person plural pronoun are used in their primary senses without any forced interpretation; furthermore, the identity of agent for both entering and evolving is logically established. Moreover, it is consistent that the act of evolving name and form is taught within the context of the creation performed by the four-faced Brahmā, as this creation—consisting of the diverse manifestations such as gods and others—is indeed the work of the Supreme Brahman itself, who has the four-faced one as His body.

Therefore, the meaning of the passage beginning with "That divinity... is as follows: "These three divinities"—namely, those consisting of fire, water, and food—"having entered through this Self," that is, through the Self characterized by the aggregate of individual souls (*jīva-samaṣṭi*), "I shall differentiate name and form"—that is, "I shall effect the manifold creation of gods and so forth, as well as their respective designations."

For that purpose—that is, for the sake of the specific creation of these elements of fire, water, and food, which were previously uncombined and incapable of producing specific effects—he resolved, "I shall make each one threefold. Therefore, this differentiation of names and forms is the work of the Supreme Brahman alone. || 17 ||

Now, it might be argued: "Because the differentiation of name-and-form (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*) has a single agent through the process of triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*), it cannot be said that its agent is the Supreme Self; for the process of triplication itself could possibly have the individual soul (*jīva*) as its agent. Indeed, after the creation of the cosmic egg, the method of triplication is taught with respect to the living beings created by the four-faced Brahmā:
'The three elements [become] objects of experience.

[By that which is qualified by the aggregate of individual souls—that is, by the body of the soul as qualified by each respective body]—it might be argued: because the instruction on triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) is given regarding the persons created by the four-faced Brahmā after the creation of the cosmic egg; and because triplication is observed in the sun and other entities created by him; and because [the scripture says], following the differentiation of names and forms: "But truly, my dear, when these three divinities reach the person, each becomes threefold; learn from me how that happens."
"Food, when eaten, is divided into three parts: its grossest portion becomes feces, its middle portion becomes flesh, and its subtlest portion becomes the mind," and so forth.
Likewise, in the preceding passage as well:

By the passage beginning, "O Agni, that which is your red form is the form of fire, that which is white is the form of water, and that which is black is the form of food," the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) is demonstrated in the fire, sun, moon, and lightning created by the Four-faced One (Brahmā). Furthermore, the tripartition is heard of as occurring after the process of differentiation (*vyākaraṇa*):
[namely] name and form...
"O Goddess, having entered these three deities with this living self (jīva-ātman), he differentiated name and form;
he made each one of them threefold, threefold"—thus [it is said].
To that, he replies:
286. Flesh and so forth belong to the earth; the same applies to the other two [elements] according to their respective names. (2.4.18)

As for what was stated—that this instruction on tripartition, "He made each of those threefold," refers to the deities and so forth created by the Four-faced One (Brahmā) after the creation of the cosmic egg—it is not possible that the tripartition is for the sake of the creation of the egg. Therefore, the meaning is that since the tripartition has the Four-faced One as its agent, the differentiation of names and forms (*nāma-rūpa-vyākaraṇa*), which has that same agent, must also have the Four-faced One as its agent.

That is not tenable; for in the passage, "Food, when eaten, is divided into three parts," since flesh and mind are designated as being subtler and more minute than feces, it would follow that they are composed of water and fire respectively by virtue of conforming to their causes. Furthermore, in the passage, "Water, when drunk [is divided into three parts]," it would follow that urine and breath—which are grosser and more minute [than the other two products]—would be composed of earth and fire respectively.

And this is not accepted [by the opponent], for [the Sūtra says]: "For flesh and so forth! It is accepted that [flesh] belongs to the earth (*bhauma*). Just like excrement, both flesh and the mind are accepted as belonging to the earth—that is, as *pārthiva* (earthy)—because of the introductory statement: "Food, when eaten, becomes threefold. And for the other two as well, according to the words [of the text]: for the other two passages as well—namely, the two sections concerning "water drunk" and "fire consumed"—the transformations are accepted according to the words [of the text]. "The water drunk is divided into three parts."

Thus, from the scriptural statement, the threefold transformation of water alone is understood. Likewise, from the statement, "So too, the food that is eaten is transformed into three parts," the threefold transformation of fire (tejas) alone is understood from the text. Therefore, it must be understood that feces, flesh, and mind are modifications of earth; urine, blood, and breath are modifications of water; and bone, marrow, and speech are modifications of fire.

Regarding the term "cause" (*kāraṇa*): even for earth, water, and fire that have not yet undergone triplication (*atrivṛtkṛta*), because they possess coarseness, subtlety, and extreme subtlety, there would likewise be coarseness, subtlety, and extreme subtlety among the respective elemental portions within those things that have been triplicated, in accordance with their own causes. Therefore, if the process of triplication were being demonstrated in the passage beginning with "Food, when eaten," then the coarsest part, feces, would be earthen; the subtle part, flesh, would be watery; and the extremely subtle part, the mind, would be fiery. But this is not tenable, because both flesh and the mind are earthen.
The meaning is that the fact of being earthy (pārthivatva) is understood from the introductory statement, "Food, when eaten," and this applies likewise to the other two sections as well.

By the phrase "and this is not accepted," the undesirable consequence (*aniṣṭa*) has been shown for the first and second alternatives (*paryāya*). However, in the third, such a consequence does not arise. The underlying point here is that in each alternative, the undesirable consequence must be applied to those [elements] taken last; since in the third alternative there is no undesirability in what is to be applied last, it need not be applied. Furthermore, in the case of the third alternative as well, the undesirability of bone and marrow being composed of earth and water will be stated later. As for the phrase "flesh and so forth": the fact that flesh and the mind are composed of water and fire, respectively, is considered undesirable.

In the second [set], urine would be earthen, blood watery, and breath fiery. In that case, the earthen nature of urine and the fiery nature of breath would be undesirable; for, according to the introductory statement, "The food eaten and the water drunk," flesh and mind are earthen, and because this does not contradict the remainder of the passage: "For, my dear, the mind consists of food, breath consists of water, and speech consists of fire. Therefore, [the text says]:
"Of these, he made each one threefold."

The manner of the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) thus described is not demonstrated by the passage beginning with "Food, when eaten," and so forth. If that were the case, since the three— mind, breath, and speech— are all subtle (*aṇīyas*) and therefore composed of fire (*taijasa*),
it would contradict such statements as, "For the mind, my dear, consists of food."

Much more so, then, regarding the triply-transformed (*trivṛtkṛta*) earth and other elements that have reached the person, the threefold transformation of each one is stated in the passage beginning with "Food, when eaten," and so forth. Furthermore, this tripartition of fire, water, and food must have occurred even prior to the creation of the cosmic egg; for those elements, if not triply transformed, lack the capacity to initiate an effect. Indeed, it is only when they are mutually conjoined that there is the capacity to initiate an effect, and that very conjunction is what constitutes tripartition. Thus it is recorded in Smṛti: "Having separate powers and being distinct, they were then unable to form a combination."

"They were unable to create living beings without coming together in their entirety. Having come together in mutual conjunction and being dependent upon one another, those principles beginning with Mahat and ending with the Viśeṣas produce the cosmic egg.
And for this very reason:

"Having entered by means of this living self (jīva-ātman), he manifested name and form"—because in this passage, the vital breaths (prāṇas) are shown to consist of water. This is also evident from the supplementary statements: "For the mind, my dear, consists of food (annamaya)," and "The vital breath consists of water (āpomayaḥ prāṇaḥ). In the third [section] as well, there would be the earth-nature of bone and the water-nature of marrow, while speech would have the nature of fire (taijasatva). However, the earth-nature of bone and the water-nature of marrow are not intended here; for the context begins with "Fire [is digested when] eaten," and the supplementary statement concludes with "Speech consists of fire. Therefore, the tripartition (trivṛtkaraṇa) is not being demonstrated [in that specific instance].
Rather, the meaning is that the transformation of food and the other [substances] is stated to be threefold for each one.

And that very thing—namely, their mutual conjunction. For this very reason, etc. Even though the means (*sādhana*) exists prior to its arising and the fruit (*phala*) exists subsequent to it, in the case of volition (*saṅkalpa*), the fruit itself is what precedes; for it is seen thus in such [passages] as "Desiring heaven, I shall sacrifice. In this context as well, in the statement "May I become many, may I procreate," the state of becoming many—the goal to be accomplished—is mentioned even before [the act], as stated in [the passage beginning with] "He desired" (du. 3). (da. 5; ta. tha. reads *anenaiva* instead of *anenaiva ca*).
The sequence of the reading, "He made each one of them threefold," is set aside by the sequence of the meaning.

The demonstration of the tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) is made with respect to fire, the sun, and so forth, which exist within the cosmic egg; for it is inappropriate to demonstrate the tripartition to Śvetaketu—who was desirous of hearing—by means of things existing outside the egg, since he was situated within it. Therefore, the tripartition is demonstrated with respect to the effects of the tripartite elements, such as fire, the sun, and so forth. || 18 ||

This might be the objection: "Food that is eaten, water that is drunk, and fire that is consumed"—since each of these, such as food and the rest, has been made tripartite and thus consists of three forms (namely, the nature of fire, water, and earth), how is it appropriate to designate them by a single form as "food," "water," or "fire"? To this, he says: 287.
*Vaiśeṣyāt tu tadvādastadvādaḥ* (But on account of the predominance [of one element], there is a designation according to that; there is a designation according to that). II.4.19.

*Vaiśeṣyam* means the state of being specific (*viśeṣabhāvaḥ*). Even though each [element] has become threefold through the process of triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*), it is observed that in each one there is a predominance of food and so forth, and thus its prior existence [as a distinct entity] is seen. This is further clarified in the *Upabṛṃhaṇa*. Therefore, in the statement of resolve, "I shall differentiate name and form; I shall make each one threefold," since the differentiation of name and form—which is the fruit of triplication—is understood first, it is established that the process of triplication itself occurs first.

The meaning is that, as seen in cases such as "He performs the *agnihotra* sacrifice" and "He cooks the gruel," the order of recitation (*pāṭhakrama*) is set aside by the order of purpose (*arthakrama*); because of the inherent nature of the sentence of resolve (*saṅkalpavākya*), because in other sentences of resolve within the same context the result is seen to occur earlier than [the action], and because of the natural force of the corroborative statements (*upabṛṃhaṇavacana*) such as "He differentiated name and form" and "He made each of them threefold," the order of recitation is set aside by the order of purpose.
It is performed; the remainder [of the sentence] is that it serves as a demonstration of the tripartition (trivṛtkaraṇa). || 18 ||

Regarding the term "vaiśeṣyam" (distinction): like the word "vikāra" (modification), the word "viśeṣa" (distinction) refers both to the substratum and to the attribute. Here, however, among the elements that have been triplicated, whatever may be the predominance of a particular [element], that very thing is designated by its respective name by the wise.
In those existing within the egg—namely, fire and the other elements existing within the egg (ta. 4)—by its own (svena) (da.
1), even the sequence (krama) (da.
1)—the demonstration (pradarśana) (da.).
In each of those cases, there is the mention of food and so forth. The repetition indicates the conclusion of the chapter. || 19 ||
Thus ends the section concerning the fashioning of names and forms (Saṃjñāmūrtiklṛpti-adhikaraṇa). || 8 ||
Thus ends the fourth quarter of the second chapter in the Śārīrakamīmāṃsābhāṣya composed by the venerable Bhagavad Rāmānuja. 4.
And the second chapter is completed. || 2 ||
Oṃ.
May there be prosperity! || śrīrastu ||
Salutation to Śrī. Salutation to Śrīdhara. Salutation to the illustrious Rāmānuja.
The first quarter of the second chapter:
The Section on Smṛti (Smṛtyadhikaraṇa). || 2-1-1 ||
The claim that the *Śārīraka-nyāya-kalāpa-saṅgraha*— on account of its contradiction with the *Smṛti*— cannot be the cause of the worlds for the sake of supplementing [the Vedas],
is worthless because it contradicts other *Smṛtis*. Furthermore, the doubt that "there is no attainment of those [other Smṛtis]" cannot even be entertained.

Brahman, being the supreme self-nature (*paramātma-bhūta*) reality, is not the cause of the worlds—it cannot be the cause of the universe—because this contradicts the Sāṃkhya scripture known as the *Pradhānakāraṇatvaparaka-pāśupata-tantra*, which is engaged in elucidating the meaning of the Vedas that has not been studied [by others], through a contradiction consisting of the rendering of it [the Veda] as having no scope. Such a doubt is baseless and unstable; for when one considers the portion concerning the ultimate reality (*tātvikāṃśa*), there is a contradiction with other Smṛtis, since [the Sāṃkhya] posits the primordial matter (*pradhāna*) as the cause of the world.

Because there would be the consequence of contradiction with the Smṛtis of Manu and others, which are established by Śruti. As for their lack of authority—that is, the absence of "authoritativeness" (āptatva), which consists of both being a speaker of truth and being a perceiver of things as they actually exist—in the case of those authors of such Smṛtis, namely Manu and others—it is not even possible to suspect it, much less prove it. || 1 ||
Adhikaraṇasārāvali (composed by the eminent Śrī Vedāntācārya)
May the illustrious Veṅkaṭanāthārya, the lion among poets and logicians, the preeminent teacher of Vedānta, dwell forever within my heart.

Although the attainment of satisfaction for those of great intellect, who are skilled in the sequence of the *Raktārkatāntra*, may be achieved through what has been stated, nevertheless, fearing an assault by rationalists (*haituka*), [the author] stabilizes the stated causality of Brahman—both its nature as cause and its nature as effect—according to each respective scriptural authority, following the method of digging around a pillar (*sthūṇākhātanyāya*). (1)
And what is their lack of attainment?

It is the failure to reach that kind of success—the joy attained by the wise (who determine the true meaning) who are skilled in a specific method within the system called Mīmāṃsā, which is dominated by *tarka* as a synonym for profound and distinctive inquiry. This [success] ought to be obtainable and consistent with the collection of meanings through the right knowledge set forth in the first chapter; nevertheless, for those of dull intellect—those of frivolous minds—who are "logicians fearing Skanda," being devoted solely to mere reasoning that does not conform to the revealed scriptures (*śruti*).

Anticipating an attack by those who speak excessively, the author of the Sūtras states: "That very causality of Brahman—the Supreme Self as the non-different efficient and material cause of the world—which has already been established; and whatever kind of effect-hood—consisting of the attainment of another state, whether it be a sentient or insentient entity within the world—characterized by modification pertaining to its nature or its essential form, which is understood through the Śrutis, that is, through Vedic statements engaged in determining matters beyond the senses, belongs to that [Self, ether, etc.]."

Even when investigated—such being the nature of the entire creation—it establishes [itself] through the method of digging a post into the ground (*sthūṇākhātakrama*), that is, by the logic of driving a post deep; it makes itself firm, demonstrating its own capacity to withstand agitation, rendering itself unshakable by any refutations (*apanītibhiḥ*). (It strengthens. || 1 ||
In the second [verse], he removes the external affliction of others for a further purpose; by means of the effect, another pair of feet arises to pacify internal agitation.
First, here, there is the refutation of the impossibility of causality for the Lord, because of His omnipresence.
The application of yoga bears fruit later on, and that occurs only after one has permanently abandoned the Vedic rites.

In the second [chapter], the pair of feet—the first two quarters (pādas) belonging to the second chapter—inform [the reader] regarding the "external affliction"—that is, the sublation and obstruction consisting of opposition raised by non-Vedic [opponents]—concerning the "Supreme Cause," which is the Supreme Brahman as the ultimate cause. The subsequent pair of feet—the second set of two quarters—[proceeds] by way of the effects.

Taking space and so forth as its effect, it arises—that is, it proceeds—for the sake of pacifying internal agitation, by means of internal [means] belonging to the Veda, or for the cessation of agitation that may occur regarding the subject matter of internal Vedāntic statements.

Thus, here in the first two quarters of this chapter, there is the "refutation of the impossibility of the Lord's [the Supreme Self] being the cause"—that is, the removal of the contradiction regarding the logical connection with causality as imputed by opponents. Subsequently, in the latter two quarters, there is the "rejection of the impossibility of that [Lordly] causality being universal," which is the dismissal of the lack of logical connection with the entire universe as its object. This bears fruit—it is established as the result of the inquiry—and that, moreover, is the refutation of the impossibility of [His] being the cause.

Setting aside that which is eternally established by Śruti—without grasping as its defining subject the collection of principles such as Prakṛti, Puruṣa, and Kāla, which are understood from Śruti as eternal—it finds its final conclusion by being defined by what remains. || 2 ||

In the introduction to the *Tantracchāyā*, [the author] himself does not prohibit the investigation of the ultimate purport (*tātparya*) of the Upaniṣads; however, because they are weaker than the Tantras, he rises up today with another argument: "one must follow them [the Tantras]. This being the case, having warded off the assault of various Smṛtis and legal codes (*naya*) with counter-missiles, he here confirms the original meaning that had wavered from its foundation.

When the *Kapila-tantra* is suspected of being the source [of the Sāṅkhya view] because its shadow is seen in the *Nidāna*, and when the alternative interpretation of the Upaniṣads—the intention of the Vedānta texts to posit a cause other than Brahman—is refuted by the author of the *Śārīraka-sūtras* himself in the section beginning with the *Ānumānika-adhikaraṇa*, then today, in the second chapter of the *Śārīraka*, the opponent—the Sāṅkhya—[is shown to be weak] because of the weakness of the *tantras*, such as the Sāṅkhya *tantras*, which ought to be followed as supplementary elaborations (*upabṛṃhaṇa*).

Since the Vedāntas, which serve as supplements (*upabṛṃhaṇa*), lack the power to subvert their own authority, one must accept that the Vedāntas follow the Kāpila system for the sake of its meaningfulness; thus he rises up—that is, he objects. This being the case—such being the situation—he transgresses the boundaries established by the opposing ranks consisting of Smṛtis and logic that do not conform to the Vedāntas; such is his intent.

The commentary (*pratyatra*) states: Having warded off—meaning having restrained—the first position (the *prācya-artha*), which was previously established as the fact that Brahman alone is the cause of all, by means of counter-smṛtis and counter-reasonings capable of refuting the respective smṛtis and reasonings; and having removed what was shaken—that is, what was made to tremble by those [opposing] arguments—he now confirms and establishes that very point from the very beginning (*pādataḥ*) through the first quarter of this [third] chapter. || 3 ||
It has been established in the *Karmakāṇḍa* that the authority of the Śrutis is unshakable when they conflict with the principles of Smṛti;

therefore, this discussion for the sake of establishing that [authority] would be redundant as the second and subsequent sections. Do not say so, for here there is a refutation [of that objection], since one who perceives that it is appropriate to follow [the Śrutis] through reasoning and the words of the Teacher—given their difficult-to-comprehend nature as determined by the various peaks of profound Śrutis—would find [the Smṛtis] sublated.

When a conflict arises between the *śrutis*—the words of the Vedas—and *smṛti*—whether by way of tradition or reasoning—then "immovability," meaning the state of having an uncontradicted meaning, has been established in the *Karmakāṇḍa*, that is, in the system of Jaimini which is devoted to investigating the meaning of Vedic injunctions regarding ritual action; it was firmly settled through the section on the resolution of contradictions (*virodhādhikaraṇa*).

For the sake of establishing that very point—that is, for the determination of that same subject matter—the "further discussion" (*punaścarcā*), which consists of a re-chewing of what has already been chewed, being undertaken in this chapter; for this reason, it is argued that the first quarter of the second chapter (named the *Smṛti-pāda*) would be fruitless—it would indeed be purposeless. [To this, the author replies: "Not so"—this is not tenable, because of the profound...

Regarding "the state of being difficult to understand": when there arises the consequence that the meanings to be determined by various Vedāntic statements—whose intended purports are hidden—are hard to comprehend, [one considers] the subsequent reflection on the meaning of the Śruti, which is assisted by both the words of authoritative persons (āpta)—such as Kapila and others who perceive reality as it is—and by reasoning (tarka) that aids those [authorities] and was set forth by them. For one who perceives this reflection as "competent" and concludes through superficial intellect that "this is logical," it is precisely in this [fourth] quarter (pāda) that the refutation—the effort to demonstrate its impropriety—is undertaken. 4.

With two [verses], he removes the contradiction with Smṛti; then, with eight [verses], he removes the sublation by reasoning (tarka), and thereby he confirms the state of being the material cause as well as the agency of the All-pervasive Lord.
This pair [of confirmations] proceeds according to the principle of the simultaneous depression of one end and the elevation of the other end of a balance scale.
One whose mind is established in investigation regarding the category of doubt restrains partiality. || 5 ||

By means of the first two sections—consisting of the refutation of Smṛti and Yoga respectively—he removes the contradiction with Smṛti, namely, the fact that their subject matter is sublated by the Smṛti of Kapila and the Smṛti of Patañjali, in due order. Then, by means of the eight subsequent sections ending with "possessing a purpose" (*prayojanavattva*), he removes the contradiction with reasoning (*tarka*)—that is, the apparent logical inconsistency regarding Brahman’s status as the material cause (and the resulting lack of authority)—and thus resolves [the objection].

It makes known [the Lord] as being non-existent in reality. By that—namely, by the removal of contradiction through what has been done—it confirms both the state of being the material cause (*upādāna-bhāva*) of the All-pervading One (*vibhu*), which consists in His being the transformative cause (*pariṇāmika-kāraṇa*) of the universe, and His agency (*kartṛtā*), which consists in His being the locus of the volition necessary for creation; that is, it stabilizes both His status as the efficient cause and His status as the material cause within certain sections [of the text].

By means of successive refutations (*kṣepa*)—that is, by demonstrating the irrationality of each individual point among the various meanings asserted by those [opponents] as appropriate—and following the sequence of the downward and upward movement of one end of the beam known as a scale (*tulā*), like the simultaneous sinking and rising of its two ends, when the multitude of doubts (*śaṅkāvarga*) has come into operation—that is, when it has manifested—the intellect of the examiner, with its mind fixed upon the investigation, casts an impartial gaze through the process of deliberating on the determination of what is correct and incorrect.
The author of the Sūtras restrains—that is, obstructs—the partiality, which is a specific form of conceit consisting of the notion of being inferior to each respective side. || 5 ||

This sage Kapila, who is wise and celebrated in the *Śruti* itself as an incarnation of Vāsudeva, is renowned in the *Rāmāyaṇa* and other texts as one of profound intellect and a devoted seeker; he proclaims the reality of Vedānta. Therefore, since that [truth] lies beyond our reach, its definitive extraction must come from his very words in the *Upaniṣads*.
It cannot be established through the many faultless utterances of Manu and others, for they do not all convey a single identical meaning regarding that ultimate reality.

The "wise one" (smartā)—the author of the Sāṃkhya-smṛti, this very Kapila under discussion—is praised by the Śruti itself, namely the Śvetāśvatara-Upaniṣad, as a seer (ṛṣi) who has perceived the true nature of supersensuous objects, as it says: "The seer born of [the primordial]...
and "He whose intellect is restrained... (ŚvetU 6.18).

[He is known as] Kapila; in the *Rāmāyaṇa* and other works—in the *Rāmāyaṇa*, *Mahābhārata*, and *Bhāgavata* (i.e., the Itihāsas and Purāṇas)—he is renowned as a partial incarnation (*aṃśa*) of Vāsudeva, specifically as an incarnation who is a portion of Viṣṇu, known as Vāsudeva, who is endowed with unsurpassed sovereignty such as knowledge and so forth; he is one whose intellect is skillful in contemplation.

One whose intellect is perfected in yoga, which consists of the resolve of the mind, speaks the truth of the Vedānta; he clarifies the very reality that is the meaning of the three Vedas through his own traditional teaching (*smṛti*). Therefore, because Kapila is the most authoritative person (*āptatama*), even for those like us who are far removed from him and for whom the subject matter is difficult to grasp with the physical eye—in the "head of the Śruti" (the collection of Vedāntic statements which determine their meaning only by depending on corroboration)—the extraction of the definitive meaning (*niṣkarṣaṇa*) can only be achieved through his own words.

(When the objection arises that [the Vedānta] can only be consistent by relying on the words of Kapila and not otherwise: The speech of the sages such as Manu—which has a single purpose, which is of the same meaning as the Vedānta, which is mutually non-contradictory, and which is clearly proclaimed in various places—is sufficient for that; for even though the words of the Vedānta are distant from us, the establishment of the true meaning is achieved through them, resulting in the attainment of certainty regarding the authoritative subject matter. (Therefore, the Smṛti of Kapila need not be pursued for the sake of corroboration. || 6 ||
Now,

in the chapter on Non-contradiction (*avirodhādhyāya*), the two subsequent sections (*pāda*)— rooted respectively in cause (*kāraṇa*) and effect (*kārya*)— have refuted contradiction (*virodha*). (70)

In the first [section], there should be a pair of caskets; by means of both [of these], through eight systems, and through tradition and reasoning, contradiction is gradually dispelled along with their causes.

"In the case of all [authoritative] explanations, when there is a desire for further elaboration regarding what has been authorized, the reasoning of Smṛti proceeds by means of the refutation of the Sāṅkhya Smṛti. Thus ends the section on Smṛti (Smṛtyadhikaraṇa). 1.72.

*Adhikaraṇasārāvaliḥ* (Yoga-adhikaraṇa): "The universe, because it possesses the three qualities (*traiguṇya*), has arisen from the three qualities; it is not [produced] from that which is devoid of them"—this is incorrect. Taking any [of these] modes whatsoever: the equality of qualities appropriate for the determination of causality—which is accepted by you—and the possession of characteristics according to those qualities; in cases such as the *gomayācika* (the insect known as *droṇa* produced from cow dung) and elsewhere, the Lord—the Supreme Self—who exists as the subtle body consisting of the subtle states of the sentient and non-sentient, having broken—that is, lost—His restrictive rule, attains grossness, that is, He assumes the state of having a gross body composed of the sentient and non-sentient.

Whatever object—such as a jar or the like—is an effect, having such-and-such clay or other material as its substrate (*upādāna*), that effect in the form of the jar and so forth does not possess qualities contrary to those residing in its cause, namely the clay; that is, it does not possess properties that are opposed to the attributes existing in the causal clay. Furthermore, this pair consisting of Brahman and this universe—the Brahman recognized as the substrate (*upādāna*) and the world recognized as the product (*upādeya*)—is characterized by attributes such as consciousness and non-consciousness, namely, being the locus of knowledge and not being the locus thereof.

If it is argued that consciousness belongs to them because they possess the quality of "seeing" (*īkṣaṇa*), which is by nature mutually opposed to their primary attributes—then, if one accepts consciousness based on the quality of "seeing" mentioned in scripture regarding fire and the other elements as being non-common to conscious beings, that consciousness, which is co-referential with "seeing," must belong specifically to those deities who are denoted by the term "those [deities]" (*tāsām*)—namely, the deities presiding over water and the rest.

"But [the effect] is not related solely to the substrate [such as the honeycomb] and so forth"—this kind of objection is not clever; it is not a skillful argument. For from a substance such as honey (*mākṣika*), a distinct substance such as a worm is observed to arise—a specific substance in the form of a worm that is of a different genus (*vijātīya*) than the honey. This is indeed established by common experience. If this necessity of being of the same genus (*sajātīyatva-naiyatyam*) were absent between the effect and the cause—that is, if it did not exist—then that would suffice for causality to be established [independently]. || 3 ||

When the objection was raised by one of dull intellect— that since the "seeing" (*īkṣā*) mentioned in the text "May I be many" is read in connection with fire and water, the world must therefore possess similarity (*sālakṣaṇya*) to them— the opponent (the Pūrvapakṣin),

denying the existence of that statement as referring to the Supreme Being who possesses those respective forms, asserted here that the term "seeing" refers generally to the activity of presiding deities (*abhimānin*). || 9 ||

It is recited [in the scripture]—it is taught in the context of Brahman, which is denoted by the word "Sat" (Being)—the thought "May I be many," meaning "May I become manifold in form. This *īkṣā*—the act of seeing consisting of volition—is precisely such a primary act of seeing in the form of volition; it is the seer of both fire and water, as they are recited [in the texts] as having entered into fire and water respectively: "Fire saw" and "The waters saw."

Therefore, because both the world and Brahman possess primary seeing (*mukhyekṣaṇavat*), there is "similarity of characteristics" (*sālakṣaṇya*)—meaning that the universe has identical characteristics with Brahman and is not of a different character. When this objection from one of dull intellect standing nearby had arisen—that is, when the doubt of the person of weak understanding was set forth—the [author] stated that this very seeing belongs to the Supreme Self alone, who possesses those various forms such as water, fire, and so on; thus it was said: "The waters saw," and "The fire saw."

The opponent—the proponent of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣin*) who seeks to deny the existence of such sentences—desiring to refute the intention behind those sentences, has stated (*vyāharat*) in this section (*asminn adhikaraṇe*) that, setting aside the particular form, there is a general usage regarding the presiding deities (*abhimānin*), namely, the character of being a presiding deity as a general attribute. || 9 ||

To remove the defects of their fallacious reasoning, which is characterized by mutually contradictory meanings and hollow pretenses, [this work is composed].
The sun of the Vedānta shines for us, filling his belly with the mass of the darkness of opposing doctrines. || 10 ||

Among the schools of Buddhist monks—namely the systems of Gautama, Jina, Kaṇāda, and Sugata—because there is an agreement regarding atoms, that is, a unity of view concerning the causality of atoms, the universe (*viśva*) would have those [atoms] as its cause; it would consist solely of atoms as its causal basis. The Sun of the Vedanta—the Aditya known as Vedanta—is shining, manifesting brilliantly before us. A person intent on denying the boundary between the individual soul and the Lord—the limit defining the essential nature and characteristics of the *jīva* and the *paramātman*—which belongs to the *Śrutis* (the Vedas) that serve as a treasury for all objects of knowledge (*prameya*) and consist of well-guarded compilations; such a person, regarding this matter of the connection between the *jīva* and the Supreme (*para*) who possess bodies, proceeds according to the logic of the sovereign and his servant, as if they were both residing within the same royal palace.

Furthermore, since the non-difference from the cause is already established, the activity of causal agents such as weavers would be rendered futile; however, this objection is not clever—that is, it is not a refined reflection—because, for that reason, [the world, which is the effect] is designated by words such as "Being," "Self," and so forth, being presented through terms denoting the cause-Brahman, such as "This was Being alone," "This is Brahman alone," and "The Self, indeed, was this."

Therefore, the effect is not different from its cause; it is indeed non-different from it. The distinction of sound and so forth—the difference in sound and other qualities in the effect relative to the cause—proceeds by relying on the distinct states of the substance, that is, by depending on the variation in the states residing in the substance. For that very reason—and because the difference in state is precisely what is to be established—there would be no pointlessness of the causal factors (*kāraka*) in producing this difference in state within the effect; nor is it possible for the employment of the activity of the causal factors to be in vain. || 5 ||

If [the effect] were other than the causal substance, like a mat from a cart due to its contrary properties, then the activity of the causal factors would be fruitless; thus, the doctrine of partial destruction (*ardhavaināśika*) is stated. [We reply: Even if there is identity of substance, let all [properties] exist through the distinction of their intended states; and as for the scriptural statement regarding non-existence (*asacchruti*), [it refers to the prior state].
Therefore, due to direct perception and parsimony, the identity of the world with Brahman as declared by the Śruti has been stated. || 12 ||

The effect (*kārya*)—the entity to be produced—is indicated by contradictory properties (*viruddhair dharmair*), such as distinct cognitions, words, and so forth, which are mutually exclusive characteristics; it is "other than the causal substance" (*kāraṇadravyato 'nyat*), meaning it is distinct from the producing substance. Just as a mat, by means of mutually exclusive properties such as being the means for sitting and being the means for riding, is other than a cart—just as the object in the form of a mat is different from the object in the form of a cart—so too is the case otherwise with the effect.

If [the effect] were non-different from its cause, the activity of the causal factors would be fruitless; thus, the specific operation of the agents and instruments—such as the agent (*kartṛ*) and the instrument (*karaṇa*)—which are established as the bringers-about of the effect, would become purposeless. In this way, when the statement of the partial nihilist (*ardhavaināśika*) has been introduced by the logician (*tārkika*), let everything be so—even though there is identity of substance (*dravyaikya*), and even though the substances of the effect and the cause, such as the cloth and the threads, are non-different, it may be due to the difference in states (*avasthāviśeṣa*) favored by them, which is the very state of the effect favored by the logicians themselves.

Let it be granted that all [arguments], such as the difference in cognition and the difference in words, have been fully established; however, there is also the scriptural statement regarding non-existence—namely, the Śruti text, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (asadevedamagra āsīt). For this reason, [the effect] is perceived as non-existent prior to its manifestation through a particular state of being produced later on.

Because the non-difference of the thread from the cloth is perceptible even in the state of being a cloth, and because of parsimony (*lāghava*)—that is, by following the maxim that "the postulation of a property is preferable to the postulation of a substratum"—one avoids postulating both a difference in substance between cause and effect and a difference in state, and instead postulates merely a difference in state; thus, [this is supported] by the parsimony resulting from such reasoning, as well as by what is stated in the Śruti...

Identity (*tādātmya*)—the non-difference between Brahman and the world as established by the Śruti text, "All this, my dear, was indeed Being" (*sadeva somyedam*), and which was explained and clarified in the Sūtra, "The non-difference from That... Adhikaraṇa 1) When the agent and the material cause possess the capacity [to act], and the collection of instruments is present, they perform the effect. Therefore, how could that which is non-existent (*asat*) alone bring about an instrument? This is due to the distinction between the power of the non-existent. One should rejoice upon seeing this illustrated by milk, the magnet, and the creeper, as well as the faces of the gods and sages.
By mere volition alone, the individual soul impels its own body, and likewise the Lord [impels] the universe-form.

When there is capacity—that is, when there is capability—and when the collection of instruments is present—that is, when there is the conjunction of the entire set of auxiliary causes—the agency of the agent and the primordial matter (prakṛti), namely the efficient and material causes, in producing their respective effects is observed in the world, and not otherwise.

Therefore—since a general cause requires auxiliary instruments (*upakaraṇa*), at the beginning of the dissolution, prior to creation, what could Brahman—the Reality denoted by the term "Sat"—which exists as one, abiding in a state devoid of anything other than itself, employ as an instrument? Or what object could it possibly take up as its own instrument?

(Thus, Brahman cannot be the cause of the world)—this objection is incorrect. Why? Because of the distinction of powers (*śaktibheda*): even in the absence of other external instruments, Brahman possesses a distinct power consisting in its suitability for producing effects; as in the case of milk, iron, and so forth...

Having observed—having thoroughly investigated—these beings who possess extraordinary powers: milk from the mouth transforming into the nature of curd; the magnet attracting iron; the spider whose nature is to emit threads from its mouth; and even the gods and sages who are capable of performing diverse deeds by mere will alone—one should rejoice in this fact—that Brahman is the non-different material and efficient cause—and remain free from doubt. Even the individual soul (jīva), though a common conscious being, [perceives] its own body...

Indeed, the body impels—that is, urges—by mere mental activity alone; likewise, for that same reason, the Lord (Īśa), being the possessor of the universal form (Viśvarūpa), creates the universe by mere volition (saṅkalpa) alone. || 16 ||

There would be a contradiction of the Vedic texts—of those scriptures such as "partless" (*niṣkalam*) and others that establish its partlessness; that is, their meaning would be sublated. Therefore, for the reason stated, Brahman’s causality is undermined in both ways—whether it possesses parts or is partless.

The claim that the status of being the cause of the world is refuted is likewise devoid of substance; such an objection is weak because of its dissimilarity—that is, due to the specific mode consisting in being of a different genus from all other things—namely, by virtue of a quality unique to Brahman (which does not entail the aforementioned defects). This is because even the Śruti texts—those Vedic utterances of the Vedānta intended to describe the nature of Brahman—make this known in that very way, teaching the nature of Brahman precisely as being of a different genus from everything else, since it possesses power (śaktimat), both in common worldly usage and in the Veda.

Because it is observed that all objects possess mutually distinct powers, and because Brahman possesses a capacity superior to all others, its status as the cause of the world is therefore unassailable. || 8 ||

If it transforms, then there would be a contradiction with the scriptural texts concerning its partlessness—the sublation of such Śruti passages as "without parts" (*niṣkalam*) which declare that Brahman is devoid of constituent parts. This objection, which depends on the dilemma of whether the transformation is total or partial, would apply equally even if Brahman were accepted as the material cause of the world as qualified by sentient and insentient beings, or as qualified by *māyā*. If it is argued that since the aforementioned defects have not been avoided, Brahman’s status as the material cause is untenable—that is, its status as the material cause consisting in being the transformative cause (*pariṇāmikāraṇa*) of the universe is not well-established—this suspicion is not justified, because the same [defect] applies equally to our own positions. The summary of the topic (*adhikaraṇārthasaṅgraha*) regarding the section on the "entirety" (*kṛtsnaprasakti*) is as follows: Having raised the objection that if partless Brahman were the cause, it would follow that the entirety of Brahman is consumed in each single effect—and thus Brahman’s causality is untenable—it is stated that Brahman’s causality is indeed tenable; for both the partlessness of Brahman and its causality of the diverse world are established by scripture, and an object established by scripture cannot be sublated by mere reasoning.

The *Adhikaraṇasārāvali* [is composed] because of the contradiction with the Sāṃkhya Smṛti, because of the refutation of the doctrine of injunctions, because of the dissimilarity of the effects, because of the contradiction of multiple systems taught for a single purpose, and because of the non-separation of the body and its experience.

He struck down [the opponent's position] which had arisen from the distinction between the effect and its material cause, from the destruction of one's own benefit, from the abandonment of the collection of causal factors, from the sublation of the arrangement of parts and the whole, and also from the fruitlessness of purposeful activity. || 22 ||

Because of contradiction with the Sāṃkhya tradition—due to the conflict between the Vedānta statements and the Smṛti of Kapila; because of the subversion of the established doctrine by the Yoga Śāstra accepted by Hiraṇyagarbha; because of the dissimilarity of the effect—the created world—which possesses a distinct nature from Brahman due to its insentience; because of the contradiction of a single meaning taught in multiple treatises—due to the fact that the meaning stated by many systems of philosophy regarding the cause of the world is mutually inconsistent; and because of the absence of bodily experience...

Because the experience of pleasure and pain dependent upon connection with a body would be unavoidable for Brahman; because of the distinction between the material cause and its effect—the necessity of mutual difference between two things related as material cause and its product, just like a cloth and its threads; because of the contradiction to one's own benefit—since if Brahman, who is non-different from the individual soul (*jīva*), were to create a world consisting of suffering, it would follow that He would be thwarting His own welfare; and because of the loss of the collection of causal factors—the disintegration of causality resulting from the failure to employ the necessary totality of conditions required for the production of an effect by a potent cause.

He [the author of the Sūtras] refuted the doubt that Brahman cannot be the cause of the world—doubt which had arisen because of the dilemma as to whether the transformation of the world from Brahman occurs in its entirety or in part (since both are untenable), and also because of the deficiency of agency (due to the absence of any purpose for Brahman, either for itself or for others) and because of its being inactive—he [the author of the Sūtras] rejected it. || 22 ||
Śrīḥ.
Salutations to the illustrious Rāmānuja. Salutations to Śrī. Salutations to Śrīdhara.
The second quarter of the second chapter: The Section on the Impossibility of Creation (Racanānupapattyadhikaraṇa). || 2-2-1 ||

Furthermore, one who is free from passion and averse to fame and the like might ask: "Why, in this second chapter (*pāda*), does he utter disparagement of others—that is, state criticisms directed toward followers of other systems? Such a doubt is not correct; for [this was done] by many renowned ancients—those famous ones active since ancient times—for the sake of quelling even a slight doubt that might arise regarding various opposing views.

For those of limited intelligence, the erroneous conviction that [other systems] possess equal authority as a means to eliminate doubt entirely is established through the delusion of equality—that is, arising from the misconception that other systems (itaratantra) have the same authority as Vedānta. This "balancing of the argument" (prakaraṇasamatā)—the suspicion that the meaning declared by Śruti is countered by an equally valid opposing argument—is to be warded off by the section on reasoning (tarkapāda); it is to be removed by the second quarter of the second chapter, which is named the tarkapāda. || 1 ||
The Sāṃkhya system, which adheres to twenty-six principles, is clearly recited in the *Mahābhārata* as being equal to Yoga;

for it is stated therein that "the Twenty-fifth is the inner self of all the principles. Therefore, having established the system of the Lord (Śiva) as one attained through the Vedas, [the author] now refutes with logical arguments the position independent of the Lord—which entails severe karmic obstacles—by means of the aphorisms.

In the *Mahābhārata*—known as the fifth Veda—the twenty-sixth principle, which rests upon the six lineages (*ṣaḍvaṃśāvalambi*), hangs suspended within the Supreme Person; and the Sāṃkhya—the Sāṃkhya scripture that proceeds from the enumeration of the twenty-five principles to be governed—is clearly recited with equal authority alongside the Yoga scripture, stated explicitly and without doubt.

Because of its abiding therein—due to the reason that it exists as the embodied soul within the twenty-fifth principle, the *jīva-tattva*—the Inner Self of all, the Supreme Self who dwells within the entire universe, is indeed the twenty-fifth; thus it is "declared," meaning established with certainty. Therefore, for the reason stated, the *Sāṃkhya-tantra* along with its Lord (*seśāna*), and the *Yoga-tantra* which is similar to it, are to be established as being indeed attained through the *Śruti*, that is, as being supported by the Vedas.

Having established the capacity [of the system], Bādarāyaṇa now, by means of the aphorisms belonging to this section—the topical rules (*adhikaraṇasūtra*)—refutes the atheistic Sāṃkhya position, which involves severe transgression, stating that it must be abandoned because it brings about sins that cannot be overlooked; thus he rejects it. || 2 ||

Establishing categories such as the Unmanifest (avyakta) through the means of inference by means of their own intellect, how could the Sāṃkhyas not seek consistency with doctrines such as the discourse on the thirty-six principles? Examining conceptual constructions that are equally subject to objection and proof, yet are liberated from the constraints of scripture, they would not deny what is perceived; rather, they would infer the subtle and accept the remainder from the authoritative teaching.
"Objects beginning with the unmanifest"—namely, "the root-nature (mūlaprakṛti), the great one (mahat), the ego-sense (ahaṅkāra), the subtle elements (tanmātrāṇi)," and so forth.

Enumerating categories that they consider to be real in essence, and employing inference as their primary means—establishing and supporting them through their own intellects, which do not conform to the Vedas but follow their own whims—the Sāṅkhyas, those systematizers renowned in the world as such, [engage] in various respective doctrines, beginning with the theory of thirty-six principles (*ṣaṭtriṃśattattvavāda*) adopted by the Pāśupatas, Vaiśeṣikas, and others, including the theory of seven categories (*saptapadārthavāda*).

How could they not desire—that is, how could it be appropriate for them not to wish for—an attachment to established matters, namely a connection in the form of their own accepted tenets? How indeed would this be logical? Those who rely on the Vedas, reflecting upon those various conceptual constructions of the outsiders who have abandoned the discipline of the Vedas and transgressed the boundaries of the scriptures—constructions that possess an equal nature of objection and resolution—should not deny what is perceived through direct experience. They should consider these [outsider] constructs as being of equal status (samānayogakṣema). Thus, those who uphold the Vedas should not reject what is evident to the senses.

They would not deny an object that is to be known; they would infer—that is, determine through inference—an object that is subtle, perceivable by the senses, and characterized by simplicity of conceptualization; and they desire—to seek to determine—the remaining specific objects that cannot be determined by perception or inference, by means of the authority of scripture (āgama), which consists of the Vedas and their supplements and is capable of determining supramundane matters. || 3 ||

Some effects are seen to be produced by weavers and others, while all other things are heard to be dependent upon a creator; nowhere, however, is there a perception of their dependence on another that contradicts this [principle].
This is illustrated by the compositions of poets, the ocean of milk, the grass-cloud (rain), lightning, wind, and the magnet.
Yet, through these examples, that which you desire does not bear fruit for us; rather, everything is presided over by a conscious being.
"But surely, at the beginning of the treatise, it was stated that even insentient things are dependent on an agent for their respective functions;

thus, what is the point of the Sūtrakāra refuting the inference regarding the Creator? This question is not entirely trivial—listen to it with attention. He thought: 'The All-Creator cannot be inferred, nor can He be denied, because no such restrictive rule is observed for either case.'"

In this context—within this section—it has indeed been stated—that is, logically established—that non-conscious entities, meaning objects distinct from consciousness, necessarily depend upon an agent—that is, they invariably require a conscious being possessing volitional effort—in order to perform their own appropriate function, namely, the production of their own effects. This was stated at the commencement of the treatise, specifically in the *Śāstrayonitva* section of the first book (*pāda*) of the *Śārīraka*, by the author of the Sūtras, who, with what intention, [affirmed] the dependence on the Ordainer—the Lord, the creator of the world?

This inquiry—such a question—dispels (vy-anudat) the attainment (siddhi) that depends upon inference (anumāna); it is not extremely trivial (atitucchā), nor is it insignificant. Therefore, because it is worthy of an answer, listen attentively (avahitaḥ) with a focused mind. The All-maker (sarvakṛt), the Lord (īśvara), cannot be inferred (na anumātuṃ śakyaḥ), nor is he capable of being established even by proof; yet he cannot be denied (na apahnotuṃ śakyaḥ), nor is he capable of being sublated even by contradiction. This is because no rule governing both is observed—that is, no necessary concomitance (vyāpti) between the existence of the Lord and his non-existence.
Because [the reason] is not perceived in any instance [of the similar class], he thus became certain that it does not exist at all. || 5 ||

Since the insentience of *prakṛti* consists in its being inert (*jaḍatva*), and since the insentience of the *puruṣa* consists in its not being a substratum of consciousness (*caitanyānāśrayatva*), how could [superimposition] be possible? For superimposition is a property belonging exclusively to consciousness; or rather, how could it be logically tenable? || 6 ||
For men, this fruit—beginning with worldly enjoyment and liberation—is all established in Pradhāna;

yet here, the capacity for seeing and so forth belongs to the Puruṣa, while the capacity for seeing and so forth belongs separately to the Buddhi. Therefore, let those devoted to Jainism mutter like a low-caste man at his wedding: "The Sage composed the scripture for the sake of the liberation of the bound, yet I am eternally liberated"—words that contradict one another.

This—seen in the treatise, beginning with enjoyment (*bhoga*) and liberation (*apavarga*), consisting of the bondage and release from *saṃsāra*—is the fruit for persons, that is, the purpose connected to the *puruṣa*. And all of that, being the purpose of the *puruṣa*, is accepted by the Sāṅkhyas as residing in *prakṛti* alone. Because of "the state of being a seer" (*draṣṭṛtva*)—that is, because the superimposition of the state of being a seer upon *prakṛti* (which is actually being observed) cannot otherwise be explained—the postulation (*kalpanā*) of the *puruṣa* as the substratum of the state of being a seer and so forth is separate; it is a distinct conceptualization concerning the *puruṣa*.

The state of being a seer and so forth resides in the intellect (*buddhi*)—when considered from the standpoint of ultimate reality, the attributes such as being a seer belong to the intellect alone. The Sage (*muni*) refers to the seer Kapila; the *Śāstra* refers to the Sāṃkhya scripture. For the sake of the liberation of the bound one—that is, for the removal of bondage from the *puruṣa*, who is the locus of bondage—he composed [it], the "Uncreated" (*akṛta*). From that Sāṃkhya scripture, [he claims]: "I am eternally liberated"—meaning, "I possess innate liberation. Such a web of mutually contradictory statements, beginning with these, [is like] a low-caste man’s marriage.

Regarding the marriage of a Śūdra woman, which serves as a locus for the employment of mutually contradictory speech, the Jaina devotees—namely the Sāṃkhyas who follow the Jaina system of ethics characterized by universal non-absolutism (sarvānaikāntya)—should mutter [the mantra] silently, that is, utter it inaudibly, but not clearly in the presence of a discerning person, out of fear of ridicule. || 7 ||
*Nayasaṅgatimālikā* (Composition:

*Aghi*) Thus, having refuted the objection (*bādha*), the opposing view (*pratipakṣa*) is now set aside. In the second quarter-verse, the doubt of a bystander is dispelled: "If the activity of consciousness (*cit-pravṛtti*) is fruitless, then it would be better for such [activity] to belong to the insentient (*acita*). This suspicion is here rejected because of the impossibility of such a composition (*racanā-sambhavāt*). Thus ends the section on the "Impossibility of Composition" (*Racanānupapattyadhikaraṇa*).

Having refuted—that is, having rejected on the grounds of its lack of scriptural authority (in the preceding section)—the principle of *pradhāna* accepted by the Sāṅkhyas as being of the nature of the "supremely great" (*paramamahat*) and all-pervasive (*vibhu*), he states an undesirable consequence regarding the postulation—that is, the inferential proof—of a multitude of material causes consisting of various types of atoms: a collection of inherent causes (*samavāyikāraṇa*) composed of atoms that possess a magnitude greater than the visible *trasareṇu* and which exhibit a diversity of qualities and distinctions of genus such as "earthness" and "waterhood."

In this section, the author of the Sūtras demonstrates the fault consisting of the undesirable consequence of an object not accepted by the logicians (*tārkika*). Previously—in the preceding section—the path of the theory of transformation (*pariṇāmavāda*) of *prakṛti* devoid of the superintendence of an intelligent being—that is, the doctrine of the transformation of insentient *prakṛti* when it is not presided over by a specific conscious entity—was refuted and established as being far removed from valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Now—in this section—he [addresses] that which contains the doctrine of dependence on a Lord (*seśvara*), namely the subtle atoms...

He grinds to dust—that is, he demonstrates as unauthoritative through a complete examination—the position of the school which maintains the doctrine of the production of the manifold of effects, such as dyads and so forth, originating from the substance called atoms (paramāṇu). || 8 ||
The assumption of a substance that was previously non-existent— which has already been refuted in the discussion on *ārambhaṇa*—
now casts aside in many ways the portion concerning the process of causes belonging to the followers of Kaṇāda;
for when the cause is divided into three parts, those who rely on inference [must account for] each respective part as is appropriate.
In this [work], he declares through the sūtras various modes of conceptual progression, such as contradictions and so forth. ||9||

To begin with—in the very first section on "Originating" (Ārambhaṇa) within the *Smṛti-pāda*—the doctrine of the Kāṇādas, the Vaiśeṣikas, which postulates the production of a substance that did not previously exist, was shown to have its subject matter refuted by being established as contradicted. Now, in this present section belonging to the *Tarka-pāda*, the portion concerning the causal process—that is, the unrefuted view of the Kāṇādas regarding the relation to the causal totality—is [examined].

He casts away the remainder in many ways—he rejects it through various means—by those who rely on inference, that is, by logicians who delight in inference (*anumāna-rasika*). Having divided and described the collection of causes into three types according to the distinctions of inherent (*samavāyin*), non-inherent (*asamavāyin*), and instrumental (*nimitta*), he [examines] each respective part—that is, the portions such as *vāyu* and so forth whose establishment depends upon the postulation of these three kinds of causes—in accordance with their suitability, in various manners following the sequence of conceptual construction (*vikalpa*).

"Contradictions and so forth"—meaning the faults of self-contradiction, unestablished premises, and deviation from one's own tenets—the venerable Bādarāyaṇa explains [them] here; that is, through the sūtras belonging to this section, the Blessed One elucidates them by means of detailed analysis. ||9||
Even those who,
by means of inference, establish that the produced dyad is minute in accordance with the form perceived, would not be able to assert its partlessness and so forth.

One should endure everything when it is subtle; or, when it is manifest to the world through its natural state of being subject to others, one may reveal its parts. However, due to the fruitlessness of memory, it should be led by another means.

The Vaiśeṣikas—establishing through inference (that is, by means of knowledge dependent on the instrument of valid cognition known as *anumāna*) that the substance called the *dvyaṇuka* (composed of two atoms), as well as the substance called the atom (*paramāṇu*) which is even subtler than that, serve as the cause for the "seen atom" (the subtle substance known as *trasareṇu* which is perceptible to the eye)—maintain this position.

Because one postulates what is unseen only by following the form that has been perceived—that is, by conforming precisely to the form already understood—it would not be possible for those philosophers who are dependent on valid cognition (*pramāṇaparatantra*) to establish, through their own words, the partlessness and so forth—namely, the eternality and lack of constituent parts—of the atom (*paramāṇu*), which is the object of such postulation. This is because they would be unable to do so regarding the subtle atomic substance (*aṇudravya*) as it is observed within the lattice of light—the sphere of the sunbeams entering through a window.

If everything—including the fact that all sounds are partless and so forth—were somehow accepted [as proven] because there is no conceptual construction regarding what is perceived, then would the *Smṛti* passage beginning with "In the sunbeams through a lattice" (*jālasūrye*), which appears at first glance to be intended merely to demonstrate the measurement of atoms and is found within the treatises on architecture (*śilpaśāstra*), proclaim those parts—that is, would it be able to establish the constituent parts of a *trasareṇu*? Certainly not; for it is fruitless, as there is no purpose in establishing those parts. Rather, by way of implication...

This [scriptural passage] must be interpreted as possessing a different intended meaning based solely on its status as a supplementary portion (*vākyaśeṣa*) to the statements concerning the objects of piercing (*vedhya*) and so forth mentioned in that specific context; it is not to be taken as establishing atoms and the like. || 10 ||

If it is argued that because the collection of parts is infinite, there can be no rest anywhere, and thus there can be no equality between a *māṣa* bean and a mountain, that is incorrect; for in an infinite series, there is certainly a gradation of difference starting from a fortnight, a month, and so on.

Indeed, in the case of two classes [of things] that are infinite due to the infinity of their individuals, why should the undesirable consequence of a lack of distinction or a total lack of sequence not apply? // 11 //

If it is argued by logicians that "if there is no resting place in some object—that is, if there is no cessation in the series of parts—then because of the infinity of the collection of parts, both the *māṣa* (the small measure of a bean) and the *kṣoṇībhṛt* (the mountain), despite their difference in magnitude, would result in an equality of size due to possessing an infinite number of constituent parts," then that is incorrect; for such an argument fails when [the series] is infinite.

Because of gradation—that is, because gradation is unavoidable even in what is incalculable—for indeed, in the case of infinite divisions of time consisting of fortnights, months, and so forth, even though their number cannot be specified as a finite quantity, there exists a fixed and unalterable disparity—a disparity in numerical gradation—which is not undesirable; that is, this disparity in numerical gradation is not disapproved by anyone, but is rather accepted by all.

Regarding the equality in the infinity of individuals (*vyakti*): even though there is an equal infinity of individuals that serve as the substrata for universals (*jāti*) such as "substance-ness" (*dravyatva*) and "earth-ness" (*pṛthivītva*), why has the mutual relationship between those two universals—their subsistence through the states of being mutually pervaded (*vyāpya*) and pervading (*vyāpaka*)—not been recounted? It has not been established by you; for, apart from the grace of the deities for those who follow the path of the scriptures, any other [explanation] has been rejected at the outset, as its postulation would require excessive effort on the part of those who know it.
If [the opponent] does not acknowledge that effort is independent of further effort, then why would they not accept it even in the case of the unperceived?
Thus, in the theory of the unseen force (adṛṣṭa) residing in the elements, the hypothesis of an unseen force inherent in the atoms that produce the dyad is here cut away.

For those who follow the path of the Vedas (*śruti-saraṇi-jupām*), there exists no such thing as an "unseen force" (*adṛṣṭa*)—denoted by the term *adṛṣṭa*—that is distinct from the grace of the deities and other such factors, and separate from the pleasure or displeasure of the Supreme Person (*parama-puruṣa*). This is because, if one were to postulate that this unseen force has a nature distinct [from God] and resides within the individual soul (*jīva-gatatayā*), then the assumption of its existence would require the exertion of further effort on the part of those who maintain such a theory of the nature of the unseen force.

The postulation of a Lord (Īśvara) possessing a specific effort (*yatna*) capable of creating a world beyond the scope of the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), which was initially rejected by Bādarāyaṇa in the *Śāstrayonitva* section at the beginning of the *Śārīraka* [Brahma-sūtras],—why do you not accept that such [effort] is independent of further effort? Why do you not admit that even in the case of the unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), it is likewise independent of another effort, just as effort itself is independent of another effort?

Even the absence of dependence on a sustainer for the unseen merit (adṛṣṭa) would indeed exist in the theory that the unseen merit resides in the elements—namely, the position accepted by the common folk, logicians, and others, which postulates an unseen merit residing in the dyads (dvyaṇuka). This position of those who maintain that the unseen merit resides in the atoms (paramāṇu) that produce the dyads has been completely refuted here in the section concerning "the large and the long" (mahaddīrghādhikaraṇa). || 12 ||

Some have declared this relation to be eternal, pervading all things as non-separately established; others, however, say that it is eternal in respect to eternal things, but merely lasts for the duration of existence in respect to non-eternal things.
For those liberated from the fixed nature of various pairs of opposites, there would be no such established order;
however, how could the postulation of another [cause] for those who possess superior qualities not incur faults such as infinite regress? || 13 ||

Some Vaiśeṣikas [assert that] it is that which is inseparably established (*apṛthaksiddha*), which persists through all [entities], which is invariably dependent on a series [of substrates], and which accompanies many objects; [otherwise], there would be no systematic order—there would be no non-confused linguistic usage (*asaṅkīrṇavyavahāra*). The postulation of another [category], namely the conceptualization (*kalpanā*) of an entity distinct from the two related relata, is indeed "heavy"—it is seized by the fault known as "prolixity" (*gaurava*). For those who accept additional [ontological] entities, the fault of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) and so forth—a fault consisting of a lack of finality that disrupts the conceptualization—how could it not arise? By what means or in what manner would it not manifest? || 13 ||

When the categories of substance—consisting of both composite wholes and atoms—have been shaken off by the authors of the Sūtras, then the "one" characterized as pervading the universe would either be non-existent or simply a non-substance.
This is not so; for the existence of the perceived atom, its aggregation, and the relationship between the two is established without contradiction.
Even scripture declares that the world originates from adventitious elements such as blood and the like. || 14 ||

By the authors of the Sūtras—the composers of the Brahma-sūtras, Bādarāyaṇa—the collection of substances consisting of wholes and atoms, which are distinct from their material causes and constitute the nature of wholes such as cloth, as well as the nature of atoms distinct from triads (*trasareṇu*), was shaken off—that is, rejected by the *Ārambhaṇādhikaraṇa* and the *Mahaddīrghādhikaraṇa*. Thus, [substance] rests solely in omnipresence (*vibhutva*), defined as the state of being conjoined with all corporeal substances, which is the single characteristic pervading the entire universe.

"Paramamahat"—that which is accepted as "paramamahat," such as the substances time (*kāla*), space (*ākāśa*), and so forth, would either be a substance (*dravya*) itself; or it would be non-existent (*asat*)—even though it is "paramamahat," it would be like a composite whole (*avayavin*) and the like, being practically non-existent; or else, it would be a non-substance (*adravya*) alone—in the end, after the exclusion of all substances, it would result in being accepted as an object of cognition (*prameya*) that is simply a non-substance! (Thus the objection raised by the author of the Sūtras.)

[If it is argued that] this [theory] has already been refuted above—do not say so; such an objection is not sound, because of the establishment of atoms through perception (*dṛṣṭasiddheḥ*).
