There is no sublation (*abādhāt*) of the cognition of the triad of atoms (*trasareṇu*) as perceived by the senses, of their aggregate, and of the connection between two atoms which is established otherwise than through aggregation; for this has not been rejected by the authors of the Sūtras. Furthermore, the Śruti itself repeatedly declares the commencement of the world—the creation of the five-fold (*pañcīkṛta*) universe—by means of adventitious qualities such as earthiness (*pṛthivītva*), which arise from the transformation of the primordial material cause (*mūlaprakṛti*).
Thus, the Śruti proclaims it again and again. || 14 ||
The Topic of the Aggregate as the Locus (Samudāyādhikaraṇa). || 2-2-3 ||
A Compendium of the Multitude of Principles of the Śārīraka:
For indeed, earth and the other elements would consist of aggregates of atoms; likewise, the sense organs and so forth would be composed of the gross elements such as jars.
This too is without substance: if all things are momentary, where could there be any aggregation, and how could the accomplishment of any effect occur? (17)

When [the opponent's position] has been shaken off—having been refuted—the author of the Sūtras refutes (*kṣiṇoti*), that is, rejects, the positions (*artha*) accepted by the Nihilists (*vaināśika*), namely the Buddhists who maintain the doctrine of destruction without residue (*niranvayavināśavādin*); this occurs prior to the rejection of the doctrines of Jina and Giriśa, and before the refutation of the Pāśupata system. || 15 ||

Śrīdhara, in his own treatise, has calculated that this Buddha, along with his incarnations, is not omniscient; thus he would neither be deluded nor would he wish to deceive any of his friends. Therefore, if it is argued that the Sātvata and other systems fall into fragmentation when subjected to the critique of what was spoken by Buddha, we say no; for [the Buddha’s] engagement in acts such as delusion proceeds from a mind intent on crushing those who oppose his own desired [doctrines]. || 16 ||

This Buddha—the Sugata who propounded the doctrine to be rejected—was enumerated by the illustrious Nārāyaṇa (Śrīdhara) in his own scripture, the *Pāñcarātra-tantra*, along with his own incarnations—namely, his births known as *avatāras* intended for the grace of the world—as one among them; he is the omniscient one, possessing unconditioned omniscience, and bears the form of a Buddha.

And the Blessed One would certainly not be deluded—he could not possibly be one whose realization of the true meaning is impaired—since he is the friend of all, possessing unconditional benevolence toward all beings; nor would he desire to deceive anyone—nor would he wish to mislead any conscious being whom he might intend to uplift. Therefore, for these stated reasons (because the Buddhist and Vaiṣṇava Tantras have a single proponent), regarding the statement spoken by the Buddha—the meaning proclaimed by the Buddha (in accordance with the Śruti...)

If it is argued that when refutation by logical arguments (*nyāya*) becomes necessary, even the scriptures of the Lord such as those of the Sātvatas and others must likewise undergo disintegration—that is, they inevitably become objects of rejection—this suspicion is not correct. For [the Lord’s] engagement in delusion and so forth, and His engagement in the subversion of the true meaning, arise from the motive of intending to subdue those wicked persons who oppose the virtuous whom He Himself favors. || 16 ||

The desire for delusion is difficult to restrain; otherwise, how could there be delusion for the Creator of all beings? Therefore, He bestows fruit according to one's karma—whether it be the awakening to reality or delusion—based on His own words and so forth.
This is established: He is not partial toward anyone without cause; therefore, His speech is impartial.
Out of compassion, He does not intend to deceive, nor would the fruit be produced by sin if it were not dependent upon the Lord. ||17||

The desire to delude the Creator of all beings—the Supreme Self, the cause of everything—is irresistible; that resolve to produce delusion cannot be described as non-existent. Otherwise—if the Lord lacked the resolve to delude—by what cause would our delusion, that specific state of intellect which grasps unreal objects, come to be? Therefore, because the Lord alone possesses the resolve to delude, He [bestows] either true knowledge or error according to the karma residing in each respective sentient being.

It bestows as its fruit either the knowledge of the true meaning or the knowledge of it otherwise—that is, it grants this as a result to sentient beings. This fact—that the Blessed One alone is the cause of valid cognition (*pramā*) for me—is established and determined by His own words, specifically from the Lord’s own statement: "From Me come memory, knowledge, and its withdrawal. This Blessed One is not uneven due to lack of qualification; He is not, by nature, possessed of partiality toward living beings. Therefore, precisely because of the absence of natural partiality, His speech is equal.

The Blessed One’s mode of expression regarding equality toward all is consistent, arising from compassion—that is, by taking as its cause the desire to eliminate suffering without any ulterior motive. If there were no intent to deceive on the part of the Blessed One, nor any desire to delude the unvirtuous, then the fruit born of evil—resulting from sin—would not be said to be "inclined toward the Lord"; that is, it could not be asserted to be dependent upon God. || 17 ||

"Is the Buddha to be conceived?"—thus those who know the Sugata’s doctrine are divided. Some hold that awakening is directly perceived; some say it is inferable from the forms of cognition; and some declare that awakening is false. Others, following the same logic, have stated that even the intellect is established only as a conventional reality.
Today, the Teacher of the Daityas [Śiva] strikes down all these Vaibhāṣikas and others with the weapons of logic. (18)

All those who know the doctrine of the Sugata and understand the intention of the Buddha—even all four [types of practitioners]—regard the object that has become known as conceptualized; it is established by mere conceptual construction.

They say it is not real—thus they speak; (due to the distinction among all those who advocate dispassion) some—the followers of that [Vaibhāṣika] school known as Vaibhāṣikas—say that the object of cognition is perceptible—they declare that the knowable object is established by direct perception itself; some—a few from among them known as Sautrāntikas—say it is inferable from the form of the cognition—they describe the nature of the [cognized] object as being inferable from a specific form residing in the cognition; some—

Some among those very followers [of the Buddha] known as Yogācāras assert that the object of cognition (*bodhya*) is unreal; they declared that the object of knowledge (*jñeya-artha*) is indeed non-existent. Others, who are likewise [his] followers but designated as Mādhyamikas, [asserted] that even the intellect (*dhī*)—that is, cognition (*jñāna*)—just like the object of knowledge, is established through conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) alone by a logic similar to that [applied to the object], being imagined solely by ignorance (*avidyā*). They described [this] to all those teachers of the Daityas—that is, to all these preceptors of the demons—and then...

In the context of refuting the opposing position, the author of the Sūtras "tears asunder"—that is, shatters—the Buddhist conceptual constructions by means of logical reasonings (*tarka*) and the instruments of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) supported by them, which are employed as proofs. || 18 ||

The Vaibhāṣika has asserted that the manifestation of aggregates such as the earth and the body arises either from atoms possessing a nature of one, three, or more [directions], or from those possessing a singular nature.
However, in that case, because they are subject to momentary destruction, the cognition and grasping [of objects] would not be established for the Buddha.
Unimpeded recognition is the churner of inference; the rest has been well stated elsewhere. || 19 ||

By atoms possessing one, two, and so forth, natures—namely, those with the single nature of tangibility (*sparśa*); those with the dual nature of tangibility and form (*rūpa*); those with the triple nature of tangibility, form, and taste (*rasa*); and those with the fourfold nature known as tangibility, form, taste, and odor (*gandha*)—that is, by the ultimate atoms (*paramāṇu*) belonging respectively to the four elements known as wind, fire, water, and earth; or alternatively, by those aforementioned atoms that possess each of those respective single natures—that is, atoms having only the single nature of tangibility, form, taste, or odor—the earth (*kṣoṇī*) [is produced].

Regarding "emanation" (*prasṛti*): it refers to the creation consisting of an expansion of the aggregate of elements such as earth, as well as the aggregate of material things such as the body—this is what was stated by the Vaibhāṣika. Within that system, regarding both the object of cognition (*bodhya*) and the cognition (*buddhi*)—that is, the atom (*aṇu*) as the knowable and the knowledge having that as its object—their momentary perishability means their destruction after a mere instant; [and thus] the grasping of objects and so forth...

The apprehension of that [object] and so forth would not be established—that is, it would not be fully accomplished; it would be "uncontradicted" (*nirbādhā*), meaning remote from any subsequent sublating cognition. Recognition (*pratyabhijñā*)—the cognition born from the contact of the sense organ aided by mental impressions (*saṃskāra*) in the form "this is that very same one"—is the destroyer of the inference [of momentariness], as it prevents the arising of the inference of momentariness, namely "whatever exists is momentary. The rest—the remaining Buddhist objections—has been well-stated (*sūkta*), that is, properly demonstrated, elsewhere—in other places and in other texts.
The earlier [proponent],

asserting that the previous object is inferred from the variety of those [cognitions]— projecting its own internal distinction of forms onto subsequent cognitions— and claiming that it is never directly perceived, speaks thus.

May he known as the Sautrāntika attain tranquility, having been subdued by those who, through their activities both before and after [him], spoke of an abundance of contradictions and an arrogance born of skill in training others. 20.

The preceding [object]—the entity existing at a time prior to the cognition that grasps it, such as a jar or other object—by imparting its own specific form (*nijam ākārabhedam*), that is, its own particular internal configuration, to the subsequent cognitions—that is, the cognitions occurring in its immediate succession—is, by its very nature, joined with them; thus, its essence is to be inferred from the diversity [of those cognitions], namely, from the distinctness of the subjective aspects (*viṣayitāvailakṣaṇya*) residing in each respective cognition. (For this very reason,) the perceptibility—that is, the state of being directly perceived—of objects to be known never occurs [in relation to the past object].

Speaking thus with such audacity, even while asserting that [the object] has not been established even in the case of a cognition [of it], this one called Sautrāntika—a member of the Buddhist school known by that name—is subject to a great deal of contradiction—an abundance of internal inconsistencies—by his fellow-sectarians: first, by those known as Yogācāras who exerted themselves to propagate their own views prior to him, and later, by those known as Vaibhāṣikas who exerted themselves after him, both of whom have entered the fold of Buddhism.

(Regarding the view that) when an object has perished and cognition has not yet arisen, [the object] must impart its own form [to the cognition]; and as for the "burden" (gaurava)—that burden which is the basis for accepting specific forms within cognition—it has been clearly proclaimed by those speaking [on this matter]. Therefore, let it be subdued and restrained from its willfulness by the virtuous members of our own school who are skilled in training and adept at discerning deficiencies and excesses among their peers;
having attained his tether, like an elephant, let him abandon his wickedness and attain peace. || 20 ||
*Nayasaṅgatimālikā*:

"In the doctrine of aggregation (*saṃghātavāda*), the fault of the theory of beginning (*prārambhavāda*) does not exist; and in the theory of the collection (*samudāyanaya*), the objection is also refuted. Thus ends the section on aggregation (*samudāyādhikaraṇa*). 3.

In some instance—whether in sleep or waking, or in any cognition whatsoever—the apprehended and the apprehender—the external objects consisting of the knowable and the knower—do not exist; they are simply not found. Even now, in this state of transmigratory existence, the nature of the intellect consists of mere consciousness.

The internal object (*antar-artha*)—variegated by diverse beginningless continuities and possessing a manifold variety produced by *vāsanās* active since time immemorial—is for this very reason threefold (*tryātmaka*). It manifests (*sphurati*), that is, appears, as if having a triple form (*trirūpa*) consisting of the knowable (*jñeya*), the means of knowledge (*jñāna*), and the knower (*jñātṛ*). Upon transcending the state of existence—that is, upon surmounting the condition of transmigratory existence—it shines forth solely as one's own self, in the form of pure consciousness alone. Such is the statement of the Yogācāra; such is the Yogācāra’s manner of describing his own intended object. This is the subject matter (*viṣaya*).

Regarding the two subjects—the object of knowledge (*jñeya*) and the means of knowledge (*jñāna*)—in their respective domains, there exist cognition (*bodha*) and its sublation (*bādha*). Wise men who consider both the cognition that establishes [an object] and the conceptual construction (*kalpanā*) that sublates it to be equal, and who reflect upon them as such, must restrain and reject these for the sake of pacifying the total collapse of reality (*tattvopaplava*). This is because, once the position favored by the Yogācāras becomes established, the distinction between self and other regarding any object whatsoever would not be proven; that is, the division between one's own and another's [perspective] could not be maintained at all due to the universal collapse of all categories. || 21 ||

The identity of the cognition and its object is not possible here for you, whether they be the truth and the knower or the fit and the yogin; for if they were distinct, you would admit the destruction of the definition of the apprehended. Nor is a unity of variegation possible here, for no one knows a variegated thing—whether substance or quality—to have a nature that is both distinct and one.
Therefore, let the theory of self-apprehension (ātmakhyāti) find its footing here, based solely on self-luminosity.

In this context—regarding the entities consisting of knowledge (*jñāna*), the object of knowledge (*jñeya*), and the knower (*jñātṛ*), that is, the two entities of the "object to be known" and the "knower"—whether these are accepted as real or otherwise, as substantial entities or their opposites (unreal), your intended identity of cognition—that is, non-difference from cognition—is not tenable; it does not cohere as a proof for your position. For if they are real, their denial is impossible; and if they are unreal, then even the unreal, distinct cognition [cannot be established].

Because it would result in [the objects] being unreal; and regarding their difference—if, in order to avoid this fault, you accept that those two are distinct from cognition, then you must consider the destruction of the definition of the "graspable" (*grāhya*)—namely, that the definition of being graspable consists in its non-difference from the respective cognitions, which takes the form of being the object of those respective cognitions. Furthermore, you must consider "variegated unity"—a unity that is different from what is seen, which coexists with difference, which is a form of non-difference between two distinct things, or a unity that is non-different from the two distinct [parts]; and this [unity] is not sought here—within this triad consisting of cognition and the other two.

No matter what philosopher it may be, no one whatsoever would consider anything—whether a substance (*dravya*) or a quality (*guṇa*), or any object whatsoever, whether of the nature of a substance or not—that is manifold (*citram*) and yet does not know [it to be] mutually contradictory, neither different nor non-different, nor both; nor would they accept it as having a form that is both different and one (*bhinnaikarūpam*), such that unity exists without suppressing difference. For this reason, due to the aforementioned incongruity, [this cannot be maintained] here in the system of the Yogācāras.

The doctrine of *ātmakhyāti*— the theory currently observed which holds that cognition itself appears in the form of both the object and the knower— should, by virtue of its mere self-luminosity, abandon a self-luminosity dependent on others (such as a jar) and instead find its final resting point in a state of self-dependent self-luminosity. || 22 ||

Because of the fault consisting in the consequence of infinite regress (*anavasthā*) resulting from cessation, even the production of a modification (*vikṛtabhavana*) means that an effect is generated from a cause that has itself undergone transformation.

Furthermore, that [position] does not attain rationality nor does it achieve consistency with logic; for it is impossible for an effect to arise from a cause—whether modified or unmodified. Thus, the statement of the Mādhyamikas—that the world (*bhuvana*) has arisen (*prabhūta*) from the void (*tuccha*), i.e., from the indefinable emptiness (*nirupākhya*)—is not true. Such a claim is certainly not correct, just like [the claim regarding] any object whatsoever that is fit to be related to a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*).

The determination of existence or non-existence—that is, the restriction of a specific state characterized either as being or as non-being—is unavoidable. For that reason stated, in the case of its opposite—the domain of the word and cognition of "existence" and the word and cognition of "non-existence"—there is a loss of insubstantiality; indeed, insubstantiality would be abandoned. If there were a loss of reality before or after, like a sky-flower, it could not exist even in the middle as an effect.

Do not say so; for if [the effect] is seen in that very [cause], then how could there be such terms as "intermediate" (*madhya*) or "action" (*kārya*)? Furthermore, even the inquiry—whether the cause is the primary origin (*nidāna*) at the commencement of the effect or whether it possesses a transformation (*vikṛti*), and so forth—is futile. Since the accomplishment of the effect depends on the causal complex (*sāmagrī*), the regressus ad infinitum of the cause attains the status of a subordinate factor (*guṇatā*). // 24 //

An effect is an entity that possesses origination; [if it were non-existent] prior to its own origination and after its destruction—after which there is a loss of existence and thus a lapse from being an object of the conventional usage of "is"—then even in the interim—the period between origination and destruction—it would be like a sky-flower, essentially void, and this must be accepted. (Thus one might object: "Not so—such an objection is not appropriate; for in that interim period, by the very fact of perception..."

This is due solely to the non-deviant apprehension [of existence]. For if that apprehension were not indicative of existence, or if existence itself—which is necessitated by it—did not exist, then how, and by what means, would these words you employ—such as the word "middle" (*madhya*) which excludes the times of origination and destruction, or the word "product" (*kārya*) and so forth which excludes the unproduced—be valid? The "cause" (*nidāna*) is the causal entity, such as a lump of clay, at the commencement of the effect. In the effect...

Whether that which is to be produced undergoes modification or not—whether only that which is endowed with an action such as destruction produces the effect, or whether the cause produces it even without undergoing modification—and so forth: even such deliberation, and even such doubt, is barren and fruitless, because effects are established through the causal complex—that is, through the perfection of all constituent causes—since effects obtain their own nature. Furthermore, the infinite regress of causes—the lack of rest in the series of causes—becomes a merit rather than a defect; it does not result in a fault. || 24 ||
If, for you, the probandum, the reason, and its members [of the syllogism] were established through mere conventional reality (*saṃvṛti*) alone,
then— following our own statement— how could faults such as "unestablished" (*asiddha*) not arise here?
If you do not accept that there is a cognition of validity therein, then do not recite the words, "That is a means of valid cognition."
If it is argued that, according to the actual state of things, that [scripture] is not a means of valid cognition, then the same applies to the one who establishes your own doctrine as well.

(Regarding the objection raised against the Buddhist that "because the Mādhyamika negates everything—including the means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*)—the object of cognition (*prameya*) called 'emptiness' is not established; for the establishment of an object of cognition depends upon the means of valid cognition," the Buddhist position is that emptiness and so forth are established by means of inference which possesses the full set of factors for conventional establishment. This [text] elaborates upon that and its refutation.)

The probandum (*sādhya*)—the object to be inferred—is the emptiness of all things; the reason (*hetu*) is the fact that serves as its proof, beginning with its constituent parts; and the "limbs of the reason" (*hetvaṅga*), such as pervasion (*vyāpti*) and presence in the subject (*pakṣadharmatva*), if these were to be established for you—the Buddhists—from *saṃvṛti* alone—that is, from the very specific defect called *saṃvṛti*—then, indeed, they would be obtained here in this means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) consisting of inference, which establishes the object of knowledge in the form of emptiness, in accordance with our own statements, that is, following our words which fall within the conventional (*sāṃvṛtika*) according to your own view.

Defects such as unestablishedness (*asiddhi*) and so forth are what constitute fallacious reasons (*hetvābhāsa*). How could defects such as unestablishedness, sublation (*bādha*), and the like not occur? Or rather, how could they not apply? They would certainly apply there—in the challenge (*āpādana*) stated by us—if the cognition of validity—that is, the awareness of being a means of valid knowledge—does not arise. Then, you should recite my statement, "That [statement] is a means of valid knowledge," which is my own word to that effect; you should say it again and again with pride.

(Just as your own position would be established merely by the recurrence of the Buddhist teaching,) if that—my statement—is not a means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) according to the actual state of things—that is, if your intention is that it is not a source of knowledge—then this applies equally even to the statement "all is empty" uttered by the proponent of your own view while engaged in establishing your doctrine; for, because it is merely conventional (*sāṃvṛtika*), its lack of validity according to the actual state of things is exactly the same. Thus, even that [position of yours] is not established at all. || 25 ||

The theory of non-apprehension (*akhyāti*), the theory of misapprehension (*anyathākhyāti*), the theory that cognition is devoid of an object (*viṣayarahitādhi*), the theory that cognition lacks a substratum (*anadhiṣṭhānabuddhi*),

the theory of the imposition of the form of external objects (*bāhyārthākārayoga*), the theory of cognition as being neither existent nor non-existent (*sadasaditaradhī*), the theory of the void (*śūnyadhī*), and the theory of the self (*ātmadhī*)—
all these various positions held by proponents of rival systems have been refuted throughout every instance of error.
For the most part, cognition is considered by those learned in the scriptures to be in accordance with reality, or else it arises from the non-apprehension of difference and so forth. (26)

In all cases of error—that is, in the general category of illusion—these various specific positions (*pakṣabheda*) have been accepted (*ādṛta*) or adopted by proponents (*vādin*) of various philosophical systems, such as the Prābhākara school and others. These positions are: *akhyāti* (non-apprehension, specifically the non-apprehension of the connection between a substrate and its qualifier); *anyathādhī* (misapprehension, the apprehension of a substrate through a qualifier that does not exist in it); *viṣayarahitadhī* (objectless cognition, synonymous with conceptual construction or *vikalpa*, which is an apprehension devoid of an object); and *anadhiṣṭhānabuddhi* (cognition without a substratum, [referring to] the substrate of superimposition).

Appearance without a substratum (*niradhiṣṭhānakhyāti*) is the appearance [of an object] even in the absence of the attribution of a property (*dharmāropa*). The appearance of form associated with an external object (*arthasaṃsargajākārakhyāti*) is the cognition that delineates the form of a jar or the like within a formless consciousness. The cognition of that which is other than existent and non-existent (*sadasaditaradhī*) is the indeterminate appearance (*anirvacanīyakhyāti*), also known by the synonym *vivarta*. The cognition of emptiness (*śūnyadhī*) is the appearance of non-existence—which is synonymous with emptiness—in the form of the world as a positive entity. And the cognition of the self (*ātmadhī*) is the appearance of knowledge itself—which is synonymous with the self—in every possible way, both externally and internally.

"Khyāti" (manifestation) is generally understood as every cognition characterized by the intellect; indeed, all such cognition is "yathārtha-khyāti" (manifestation in accordance with reality), which is precisely what is accepted by those learned in the Vedas—that is, agreed upon by the knowers of the Veda. However, in certain instances—namely, in cases where the establishment of correspondence with reality is impossible, or in specific types of perception involving both valid and invalid cognitions—"akhyāti" (non-manifestation) occurs, consisting of the non-apprehension of difference (*bhedāgraha*) and the non-apprehension of non-relation (*asaṃsargāgraha*). || 26 ||

Summary of the Section on the Impossibility in Every Way (*Sarvathānupapattyadhikaraṇa*): Since existence and non-existence are merely specific states [of a thing], even when the proposition "it is non-existent" is asserted, the kind of "emptiness" (*tucchatva*) favored by the Mādhyamikas is untenable—just as it is untenable when the proposition "it is existent" is asserted. Thus, it was stated that their doctrine is logically inconsistent.

*Nayasaṅgatimālikā* (The Garland of Logical Consistency): "Indeed, no fault whatsoever attaches to the doctrine of universal non-existence; thus is the Mādhyamika position refuted through the application of counter-examples. Thus concludes the section on the impossibility [of the opponent's view] in every respect. 5.
(51) The Section on the Impossibility [of Multiple Cognitions] in One [Mind] ||2.2.6||
The *Śārīrakanyāyakalāpasaṅgraha* [states]:

"Everything, such as existence (*sattva*) and so forth, is both different and non-different from states such as 'cloth' and so on, and is both stable and unstable"— this too is false, because [it involves] contradictory properties.
Cognition produced by something other than its own substratum is not [valid]. || 20 ||
And every single thing, without exception, is non-different from the states of existence such as being (sat) and is stable.
3. PE

"By means of general properties such as existence (*satva*), substantiality (*dravyatva*), and so forth, [the object] becomes devoid of difference and long-enduring; yet, by means of specific properties such as cloth-ness (*paṭatva*) and jar-ness (*ghaṭatva*), it possesses mutual differences and is quickly perishable. (Therefore, only the doctrine of non-absolutism [*anekāntavāda*] is appropriate). This too is incorrect—such a reflection is also improper—because for whatever reason two contradictory properties—two properties that are mutually opposed—would not have a single locus, nor would they be co-instantiated (*samānādhikaraṇa*) within one and the same substratum (*dharmin*). This is what is perceived.

Cognition that apprehends contradictory properties is caused by another [factor], such as a difference in place, time, or other limiting conditions (upādhi), but not by inconclusiveness (anaikāntya). || 20 ||
In some portion, regarding certain aspects such as non-violence and other common duties of human beings, [there is] the word of the Jina-muni.

Because of the agreement—due to the consensus regarding the words of the sage known as Jina—the remainder [of his teachings] should also be accepted as authoritative; that is, the rest of the speech declared in the Jaina scriptures should be recognized as valid. Therefore, since their equality as authoritative sources is established, the claim of the Vedāntins—that the Upaniṣads are contradicted by the words of the Jina-muni—might even be refuted in some instances. Thus, the "evil hope"—the wicked expectation—of the "pluckers" (ulluñchanas), namely the Jainas who are devoted to the plucking out of hair, might be realized.

That [validity] would not be fruitful, because even in the case of inconsistency—since it is observed that the words of the Jina also convey meanings contrary to those of the Vedas (due to the absence of agreement in all respects)—if the words of the Jina were not defective despite contradicting the Veda, then likewise the speech of the Sugata—the language spoken by Śākyamuni—would also be true, meaning its authority would be accepted. Therefore, since there is no distinction regarding the aspect of contradicting the Veda, between the two human utterances—the words of the Jina and...

Because the words of the Sugata and [the Veda] are mutually contradictory—due to their mutual opposition resulting in sublation—the Vedic word, which for us is the authoritative, authorless speech of the Vedas, remains awake as something unshakable, its validity being irrefutable. || 27 ||

The sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*)—consisting of "is," "is not," and so forth—is proclaimed by those whose speech is as vast as the sky; it comprises two truths, and that [set] is augmented by two along with the previous ones. If contradiction is accepted by them, it is their own system's refutation; if it is not accepted, it is the opponent's statement.
"Therefore, there is no harm [to our position] by those statements, nor is there any connection with non-existence or the like that is devoid of qualifications. ||28||

"Clad in the sky" refers to the Digambara Jains, who dwell in the open air. Their own established path of doctrine accepts the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgī*), which possesses seven types of modes (*bhaṅga*) [of non-absolutism], expressed through such statements as: "In some sense it exists," "in some sense it does not exist," "in some sense it both exists and does not exist," "in some sense it is inexpressible," and "in some sense it exists and is inexpressible."

By means of such a mode of expression as "it may be non-existent and inexpressible," and "it may be existent, non-existent, and inexpressible"—[where] "existent" (*sat*) and "non-existent" (*asat*) mean both being like existence (*sattāvat*) and being other than existence; and "both" (*dvaya*) means both being like the duality of existence and non-existence and being distinct from that stated duality (i.e., the inexpressible, *anirvācya*); and [finally], together with all those preceding and following [positions], it is proclaimed as being like the inexpressibility that consists in being distinct from all of them—thus is it established by them for this purpose.

If the fault called "contradiction" (*vyāghāta*)—which is to be pointed out by disputants—is accepted as a fault even by the proponents of the sevenfold predication (*saptabhaṅgīvādin*), then there is a violation of their own system (*svasamaya-vihati*), that is, a fall from their own established doctrine (since the sevenfold predication itself consists of contradiction). If, on the other hand, it is not accepted—that is, if it is not agreed upon as being a fault—then there is no damage to the opponent's statement; that is, there is no harm to the position of the proponent of the doctrine asserted by your adversary through your own words intended to expose that fault.

Let there not be a contradiction anywhere—in any single object—regarding the connection with non-existence and so forth that is unconditional (*nirupadhika*), meaning independent of distinctions such as place and time (i.e., natural); for it is impossible for contradictory properties, such as non-existence, to coexist with existence inherent in the same thing. || 28 ||

Those who, by means of fallacious arguments, imagine that for living beings there is an increase in size according to their respective bodies, that there is a celestial vehicle (vimāna) upon the destruction of the body, or that in liberation there is either eternal upward motion due to heaviness or eternal falling due to the weight of the earth and so forth; or those who imagine that qualities such as dharma are all-pervading like space, or that the soul possesses a "pudgala-nature" similar to it—they are to be driven away by those skilled in the method of the Śruti. || 29 ||

For living beings (*bhavinām*)—that is, for souls wandering in saṃsāra—in each body (*pratitanu*), increase and decrease (*vṛddhihāsau*)—meaning growth and decay (or large and small dimensions)—are observed according to their fitness (*yathārham*). When the destruction of the body occurs (*dehabhaṅge*), that is, when the connection with the body is severed, there is a state of uniform dimension (*vimānam*)—this being a reference to the abstract state (*bhāvapradhānanirdeśāt*). In the state of liberation (*muktau*), there is eternal upward movement and so forth (*nityordhvayānaprabhṛti*) as a result of [the cultivation of] forbearance and the other virtues.

—of the earth, planets, spheres, and so forth; by the reason of "heaviness," that is, by possessing the property called gravity which is the cause of falling; [there would follow] "constant falling," meaning an uninterrupted succession of falls. Furthermore, of dharma and adharma, there would be "pervasiveness"—the occupation of all places and all times—by virtue of their similarity to the sky (ākāśa). Or else, "unlike that," meaning the opposite of pervasiveness, namely "pudgala-nature," which is the state of having a limited dimension (paricchinnaparimāṇatva). By wicked logicians...

These Jains, who determine that [the Veda] is not authoritative by means of reasonings contrary to the Śruti, should be driven far away—meaning they should be refuted so as never to sprout again—by those skilled in the method of the Śruti, that is, those proficient in Vedic logic. || 29 ||
The Section Concerning Paśupati (2.2.7).
This compendium of the collection of principles concerning the embodied soul is the doctrine of the Lord of creatures, worthy of respect because of His omniscience and His acceptance [of it].
This too is false, because it propounds doctrines such as the supreme and the inferior that contradict the Vedas. || 21 ||

The claim that the Pāśupata doctrine—so called because it proceeded from the instruction of Śiva, the Lord of Beasts (Paśupati)—is invalid for the following reasons: first, because its teacher, Śiva, possesses omniscience and thus knows the true nature of all principles (*tattvas*); and second, because of its acceptance (*parigraha*)—as evidenced by the fact that certain Vaidikas have accepted the scripture composed by him as authoritative through the means of instruction and practice—it is also untenable to argue that it is unworthy of acceptance merely because it is a scripture that expands upon the venerable Vedas.

Such a reflection is also improper and contrary to the Vedas... by establishing that the two principles known as Īśvara and Pradhāna possess the characteristics of being both efficient cause (*nimitta*) and material cause (*upādāna*), which is not accepted by the Śruti; [this is because] this doctrine is to be disregarded by the followers of the Veda. || 21 ||

For, having been commanded—ordered—by the Lord, the Blessed Mahāviṣṇu, who delights in crushing the Daityas—that is, who desires the destruction of the Danujas—to "compose delusive scriptures," meaning to set forth those scriptures that cause the delusion of the Asuras; being thus instructed, [he acted].

This one—Śiva, known by the name Paśupati—composed his own Pāśupata Tantra; therefore, for that reason, that Pāśupata Tantra intended to delude the Asuras is not to be relied upon as authoritative by those who follow the true scriptures, nor is it to be lived by by the learned. || 30 ||

Indeed, in the dialogue concerning Prajāpati, the Upaniṣad clearly set forth the doctrine that the body is the self; that was the Lokāyata system which Suguru (Kapila) destroyed by teaching "I am not the body" (ahanmo). Furthermore, the preeminent Lokāyatikas are sung of even in the Mahābhārata at the place of Kaṇva; thus, the deception regarding the purpose of creation on the part of Paśupati is likewise established here.

The *Upaniṣad*—the *Chāndogya Śruti*, specifically the passage concerning Prajāpati, which was taught by Prajāpati to Indra and Virocana and is devoted to revealing the nature of the Self (as a supplement to the *Dahara-vidyā*)—contains a discourse on the identity of the body with the Self (*dehātmavāda*), a statement that teaches that the body alone is the Self. Indeed, it speaks clearly—it declares this explicitly—and thus, that very identity of the body with the Self as spoken by Prajāpati was formulated by the Teacher of the Gods (*suraguru*), Bṛhaspati, into what became known as the *Lokāyata* system.

Mukunda—the bestower of liberation (mukti-dāyaka), namely Janārdana himself—assumed or took upon himself the state of being a deluder (mohanatva), either in the form known as Mohinī or in forms such as Buddha that serve as means for deluding; and even in the hermitage of the sage Kaṇva, he encountered the leaders of the Lokāyata school, who are celebrated even in the Mahābhārata.

This has also been made clear in the *Mahābhārata*. For that reason, here—in this *Pāśupata-tantra* as well—it is entirely appropriate (*upapanna*) that there should be a "deception" (*vipralambha*), which is to say a delusive activity directed toward a specific primordial nature (*prakṛti-viśeṣa*) for the sake of a particular task, on the part of Paśupati—that is, Śiva who bears the name Paśupati. This is justified because it serves the purpose of fulfilling the Lord’s true resolve (*satya-saṅkalpa*). || 31 ||
The *paśupati* tradition is fourfold through its various specific designations, or otherwise [it may be] different;

here, the mutual contradiction with the Veda is clear, and thus it is said to be corrupted by a curse. Those who follow the Vedas [should] not accept those who have entered that [tradition], even though they remember the scriptures;
likewise, regarding the truth here, the teaching of the Sugata—the Jina—is mentioned immediately after, as it follows in sequence.

The *paśupatisamaya*—the established doctrine of Paśupati Śiva—is divided into four types through specific designations such as Śaiva, Pāśupata, Kāpāla, and Kālāmukha; or it may exist otherwise, as having only a single form. (We have no concern for that here. In this Pāśupata system, contradiction between the Vedic revelation (*śruti*) and [its own internal] statements is evident.

—And its contradiction with the Veda, even when mixed within itself, is easily discernible by those who possess discrimination; therefore—for the reason stated above—that Pāśupata doctrine is fit only for the service of those corrupted by a curse, namely, by the curse received from the sage Gautama.

It was stated that they are not for the Vaidikas—meaning they exist as determined by the Vaidikas; "those who follow the Nigamas" refers to the Mantras and others who rely on the path of the Vedas; "those who have entered therein" refers to those who have entered the Pāśupata discipline. [The sages] declared them "unacceptable to the Vaidikas"—that is, as being unworthy of adoption by those who have entered the Vedic path—and thus they made this known in their own Smṛtis. Here, even regarding the truth which is the object to be determined by those seeking liberation, there is "otherwise-ness"—that is, a contradiction with the Śruti.

(Not only regarding the section on conduct) there is the statement of other views within the Sugata-Jina’s system: the logic of refutation that follows the refutation of the Buddhist ultimate view (*bauddhāntamata*) in this tantra, which proceeds according to the sequence of gradations once its non-Vedic nature has been established.
It is established. || 32 ||

Because of the statement that Nārāyaṇa is the ultimate goal of all, and because it is stated that He cannot be slain by any cause, as well as by the declaration of His invincibility, other tantras are also honored like the Vedas in the Mahābhārata and other texts. If it is argued that there is no refutation of them—as there is for the Buddhists and others—this is true; however, there may be contradiction regarding certain parts.
Such [contradiction] does not exist anywhere in the Pañcarātra; therefore, its acceptance here is equal to that of the Veda.

In all [systems]—even in all the systems such as Sāṅkhya and others—the final goal (*niṣṭhā*) is Nārāyaṇa; that is, Nārāyaṇa alone is the ultimate ground. This is known from the statements in the *Mahābhārata* and other Itihāsas and Purāṇas, which are universally accepted as authoritative sources, where it is described that "Nārāyaṇa is remembered as the final goal. Furthermore, this is established by the declaration of his invulnerability to logical arguments: "Likewise, the Pāśupata [teaching] is not to be refuted by reasons," because its immunity to subversion by mere reasoning is determined, and because its status as a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇatva*) has been stated.

And [it may be argued]: "Since these are established as valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) by the statement 'these are the measures of the Self,' other systems (*tantrāntara*)—that is, systems other than the *Pañcarātra*—are also honored like the Veda, meaning they possess excellence due to their similarity to the Veda. Therefore, for the reasons stated, just as in the case of the Buddhists and others—that is, with the notion that they are equal to the followers of the Buddha, the Jains, and so on—their refutation is not [appropriate]; thus, the refutation of the *Tantras* of Kapila and others is not at all logical. [The author] raises this objection. [The reply is: True—this statement must indeed be accepted in certain respects, but in other respects...

There would be contradiction [with scripture]. Because Īśvara is merely the efficient cause (*nimitta*) and not the material cause (*upādāna*), the contradiction with the Vedas in certain respects is indeed unavoidable. However, in the *Pañcarātra*—the system (*tantra*) called Pañcarātra proclaimed by Nārāyaṇa—that contradiction with the Śruti does not exist even in the slightest degree; it does not even deserve to be suspected in any part whatsoever. For that reason, here in the Pañcarātra, its acceptance is equal to the Veda—it is to be accepted by the followers of the Veda on the basis of its equality with the Veda, and not through any hierarchy of superiority. || 33 ||
Indeed, conventions are seen to be adopted in the world, and they must be upheld by kings;
therefore, partiality toward us is inappropriate in any case—such is the objection raised by those who are like children.
Let other conventions be adopted by the simple-minded, but let the statement regarding the preservation of a convention be applied to that which is righteous.
The statement regarding the oneness of the ultimate reality is intended to exclude anything other than that, because it is observed to be a declaration opposed to such [other] things. (34)

For, in this world, various systems of tenets (*samaya*)—meaning diverse established doctrines—are seen to have been compiled and set down together in the form of texts; these are found [to have been composed] by various Tīrthaṅkaras, and all those systems of tenets must be protected by the king—that is, they must be preserved by the monarch just as he protects his subjects. Therefore, because they must be protected by the king, we too should not harbor partiality toward any single one of our own philosophical views.

"Unfit"—meaning that pride regarding what is distinguished is improper—this is the objection of those who are like children; such a suspicion belongs only to those equal to fools. Other non-Vedic systems have been grasped by the deluded, that is, accepted only by those who have fallen into confusion (not by the discerning). And as for the statement regarding the preservation of one's own system—the claim that "all philosophical tenets (*siddhāntas*) must be upheld"—let it be so, provided it concerns tenets that do not contradict *dharma*; let it be certain that this refers to such matters. As for the statement regarding the unity of the ultimate goal (*niṣṭhaikya*), [it applies] to all...

The statement, "The culmination of the Tantras is Nārāyaṇa, the Supreme," which asserts that the finality rests in Nārāyaṇa alone, is intended to exclude other [deities]; it proceeds with the aim of negating the notion of supremacy in anyone other than Nārāyaṇa (i.e., another deity), because such contradictory statements are observed in other Purāṇas and among people, and because the wise must therefore undertake the refutation of those [contradictions]. || 34 ||
Section on the Impossibility of Origination (Utpattyasambhavādhikaraṇa) 2.2.8.

The *Śārīrakanyāyakalāpasaṅgraha* [is so called] because it is seen to contradict the Vedas through such statements as "the individual soul (jīva) is from the Supreme [Self]," and "the mind is from the individual soul."
It might be argued that "the five nights are not real" because they are merely a designation for a ritual arrangement (vyūha) and because they are subject to awakening [from sleep]. (22)

However, from another [source]—namely, from Vāsudeva, the supreme cause, who is Brahman itself, the individual soul (jīva) arises; and the mind (manas), that is, the sense organ of the mind, arises from the individual soul—by means of such statements found in the Śrī Pañcarātra which convey these meanings, and because of the observation of contradiction with the Vedas—due to the perception of conflict with the Śruti which asserts the eternity of the soul and the Śruti which asserts that the mind has the Supreme Self as its cause—the Pañcarātra, known by that name, is not true.

The claim that the Tantra is not sound (i.e., not authoritative) is baseless; such a suspicion is not logical because of the mention of the *vyūhas*. This is because those passages are intent upon propounding the manifestation of the Lord’s *vyūha* forms presiding over the principle of the individual soul (*jīva-tattva*), and the manifestation of the Lord’s *vyūha* forms presiding over the principle of the mind (*manas-tattva*). Furthermore, there is an indicative proof (*jñāpaka*) within the Pāñcarātra itself, where the origination of the individual soul is explicitly barred by the direct statement: "He is beginningless and endless. || 22 ||
Kapila, Kaṇabhuj, and the Buddhas, along with the Arhats and Śambhu—those of harsh intellects—have been struck down by these arguments sharpened like thunderbolts.
Furthermore, it has been established that this path of the venerable Śrī Pañcarātra, as seen by the Blessed One, is indeed not at all similar to other external systems. || 23 ||

Kapila, Kaṇabhuj, Buddha, and Arhat—namely Kapila, Kaṇāda, Sugata, and Jina; the teachers of the Sāṃkhya, Vaiśeṣika, Buddhist, and Jain traditions—along with Śambhu, that is, together with Paśupati, the teacher of the Pāśupatas; because their intellects were not sharp—that is, due to their lack of acute intelligence—these [teachers], having been awakened by the *Śārīraka* (the *Brahma-sūtra*), were struck down by arguments as sharp as a thunderbolt—that is, by reasonings employed as means of proof—which were exceedingly keen like a diamond, [and thus] their respective doctrines were destroyed.

They are refuted by way of rejection; moreover—furthermore—this course of the Śrī-Pāñcarātra, namely the system of the Śrī-Pāñcarātra under discussion, was directly perceived by the Blessed One, Vāsudeva. Therefore, it is certainly not similar to, nor does it coincide with, other tantras excluded from the Vedas; this has been thoroughly established and correctly determined. || 23 ||

The authority of the *Sātvata* [Pāñcarātra] is established even in the section on ritual (*karmakāṇḍa*) by virtue of the principles of the *Smṛti* texts; and if it is argued that there is no connection for this [Pāñcarātra] in this [first] chapter because it does not subdue rival systems, we say: no, for the hostility of the opponent is warded off by the Pāñcarātra dispelling the delusion of contradiction.
By means of speech arising from wickedness or gambling, and at times other than those [prescribed], success was not achieved for him. || 35 ||

The authority—that is, the capacity to produce knowledge of the true nature of reality—of the *Sātvata* system, also known by the synonym *Pāñcarātra-tantra*, is established—that is, already attained—in this section (*pāda*) of the second chapter, specifically the second quarter (*caraṇa*), which is intended for the refutation of opposing views (*pratimatadamana*), by virtue of the principles of the *Smṛti-adhikaraṇa* from the *Karmakāṇḍa* of the *Pūrva-mīmāṃsā*. This refers to the present [section] which serves to support the authority of the *Pāñcarātra*.

Regarding the section on the impossibility of origination (*utpattyasambhavādhikaraṇa*), there is no connection [to the previous topic] in the sense of whether or not there exists a relationship conducive to its being defined. If one objects that such a doubt is also inappropriate—given that the author of the Sūtras was intent on removing and warding off the delusion of contradiction (the error of thinking that this *tantra* called Sātvata, namely the Pañcarātra, teaches matters contrary to what is established by the Śruti)—then it must be maintained that its opposition (its lack of conformity with the Vedas) is to be warded off (refuted).

In this context (*asminn adhikaraṇe*), at other times—that is, regarding non-Vedic systems (*vaidetara-siddhānta*)—their status as opponents (*pratyarthitva*) is established by demonstrating that they arise from unstable and fallacious arguments (*dustarka-dyutthato-ktiyā*), meaning they lack the capacity to withstand the Vedas; this [status] is to be warded off (*vāryam*), that is, avoided, according to the method already stated. Thus, the accomplishment of the underlying thread (*anusyūta-siddhiḥ*) consists in the removal of contradictions.
The attainment of a single, recurring referent (pādārtha) occurs. || 35 ||

If it is argued that the Sage [Bhāskara] disapproved of the Veda because he saw its censure in this [Sātvata-tantra], such is not the case; for there is no loss of Vedic flavor in a statement intended to offer praise based on clarity.
Indeed, the Blessed One, compassionate toward his devotees, composed this work having extracted the essence of the sacred tradition (Āmnāya).
And here, the All-pervading Lord divided the Vedic [dharma] into the Śrauta, Smārta, and so forth, as well as the Tāntrika.

In this [work], the *Śrīpāñcarātra*, because the censure resulting from the description that it does not produce the attainment of peace through the reviling of the Vedas has been observed—that is, perceived—for that reason, its status as Vedic (*vaidikatva*), meaning its conformity with the Vedas, is undesirable to the Sage (*ṛṣi*), namely, to Bādarāyaṇa, the author of the Sūtras; it is not accepted by him.

Not so—such a suspicion is not correct. For in the statement "not finding stability in the Vedas with their auxiliary limbs," which is intended as praise for the Pāñcarātra and is devoted to praising [the scripture] based on its clarity, the capacity to generate a clear comprehension regarding the reality of the principles (*tattvārtha*) is the intended ground; thus, there is no possibility of it having the sense of being contradictory to the Vedas, which would result in a loss of the Vedas' excellence. Indeed, because...

The Lord Nārāyaṇa—compassionate toward his devotees and whose sole nature is affection for those who have sought refuge—having extracted the essence of the Āmnāyas, the preeminent meaning within all the Vedas, and having condensed it into one place, the omnipresent Lord Nārāyaṇa, the founder of the Pāñcarātra, composed this Pāñcarātra. Herein, in this Pāñcarātra-tantra, both Vedic and Tantric [practices] are included; "Vedic" refers to those among the ritual acts of the Śrauta and Smārta traditions that are categorized as Vedic, while "Tantric" refers to those categorized as Tantric.
He divided, that is, he partitioned [the dharma] into the categories of *śrauta* (Vedic) action and *smārta* (traditional/smṛti-based) action, just as one uses an instrument for division. || 36 ||

Because the authority of the Vedas is proclaimed and because it is stated that one's own [tradition] is rooted in them, a distinction from external scriptures (bāhyāgama) appears; thus, there is no scriptural statement [to the effect] that they are equal.

What loss is there in this? Just as various minor sciences (kṣudravidyā) are mixed in such a portion of the Veda for the sake of providing conviction regarding liberation, so too have the various types of supernatural powers (siddhi) been enumerated in the Sātvata [Tantra]. || 37 ||

Because the authority (*pramāṇatā*) of the Vedas—those non-human utterances in the form of the *Ṛg* and other Vedas—is proclaimed in the *Śrī Pāñcarātra*; because its own [authority]—that of the *Pāñcarātra*—is established through following them—that is, by conforming to the Vedas; because it declares its being rooted in those [Vedas]—by stating that it has the Vedas as its source; and [it is superior] to the non-Vedic scriptures (*bāhyāgama*), which are excluded from the Vedas.

Because a distinction appears—that is, a difference is perceived—for this reason, the statement of its similarity [to other systems]—the rhetorical claim that the Pāñcarātra is equal to external [systems]—is not accepted as being *ārṣa* (of the Sage), meaning it is not approved by the Sage who composed the Sūtras. As for the phrase "intermingled with lowly sciences" (*kṣudravidyāśabalam*): even if this Tantra is mixed with many sciences favored by those seeking worldly enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*), what loss is there? What loss could there be regarding its acceptability to those seeking liberation (*mumukṣu*)? Certainly none, just as in the case of such a portion of the Veda [which is accepted] by both those attached to it and those detached from it.

Just as there is no loss of authority for a portion of the Vedas when it is combined with venerable branches of knowledge—namely, meditations (*upāsanā*) that have the attainment of Brahman as their fruit, and ritual injunctions for optional sacrifices (*kāmyeṣṭi*)—so too, in the *Sātvata-Pāñcarātra*, the various types of supernatural powers (*siddhibhedāḥ*) are merely specific accomplishments to be cultivated by those seeking worldly enjoyment (*bubhukṣu*). They are enumerated as "powers" only according to the maxim of the "candy on the tongue" (*guḍajihvikānyāya*), solely for the purpose of generating conviction regarding liberation (*mokṣapratyayārtha*).

It functions as a cause; therefore—because it propounds these meanings that contradict the Vedas—the Pañcarātra, the scripture known as Pañcarātra, cannot be *māna*—it is not at all fit to be a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

Not so—such a doubt is not appropriate, because the words for "living being" and so forth—the terms *jīva*, *manas*, and *ahaṅkāra*—occurring here in this sentence, denote the threefold divisions of the manifestation known as *vyūha* of the all-pervading Lord Vāsudeva, namely those called Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha; they signify these. Among those aforementioned specific manifestations of the *vyūha*, each respective name arises from the presiding over that particular principle (*tattva*), [the first being] the living being (*jīva*).

Among those various principles known as mind (*manas*) and ego (*ahaṅkāra*), [the word "mind"] has attained a specific restriction (*niyati*) due to its particular relationship with the state designated as "self-conceit" (*abhimāna-pada*); it exists as being governed by a rule that restricts its denotation to those [principles] alone, through both the exclusion of non-connection (*ayoga-vyavaccheda*) and the exclusion of connection with others (*anya-yoga-vyavaccheda*). || 38 ||
Since it is stated here that the individual soul (jīva) is without beginning or end, the position that it is produced is not accepted;
for the term "Saṅkarṣaṇa" and so forth does not in any way apply to the mere individual soul.
Furthermore, the scriptural order of creation has not been recited by [the author] himself, and one should not postulate anything contrary to that.

Therefore, there is no contradiction here between [the two] statements, either directly or indirectly, because we perceive that their intended meaning (tātparya) is dependent upon each other. || 39 ||

In this regard—in the *Pañcarātra*—it is clearly stated by the scriptural declaration, "He is without beginning and without end," that the *jīva* (the individual soul), which is conscious (*cetana*), is "without beginning and without end" because it is devoid of origination and destruction; for this reason, the position that accepts the birth of the *jīva*—the view that the *jīva* is produced—is certainly not desired or accepted in the *Pañcarātra*. Furthermore, words such as *Saṅkarṣaṇa* and others do not, in any way, refer merely to the *jīva* and its adjuncts—namely, the forms of the individual soul, the mind (*manas*), and the ego (*ahaṅkāra*).

It cannot be connected in any manner as a means of proof; furthermore, the sequence of creation established by the Śruti is itself the very mode of creation [of the twenty-four principles], which, though not explicitly recited here, is nevertheless set forth by direct statement. That which contradicts this should not be postulated—it is not fit for postulation on the grounds of being established by such statements as "the individual soul is born," as that would contradict the sequence stated directly. Therefore, through such analysis and from the perspective of the intended purport of those respective texts:

Because the essential purport of the *Pāñcarātra-tantras* has been understood here—in this system—there is no contradiction, nor any teaching of mutually inconsistent meanings, whether with the *Śruti*, or among themselves, or with the Veda, or within their own texts. (39) The Sāṅkhyas and Vaiśeṣikas desire the dharma proclaimed by the *Śruti*, but not its true reality (*tattva*). However, in the teachings of Buddha, the Kṣapaṇakas, and Paśupati, both the principles (*tattva*) and the conduct (*ācāra*) are devoid of the *Śruti*. In the *tantra* named *Pāñcarātra*, which supplements the Vedas like the *Viṣṇu-smṛti*, the reality established by the Upaniṣads (*trayyantāsiddha*) is found, and the practice (*caraṇa*) is likewise consistent, according to the rules of the various *Gṛhya-sūtras* and so forth. (40)
The Sāṅkhyas and Vaiśeṣikas—the followers of Kapila and the followers of Kaṇāda—[reject] the dharma recited in the Śruti, that is, the dharma declared in the Veda.

They desired—that is, they accepted—the goal consisting of the means to the highest good (*śreyas*), such as the performance of prescribed duties and the avoidance of prohibited ones; however, they did not desire—that is, they did not accept—the supreme object of knowledge (*prameya*) declared in the Śruti. But in the teachings of the Buddha, the Kṣapaṇakas, and Paśupati—namely, in the scriptures (*āgama*) of the Saugatas, Ārhats, and Pāśupatas—both the supreme reality (*tattva*) and the practice (*ācāra*), that is, both the object of the scripture and its ritual application, are devoid of the Śruti and far removed from the Veda. This is because, like the *Viṣṇu-smṛti* which supplements the Veda, [the Buddhist and other scriptures] serve merely as expansions (*upabṛmhaṇa*) of the Veda.

Just as in the *Viṣṇusmṛti*, so too in the Vaiṣṇava tantra known as the *Pañcarātra*—in this *Pañcarātra* system as well, both [the knowledge of] reality (*tattvam*) and the practice (*caraṇam*), that is, the performance of rites, are the objects of authority of the scripture; both are established by the *Trayyantavedānta*, meaning they are understood precisely through the statements of the Upanishads. They are "equal" (*samam*), meaning undifferentiated, when considered in accordance with the sequence found in specific *Gṛhyasūtras* such as those of Āśvalāyana and Āpastamba, according to the rules of various *Gṛhya* traditions. Thus, it is "unfailing" (*avitatham*);
even if one were to find an inconsistency within itself, it would not incur the fault of redundancy, for it merely reiterates what has already been declared in the Vedas. (40)

The five sacrifices are remembered even by the sages as being performed for a Śūdra with the mantra of salutation (namaskāra). In that regard, the terms beginning with *haviṣkṛt* are studied; thus, his entitlement here is partial. The sequence of time mentioned by Dakṣa should be applied according to the distinctions such as *abhigati* and so forth as stated therein.
Having logically synthesized the entirety of what is to be grasped, beginning with the animal sacrifice and so forth, [one should understand it] as being equal [to the other]. 41.

For a Śūdra—a qualified person belonging to the fourth caste—the five great sacrifices (*pañcamahāyajña*), known as the sacrifice to the gods (*devayajña*), the sacrifice to the ancestors (*pitṛyajña*), the sacrifice to humans (*manuṣyayajña*), the sacrifice to beings (*bhūtayajña*), and the sacrifice to Brahman (*brahmayajña*), are to be performed using only the mantra of salutation, namely the mantra "Namaḥ. This is recorded by the sages who are authors of the *Smṛtis*—by the seers (*ṛṣis*)—in the traditional law: "One should conclude the five sacrifices with the mantra of salutation. Thus, it is made known through the *Smṛti* regarding the case of the Śūdra.

The term *haviṣkṛt* and others: the word *haviṣkṛt* is fit for use in the sentence uttered at the time of the *preṣa* (direction), based on the reason of being the agent of the sacrificial oblation (*yajñīya-havis*); likewise, at the time of constructing the hall suitable for bringing the fire, the word *bahuyājin* is studied based on the reason of being the performer of various sacrifices—as it is recited in the *Kalpasūtras* and other texts: "For a Śūdra, [the fire is taken] from the *haviṣkṛt*'s hearth," and "From the house of a *bahuyājin*, excluding a Śūdra. Therefore, here too, even in a Vedic rite, for this—

A member of the Śūdra caste possesses a partial entitlement—that is, the fitness for performance—only in certain specific actions appropriate to his own varṇa (it certainly exists, though not everywhere; likewise, even regarding the rites taught in the Pañcarātra, there remains a partial entitlement for those other than the three higher varṇas). As it is stated regarding the specific set of five-fold daily rites (pañcakālika-kriyākalāpa) consisting of the divisions beginning with *abhigamana*—namely, *abhigamana*, *upādāna*, *ijyā*, *svādhyāya*, and *yoga*—there is the sequence of time as prescribed by Dakṣa, namely the *aṣṭakā* sacrifices mentioned in the *Dakṣasmṛti*.

The procedure for the sequential performance of rites should be applied—meaning it must be established as something to be performed without mutual sublation—encompassing all actions: those based on the Śruti, the Smṛti, and the Tantras. Just as the various distinct rites known as Paśu, Iṣṭi, and Soma are included within the Vedic fold and must be performed by a single qualified person at specific times (or places) without mutual contradiction, so too [should this procedure be applied].

"By way of logic"—that is, by means of the proper method—it should be grasped by synthesizing [the various sources]: having correctly combined them, one must understand that the term "Ācārya" is used in certain instances [as a title]. This is not so in cases such as the Vedic injunction "The teacher is like a god," for its application is restricted by the definitions established in the Smṛtis. Similarly, in the case of the Sātvatas and others, where there is no other recourse, breaking with conventional usage (rūḍhi) is not a fault;
furthermore, the status of Brahmins and others in this scripture is well-known in many ways from the Mahābhārata and other texts. || 42 ||

Regarding the word *ācārya*: this word "ācārya" is sometimes used in a specific worldly convention, namely, in reference to a particular caste—such as a person belonging to the *takṣan* (carpenter) caste—and merely by that much; even in the case of the word *ācārya* found within the scope of Vedic usage, such as in the traditional injunction "be one for whom the teacher is a god" (*ācāryadevo bhava*), there is no such cognition—that is, no understanding of a person possessing that specific caste—as there is in worldly usage. This is because [the meaning] is restricted by the definition established in the Smṛtis: "Having initiated [a student]... (*upanīya tu...*) [and so forth].

Since the word *ācārya* functions to convey its own primary meaning by relying on the well-established definition found in such Smṛtis as, "He who [instructs] the disciple... him they call an *ācārya*," and following that very same method, there is no fault in breaking the conventional usage—that is, abandoning the collective power (*samudāya-śakti*)—in the case of words that have no other recourse, such as *sāsvata*, *sāntva*, *bhāgavata*, and so forth, which fall within the scope of usage in this system (Tantra) and whose meanings cannot be conveyed by the collective power alone.

There is no fault of violating grammatical derivation; for even here in this scripture, the *Pāñcarātra-tantra*, the status of the Brāhmaṇas and others—the established position of the social classes beginning with the Brāhmaṇa (as well as their boundaries)—is well-known in many ways in the *Mahābhārata* and other such works, which are renowned as the foremost authorities (specifically in the sections concerning the *Pāñcarātra*). || 42 ||
Conclusion of the [first] quarter:
A Compendium of the Collection of Principles of the Śārīraka.

Having established the non-contradiction with tradition and reasoning, as well as the refutation of the opposing view, the nature of the effect is then considered in the following two verses. || 24 ||

Having established the non-contradiction with Smṛti and Nyāya—the fact that the doctrine of Brahman as the cause, propounded by the Vedānta, cannot be refuted by the Smṛtis of Kapila and others or by the Nyāyas of the Vaiśeṣikas and others—and having effected the refutation of opposing views—the rejection of the positions of those outside the Vedic fold such as the Buddhists—he establishes the nature of the effect—the fact that ether, the vital breath, and so forth, are effects of Brahman—by means of the first two quarters [of the second chapter], and subsequently, by means of the latter two—the third and fourth quarters—he reflects upon and settles this matter through inquiry. || 24 ||

In this chapter, by the followers of Kapila, those who follow Kaṇabhuj, the elder Vaibhāṣikas and others, and those called Yogācāras— all of whom are detractors of the Sugata’s doctrine and are prone to the doctrine of emptiness— [the following is addressed].
Then, having set aside the objections raised by those devoted to the doctrines of the Arhats and those established in the tradition of Paśupati,
he who perceives the fifth Veda proclaimed the *Pañcarātra* as the path of the revealed scripture (*śruti*).
Śrīḥ!
Salutations to the illustrious Rāmānuja. Salutations to Śrī. Salutations to Śrīdhara. The third quarter of the second chapter. (2-3)
The Section Concerning Space (Viyan-adhikaraṇa). 2.3.1.
A Compendium of the Collection of Logical Principles Concerning the Body (the Self).
"If the Śruti says, 'Souls do not possess origination, just as space does not possess origination because of its non-destruction,' that is indeed insubstantial."
It would be exactly so, and not merely through the refutation of reasoning. || 25 ||

The individual souls (*jīvas*)—that is, the inner selves—are devoid of parts (*aṃśahāni*) because they lack constituent members; therefore, just as they do not possess birth—that is, in whatever manner they are not subject to being born—in the same way, the ether (*nabhas*) or the sky also does not possess birth, nor is it an effect. Such an objection, however, is without substance, being devoid of supporting reasoning. If the Vedic scripture (*śruti*) declares it so—if it speaks of their lack of birth—then that must be the case, and thus the ether is indeed eternal.

This would follow from the refutation of the argument—merely on account of the contradiction with the pervasion imagined by oneself alone, namely, "whatever is partless is unproduced"—but not because the sky is incapable of being unproduced; therefore, the fact that space is an effect of Brahman is difficult to deny. || 25 ||

The three Buddhist schools, beginning with the Vaibhāṣikas, assert that everything—indeed, all things without exception—is momentary; they maintain that from the very moment of their arising, they perish in the second instant. In contrast, the Jains—who daily recite the *saptabhaṅgī* (the sevenfold predication) taught by the Jina—the Lord of Sages—hold that everything is both eternal and non-eternal, being eternal in its aspect as substance (*dravya*) and non-eternal in its aspect of states (*avasthā*).

The Vaiśeṣikas and others—the followers of Kaṇāda and Gautama—though they have indeed divided the multitude of entities into the eternal and the non-eternal, having analyzed them as such, nevertheless speak perversely; that is, having inverted the scriptural doctrine of the division between the eternal and the non-eternal (by asserting that knowledge and so forth are eternal, while the object consisting of configuration is non-eternal, and the object in the form of the universal is eternal), they speak of those [entities] as if their very nature were derived solely from the authority of the Śruti.

Regarding the statement that "just as there is origination [of ether], so too is its persistence," some opponent objects that this is contradicted by scripture. The proponent replies: "The creation of ether is established by hundreds of Vedic texts; its establishment cannot be otherwise.
He states the disparity in the arguments by citing the scriptural declarations regarding wind, ether, and nectar, which show that birth is diverse. || 46 ||

In the preceding section on eligibility—that is, in the previous section concerning the impossibility of origination—the statement from the Pañcarātra that appears to indicate the birth of the individual soul (*jīva*), namely "the *jīva* is born," is [refuted] by the declaration of its eternity, through the passage from the Pañcarātra which teaches the eternality of the *jīva*: "Indeed, it is beginningless..."

By demonstrating this statement, a resolution was established through an exposition of the appropriate meaning regarding the origin of space (*vyoman*)—that is, concerning the status of space as an effect—even when there is a contradiction (*vyāhati*) between two statements that respectively establish its being "born" and its being "immortal. Such being the case, the actual state of affairs is that the statement regarding its being "born" is to be understood figuratively (*aupacārikatvena*), while the statement regarding its immortality is the true state. Thus says someone.

The proponent of the prima facie view (pūrvapakṣin), being unskilled in the thorough investigation of the meaning of the scriptures, asserts [the following]; whereas the proponent of the established conclusion (siddhāntin), who is adept at reflecting upon the purport of the Vedānta, maintains that the creation of space—the origination of ether—is established by hundreds of scriptural passages (*nigamaśatamitā*) and is accepted by many Śrutis. In this scripture which speaks of origination, there can be no "establishment through another means" (*anyathāsiddhi*), nor can it be rendered purposeful by any other interpretation. Furthermore, the scriptural statement regarding the immortality of air and space—namely, the Vedic utterance, "Air and the intermediate space are indeed immortal"—[refers to] birth...

"Sublated by the injunction" means sublated by the sentence that prescribes the origin; he states the disparity in expression—namely, that he asserts a difference in nature between the statement regarding the origin of the individual soul and the statement regarding the origin of space. || 46 ||

[Objection: "Because of its being mentioned first, because of the statement that it is immortal (*amṛta*), and because it is a partless substance, the statement regarding the origin of space must have as its object only that which is conditioned (*upahita*), just as in the case of the Self (*ātman*). [Reply: This is not so. For its being "first" is not explicitly stated in the scripture; if one were to assume it based on its being read first, that would be sublated by other [scriptural] passages. Furthermore, the term *amṛta* here is equivalent to the expression "immortal" (*amartya*) due to the uniformity of purpose across many sentences. (Verse 47)

Regarding the ether (*vyoman*): the statement concerning its origin—the scriptural text declaring its birth—is like a common worldly expression regarding the self, such as "the potter is born," which conveys the birth of the self only with respect to a conditioned state (*upahita*). It refers only to the ether as connected with limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as pots and cloths, and not to the pure ether. (If one asks why? There are three reasons here: because fire is seen to be first in creation, as the scripture "It created fire" (*tattejo'sṛjata*) shows that fire occupies the initial position in the process of emanation.

Regarding the argument from the statement concerning immortality—namely, that because immortality is explicitly stated of space in the passage, "And this intermediate space is immortal," and because of the nature of space as a partless substance—that is, because it is a substance without parts—if you say this, we reply: such a doubt is not tenable. This is because the primacy—the status of being the first in the creation of fire—is not established by scripture (*aśrutatvāt*), meaning it lacks scriptural authority; for merely on the basis of its position at the beginning of the narrative of creation—the fact that the creation of fire is mentioned first—no inference (*kalpane*) can be made by another [means].

Because the statement of "being born" would result in the sublation (*bādhā*) of inference by means of the perception [of birth], and furthermore, upon careful reflection, the term "immortal" (*amṛta*) here refers to immortality in relation to space; however, its usage is exactly like the application of the word "immortal" (*amartya*) to the gods due to their long duration, as evidenced by the harmony of many statements that teach [their] origin. || 47 ||

The doctrine of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*) is consistent with the Śrutis; there is no such thing as a composite whole (*avayavin*). The theory of creation is that various substances assume different names while remaining co-existent within their respective substrates.
For you, states such as sound and so forth are accepted even within the class of partless substances;
therefore, the origin of space mentioned in the Śrutis—being equal to the origin of other things—is not to be contradicted. (48)

The theory of the pre-existence of the effect (*satkāryavāda*)—the doctrine that the effect exists even prior to its manifestation—is logical, as it is established by reasoning (since the clay remains present even now); it is sanctioned by the scriptures, being authorized by Vedic statements such as "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (*sadeva somyedam agre āsīt*); the object to be created (*sṛjya*) is not non-existent at all prior to its production; and the "whole" (*avayavin*) as a distinct entity from its parts, as accepted by the logicians (*tārkikas*), is a novel concept that does not exist at all within the scope of valid means of knowledge. As for the doctrine of creation—the worldly view concerning origination—it is merely conventional.

Or, according to the technical usage of the treatises (*śāstra*), in those various substances such as clay, threads, and so forth, the acquisition of specific denotative names depends merely upon a connection with adventitious properties capable of assuming those particular states. This is your view, O Vaiśeṣika, even regarding that class of substances held to be partless—such as time, the self, and space—even though they are devoid of parts; for instance, the state of sound in space, or knowledge in the self.

Conjunction and other such adventitious properties (āgantuka-dharma) in time, atoms, and so forth, are indeed accepted and agreed upon. Therefore—since the very attainment of a particular state is what is denoted by the term "origination" (utpatti)—the origination mentioned in the Śrutis, that is, declared in the Vedas, regarding the void (vyoman), i.e., with respect to space (ākāśa), is not to be sublated; it is not capable of being refuted, because it is equal to the origination of other effects and accompanied by the same characteristics as the origination of air and the rest. || 48 ||
