The Section on Light (Tejo’dhikaraṇa) || 2.3.2 ||
The Compendium of the Collection of Principles on the Śārīraka [Upanishads]:
All effects likewise arise from the Cause, because it is so heard in other scriptural passages.
It is not so; for, according to the scripture, they exist beyond their respective bodies when viewed without any intervening space. || 26 ||

All effects produced from wood—namely, all things understood from both worldly experience and the Veda as being born therefrom—are likewise [produced] because it is so heard in scripture: "From ether, air; from air, fire."

Because they are described as being the causes of their respective entities, such as space and so forth, and because in another place—in the place where the word "food" occurs—the different word "earth" is heard—[the elements] arise from their causes; that is, they are born solely from their own respective prior causes, not from Brahman.

It is not so—it is not appropriate to raise such a doubt—because of the Śruti: "All this, indeed, is Brahman," and because of other Śrutis such as "From this [Brahman] it is born," etc. Since, from the perspective of non-intervention—that is, without any mediation by anything other than itself—it is understood that all effects arise directly from Brahman alone, they "come forth from beyond" their respective bodies—the bodies of the elements such as ether and the rest—from the Supreme Brahman itself. || 26 ||
From such scriptural passages as these, [it follows that] there are two breaths.

"Easy to understand" (*sugama*) means capable of being connected [to the meaning] without difficulty; such is the kind of reasoning (*ūha*) consisting of intellectual deliberation (*tarka*). "Delusion" (*moha*) here refers to a contrary determination regarding the fact that the world is an effect of Brahman. "In due order" (*kramataḥ*) means merely following the sequence of the scriptural recitation beginning with "Prāṇa, Manas," and so on. "In causing confusion regarding the other" means in subverting the sequence as understood from the *Śaubāla-śruti* and other texts. This is because of the fallacy of over-extension (*atiprasaṅga*), since in the absence of a decisive criterion (*vinigamanābhāvataḥ*), there would result a state of total confusion among all the *śruti*, *smṛti*, and other authorities.

(Because such an instrument is impossible: on account of the observation of the continuity of "seeing" in such passages as "It thought," "The fire thought," and "The waters thought"—since we observe the uninterrupted persistence of this "thinking," which consists of volition suitable for creation—the first [cause], the primary principle, is indeed the Supreme Brahman; and just as it creates, so too does it create the subsequent objects of creation, such as the Mahat and the rest, while itself having those respective preceding principles, such as the Pradhāna, as its body.
Brahmā alone, O Sauti, produces [the world] directly by himself, and not according to the manner of sons, grandsons, and so forth. || 49 ||
— 0— Summary of the Meaning of the Section:

In the section concerning fire (*tejo’dhikaraṇa*), having raised the doubt that because the scriptures state "from air, fire" (*vāyor agniḥ*) and so forth, the production of fire and the other elements occurs from air and the rest alone, [the Sūtra refutes this].

It has been stated that because the act of seeing—which is unique to Brahman—is heard in such passages as "Fire saw" and "The waters saw," the origin of fire and the other elements is from Brahman alone, who possesses those respective bodies.

In the *Adhikaraṇasārāvali*, it is stated that all substance is indeed eternal through the destruction of its constituent parts; yet, why does the author of the Sūtras further declare the eternity of the Person (*puruṣa*) specifically? True; here, by means of another name, he removes the state of being an insentient object from the conscious Self, which is devoid of limiting adjuncts (*anupādhi*).
Thus, here, the two attributes of inwardness and sentience are eternally restricted to the Knower of the Field as well. (50)

In the previous section concerning "the large and the long" (*mahaddīrghādhikaraṇa*), by means of refuting the composite substance (*avayavidravya*)—specifically through the negation of a composite whole such as a pot that is distinct from its constituent parts such as clay—it was indeed stated and established that all substances, comprising both the sentient and the insentient, are eternal (*nitya*) insofar as they are devoid of origination and destruction. This being the case, the author of the Sūtras—the venerable Bādarāyaṇa, the composer of the *Śārīrakasūtra*—[proceeds to discuss] eternity (*nityatva*) with respect to the Person (*puruṣa*), that is, the individual self (*jīvātman*).

What does it further—that is, yet again—state regarding eternity, which consists in being devoid of birth and so forth, specifically by taking up the particular form known as "selfhood," and for what purpose?

Does he state [this]? (The meaning is that it is redundant and fruitless. (Thus he objects. It is true—it is indeed natural; however, here—in this context—he removes—that is, sets aside—the other state, which is conducive to assuming another name, for the conscious one who is without adjuncts—the Self whose form is pure knowledge and who is untouched by adjuncts such as the instruments and the body. That [is so] because of the aforementioned difference between the conscious and the unconscious; even for the "owner of the field" (kṣetrin)—that is, for one who has obtained a body.

In this section, these two attributes of the individual soul—namely, its nature as the inner self (*pratyaktva*) and its nature as a knower (*jñatva*), which consist in its being manifest to itself and its being the substratum of knowledge—are established as eternal, meaning they persist as long as the self exists; thus, they have been firmly and effectively demonstrated. (Therefore, there is neither redundancy nor futility. || 50 ||
It is established by such texts as "All this has that as its self" (*aitadātmyam*) that everything other than the object of desire (the Self) is subject to birth;

thus, creation has been described. Furthermore, the doctrine of [the Self] being partless has been refuted in the case of space and so forth. Therefore, it cannot be that the individual soul (*jīva*) is produced from that [Self], for that would entail the fallacies of the uncreated acquiring [what was not previously its own] and the like.
Even though his eternity and lack of birth have been explicitly stated, there is nevertheless the manifestation of this [Self] through the conjunction with a body and so forth. // 51 //

Everything other than that which is denoted by the word "sat"—the entire collection of objects understood by the term "sat," namely Brahman—is possessed of birth (*janimat*), meaning it possesses the quality of origination. This is established by such scriptural passages as "All this has that as its self" (*aitadātmyam idaṃ sarvam*) and "All creatures have Being as their root" (*sanmūlāḥ sarvāḥ prajāḥ*). Furthermore, the creation of the individual soul (*jīva*) is also declared; indeed, the fact that the individual self also possesses the nature of being born is explicitly stated in the scripture: "By water he emitted the living beings" (*toyena jīvān vyasasarja*). However, as for the doctrine of partlessness (*niravayavatva*): "That which is partless... [is the subject].

As for the argument that [the soul] is "not produced by that" (by God), it has been refuted regarding space and so forth—that is, concerning the subject of ether and the like—on the grounds that it is inconclusive due to observed deviation; therefore, the claim that the production of the soul would follow from the aforementioned set of reasons—that is, the birth of souls consisting of the acquisition of another name and a different state—is entirely unimpeded, yet this is not true—it is not correct—because of the consequence of [the soul being] uncreated, namely, that pleasure, pain, and so forth would occur even without the performance of prescribed and prohibited actions.

This follows from the logical consequence [of the soul's eternity], and even by explicit statements regarding its eternality and birthlessness—such as the clear declarations in "Unborn, eternal, and everlasting"—which serve as indicators. However, the "birth" of this [Self]—that is, the Self's origination—is merely its conjunction with a body and so forth, a connection with the instruments (the senses) and the body; it is not a transformation of its essential nature (*svarūpa*) like that of a jar or similar objects. || 51 ||

If the body were the self, there would have to be birth [of desire]; yet that is not possible here for one who has just been born, because of [the presence of] passion. The theory that knowledge arises from yeast and so forth, or from a variegated cloth like a rain-cloud or a stone, is extremely untenable. The sense of "mine" regarding the body is as [natural] as [the sense of ownership] regarding a house; the delusion of identity is due to defects.
Furthermore, the inference of identity is refuted by powerful counter-inferences derived from scripture and reasoning. (52)

If the self-nature [ātmatva] were located in the body—that is, if the nature of being a self resided in the body—then birth would occur; that is, the production of the self would be logical. But that is not possible here; the nature of being a self is not tenable in the body. For even at the moment of birth—for the embodied being as soon as it is produced—one observes activity preceded by desire, such as [the desire for] suckling breast milk. Furthermore, there persists an unimpeded awareness of "mine-ness" toward the house and so forth, experienced as being similar to the thought, "This is my house," which is like the notion of ownership regarding a home. As for the delusion of identity—

The misconception that "I am fat" or "I am white," which apprehends the identity between the referent of the "I" (the self) and the body, is produced by defects—specifically, the defect consisting of beginningless sinful tendencies (*vāsanā*). The inference for identity—"The body alone is the self, because it is the object of the notion of 'I'"—is countered by a stronger inference establishing the body's distinctness from the self, namely: "This is my body."

Because it is strengthened by the support of direct perception (*pratyakṣa*), because scripture (*śāstra*)—such as the aforementioned scriptural passage—reveals the distinction between the self and the body, and because it is refuted by reasoning (*tarka*) as well—namely, by the reasoning made known through sūtras such as "the birth of one free from passion is not observed"—it is cast aside, rejected, and overturned. || 52 ||

Those who desire the soul to be the body itself, or that which transcends the body yet is restricted by it as its limit—consisting of breath, intellect, and the senses—or who desire it to be the stream of consciousness, eternal until liberation, or even stable and persisting through dissolution; or those who, like foam upon the ocean, desire the living being to be a real modification within the unchanging reality—all such views are here utterly dispelled by the Śruti, which is free from the defect of contradiction, just as other [erroneous] views are. (53)

"Body"—meaning the very physical frame, whose nature is beyond doubt as being perishable; "desiring [it] to be the living soul"—accepting it as the individual self (*jīvātman*); "even though there is a difference of the self from the body"—that is, even when the self is distinct from the body, up to that limit...

Regarding *rūpa*: those who accept the living being (*jīva*) as having the nature of the vital breath, the intellect, and the sense organs, whose existence is necessarily bound to the existence of the body; those who accept the living being as a permanent stream of cognition—an undisturbed stream of consciousness; those who accept the living being as a form of the stream of consciousness that persists until dissolution and undergoes cessation at the time of cosmic dissolution (*pralaya*); and even those who accept it as persisting until final liberation (*āpavarga*), remaining from beginningless time until it perishes in its essential nature upon reaching liberation.

Accepting the individual soul (*jīva*), and likewise [accepting] the "unfailing transformation"—the locus of modifications that are necessarily employed for effects—and the "existent ocean" (*sad-abdhi*)—the ocean of Brahman denoted by the word "Being"—they acknowledge the soul to have a nature resembling foam, bubbles, and the like. Thus, all these [schools], from the Cārvākas up to those of Yādavaprakāśa, by accepting the nature of the eternal Self as established by the Śrutis and other authorities, are here—in this section on the Self—[refuted] by means of Śrutis that are free from the defect of contradiction.

By the words of the Vedas—which are remote from human defects such as error and which are supported by means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*), logical reasoning (*tarka*), and so forth—they have been utterly cast away, that is, completely eradicated along with their roots, just like the positions of the Sāṅkhya and other schools. || 53 ||
Section on Knowledge (Jñādhikaraṇa) || 2.3.4 || A Compendium of the Logical Threads of the Śārīraka [Brahma-sūtras] || From the word "vijñāna," because it is not observed in dreams,
[the self] is either consciousness alone or adventitious sentience.
The scriptural statement regarding knowledge in deep sleep is not thus restricted; rather, it occurs because that state consists essentially of that quality [of knowledge]. || 28 ||

The self—the individual soul—is denoted by the word "consciousness" (*vijñāna*), because it is expressed by that term in such passages as "that which is in consciousness" and "consciousness is the sacrifice. Furthermore, because it is not perceived during sleep—that is, in states of deep slumber—even though its attribute of being of the nature of knowledge is absent, it is "pure consciousness," having the essential nature of pure *cit* alone; it does not possess knowledge as an adventitious attribute. Or rather, it is "accidental consciousness," meaning it possesses the quality of consciousness contingent upon a collection of causal conditions.

[If one] objects that [the Self] is not the substrate of intrinsic consciousness, [we reply: such an objection is not appropriate, because of the scriptural authority of the Śruti: "There is no loss of consciousness for the knower. In deep sleep—the state of slumber—that which is contracted, namely knowledge as an attribute (*dharmabhūtajñāna*) whose expansion has not yet been attained, is not non-existent. Its designation by the term "knowledge"—that is, its being denoted by a word signifying knowledge—is justified because it has that quality as its essence; that is, it is established because it is the substrate of the quality called knowledge, which persists as long as the Self exists. || 28 ||

Bādarāyaṇa [says]: "By the previous reasoning"—that is, by the logic of the preceding section concerning the Self (*ātman-adhikaraṇa*)—regarding this [Self], namely the individual soul (*jīvātman*), which has been established as being devoid of birth and dissolution (i.e., as possessing the absence of origination and destruction), and in this present section concerning the Knower (*jñā-adhikaraṇa*), where eternal consciousness has been declared (determined to possess innate knowership)—for this individual soul, even the statement of its being a modification (*vikṛti-vacana*), that is, the description of it as an effect, is mediated (indirect) because of its intellect being subject to contraction and expansion (due to the cause of its intellect being capable of contraction and expansion).

It may be that [the transformation] occurs by means of knowledge which is its own attribute (svadharmabhūtajñāna); however, it is not caused by a change in its essential nature (svarūpa), as is the case with ether and other elements. || 54 ||
The state of being a knower and the nature of knowledge are declared by the Vedas; we do not fall into error here in this position.

Why would the Self not shine everywhere? For the atomicity of the embodied soul is established in the Nigamas. It is accepted that the Self, whose own form is solely self-luminous and whose "I-consciousness" is always present though indistinct, shines at all times;
however, during states such as deep sleep, there is merely an obstruction to its distinct manifestation due to the contraction of the intellect.

And the exclusion of absolute non-connection (*atyantāyoga*) takes three forms according to what is appropriate, based on its occurrence in the subject (*dharmin*): when the particle *eva* is connected with the qualificand (*viśeṣya*), there would be the loss of that [other] property—that is, the establishment of the absence of that property—in the case of something other than that, namely in the case of a subject other than the one under discussion. For example, in the expression "This person knows indeed" (*jānāty evāyaṃ puruṣaḥ*), this very particle *eva* implies that he is not a non-knower; [the soul] never...

The meaning is: "He does not lack the nature of knowledge. Insentience (*jaḍatā*)—that is, the state of being non-conscious in the Self—is to be excluded by the statement that He consists of pure consciousness; this is excluded by the specific expression "consisting of consciousness" (*vijñānamaya*), which asserts His singular form as knowledge. This very particle *eva*—even though the particle *eva* is attached to the verb in the phrase "He knows indeed" (*jānātyeva*)—attains the status of being the primary subject (*abhidheya*) in accordance with the scriptural passage, "For there is no loss of the knower's consciousness" (*na hi vijñāturvijñāterviparilopo vidyate*). [This] subject (*viṣaya*)—the one to be expressed—reaches [this status]. || 56 ||

From the scriptural statements regarding its departure, vibration, and comparison to an atom, the [individual soul] is smaller than an atom; yet, through the abundance of its powers, simultaneity occurs when perceiving multiple forms, according to the view that it possesses parts.
Wherever all-pervasiveness is taught, this appears to have as its purport the Supreme [Self], as indicated by the internal evidence of the context.
The doctrine of [the soul's] pervasiveness in terms of speed is intended to express either the greatness of its intellect or its nature as pure clarity. || 57 ||

On account of the scriptural statements regarding departure—namely, the mention in the Śruti of the soul's exit from the body, its movement, and the comparison of its subtlety to a hundredth part of the tip of a hair—the extremely subtle (aṇīyasaḥ) individual soul (jīva), when it has attained power—that is, the capacity for entering another body and so forth—is able to assume multiple forms simultaneously (yaugapadyam), even while taking on various bodies at once.

The unification of pleasure, pain, and so forth, as delimited by the entire body, is not contradicted by the expansion of *dharmabhūtajñāna* (attribute-knowledge) through its abundance in a single body—just as it occurs in the various limbs such as the hand and feet—in that scriptural passage where it is taught: "He, indeed, is this great, unborn Self" (*sa vā eṣa mahān aja ātmā*). In this [passage], all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*), which is synonymous with greatness (*mahattva*) and omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*) [meaning unlimited dimension], is recorded and taught; this is that very word of the Śruti.

By means of the indicators of purport (*tātparyaliṅga*)—such as the context of the subject matter and so forth—which determine the purport of the scripture, it clearly appears that the subject is the Supreme; that is, it becomes manifest as the Supreme Self alone. As for the discourse on the pervasiveness of the individual soul—the conventional usage of pervasiveness regarding the individual self in such statements as "the Self is eternal and pervasive in every body"—this is intended to describe the greatness residing in the Self by way of its being the substratum of the greatness called "pervasiveness" which exists in knowledge, which is an attribute of the Self.

Or it is "engaged" (pravṛttaḥ), meaning it is engaged in demonstrating its own purity and other such qualities; that is, it is engaged in demonstrating its capacity to enter within all insentient things without obstruction—an ability existing within itself—which is another synonym for purity. || 57 ||
A summary of the subject matter:
A compendium of the essence of the topical sections (*adhikaraṇa*).

Let it be that the person possesses the nature of a knower; nevertheless, agency is not established for him, because it is negated by scripture and other authorities, and because he is devoid of modification (*vikṛti*), which would contradict what is observed. Indeed, the denial of agency and the statement regarding his lack of modification have been declared to possess another meaning (*anyaparya*).
An agent exists because the scripture has a purpose; otherwise, there would be no injunction here for one who is not an understander.

The subjectivity of the person—the individual soul's status as the locus of knowledge—may indeed be established in this manner; that is, let it be proven according to the method stated for the locus of knowledge (*jñādhikaraṇa*). Nevertheless, even so, the agency of this individual self is not thereby established.

The acquisition of agency cannot be asserted on the basis of valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), because it is negated by the Śruti and other sources accepted as authoritative—such as the Śruti and Smṛti—which make known the absence of agency in that [Self] through such statements as "This one does not kill" and "The deluded soul thinks, 'I am the agent'" (Gītā 3.27). Furthermore, it is due to the absence of modification—that is, because the individual soul (*jīva*) is changeless (since agency itself falls within the category of modifications)—[that it lacks agency]. Such a doubt is incorrect, because it is contradicted by what is perceived (*dṛṣṭabādha*) through direct perception (*pratyakṣa*).

Because the apprehension of the absence of that [agency] is sublated by the apprehension of the agent; for, since there is the statement denying agency—the scriptural passage negating agency—and likewise the statement of non-modification—the passage establishing changelessness—these have a different purport (*ānyaparya*): namely, the intention that agency depends upon association with *prakṛti*. This is understood from the Gītā statement: "But he who [sees] the Self as the sole agent... Therefore, this one here is the agent; thus, this *jīva* [is the agent] in action.

It is precisely the locus of the attribute of agency, because the scripture has a purpose; for the scriptures, which are devoted to injunctions and prohibitions, must necessarily be effective, and because the soul (jīva) must be described as the one who partakes in the fruit of the scripture. Furthermore, there could be no mandate for that which is not a knower—the primal matter (pradhāna) and so forth—which is not the locus of knowing; for neither the enjoining scripture nor the instruction established by the scripture would attain its own nature or its effectiveness. || 58 ||

Furthermore, if the negation of agency belonging to the "I" (*aham*) spoken of by the proponent refers to an "I-sense" other than [the one under discussion], then this is merely proving what is already established for those who know the Upaniṣads.
Moreover, if the state of being an enjoyer (*bhoktṛtva*) were also absent, the scriptures concerning bondage, liberation, and so forth would be rendered futile.
The agent [is so called] because of taking breath, because of movement, because of the thought "I am superior to nature," and because of yoga. (59)

Furthermore: Moreover, the negation of agency belonging to the "I-sense" (ahamartha)—which is the doctrine that agency is impossible for the individual soul (jīvātman)—is contradicted by the speaker himself through his own statement and inference, both of which involve the agency of the speaker. If it is argued that this negation of agency refers to something other than the "I-sense"—that is, if it is said that this negation of agency has as its object something distinct from the individual soul which constitutes the "I-sense"—then this very statement that there is an absence of agency in anything other than the "I-sense" belongs to the knower of the Upaniṣads.

For those who know the Vedānta, that which has an already established object of proof—that is, one whose probandum is a determined fact—is indeed fruitless, even with respect to the state of being an enjoyer.

If existence [is denied]—that is, when the negation of "enjoyership" (*bhoktṛtva*), which is pervaded by "agency" (*kartṛtva*) that serves as its pervader, results in the negation of everything—then the entire body of beneficial instruction consisting of the scriptures on bondage, liberation, and so forth, which inform us of the nature of transmigratory existence (*saṃsāra*), its cessation, and the means thereto, would follow as being false; it would become purposeless (because all of that depends upon enjoyership). [This applies to] "taking life"—the impelling of the senses for the sake of one's own enjoyment—and "sporting"—[acting] for that very same purpose.

Because of the impelling of the body as declared by the Śruti, because of the yoga consisting in the thought "I am superior to Prakṛti," and because of being the locus for the meditative absorption (*samādhi*)—which is intended as a means to liberation and takes the form "I am other than Prakṛti"—the agent (is) the individual self (*jīvātman*) alone, possessing agency, and not the intellect (*buddhi*) or other such factors. || 59 ||
Activity, knowledge, desire, feasibility, effort, and the application of means— when these are weak,
there occurs in the world a worldly engagement regarding an action that depends on a collection of causal factors, whether it be according to scriptural injunction or otherwise.
That state which is suitable for scripture is one where activity is directed by the meaningful speech of the treatises and is regulated by destiny.
Thus, this person here appears as the knower, the agent, and the enjoyer through all means of valid cognition. || 60 ||

The argument regarding *vyāpāra* (activity) is as follows: it is the reasoning demonstrated for the purpose of establishing that activity—as described in the sūtras concerning material cause (*upādāna*) and so forth—along with the knowledge of the means thereto, the desire produced thereby, the capacity to accomplish the task to be achieved, and the effort that impels it, are all impossible in the case of the individual soul (*jīvātman*). Furthermore, this is a weak argument, being merely a semblance of reasoning (since it is intended to prove both omnipresence and changelessness). This applies to both the injunction (*vidhi*) and its opposite: namely, the injunction "Do this" and [the prohibition] "Do not do this."

And regarding negation, when an action depends upon a causal complex—that is, when its object consists of activity or cessation based on the convergence of causes—activity directed toward such an end is observed to be established in the world and common to all people; it is the engagement of those qualified for specific tasks. Whether secular or Vedic, scripture (*śāstra*)—meaning instruction—becomes meaningful and fruitful through beneficial discourse, that is, by providing knowledge of the means to achieve human goals; such is the state suitable for scripture.

And there is a distinct state, fit for the performance of beneficial acts taught by the scriptures, which is regulated by destiny—that is, dependent upon the adherence to specific rules such as caste (varṇa) and stage of life (āśrama) ordained by fate. For these aforementioned reasons, this person—the conscious being who presides over the body, senses, and so forth—is known in this scripture through all means of valid cognition (pramāṇa), such as perception and others that determine reality; appearing as the knower, the agent, and the enjoyer, he is established as the substratum of knowing, acting, and experiencing. || 60 ||
Furthermore,

because passages such as "Actions are performed by nature" (Gītā 3.27) are intended to demonstrate that the transmigratory agency of the individual soul (jīva) is dependent upon its association with the *guṇas*, it has been stated that "the Self is the agent."
And its essence is this:
from the very beginning, by means of the very power of autonomy granted by the Lord, the person exists while himself generating various cognitions, desires to act, and efforts.
In that regard, Hari bestows the fruit of each respective action upon every person by first observing, then approving, and finally ordaining their restraint or favor. 46.

The *puruṣa*—the conscious transmigrating being—at the very beginning, at the time of creation consisting in the provision of the instruments and the body, by the power of independence (*svātantrya-śakti*)—which is synonymous with autonomy and is inherent within himself as the capacity for accomplishing effects—granted solely by the Lord and through the grace of the Supreme Person, [acts] "himself," that is, by his own free will dependent upon prior latent impressions (*pūrva-vāsanā*), spontaneously, [producing] those respective cognitions...

Hari—the Lord of all, Nārāyaṇa—exists as the presiding deity of the body, producing within himself the knowledge regarding each respective desired object, as well as the corresponding desire and the corresponding effort; yet, having remained indifferent—that is, having resorted to neutrality in the form of silence—toward that initial effort of his which conforms to his own will, he subsequently grants his approval and impels him toward the second and subsequent efforts directed toward those same objects which arise immediately thereafter.

Having nourished him by means of such assistance and so forth, and thereafter—performing upon him both restraint and favor, manifesting anger or favor toward him as is appropriate—he bestows upon every person—that is, upon the entire class of sentient beings—the specific fruits of their respective actions, ranging from the highest to the middling to the lowest, extending from the granting of their own self up to the attainment of a place filled with the great darkness [of ignorance]. He distributes these [fruits] free from any sense of partiality toward those who are liked or disliked. (46)
When a person consents to the non-cessation of evil deeds, Acyuta performs it through his unimpeded sovereignty; thus, there is no fault in Hari according to the Śruti.
Just as in the world, the restraint of waters is considered a virtue and not a defect.
The foundational premise would not be established, were it not for the Upaniṣadic word being our authoritative means of knowledge.

Acyuta—the Lord Nārāyaṇa—by means of His unbridled sovereignty—that is, by His unimpeded independence—effects the non-prevention and the subsequent authorization of a person’s engagement in evil deeds; that is, He does not restrain one who has set out toward sinful acts committed by a conscious agent which are contrary to His own command, and He grants permission for them. Such a state of independence is understood through the Śruti—the Vedic word—as being merely an excellence (*guṇa*) that brings about superiority. That [state] is not a defect in Hari; such is the case.

The independent nature of Hari does not contradict His supreme excellence (as is understood from scripture); for the exercise of restraint over enemies—the act of punishing those who cause harm toward foes—is seen as a virtue even in the world, experienced as a cause for praise and not perceived as a defect or a cause for censure; thus, the Upaniṣadic word—that is, the Vedāntic statement which apprehends such a Lord—is indeed a valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*).

If [the Lord] were not accepted as the means for attaining the knowledge of the true nature of reality, there would be no "unestablished locus" (*āśrayāsiddhi*) [for the argument against Him]; rather, there would simply be the non-apprehension of the very Lord asserted by the nihilists (since, if He were established by valid cognition, there would be a contradiction with the evidence grasping the subject, which is precisely what constitutes the refutation of the Lord). || 47 ||

But for that man who has desisted from the pursuit of evil deeds, disregarding the countless sins accumulated through many previous births, even Lakṣmī’s Consort himself strives for the attainment of his infinite bliss; and this multitude of virtues, preceded by His compassion, unfolds within him. (48)

But as for that very conscious being who has desisted—that is, whose mind has turned away—from the undertaking of evil deeds, from the effort toward sinful action—for that person, that conscious being, previously...

Disregarding—that is, not counting as grounds for punishment—the accumulated sins from many previous births, which are countless and impossible to enumerate; and for the sake of that man, even though he is an offender, who has ceased his efforts toward evil deeds, so that he may attain infinite happiness and reach limitless great bliss, Lakṣmīsahāya—the Lord of Śrī, Nārāyaṇa—strives himself, making an effort of his own accord; therefore (tat).

Of that Blessed Viṣṇu—this multitude of qualities, headed by compassion, consisting of the collection of attributes such as unconditional mercy established in the scriptures—unfolds; being ever-increasing, it shines forth in full splendor. || 48 ||

And having accepted that fruit—having admitted both independence in action and participation in the results of action—one should not harbor such hatred toward the Supreme Person, the Lord of the Self, who is known through hundreds of scriptural texts, who is established by many Vedas, and who is the controller of all selves; for such a state of opposition, which is incompatible with His being the cause, has a miserable end—that is, it leads to disastrous consequences—and therefore [hatred] should not be practiced (and thus the individual soul possesses dependence on another even regarding its own independence). || 61 ||
The all-pervading cause is common to all the sprouts of effects, like water;

however, the diversity [of results] from Brahmā downwards arises from the seeds of the karma of living beings, which yield specific fruits. Although its own uniformity is proclaimed and heard here in the scriptures, there is nevertheless a distinction based on the desire to remove sins and so forth;
thus, the fruit conforms to such karma, and this beginningless stream is fixed.

Just as water is the common cause for all sprouts of every effect—indeed, for all sprouts whatsoever that arise in connection with their respective seeds—in the same way, the All-pervading Lord, the Sovereign of All, the Supreme Self, is the cause, acting as the causal basis for all objects whatsoever that possess birth, by virtue of their commonality in the form of the universal property of being an effect; yet there is diversity among the things created.

As for the diversity [of the world], extending up to Viriñca—that is, starting from Hiraṇyagarbha, the creator of individual creation, it arises through the very specific actions of all embodied beings; these actions, which possess well-ordered and distinct fruits, are like their particular seeds, being distinguished by those respective karmas alone.

(But not by the Supreme Self as a common cause) "His own"—that is, the Lord's own—"equality"—meaning His impartiality toward all equally—is "sung by Himself," clearly stated by Him (the Supreme Self alone): "I am equal toward all beings"; and it is also "heard"—described even by the Śruti: "The Teacher of all people, the Self of all. For that reason, here—in the Blessed One (established by the Śruti as being present)—there is no distinction such as the desire to lead some downward and so forth.

The state of being an object consists of mental constructs such as the vision of the lower worlds or the vision of the higher worlds; the fruit corresponds to such karma. Therefore, this stream—consisting of the succession of cause and effect in the form of fruits corresponding to the respective karma of each individual soul, characterized by "distinct merits and demerits, and distinct pleasures and pains"—is to be understood as beginningless, fixed (niyata), having no known starting point, and possessing a nature and essence that are mutually unmixed and absolutely well-established. || 62 ||

At the proper time, the Blessed One brings about the pacification of suffering by relying on mere skillful means; that very desire of one whose mind is intent on the welfare of others to eliminate suffering is his compassion itself.

By that same [compassion], he bestows upon men the "union" with the body and so forth, instructs them in the Nigama, speaks the essence of the Vedānta, and at the time of the unconditioned, produces for them the yoga of limitless bliss.

The Blessed One, the Lord of all, who is fully endowed with the sixfold sovereign powers, at the proper time—the moment when the fruits of past deeds ripen—causes the cessation of suffering. Taking even a mere semblance of a means—such as the resolve to practice the methods for attaining the Blessed One and the subsequent engagement therein (which, in reality, lacks the capacity to bestow the fruit)—and regarding it as a valid means, He generates peace, which consists in the complete abandonment of all suffering, thereby awakening the consciousness of sentient beings to that state of tranquility.

The Supreme Person, whose mind is intent on the welfare of others and whose heart is devoted solely to the benefit of others—His natural inclination (*apekṣā*) to desire to remove the suffering of others, which takes as its object the uprooting of their pain, is itself *anukampā*; that very *anukampā* is called compassion (*dayā*). By that very compassion, He bestows and favors upon sentient beings (*puṃsām*) the connection with bodies and so forth (such as the desire for liberation and the practice of the means to liberation), as well as the Veda (*nigama*).

He bestows the lamp of the Vedas, which reveals the directions, the principles, and the goals of human endeavor; he expounds the essence of the Vedānta—(which is the means for attaining the realization of the method for reaching the Lord without delay)—and having entered into the hearts of virtuous teachers and others, he makes manifest even the supreme and primary meaning of the Vedānta. At the time of the cessation of limitations such as the body and senses, he brings about union with boundless bliss and grants the attainment of supreme bliss that is one's very nature. || 63 ||
If it is argued that there would be the fault of partiality on the part of the Controller, we say no, because there is no suppression [of others].

For His own disadvantage does not attach to the Lord, nor does the disadvantage of others, since He is opposed to it. Compassion has its scope in certain cases; thus, His status as a Witness and so forth is well-established.
And this is consistent with the understanding that He bestows fruits when His nature is perceived as such. || 64 ||

If it is argued that for the Restrainer—the Lord of All who possesses the sovereignty of universal control—there would be a "portion of restraint" (nigrahāṃśa)—that is, one of the two aspects of restraint and favor, namely restraint—and that this would constitute a defect (doṣa), such that it would obstruct [beings'] recourse to Him; then we reply: such a thought should not be entertained. Why? Because it cannot withstand refutation. How could there be a defect? What kind of defect? Whose defect?

In this manner, since it cannot be established that [the Lord's action] constitutes a fault during the process of purification—because, for (*hi*)—in the case of the Lord, the Controller, the Supreme Self, no undesirable consequence arises; that is, nothing disagreeable to Him occurs as a result of His restraint. Furthermore, any undesirable thing belonging to another that might be incurred through such restraint does not oppose Him; it does not constitute a fault in the Lord. This is because compassion—the Lord’s mercy, which may be either causeless or caused—is present.

Its own nature (*svarūpa*) is sometimes said to be "with scope" (*sāvakāśa*); thus, it was stated in the preceding verse that at the beginning of creation (for the sake of acquiring appropriate instruments and bodies), and subsequently (through the performance of means for the sake of heaven and liberation, for the attainment of their respective fruits), it unfolds only as having an object. Furthermore, its roles as witness and so forth—namely, being a witness, an approver, an instigator, indifferent, and a collaborator—with respect to the good and evil deeds performed by the individual soul (*jīva*) toward the Blessed Lord—were also explained.

The entirety [of His nature], such as being the bestower of fruits and the source of all fruits, is well-established—meaning it is free from defects and unshakable. When this entire nature of the Lord has been understood through the scriptures and the teacher, then taking refuge in that Lord—that is, seeking shelter in Him—with the thought "He is the giver of fruits"—that is, with the conviction "The Lord is capable of bestowing the fruit"—is appropriate; it becomes logically sound. || 64 ||

The inner self (*pratyaṅ-ātman*) is the referent of the "I" (*ahamartha*) for those who possess valid cognition; it possesses agency and so forth because its activity is preceded by its own will. To that extent, this [self] is distinct from insentient matter and equal to the Lord (*īśvara*). However, since the Lord exerts effort solely through His own will, everything else is subordinate to Him.
The activity of the three [factors] proceeds with a specific destination determined by the sequence beginning with the charioteer. || 65 ||

For those who rely on valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa-parādhīna*), the referent of "I" (*ahamartha*)—the conscious self (*pratyag-ātman*) whose nature appears to itself—is that consciousness in which agency and other qualities, such as being an agent, an enjoyer, and a knower, reside. This [self], possessing agency and so forth, acts according to its own will.

Because its nature is active (*pravṛtti-svabhāvatvāt*), it is superior to the non-conscious (*acetana-vilakṣaṇaḥ*) and excels it; in that respect, it is equal to the Lord (*īśāna-tulyaḥ*). To this extent it resembles the Lord (*īśvara-sadṛśaḥ*), for the Lord exerts himself solely by His own will—He is the Supreme because His activity depends on His mere volition (and thus He is superior even to the individual soul). Everything else—all that is distinct from the Lord—is subordinate to Him (*tad-ninam*), being dependent upon the Lord. Such is the activity of the three: the conscious (*cit*), the non-conscious (*acit*), and the Lord (*īśvara*).

There is activity for all three as well; through the sequence beginning with the charioteer, there would be a determined movement according to the manner of the charioteer, the warrior, and the driver—their well-ordered nature remains ever vigilant. 65.

If agency were to exist [in the soul], it would sometimes depend upon an instrument; if it did not depend on the instigation of another, how could there be its restraint and so forth? If you say this is not so, it is because the same logic applies to your own preferred position as well. For those who are compassionate would not cause one who has engaged in what is unwholesome to do it again.
If that [agency] belongs to his very nature, why would the other [lack of agency] not also belong to him? Thus, the destruction of the study [of scripture] is fruitless.

In the case of the *jīva*, who possesses instruments such as the body and senses, at some time—that is, at the moment of initial activity—an agency independent of the instigation of another (i.e., an agency not dependent on the prompting of the Supreme Self, but solely self-dependent) is possible; otherwise, if even at the initial activity it were dependent upon the Supreme Self, then how could there be its restraint or favor? For if [the soul] possessed an activity dependent solely on its own instigation, how could there be restraint or favor for that conscious being by [the Supreme Self] alone? If [it were so]:

If it should be suspected: "How could [the Lord's] impelling toward punishment and so forth be appropriate, given the possibility that he might act like a madman?"—then this suspicion is not tenable, because it applies equally even to our own accepted position; for even in the view we ourselves favor—that subsequent activities depend upon the Lord—[the same objection would hold].

Since this fault is common [to both], those whose hearts are softened by compassion—being intent on the desire to remove the suffering of others—would not cause a person who has spontaneously engaged in what is unwholesome—that is, one striving toward an action with harmful results—to engage in it again, even for a second time; they would certainly not incite him to perform such an unwholesome act. If that [refraining] arises from his own nature, then the Lord’s role as an instigator pertains to the second and subsequent occurrences.

If it is resolved that [the first activity] is not subject to objection because it is produced by its own nature (*svabhāvakṛta*), then why is it not likewise resolved that for the second and subsequent activities, its being prompted by dependence on its own prior latent impressions (*prāgvāsanā*) at the time of the initial engagement, as well as its undergoing approval or punishment during those subsequent engagements, are also produced by its own nature? [This would result in] the collapse of what has been studied—an effort to subvert the omnicausality and other attributes of the Supreme Lord as declared in the Vedas and other scriptures; it is purposeless (*niṣkala*).
Thus, the soul's perpetual dependence on another for its agency is established beyond dispute. || 66 ||

The inequality of the field-knower (*kṣetrajña*), though they are equal, arises from such a difference in unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*); however, no other unseen force is required as a regulator, for that is already established by the distinction of the Controller.
Furthermore, the Lord’s role as an impeller, which is supported by the consensus of the scriptures, is not contradicted by His being a witness.
Even a mere fragment of a work such as the Bhāṣya would, for one with an attentive mind, possess this same significance. || 67 ||

Regarding the knowers of the field—the individual selves (*jīvātman*)—even though they are equal, being non-different in terms of their essential nature (*svarūpa*) and inherent character (*svabhāva*), there exists a diversity of bodies (*viṣamayatanatā*), which is to say, a disparity in activity (*pravṛttivaiṣamya*). This arises from the distinction in such unseen merit/demerit (*adṛṣṭa*), that is, from the disparity in the unseen forces corresponding to those [past actions]. (Thus, in the first instance of activity, the agency of the soul is indeed dependent solely upon the unseen force.)

(An objection is raised: "Agency does not depend upon the Supreme Self. [The response: But as for *adṛṣṭa*—that which is denoted by the term *adṛṣṭa*—it is something else, namely, that whose nature is accepted by the Vaiśeṣikas, Mīmāṃsakas, and others; it is not desired (*iṣṭa*) nor admitted by the Vedāntins. In that regard—at the time of the beginning of creation—it must exist in the form of *adṛṣṭa* through a specific volition (*saṅkalpa-viśeṣa*) denoted by the word "governance" (*niyamana*), belonging to the Governor, the Lord who is the ruler of all.

Not by another; [therefore, it rests solely upon God as the cause through the door of restriction]. Of the Lord, who is the motive for the activity of the Guide—His being the Witness and so forth, meaning His state of being a mere observer at the initial impulse—and His being measured by the *samanigama*—meaning His impelling nature as established by a means of knowledge similar to that which establishes His witnesshood, namely His unconditioned status as the efficient agent (*prayojaka-kartṛtva*)—this does not obstruct or preclude [the other]; even a small portion of the *Bhāṣya* and other texts concerning this section of the *Śrībhāṣya*...

Even a single portion from ancient treatises such as the *Tattvasāra*, when reflected upon by those of attentive mind—meaning those whose minds are focused solely on that [truth]—will possess this very purpose; it will attain its purport (*tātparya*) precisely in this stated meaning, and not in any other. || 67 ||

Because it would contradict all scriptural injunctions and so forth, there is neither the performance of ritual action nor its fruit for one who practices evil. For it has been stated by the author of the Commentary that even the thoughts and such of living beings are dependent on karma; he will explain this very point as being presided over by the aggregate of the sense organs even for deities. (68)

The Lord is the sovereign of all, the maker of fruits—that is, the bestower of the fruits of actions—but He is not the agent who possesses instruments nor the impeller; yet it is improper to object that [the Lord] is also not the instigating agent of the actions of a conscious being endowed with a body, senses, and so forth—such a doubt is incorrect.

Because of the contradiction with all the Śrutis and Smṛtis, such as "The Teacher of men, the Lord of the lords of the senses, impelled by the Lord," it cannot be said that the fruit of past karma—that is, the performance of evil deeds in this life—is not [the result]; for it cannot be said that it does not take the form of a ripened purpose, since even the deliberations and so forth regarding the good and the bad of a bound soul (bhavabhṛta) [are determined by it].

However, [the functioning of the organs] is dependent on karma, being strictly contingent upon specific past actions and not merely upon the present moment; this has been stated by the authors of the *Bhāṣya*—elucidated by the venerable Rāmānuja, the author of the *Śrībhāṣya*.

For all living beings, including deities, for all embodied creatures, and even for Indra and others, the presiding over the collection of instruments—the presiding over the body, senses, and so forth (as well as the presiding over speech and other faculties related to all living beings in the case of deities like Agni)—is thus dependent solely on the impulsion of the Lord (*īśvara-preraṇāyatta*); the author of the *Bhāṣya* will state this, that is, he will make it manifest. || 68 ||
Regarding the *Adhikaraṇasārāvali*,

in the section on dependence (*parāyattādhikaraṇa*), having raised the objection that since the individual soul lacks the power of independent initiative, the scriptures prescribing injunctions and prohibitions would otherwise be rendered meaningless, [the author] considers the soul’s agency to be independent.

Because the dependence on the Supreme Self is heard in passages such as "He has entered within," and because if the individual soul were independent in its initial activity while being dependent [on the Supreme], the scriptures would be rendered purposeless, it has been stated that agency is indeed dependent on another.

Because of difference—since the distinctness of the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*) is established by scripture, the individual soul is not a part [of the Supreme]. Thus, the individual self is not of the nature of a part of the Supreme Self; this is indeed the intention of the Vedic texts. However, regarding the Vedic words engaged in revealing the true natures of the individual and the Supreme, a mutual contradiction is observed—a lack of unanimity and a clear perception of a difference in intended meaning (this being the prima facie view). [The conclusion follows] from the teaching by way of a "foot," according to the scriptural text: "A foot of Him... (*pādo 'sya*).

Because everything is understood to be a limb [of Him], and because of the Smṛti regarding limbs—namely the Gītā Smṛti statement "a portion of Me alone"—the individual soul (jīva) must indeed be a limb of this Supreme, the Paramātman under discussion; that is, the individual self possesses the status of being a limb in the sense of being a constituent part of a single, qualified entity. || 31 ||

—0— What else is to be established by the Upaniṣads? To this question, [the answer is] non-duality (*advaita*). Non-duality is precisely that which is of the nature of identity, opposed to duality as it is known through direct perception; let it be accepted as that which is to be known because it is not within the scope of anything else—that is, because it cannot be reached by means other than the Śruti, let it be admitted as "that which is to be known by the Upaniṣads. For indeed, scripture is purposeful only regarding a subject matter not already attained—that is, regarding a subject matter not known through other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*); thus, the effort [of the scriptures] takes the form of such practical discourse.

A special effort is futile—it does not bear fruit through the proof of non-duality as you intend—because, for that reason, a difference other than the well-known one—that is, a difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*) distinct from what is established in the world, which necessitates the relationship of the governed and the governor—is like your own non-duality; for it is the subject matter of scripture alone, being unknown to the world. || 50 ||

As for the Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad stating "a plurality of men" (*nṛbahutā*) and asking "who among the many?", there a rule applies to a specific subject, just as in the case of the eight-pot-sherd offering (*aṣṭākapāla*) and so forth.
Since this plurality is eternal, how do we know it from other scriptural passages (*nigama*)?
The distinction between self and other, and between bondage and liberation, is clear through the states of inwardness and outwardness. || 51 ||

The Śvetāśvatara Śruti states: "He is the eternal among the eternals, the consciousness among the conscious, the one who ordains the desires of the many. Regarding this scripture, the phrase "the one among the many"—a portion of the mantra stating "the one among the many"—speaks of the plurality of men; that which establishes the diversity of conscious beings therein contains an injunction. In the case of the plurality of conscious beings, there is the function of making known what was previously unknown, just as in the case of the eight-pot-sherd [offering] in such sentences as "That which belongs to Agni is on eight potsherds," where the number eight applies to the potsherds.

Just as there is an injunction regarding a specific sacrifice characterized by the time of the new moon and full moon, which is further qualified by the sacrificial cake (*puroḍāśa*) dedicated to the deity Agni—a prescription whose scope is thus qualified—so too here [in the Vedic passage], the scope is indeed qualified by the fact that it prescribes a fruit connected to a conscious being qualified by eternality and plurality; specifically, it has as its object a single eternal conscious being (referring precisely to the qualified object understood through the entire sentence). In this sentence, that which is intended to be enjoined—the plurality consisting of eternality—is [qualified] by eternality (through grammatical coreferentiality).

How can we know the plurality of selves (*ātmanānātvam*) from anything other than the *Nigama*—that is, setting aside the Veda, by what other means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*) or by what argument do we understand it? Furthermore, even in the state of liberation (*mukti*), when one has transcended the cycle of existence (*saṃsāra*), there remains a distinction between the individual self (*jīvātman*) and the supreme self (*paramātman*)—between "self" and "other"—consisting of internality and externality, respectively, as characterized by the notions of "I" (*ahambuddhi*) and "this" (*idambuddhi*). This separate state, produced by their being objects of cognition, clearly and unmistakably persists. || 51 ||

Regarding all collections of words that participate in grammatical coreferentiality (*sāmānādhikaraṇya*), the Advaitin must state for each individual word what it signifies as distinct [from the others];
or else, if he says "no," then because of its lack of meaning, no word would be anything other than a single [meaningless] entity.
Otherwise, however, the argument would belong to the opponent rather than to oneself. || 52 ||

In all collections of words that share grammatical coordination—that is, those in which the case endings are identical—such as "Truth, Knowledge" (*satyaṃ jñānam*), "That thou art" (*tattvam asi*), "This Self is Brahman" (*ayam ātmā brahma*), and "All this, indeed," and so forth—the object to be conveyed by all these words is...

—Each word must be understood by itself; that is, regarding every single word, the question arises as to whether it is distinct or not—that is, whether it differs or does not differ. What must be said by the Advaitin? Or what response can be given by the proponent of the non-dual identity of the self and Brahman without attributes? (Nothing at all). If the answer "it is not distinct" is given, meaning "it does not differ," then there would be pointlessness—the lack of purpose—in the collection of more than one word, since no difference in the object of understanding has been produced.

Due to the absence of a fruit [of the sentence], one would not perceive a word exceeding the number one, nor would a collection of words exceeding one be recorded in the Śruti; otherwise, if the reply were given that "it exceeds at every step," then the opponent's argument—that the argument you have presented as a refutation of the opponent, namely the failure to establish an indivisible object (*akhaṇḍārtha*) which is the fruit of grammatical coreferentiality (*samānādhikaraṇya*)—turns upon itself, pursuing its own self; for it lacks the power to prove an indivisible object. || 52 ||

Regarding those who have declared, citing as an example "silver superimposed on mother-of-pearl," that "what is censured is unreal because it is perceptible," we reply to them as follows: This [argument] is refuted by the very means of knowledge that apprehends its own subject; furthermore, this "having a limiting condition" (sopādhikatva), which is clearly established in the Sūtra, serves as an unfailing mark for the refutation of your [position]. // 53 //

Some—namely, the adherents of Advaita—here, regarding their own stated position on the falsity of the universe, citing the example of silver superimposed upon mother-of-pearl—that is, silver falsely attributed to the substrate known as mother-of-pearl—and using it as an illustration for the falsity to be proven, have asserted—that is, they have established—that the "disputed" world, which is the object of conflicting views due to its being characterized by both reality and falsity, is "unreal"—that is, false—because it is "visible," meaning it is within the range of perception. Regarding that which they have thus asserted: [the following applies].

We shall now state the collection of defects regarding that subject; we shall demonstrate them as follows: this inference of falsity based on the reason of "being an object of perception" (*dṛśyatva*) is sublated by the very means of knowledge that apprehends the locus (*dharmin*), namely, the perception that apprehends the world which serves as the locus for the property of falsity. It is thus contradicted by perception, just as [the argument] "fire is not hot" [is sublated].

Just as the inference "because it is perceptible, like water" is sublated by the tactile perception grasping its heat, so too is there the fallacy of being "vitiated by a limiting condition" (sopādhikatva)—that is, the inference being overwhelmed by a condition that renders it sublated. This is established by the Sūtra, "And because of dissimilarity" (*vaidharmyācca*). It is clearly evident, unbreakable, and unavoidable. Furthermore, even "visibility" (*dṛśyatva*), which is adduced as a logical mark (*liṅga*) or reason, proves to be inconclusive (*vyabhicārin*), as stated in the scriptural text: "But it is seen by you through [this] ignorance."

Since you do not admit the falsity of Brahman—which possesses visibility as established by scripture—the flaw of deviation (vyabhicāra) that would otherwise result remains; this serves for your ruin—that is, for the subversion of your intended position and your defeat. || 53 ||

If you indeed seek to prove that the world is false, established through delusion, then the reason is one for which the probandum is already established; or if the phenomenal world is real, then non-duality is lost. If the probandum is the very nature of Brahman, then it too would simply be a case of proving what is already established.
Thus, your path toward the negation of the phenomenal world is discarded from afar.

If the falsity (*mithyātva*) of the world—the phenomenal universe (*prapañca*), which is established through delusion—is indeed proven as something false, and if it is rendered the predicate (*vidheya*) of an inference based on the reason (*hetu*) of "being visible" (*dṛśyatva*), then the reason—that is, the object consisting of "visibility," which is intended as the means of proof (*sādhana*)—would be a case of proving what is already established (*siddhasādhya*), because the subject (*pakṣa*) would lack the necessary qualification (*vaikalyavat*; since it is established by delusion, there is no room for doubt). Furthermore, the world—the object that serves as the locus (*dharmin*) for the property of falsity to be proven (the world itself)—would be real.

It would be true—indeed it would be the case—if "falsity" (*mithyātva*) were to be made the object of inference as something ultimately real (*satya-pāramārthika*). In that event, there would be a loss of non-duality (*advaita-hāni*), resulting in the collapse of the doctrine of the falsity of everything other than Brahman (since one would have admitted falsity as an ultimate reality). If the "probandum"—the falsity that constitutes the object of inference—is of the very nature of Brahman, then it would necessarily be admitted as being non-distinct from the nature of Brahman; in that case, there would be the fallacy of proving what is already established (*siddha-sādhyatva*).

Since Brahman, whose nature is already determined by scripture (*śruti*) and other means of valid knowledge, is accepted as being inferable, the fallacy known as *siddhasādhana* (proving what is already established) befalls inference. And thus, given the aforementioned deficiencies in the inference of falsity (*mithyātva*), the monist’s path for eliminating the phenomenal world (*prapañca*)—that is, their method of refuting everything other than Brahman—would be cast far away; it would be entirely unestablished in its own nature. || 54 ||
In the view of the Yogācāras, all entities other than pure consciousness (*cinmātra*) are proclaimed to be false;
when it is sought to make this [view] conform to the Upaniṣads,
it is then drawn in by the Māyāvādins, who [employ] the logic of the scriptures and other means of valid cognition (*pramāṇa*) that have not been perceived [by others].
For indeed, by means of their methods and logical arguments, they cast aside those very means of valid cognition! || 55 ||

In the Yogācāra system—that Buddhist tenet known as Yogācāra—it is proclaimed with a great multitude of words that everything other than pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), including the entire range of objects consisting of the knower and the known, is ultimately false and unreal. This is done in order to establish the unreality of whatever exists apart from pure consciousness, thereby bringing it into the fold of the Upaniṣads and elevating it to the status of the ultimate truth of the Vedānta. This [reality] which is not perceived...

By those proponents of Māyā—the upholders of the Advaita system—who have gained no confidence in the inherent capacity of the means of knowledge, such as scripture, logic, and perception, to determine the true nature of reality, the Vedas and other authorities are forcibly dragged away and attempted to be led toward a different purpose; that is the Yogācāra view. All means of knowledge—namely perception, inference, and scripture—when joined with their respective supporting arguments (nyāya), cast them aside and expel them far from the path of valid cognition. || 55 ||

If it is argued that there is a disparity between the cognitions regarding multiplicity and momentariness on the one hand, and unity and permanence on the other— both within one's own system and in the system of another— it is not so, because this [disparity] does not exist in the Māyāvāda system compared to the Buddhist system in terms of ultimate reality.
In both of those two views, there is no dharma whatsoever that arises from the intrinsic nature of cognition.

If it is argued that there is a difference between the Māyāvāda view and the Buddhist view because, in one system—the Yogācāra view—consciousness (*dhiyaḥ*) is accepted as having multiplicity and momentariness (due to the acceptance of a momentary stream of consciousness), and in the other—the Māyāvāda view—unity and permanence are accepted (due to the acknowledgment of an indivisible, singular nature and indestructibility)—then [the response is: with respect to the Buddhist view...

One might raise the objection that there indeed exists a distinction from the Advaita position; however, this is not so. This statement regarding the disparity is not correct because—in both of those systems, namely the two established doctrines of certain Vedāntins who maintain the reality of pure consciousness (*saṃvinmātra*)—there is no real attribute whatsoever, no ultimate entity denoted by the term "attribute" (*dharma*), which is dependent on consciousness, apart from the nature of consciousness itself—that is, excluding the single substratum (*dharmī*) consisting of cognition (*vijñāna*).
It is not accepted at all, because of the impossibility of dissimilarity (for if it were so, properties such as permanence and unity would not be distinct from the substratum). || 56 ||
There are indeed four possible positions: the beginninglessness of its own nature, the difficulty of its conjunction with itself and others, the beginninglessness of its stream,
or the avoidance of infinite regress by declaring that ignorance is non-existent.
These are clearly considered equal on the path that has the unreal as its support. (57)

O you, O Khaṇḍanakāra!—O base one, author of the treatise named *Khaṇḍana*! Refute!—thoroughly criticize the doctrine of those who maintain that everything is ultimately real; your position is being rejected—your own position, which is intent on subverting ultimate reality, is being cast aside.

(How so? By the arguments stated by you—that is, by the very arguments put forward by you for the purpose of refuting the Mādhyamikas, serving as the means of proof—if you ask, "What follows from that?"—or if you ask, "What is your gain in refuting the *Khaṇḍana* treatise?"—our position remains; our doctrine of the world's purposelessness (*jagat-pārārthya*) stands unrefuted. Just as... [the Mādhyamikas... remain.

Therefore—because of the refutation of the negation of consciousness as described by the Mādhyamika Buddhists—your own position remains; indeed, your doctrine of the ultimate reality of consciousness, which is the substratum for the world-appearance, stands unassailed. Understand it to be just like this: just as in the world, when a crop or similar thing is subjected to the destruction of its obstructors—that is, when its destroyers are countered—the persistence of its own nature, the continued existence of the crop in its own form, is established; so it is here. || 58 ||

If someone here were to say, "It follows that cognition must be an object of knowledge, just like a jar; therefore, its own establishment [as an object] is due to its being a cognition," that is incorrect.
For "establishment for itself" means only in relation to its own substratum (the self), not even in relation to another person.
This [cognition] is indeed to be known by another; even so, its status as cognition is not undermined. || 59 ||

If consciousness (*saṃvit*, i.e., knowledge) were to have the nature of being manifestable by another cognition—just like a jar—it would follow that it possesses the quality of being an object of cognition (*adhī-tva*), which is to say, it would result in its being insentient (*jaḍatva*). By this line of reasoning, and likewise because that consciousness is itself consciousness, its own establishment (*svasiddhi*) is self-luminous (*svaprakāśā*), independent of anything else; and by this line of reasoning as well, here—in Brahman (taking pure consciousness as the subject)—some adherent of the Advaita school [establishes this].

Someone says: [The claim that] Brahman, whose nature is consciousness (*saṃvidrūpa*), is both unknowable and self-luminous is incorrect; for this [claim] is produced by a failure to distinguish between the nature of the object and [the nature of cognition]. Indeed, because the self-establishment—that is, the self-luminosity—of cognition (*dhiyaḥ*) is only with respect to the person who is its own substratum—the conscious being who serves as the locus of cognition—and not even with respect to another person; it does not [establish itself] even with respect to another conscious being who is not its own substratum.

Therefore, this very consciousness (*saṃvit*) under discussion—this experience (*anubhūti*)—is cognizable by another, meaning it is to be known by a subsequent cognition (*jñānāntara-vedyā*), even though it is itself an object of experience (*anubhāvya*). Nevertheless, even while being an object of experience, its nature as cognition (*matitva*)—that is, its nature as consciousness (*saṃvit-tva*) or its nature as awareness (*dhī-tva*)—is not destroyed; it does not cease to exist, because there is no mutual contradiction between being an experience and being an object of experience. || 59 ||

For indeed, if the nature of entities as revealed by the group of means of knowledge beginning with perception were to depart from them, what would remain? If their nature were dependent upon being perceived, then, by virtue of that perceptibility, it would follow—just like a jar—that they would lack the status of being "non-pots" when they are objects of cognition for another. (60)

For it has been stated exactly thus: [it] does not contradict [this]. Because those entities (*bhāva*) are objects of cognition (*vedya*), on account of their being merely objects of cognition (*vedyatvamātreṇa*), does the nature (*svabhāva*) of those various things—which is manifested through perception and established by the collection of means of knowledge such as perception—depart? Does the specific characteristic (*asādhāraṇadharma*) recede far from that entity? (Certainly not). On account of their being objects of cognition—that is, merely by virtue of being knowable—their own nature remains close at hand.

This is a contradiction with its own unique property (*svāsādhāraṇadharma-viparyāsa*). If it were the case that "it exists"—that is, if this existence were intrinsic—then, when the cloth's status as an object of knowledge (*jñeyatva*) is attained—that is, when the entity in the form of the cloth becomes accessible to cognition—it would follow, just like a jar, that it is "non-cloth" (*apaṭatva*), meaning either something other than a cloth or the absence of cloth-nature. (For one property cannot coexist with the negation of another property residing in the same substrate;
otherwise, there would be the undesirable consequence of destroying the relationship between the pervaded and the pervader, etc. || 60 ||

Light exists in objects such as jars, which possess insentience, and its object is that [insentient thing]; its concealment is its non-cessation in the non-insentient Brahman. Furthermore, [Brahman's] essential nature is pure consciousness (*cinmātra*), and its manifestation is also its own cessation;
it would be either insentient or Brahman devoid of concealment, otherwise. (61)

In an insentient object—such as a jar or the like, which possesses inertia—the "manifestation" (*prakāśa*) is the state designated by the term "manifestation"; "having that as its object" means it is simply the valid cognition (*pramiti*) directed toward that [jar, etc.]. Furthermore, "concealment" (*tirodhi*)—the state designated by the term "concealment" regarding [the jar, etc.]—is the cessation, that is, the absence, of this [valid cognition] directed toward it. On the other hand, in the non-insentient Brahman—indeed, in Brahman designated by the term "non-insentient"—there is "radiance" (*sphuraṇa*), which is of the nature of manifestation.

Abiding is pure consciousness—Brahman itself, whose nature is non-dual consciousness, and not that which has the form of an object of cognition (because it is not an object of knowledge). Furthermore, concealment—the state of Brahman’s veiling—is simply the destruction of that manifestation which is non-different from Brahman (resulting in the destruction of Brahman itself). Otherwise, if one were to admit both the manifestation of its own nature and its concealment—as in the case of a jar or other objects—then even the Supreme Brahman would become insentient.

It would either be insentient like a jar and so forth, or it would be devoid of concealment—that is, entirely untouched by obscuration; for both the positions of its being insentient or its destruction of its own nature are undesirable. || 61 ||

Even the manifestation of the substance present before one is susceptible to the error of silver; the manifestation of "shell-ness" alone is what is capable of dispelling the error. Likewise, if Brahman were not [manifested] as it was before, there would certainly be no cessation of the superimposition of the world.
Where could superimposition be established if there were something resembling the nature of mother-of-pearl? (62)

The prior manifestation—the appearance of the substratum (dharmin) such as mother-of-pearl in close proximity to the eye—is indeed capable of producing an error characterized by the mode (prakāra) of "silverness" or the mode of "non-difference from silver," even though it is itself incapable of sustaining the error of silver; it does not prevent it.

The manifestation of "shell-ness"—the cognition of shell-ness in the object present before one—cannot tolerate the delusion of silver. Why? Because that manifestation of shell-ness is capable of counteracting the delusion—that is, it is competent to prevent the arising of the delusion of silver (due to the mutual opposition between these two specific attributes).

And because there is no contradiction between the two attributes consisting of the universal and the particular: if Brahman were—as before—that single-flavored self-luminous manifestation, then this [manifestation] would be equivalent to the manifestation of a universal attribute that lacks specific form; in that case, since it would tolerate error, there could certainly be no cessation of the superimposition of the world—meaning that the repose of the bondage of saṃsāra, which consists of the superimposition of the phenomenal world, would not occur—and thus liberation itself would be impossible. If, however, it were like the "shell-ness" [of mother-of-pearl] in relation to the object present before one...

If [Brahman] were like the manifestation of a specific property such as the nature of mother-of-pearl (*śuktitva*), then since Brahman is non-different from that manifestation and is of the nature of self-luminous consciousness, where would superimposition—the superimposition of the world consisting of transmigratory existence—be established? That is, upon what substrate (*adhiṣṭhāna*) could it arise? (Just as an error such as "this is mother-of-pearl, this is silver" is impossible when the specific nature is manifested, so too an error such as "Brahman is the world" cannot arise when the specific nature is manifested. || 62 ||
These various refutations have been voiced here against the doctrine of Māyā;
but if Brahman is self-luminous and devoid of all distinctions, how can this be? For in that view, as it appears to us, the Puruṣa is indeed possessed of distinctions.
Thus, such things as the superimposition of that form and the cessation thereof are logically consistent. || 63 ||

This has been declared—this manifold refutation, consisting of various types of demonstrations of fault, described in these few verses, has proceeded here in this very system, directed toward the doctrine of Māyā, namely the non-dualist school (*advaitasamaya*). [Furthermore, there exists another collection of refutations: if the Self-luminous Brahman—the Supreme Brahman whose essence is self-manifesting—were devoid of distinctions, that is, if it were of the nature of pure, attributeless consciousness (*nirviśeṣacinmātra*), then...!

In our view, however, within Brahman itself—which manifests in the form of the "I" (ahantva)—there is a "qualified person" (*saviśeṣaḥ puruṣaḥ*); that is, one who is capable of being designated by the term "person" (*puruṣa*) through its engagement with specific attributes (*viśeṣadharma*).

How can all this collection of worldly transactions (*vyavahāra*)—which establishes bondage and liberation, such as "the superimposition of a form not belonging to that [object]" (i.e., the superimposition of specific attributes like *puruṣatva* upon Brahman, which is devoid of such qualities), and "the cessation of that" (i.e., the cessation of such superimposition, which is *mokṣa*)—be possible or consistent within that system, namely the position of Māyāvāda? (Because all worldly transaction consists of mutual contradiction. || 63 ||
When the Self shines forth as "I" within its own substratum,

there occurs the superimposition of various forms, such as "I am an animal," "I am a human," and so on. However, when one is established far beyond the confusion of the body, which is the doctrine of the atomic soul (aṇuvāda), [the true nature is revealed].
Is concealment not indeed the contraction of the cognition directed toward that [object], or rather, [is it] when [the object] is covered? 64.2.1–2.

The phrase "I am" (*ahamiti*) means that in the form of egoity (*ahaṃtva*), it shines forth by itself—that is, manifesting spontaneously without dependence on any other illuminator—in the Person (*pums*), the conscious substratum (*adhiṣṭhāna*).
