Upon this conscious support, there occurs the superimposition (*adhyāropa*) of the modes of the body, such as "I am an animal," "I am a human," or "I am an animal, I am a human. This is an error consisting in attributing to the referent of "I" qualities such as animality or humanity belonging to the body, which do not actually exist in reality within that referent of "I. [This occurs] regarding that which is enjoined—that which is made known solely through scripture—and the body...

And "far away" means: in every respect, there is a concealment—that is, a disappearance (the non-manifestation of the shining *aham-artha* in its restricted mode)—of the attributes residing in the Self, such as atomicity, eternality, and partlessness; this occurs because the intellect (*buddhi*), which has as its object the Self qualified by those respective attributes and constitutes an attribute of the Self, undergoes contraction. Indeed, that which is denoted by the term "contraction" must necessarily be a particular state. || 64 ||

Surely agency and knowership are attributes of the Person (puruṣa) and not qualities of the body; such is the actual state of things. Yet, even so, that is not their true nature, for they are understood through beginningless superimposition (adhyāsa). Now, by means of the method of scripture and one's own yoga, the Person shines forth as distinct from the body and its like.

As for "I-ness" (ahaṃtva) and "knowership" (jñātṛtva)—namely, subjectivity and the state of being the substratum of knowledge—surely these two are attributes of consciousness (*cetana*) alone according to the actual state of things; they are not qualities of the body, nor indeed are they attributes of the physical form. Nevertheless, both of these—I-ness and knowership—are likewise devoid of being bodily qualities, or rather, have the Self alone as their locus. This fact is certainly not understood due to the cause of the delusion that the body is the Self, which has arisen from beginningless worldly existence (*saṃsāra*).

It was not known at all; now, however, through the ripening of past merits, having obtained this distinguished birth, the person—the conscious self—shines forth, becomes manifest, as distinct from the body and so on, by means of the scriptures, logic, and one’s own yoga—that is, by the scriptures which grasp the discerned reality, by correct reasonings consistent with them, and by the yoga of knowledge which is the means for perceiving the Self, [thereby] being distinct from the body, senses, mind, vital breath, and intellect. 65.

Since the doctrine of liberation-in-life does not truly live— being cut down by the weapon of scripture and because its attainment is opposed to worldly consensus— it was therefore rejected at the very outset by Āpastamba, who followed the Upaniṣadic path.
Indeed, the preceptor, the sage known as Dvaipāyana, refuted that [view]. || 66 ||

The doctrine of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*)—the view of the Advaitins that "liberation is attained even during the state of being alive"—is not [correct], because [the one who has attained knowledge] does not attain his true nature while living. For what reason? By means of the "weapon" which is the scripture—that is, by the means consisting of the scripture which teaches that the delay [until final liberation] lasts only until the fall of the body, and which is thus like a weapon—he is "cut," meaning his true nature is shattered. Furthermore, because there is an accomplishment contrary to worldly experience and a certainty obstructed by perception (since he too possesses the three-fold affliction in this world), therefore, that very [state]...

Having demonstrated this by way of its cause, [it is shown] even at the outset—that is, prior to the commencement of philosophical systems in the manner in which they are observed to exist now—this doctrine of liberation while living (*jīvanmukti*) has been rejected by Āpastamba: "If it is the attainment of security upon awakening... (*Buddhe cet kṣemaprāpaṇam*).

The sage named Āpastamba, who composed the aphorism "one would not experience suffering even here [in this very life]," rejected [this view]. Furthermore, the sage known as Dvaipāyana—the seer named Kṛṣṇadvaipāyana, the founder of the Vedists who follow the path of the Upaniṣads—indeed refuted that doctrine of liberation while living (jīvanmukti); he clearly made it known as being contrary to his own view in the words: "Because until that [final dissolution], there is the designation of transmigratory existence" (Brahma Sūtra 4.2.8). || 66 ||
O you who desire the Vedāntas, whose minds are fixed on the doctrine of Śaṅkara,
yet who declare that the authority of the Vedic words is but a manifestation of delusion— alas, how it is just like those who proclaim the compositions woven by the Buddha! And yet, you are the same.
The Vedāntins have counted [the opponents] as being seized by the crocodile of ignorance. || 68 ||

Where are the Vedāntas? Where are the words of the end of the three [Vedas]? Those who claim authority for the words of the Veda—the utterances of Śruti—which are merely the play of delusion (*bhrama*), that is, the manifestation of ignorance (*avidyā*), while professing them to be valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*); those whose minds are fixed on the system of Śaṅkara, placing their trust in the Māyāvāda of Śaṅkara; where are these people?—the Advaitins? (In their view, the authority of the Vedāntas is indeed precarious. They are like the strings of bells tied together by a Buddhist.

Whatever authority belongs to the words compiled by the Buddhas, that very same authority belongs to the words of the Vedas as well—alas, this is indeed a source of despair! And yet, even while this is the case, those Vedāntins—that is, the proponents of non-duality (Advaita)—are reckoned and flourish among certain people whose minds are obscured by the crocodile of the Kali age, which, in the form of the Kali era, conceals the truth. || 67 ||

—0— Regarding the mutual difference and non-difference between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme (*para*), the contradictions perceived at first glance in the Vedic words that teach these [respective] views—even those found in the Śāstra—are removed by means of the *ghaṭaka* (reconciling) scriptures. By taking up scriptural statements such as the Antaryāmi-brāhmaṇa and the Sauca-lāṅgala, [the contradiction] was set aside (by the author of the Sūtras through the demonstration of principles such as "Because of the abiding [of the Self in all], so says Kāśakṛtsna"). Thus, the resolution to the aforementioned objection has been established, along with the nature of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) and the final conclusion (*siddhānta*).

"An additional reason"—a reason superior to or exceeding what was previously stated (a specific argument)—is not present here; that is, it has not been demonstrated in this section of the treatise. (If this is so, one might question: "Why then is this section commenced? True—it is indeed appropriate to raise this objection; nevertheless, the portion of the chapter...

However, for the sake of refuting the views of those who wander in error—due to their misinterpretation of the word "quarter" (*pāda*) in the Śruti concerning the individual soul (*jīva*), as well as the word "part" (*aṃśa*) in the Gītā—the investigation into the nature of the part (*aṃśa-cintā*), which constitutes the section on parts (*aṃśādhikaraṇa*), has been undertaken solely to reveal the defects in those other systems. || 69 ||

The status of being a "portion" (aṃśatva) in the case of Rāma, Kṛṣṇa, and others arises from their being incarnations as partial embodiments (vigrahāṃśāvatāra); however, the statement that the individual soul (jīva) is a portion of Brahman cannot be logically maintained for a speaker who asserts that Brahman is partless.
Therefore, it is untenable to claim that Brahman is the collective totality of consciousness (citsamaṣṭi) and that there is a state of being a portion with respect to each individual soul.
For the creator of the universe, who meditated on becoming many with the thought "May I become many," the state of oneness is established.

"Being a part" (*aṃśatvam*) means being a portion (*ekadeśatva*). Regarding "in the forms of Rāma and others" (*rāmatiṣu*): because there is an incarnation as a portion of the divine form (*vigrahāṃśāvatārāt*), since they are of the nature of incarnations that are portions of the single divine form of the Supreme Vāsudeva abiding in the highest state (*paramapada*), let it indeed be so—that is, let it be logical—for the Vedāntins who maintain that Brahman is partless (*niravayava*) to speak of the individual soul (*jīva*) as a part of Brahman, [given that] the inner self (*pratyagātman*) is an eternal entity distinct [from Brahman].

The description of [the individual soul] as being a single part (*ekadeśa*) of Brahman would not be possible; indeed, it would not be tenable in any way. Therefore, since the statement regarding its being a "part" (*aṃśa*) must be reconciled, it is logical that the reality denoted by the term *brahman*—which serves as the substratum for the state of being a whole (*aṃśin*) relative to the individual souls (*jīva*)—is precisely the aggregate of consciousness (*citsamaṣṭi*), consisting of the entire collection of sentient beings. Furthermore, even within each individual soul, "being a part" here means having the status of a single portion relative to the collective Brahman (just as a soldier is a part of an army).

[The objection that] "it is like [the parts of] a tree or the like being portions of a forest in one part of the forest" is incorrect—such a formulation of the prima facie view (*pūrvapakṣa*) is not sound. This is because for the Creator of the universe, Brahman, the cause of the world—who resolves, "May I become many," so that He Himself may indeed become manifold—the oneness (*ekatva*) is established; for from scripture we understand that He is the substratum of the number one (and because attributes such as being a collective whole would contradict scripture and other authorities). || 70 ||

It is incorrect to claim that Brahman is a single void that becomes manifold through various limiting adjuncts (upādhi) such as jars and the like, and that upon the removal of these adjuncts, this embodied being attains the state of Brahman;
for this would entail the absurdity of one’s own suffering originating [from another], and because we do not perceive the recognition of specific qualities or other such evidence [to support it].

Just as the single sky—though in reality devoid of multiplicity—becomes distinct through various limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as jars and huts, appearing in the forms of "jar-space," "hut-space," and so forth, thereby becoming the locus for various conventional designations; even so, by the same principle demonstrated regarding space, Brahman—the Supreme Brahman—though in reality partless (*niraṃśa*), appears to possess a multiplicity of parts created by limiting adjuncts. In that [Brahman] which possesses a multiplicity of parts produced by adjuncts...

Regarding Brahman, upon the removal of limiting adjuncts—that is, when the limiting adjuncts such as the body that give rise to the conventional usage of "diverse individual souls" have ceased—this bearer of existence, this transmigrating soul who is a portion of Brahman, would attain the state of Brahman; it would reach the nature of Brahman free from all adjuncts. Thus, the objection raised by the proponents of the identity of Brahman and the individual soul (brahmajīvavādins) is untenable, because... [svāna...]

Because of its flawed nature—it fails to resolve the question, "How could Brahman, being such [as it is], initiate the act of creation?"—and because the experience of pleasure, pain, and so forth, restricted to specific bodies, would not be established for Brahman as conditioned by those respective bodies (as is the case with Saubhari and others), this doctrine is untenable. Chinnā...

This [doctrine] is also untenable because it leads to various contradictions dependent upon such investigations as: "Is the entity in the form of the individual soul (*jīva*) a fragmented part of the complete Brahman, or is it an unfragmented part? Furthermore, regarding liberation—at the time of the soul's release—the term "equality" (*sāmya*) implies that the soul attains equality with Brahman; yet, since the scripture states, "He attains supreme equality," this refers specifically to an equality constituted by an inherent distinction [between the two]. Therefore, this doctrine of the conditioned Brahman being the individual soul (*upahita-brahma-jīvavāda*) is incorrect. (71)

This is incorrect—for one who perceives the present [world], it is an undesirable consequence that the nature of being a transmigrating soul (*saṃsāritva*) would be merely adventitious (*aupādhika*). Regarding this, some say: "The moon of Brahman reflects in the various waves of the ocean of Māyā;
its reflected parts are the individual souls (*jīvas*). This must be examined.

Brahman is not the seer of those [objects], for it is insentient; nor can the individual soul (jīva) be so conceived by itself, because prior to its own manifestation, no conceiving agent superior to the triad [of categories] can be found there. || 72 ||

In the shoreless ocean of illusion (*māyā*), whose banks cannot be reached and which consists of illusion itself, within the waves of falsehood—(which are worthy of being reflected and appear like waves, though they are unreal transformations of the intellect)—the moon of Brahman, that is, Brahman resembling the lunar orb, shines forth as a reflection. Of that reflecting Brahman, the individual souls (*jīva*—the transmigrating selves) possess portions similar to shadows, that is, they consist of parts resembling reflections.

"Some maintain that [the individual souls] are not other than the reality, meaning that Brahman and the individual soul stand in the relation of the original object and its reflection"—thus some Advaitins accept this; however, this view must be examined: it is merely a matter for contemplation, but not something fit for formal acceptance.

For this reason: that which fashions those portions of Brahman which consist of the forms of reflections of the Seer is not Brahman—the original prototype—since it is impossible for Brahman itself to be such [a fashioner] (because conceptualization is incompatible with that [Brahman], which is the undifferentiated, pure Consciousness); nor can even the non-sentient (acid), being of the nature of matter, be capable of being the Seer (because the quality of being a Seer is an exclusive attribute of Consciousness). Likewise—and just as it is with both Brahman and the non-sentient—so too with the individual soul (jīva), who is itself a reflection.

The soul cannot be postulated as its own self, for there would be no postulation at all, since that would entail the loss of its own nature; furthermore, because the postulator is unestablished prior to the act of postulation, the postulation itself cannot be accomplished. As for a postulator distinct from this triad—that is, a supreme postulator of the soul beyond these three—he must simply be sought within that system. Therefore, this view as well is fundamentally untenable. (72)

"Brahman is pure existence (sanmātra) pervading all; moreover, there are three eternally established parts—the individual soul (jīva), the Lord (īśa), and consciousness (cit)—due to a distinction within consciousness. This [view] of some is not to be raised [as an objection]. Because the Lord, whose form exceeds mere existence, is declared to be Brahman due to the persistence of pure being (sattāmātrānuvṛtti), the statement regarding the threefold nature of Brahman must have another intention, since Brahman is determined to be partless. || 73 ||

Brahman is pure existence (*sanmātra*)—the reality of Brahman understood in the Śrutis as having the single form of "Being," which is all-pervasive, appearing as that which persists through all principles (*tattva*). Furthermore, within this very reality of Brahman, by resorting to the distinctions of individual soul (*jīva*), Lord (*īśvara*), and insentient matter (*acit*)—that is, the mutually distinct forms—the three parts or three divisions are eternally established.

Some maintain that [these three] have been established from time immemorial, independent of any conceptualization or causal agency; even so, certain Advaitins hold this view, yet it should not be raised [as a valid position], for this doctrine is not to be respected either. This is because of the persistence of mere existence (*sattāmātra-anuvṛtti*)—since the property whose nature is existence, consisting simply in being the object of the linguistic usage "it exists," is the only one that persists through all three [of these categories], and because it is logical [to accept this]. A body beyond that—that is, a nature superior to both [existence and non-existence]—is not [required].

Since the term *brahman* is taught in the Upanishads as denoting the Supreme Self (*ātma-viśeṣa*) alone—the Teacher and Controller of all—and since it is determined to be partless (*niravayava*) and established as being without components (*niraṃśa*), the statement regarding the threefold nature of Brahman—namely, the sentence "This Brahman is threefold"—must have another intention; it would be intended to refer to a single portion of that qualified reality. || 73 ||

In the view close to the Āgama, the statement that [the Lord] is a "portion" (aṃśa) of Maheśvara— expressed as "by means of the crown and so forth"— is intended to be understood as based on a common nature and a small degree of difference,
since He is eternally non-different; for to those of subtle intellect, such a statement of "portion" would be secondary, as it refers to a single part of a single reality.
Therefore, the individual soul (jīva) is described as a specific mode and a part of the Blessed Lord, who possesses all attributes. || 74 ||

The phrase "beginning with the crown" means the golden crown and so forth; "a portion of Meru" means being a part of the golden Mount Meru—according to this principle—that is, when reflecting in accordance with such a mode of conventional usage, the statement regarding being a "portion" applied to an entity that is eternally distinct—that is, characterized by natural and absolute difference—is understood to be appropriate as being based on similarity and smallness, having taken as its grounds the fact of belonging to the same genus and being smaller in comparison to it.

"In some way they ought not to be led away"—thus, in the view of those close to the *Āgama* (the scriptural tradition), namely in the opinion of those who dwell near the *Śruti*, the statement that "the individual soul (*jīva*) is a part (*aṃśa*)"—a term found in the *Śruti* and other texts—would be non-primary; that is, it would be figurative (*gauṇī*), because, according to the view of those of subtle intellect (*nipuṇadhiyaḥ*), that referent of the word "part" is a single portion of one entity—a portion of a single reality qualified by its attributes.

It is indeed of the nature of a single part; therefore—for the reason stated above—in the distinguished Blessed One, that which is called consciousness (cetanā) is a non-separately established attribute (*viśeṣaṇa*) in the Supreme Brahman. Like a quality in a substance, it is an object that exists as a fixed mode (*prakāra*); thus, it is called a "part" (*aṃśa*), being designated by the term "part. || 74 ||

It has already been stated previously that, according to the opponent's view, undesirable consequences such as constant perception and so forth have been repeatedly pointed out here; why then mention again the confusion of enjoyments and the like?
Do not say so, for while previously [the argument] quelled the outward proliferation [of objects], it now [addresses] the doctrine of Brahman.

And there may be an avoidance of those who are arrogant due to their fallacious views regarding future doctrines. Regarding the "opinion of others" (*paramate*): in the view of those who maintain the all-pervasiveness (*vibhutva*) of the self, [the consequences] beginning with "perpetual perception"—such as the manifestation of "I" at all times and in all places—are "undesirable," meaning they entail an unintended conclusion. This was already stated previously, having been described in the very section on knowledge (*jñādhikaraṇa*). Furthermore, here in this section on parts (*aṃśādhikaraṇa*), such [arguments], which are intent upon refuting the opinion of others, [apply] to the confusion of experience (*bhogasaṅkīrṇatā*) and so forth.

An objection is raised: "Why was this *prasaṅga*—the operation of refutation consisting in the production of a confusion of enjoyments (*bhoga-sāṅkarya*)—previously mentioned and clarified? Is it not redundant? This doubt is not appropriate, because previously, in the *Jñādhikaraṇa*, he [the author] quelled the expansion of the Sāṅkhyas and others who do not conform to the Śruti; whereas now, however, he [addresses those] who are arrogant under the pretext of being proponents of Brahman (*brahmavādin*), merely by way of a pretense toward the Upaniṣads.

"Having relied upon the discourse on Brahman, those of evil views—possessing the pride of thinking 'we are Vedāntins' and harboring intentions contrary to the Śruti—[the author] pacified those who follow the doctrine of non-duality (advaitamatīya). Therefore, there is no tautology. This is the resolution; and such a method of resolution may also apply to future cases—it would be appropriate for subsequent sections as well. || 75 ||
For a living being whirling like a constellation in the wind-wheel of false knowledge and the like, [the author],
in order to remove worldly existence through the realization of the inner reality— a fact uncontradicted by any philosophical system—
will speak of the worship of the Supreme, which contains the knowledge of the pure Self, as well as the distinctions between the limbs and the divisions of the limbs.
Furthermore, he purified the individual soul (jīva), whose form was established through the commencement of Mīmāṃsā.

In the wheel of false knowledge and the rest—which revolves continuously like a wheel—within this mass of causes and effects consisting of the succession of connections with the *prakṛti* (primordial nature) based upon: the cognition of one thing as another (*atasmiṃs-tad-buddhi*), the karma dependent thereon, the latent impressions (*vāsanā*) dependent thereon, and the specific inclinations toward liberation produced thereby; for the living being who is thus whirling—helplessly wandering about—in this cycle, like the constellation of planets, stars, and other luminaries in the circle of the wind (*maruti bhagaṇavat*).

For all living beings, because of the realization of the nature of the inner self—that is, by reason of the knowledge of the true essence of one's own nature—there exists the cessation of existence, which is the abandonment of the wheel of saṃsāra. This state stands uncontradicted by any system (sarvatantrāvigīta), being a point where no disagreement among any philosophical schools can find footing; yet, even while this is established, [this work] contains within it the knowledge of the pure Self, being composed of contemplation on the Self as distinct from the non-sentient. *Pañca*...

Bādarāyaṇa, intending to explain—meaning, to deliberate upon in the third chapter after first establishing the principles of reasoning—the various forms of the worship of the Supreme Self and its constituent parts—that is, the specific sets of ancillaries suitable for that worship—further refined the individual soul (*jīva*), even though its nature had already been determined at the very commencement of the *Karma-mīmāṃsā* as distinct from the body and so forth for the sake of being the enjoyer of the fruits of sacrifices and other rites; he investigated it once again in this *Śārīraka* [Mīmāṃsā] in order to achieve the certainty of its fitness for liberation (*apavarga*). || 76 ||

The dependence of agency upon another—that is, the fact that the agency residing in the individual soul (jīva) is subordinate to the Supreme Self; 7) the soul’s being a part in relation to the Supreme—that is, the soul’s status as a part defined by the Supreme Self—all these points have been stated; all these seven points have been reflected upon and determined through reasoning by this quarter—the second and third foot [of the verse]. || 32–33 ||
The first, second, and third [sections] are connected here;
the remaining four [sections] of the third [chapter] are considered as incidental discussions (*prasaṅga*) in this context. (34)

The first three principles (nyāyas) have a direct connection with this [subject], while the remaining four principles, being auxiliary to the third principle, have been described incidentally and do not possess a direct connection. || 34 ||
6) -0- A Garland of Legal Issues (*Adhikaraṇamālā*)

Even regarding creation and so forth, as well as the sequential stages of the Lord, [the following seven points]—namely, that the birth and dissolution of the individual soul (jīva) are merely due to limiting adjuncts (upādhi) when distinguished by the primordial principles; that its nature is a mass of consciousness and pure subjectivity;
that its agency is dependent on another; that it possesses a portion of the universal form through the logic of the body of attributes (guṇatanu);
and [the rest]—are established by the feet of the sky-like [scripture] which removes mutual contradictions between the various Vedic traditions. || 77 ||

1) Even in the case of space and so forth—meaning even in the case of ether (*ākāśa*) and the like—the "postulation" (*klpti*) of the all-pervasive one refers to the very origination of the Supreme Self; and 2) even in the case of the class of principles (*tattvajāti*) such as air and fire, which are perceived as being produced in succession through a lineage of emanation, the postulation of the all-pervasive one occurs from that which is characterized by primordial existence—namely, from the previously mentioned ether.

1) The origin of the subsequent principles from the Supreme Self, which is bodiless; 2) the birth and dissolution of the individual soul (*jīva*), the inner self (*pratyagātman*)—that is, the conventional designations of production and destruction dependent upon limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) consisting of the arrival and departure of the body; 3) its nature as a mass of consciousness and knower—that is, the individual soul’s status as the substratum of knowledge conjoined with the form of cognition; 4) agency—the independence of the individual soul regarding actions it has undertaken; 5) dependence—the [dependence] of the individual soul.

Agency is dependent upon the Supreme Self (paramātmanighna); 7) from the perspective of the principle that qualities inhere in a substance—just as a quality relates to its substance, or the body relates to the self—the individual soul possesses the status of being a part of the universal form, meaning the soul is a constituent part of the Supreme Self who has the universe as His body, according to the manner stated above; thus, the seven objects of inquiry, which are to be established by the section on ether (viyatpāda) through the resolution of apparent contradictions appearing in the scriptures, exist in a number of seven. || 77 ||
|| Translation: ||
Salutations to Śrīmat Rāmānuja. Salutations to Śrī. Salutations to Śrīdhara.

Because it serves a purpose—namely, because the commencement of the [first] chapter is established as being meaningful through the refutation—that is, the rejection—of those who assert that even a single thing is not an effect of Brahman, or who maintain that nothing whatsoever is produced from the Supreme Self; therefore, regarding the state of being an effect...

Due to the "support" (*samarthanāt*) of the first and the last—the first section (*prāṇotpattyadhikaraṇa*) and the final section (*saṃjñāmūrtiklapti*)—there would be a direct connection; that is, the connection to the chapter (*pāda*) would be immediate and uninterrupted. However, for the intermediate sections—that is, for the other sections situated between these two—the connection would be by way of occasion (*prasaṅgāt*); it would be an incidental connection (*prāsaṅgikī saṅgati*), not a direct one. || 1 || There are eight topics here. In the first, the principle regarding space (*viyat*) has been stated; [the subsequent sections] strengthen the principle regarding fire, water, and food mentioned [in the second], while in the last, the creation of the individual group (*vyaṣṭi*) is described.
Even in the case of reflections on number, measure, and so forth, there would be a fruit through meditations and the like based upon them;
furthermore, this section (pāda) is also intended to clarify that the knower is distinct from the vital breaths and other such entities. || 2 ||

In this context—within the second chapter, the *Prāṇa-pāda*—there are eight topical sections (*adhikaraṇas*). Among these, here—in the first, proximate, and initial topical section—the principle regarding the "ether" (*viyat*) is stated; that is, the principle established by the *Viyan-adhikaraṇa* concerning both types of faculties—the organs of action and the organs of knowledge—which have the *sāttvika-ahaṅkāra* as their material cause.

The fact that space (*ākāśa*) is an effect of Brahman has been extended [by analogy] by the statement, "In the same way, the vital breaths (*prāṇāḥ*). Finally, in the concluding section of this chapter (*saṃjñāmūrtiklṛptyadhikaraṇa*), regarding the creation of individual distinctions—the production of specific individual forms such as gods and humans—it confirms the principle stated in the section on fire (*tejo'dhikaraṇa*) concerning the nature of the elements of fire, water, and earth as being effects of Brahman; it stabilizes this through the extension [of the argument] that the bodies of Brahmā and others are effects of Brahman. This is the number [of sections].

Even when investigations are conducted regarding the enumeration of the senses—such as their being seven, six, or eleven—and regarding their modifications according to modes such as minuteness (*aṇutva*), the fruit—the purpose—is indeed obtained through the worship and other practices directed toward Him who is conditioned by those [senses], that is, by means of the Lord’s being qualified by the specific attributes of the senses and their respective numbers and transformations; for the knower—the individual soul (*jīva*) who is the substratum of attribute-become-knowledge (*dharmabhūtajñāna*)—is distinct from the vital breaths (*prāṇa*) and so forth. Thus, [the soul is] distinct from the vital breaths, the senses, and...
This fourth Prāṇapāda is employed to clarify and also to make explicit that [the Self] is distinct from these things beginning with [the body], which serve as its own instruments. || 2 ||
The Veda, speaking of the existence of the sages at the beginning, declares that they possess vital breath;
therefore, it is Brahman alone who is the object denoted by the plural number, and thus the eternity of the Akṣapādas is established.
This is not so, for because their creation is firm, this plural number is to be understood according to the rule regarding fetters (*pāśa*).
For [the term *prāṇa*] is indeed well-established as referring both to the vital breath and to the Supreme Self, due to the similarity in its etymological derivation and other such factors. || 3 ||

The Śruti—namely this passage from the Śatapatha Brāhmaṇa, "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent... the Ṛṣis are indeed the vital breaths"—declares that the Ṛṣis (the entities denoted by the word 'Ṛṣi') possess the nature of the vital breaths; it speaks precisely of their being of the nature of *prāṇa*. Here, Brahman alone is not the primary meaning. It cannot be said that the Supreme Brahman itself is intended by the words 'Ṛṣi' and 'prāṇa', because of the contradiction with the plural number—that is, due to the lack of connection with plurality.

(Since Brahman is one,) there would be the fallacy of contradicting the plural number; therefore, by this reason stated [by you], the establishment of eternal sense organs follows from the presence of plurality among the senses, and thus the establishment of eternal sense organs occurs (so he objects). Let it not be so—let such an objection not be raised—because their being created by Brahman is beyond doubt (due to the Śruti: "From Him are born the vital breath, the mind, and all the sense organs"), and because these plural terms—"the vital breaths" (*prāṇāḥ*) and "the sages" (*ṛṣayaḥ*)—[refer to them].

The plural number is to be understood according to the very logic of the section on "nooses" (the *pāśādhikaraṇa*); it is not to be explained merely as a figurative usage. For even in the case of the Supreme Self—the Supreme Brahman whose existence prior to creation is beyond dispute—both the state of being the vital breath (*prāṇatva*) and the state of being a seer (*ṛṣitva*) apply, due to the similarity in their etymologies: He is called "Prāṇa" because "He causes all to breathe," and He is a "Seer" (*ṛṣi*) because "to see (*ṛṣa*) means to know," thus possessing the quality of being the instrument of breathing.

Because the meanings of the individual components—namely, "seeing all objects" and "the state of being a seer"—as well as the collective power of those words, are identical [to those in the other case], they are indeed "well-joined" (sughaṭite), meaning perfectly consistent. || 3 ||
—0— Summary of the Topic of the Section:
Thus, the origin of ether and the other elements has been described; immediately following this, the origin of the instruments of the individual soul (jīva) is described in the fourth [section].
Regarding the section on the origin of the vital breath (*prāṇa*):

In the section concerning the origin of the vital breath, a doubt was raised that the sense organs do not originate, because in such passages as "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent" (*asad vā idam agre āsīt*), the sense organs designated by the word "vital breath" (*prāṇa*) are perceived to persist even at the time of dissolution.

In response, it was stated that the sense organs do indeed originate, because their origination is heard in passages such as "From this [Self] they are born," and because in the passage "In the beginning, this was indeed non-existent," the word "vital breath" refers to the Supreme Self.

From the statement beginning with "When" (yadā)—specifically the passage from the Kaṭhavallī, "When the five [senses]... the supreme goal"—and also from the Vedic scripture stating "there are seven prāṇas," namely: "Seven prāṇas come forth..."

Even from the indicative statement of the *Muṇḍaka* Śruti, "Seven, seven," it is understood that there are indeed seven senses which serve as instruments for the individual soul (*jīva*). However, such a doubt—that there are only seven—is not appropriate, because the number seven is mentioned in reference to their primary status as instruments for the soul; furthermore, from the scriptural statement, "These ten vital breaths (*prāṇas*) and the self as the eleventh," the number eleven is made known (and thus the number eleven remains uncontradicted).

Some—certain partial proponents of philosophical systems—maintained that the sense organ (*akṣa*) is "pervading the body," existing by extending across the entire physical frame; and that it performs "different functions in different parts"—meaning that through its various locations such as the ear and so forth, it effects distinct operations like speaking and hearing by means of its own specific portions; thus they asserted that the sense organ is "one," being non-different in its essential nature. Some others, however, who are "averse to the path of scripture"—those such as the Vaiśeṣikas who do not rely on the Veda alone—employ "petty logic," that is, mere trivial reasoning.

Relying on them as the means for attaining certainty, some—the Paurāṇikas—abandoned, that is, rejected, the five organs of action beginning with speech. Others—certain [Sāṅkhyas]—having combined the group of causes belonging to the Knower of the Field (the *kṣetrajña*), namely the collection of organs which serve as the instruments of the individual soul (*jīva*), together with intellect (*buddhi*), ego (*ahaṅkāra*), and mind (*citta*), say—that is, they describe—that there are fourteen organs in total, excluding the mind (*citta*) from that collection of organs.

— "Having excluded the mind (along with the internal organ known as the intellect, ego, and manas), they declared"—that is, they spoke—for this reason, all those who propound objects of knowledge that contradict the Vedas were refuted here in the seventy-second section by demonstrating their non-Vedic nature through the actual realization of the truth. || 5 ||

As for those senses called *prāṇas*, it is correct that they are "all-pervading" (*vibhu*); indeed, it is proper to say they are "all-pervasive," because of the scriptural hearing: "All these are indeed equal, all are infinite"—for it is precisely this "all-pervasiveness" (which is synonymous with infinity) that is declared by scripture. [Objection: This doubt is not tenable, because of the very scripture concerning departure: "When he departs, all the *prāṇas* depart after him. And regarding this departure—

Since it is established that the sense organs move together with the *jīva*, they possess atomicity (*aṇutva*)—which implies being limited—and extreme transparency (*atisvaccha*); therefore, because the teaching of their infinity is for the purpose of meditation—having the result of making known the duty to perform the meditation on the vital breath (*prāṇa*) through its specific form characterized by manifold functions [of the senses]—[the atomicity remains]. || 37 ||

Summary of the Topic (*adhikaraṇārthasaṅgraha*) on the Prāṇas: In the section concerning the Prāṇas, having raised the doubt that the sense organs are all-pervading because of the scriptural hearing of their infinity in passages such as "All are indeed equal, all are infinite," it is stated that they are atomic. This is because of the scriptural hearing of their departure in the passage, "When the prāṇa departs, all the prāṇas depart after it," and because they are not perceived by bystanders at the time of departure; furthermore, the scriptural hearing of their infinity refers to the infinity of their functions for the purpose of meditation.
*Adhikaraṇasārāvali* (The Section on Vāyu):

It has been established by the previously stated reasoning that Prāṇa is produced by another; however, it is not distinct [from Vāyu] because of the doctrine of its production along with it—[the view] that it is merely Vāyu within the body or its activity. Its status as a substance is appropriate due to its enumeration among the category of substances; it would not be a separate principle (*tattvāntara*).
Or rather, just as there is no abandonment of the state of being air when it exists as fire, here too there is never any abandonment of that [nature].

Prāṇa—the supreme vital breath—is established as being produced from the Supreme (Brahman) according to the previously stated principle and the logic of the *Viyan-adhikaraṇa* mentioned earlier; this has been firmly settled in the *Prāṇa-adhikaraṇa*. Is that prāṇa, which is an effect of the Supreme Brahman, merely the air within the body—simply the wind whose nature is to circulate within the physical frame—or is it the activity of that [air] within the body, consisting of the winds in the form of inhalation and exhalation whose nature is to operate continuously within the interior of the body?

The determination of either alternative—namely, that it is an action (*kriyā*) or not—is not correct regarding this *prāṇa*, which is the subject of dispute. This is because, together with the air (*vāyu*) that is the object of the possibility of its non-difference from it, there is a separate mention of its name; and because of the doctrine of its origination—from the very scripture stating its origin, "From this [Self] is born *prāṇa*... ether, air" (*Taittirīya Upaniṣad* 2.1)—it possesses substantiality (*dravyatva*), meaning that setting aside the nature of being an action, it has the essential nature of a substance that is the substratum of action, and thus belongs to the category of substances.

From the perspective of scriptural recitation—since it is traditionally taught in the Śruti as being included within the collection of substances in the passage "Space, air, fire, water, earth"—it is appropriate, that is, necessarily to be accepted, that this aforementioned preeminent *prāṇa* is not a distinct principle. This is because it cannot be the direct substratum of a differentiator of principles (and thus does not deserve to be enumerated as a separate reality), just as [air] would not [be distinct] when it has attained the state of fire (*tejastva*).

Just as there is the abandonment of the state of air—just as the state of being air is relinquished when [air] has set out [to move]—so too here, in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), at any time whatsoever, because that abandonment—the relinquishing of the state of air—is not observed, the *prāṇa* is not even a distinct principle; rather, it is simply air that has attained a particular state. || 7 ||
In the *Nayasaṅgatimālikā*,
within the section concerning Vāyu, a determination of the truth is reached as a consequence of the numerous disputes regarding the essential nature of the primary vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*). (106)
Thus ends the section concerning the activity of air (vāyu-kriyādhikaraṇa). 4.

Let it be so; this [objection] is improper—such a suspicion is incorrect—on account of the analogy of the individual soul and its senses (*jīvākṣanyāyataḥ*). For, due to the contradiction that would arise from the departure of the vital breath (*prāṇa*) and its subsequent coming and going—which are taught in scripture as occurring in association with the individual soul and its senses—the [vital breath] would necessarily be subject to destruction along with them. [This is because it would be a mere instrument...]

Regarding the cause—in the vital breath (*prāṇa*), which serves as the means for sustaining the senses and the body—there is the scriptural statement of universal equality: "He is equal to this entire world. This scriptural declaration of equality with all worlds has the purpose of praise, resulting in the understanding of commendation, rather than the realization of a vast physical dimension. Furthermore, within this body, its specific activities are divided and well-established through its various functions (*vṛtti-bheda*) in a tenfold manner, consisting of the fivefold group beginning with *prāṇa*.

Possessing ten forms through the nature of the five [deities] beginning with Nāga, it is of immense benefit; an inexpressible and great gain of purpose (serving all human goals) shines forth—it unfolds throughout both the world and the Vedas. || 8 ||

In this context—"in this body"—the presiding deities (abhimānidevatās) of fire and the other elements, in their respective forms such as Agni and so forth, would have their presiding over speech and the other organs—that is, their role as the activators of the organs of action and knowledge—along with the individual soul (jīva), be "self-dependent" (svataḥ syāt), meaning it would belong solely to themselves and not be dependent upon the Supreme Self (paramātman). This is not so; such a description of absolute self-dependence is not correct. For these deities, such as Agni and the rest, as well as for the individual soul, this aforementioned presiding is [dependent on the Supreme].

However, because of the contemplation of the Supreme Self, [the attainment] occurs solely through the will of the Supreme Person and not by itself; for it is so stated in the Śruti: "He who dwells in the fire," and "He who controls the fire from within," since the Śruti makes known both His abiding within those [elements] and His status as their controller. || 40 ||
Summary of the Topic (*adhikaraṇārthasaṅgraha*) (Jyoti-adhi):

In the section concerning the presiding over [the elements] such as light (*jyotirādyadhiṣṭhānādhikaraṇa*), one might raise the objection that the individual soul (*jīva*) and the deities such as Agni possess independent control over the domain of the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), because they are perceived to be self-sufficient. Having raised this doubt:

In passages such as "whose body is fire," since it is established that the nature of fire and the other elements is dependent upon the Supreme Self, it is stated that their substratum is dependent upon the Supreme Self.

*Adhikaraṇasārāvali*: (On the Senses) Prāṇa too may be considered a sense (*indriya*) because it is an instrument (*upakaraṇa*), due to the statement of its primacy among them, and because of its assistance in the final departure [of the soul] and so forth; yet this is not so, for it is distinct from the others by its specific designation. Since the status of being a sense is explicitly stated for the mind (*manas*), the maxim of "the cow and the bull" applies there; but it does not apply to prāṇa, as its being a modification of the sāttvika-ahaṅkāra is weak, given the similarity of the term "sāttvika. (10)

The vital breath (*prāṇa*) as well—the chief vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*)—should also be considered a sense organ (*hṛṣīka*), that is, it ought to be an organ (*indriya*) because of its similarity [to the others] in being an instrument for the individual soul (*jīva*). This is because it is an exceedingly effective instrument; because there is a doctrine of its primacy among them; because it is designated as the foremost among the senses due to its superior service to the soul; and because it provides assistance during departure from the body and so forth—that is, by rendering aid during the exit from the body as well as during the processes of going and returning—if this were not the case.

That suspicion is not correct, because of the distinct designations found in the Śruti using separate terms—namely, the specific mentions of "prāṇa," "manas," and "indriyas"—due to the difference between them, that is, the distinctness of prāṇa from the sense organs. As for the mind (manas), however, it is established by the explicit statement in the context of the mind: "The senses have the mind as the sixth"; thus, because the mind is included within the category of the sense organs, the principle of "the cow and the bull" applies—that is, to avoid redundancy, [the term "mind"] refers to a subject distinct from those already mentioned by their respective words.

When a general term and a specific term are used together, there is a well-known principle that their co-occurrence avoids redundancy through the function of restricting the scope of the general term; thus, [the statement] "the mind and all the senses" is consistent and appropriate. Furthermore, [the claim] that the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—the foremost among the vital breaths—is a modification of the *sāttvika* ego, and that it possesses the nature of being a substance derived from the *sāttvika* ego as its material cause (which constitutes the defining characteristic of a sense organ), is neither consistent nor appropriate, because the names are identical for both the sense organs and the principal vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*).

But the grounds [for identity], such as the oneness of the word "prāṇa" and so forth, are weak—(because they are inconclusive in cases of multiple meanings, and because that [oneness] does not establish the intended point)—therefore, that is useless. || 10 ||

—0— *Nayasaṅgatimālikā* (The Garland of the Coherence of Methods): [Section on the Faculties] "An investigation [into the nature of the self] by means of distinguishing the vital breath (*prāṇa*) from the faculties (*indriya*) would be fruitless. To refute this objection, the method concerning the faculties (*indriyanaya*) arises. (109) Thus ends the section on the Faculties (Indriyādhikaraṇa), the seventh.

It is made known in the Smṛtis that [the Lord] enters by means of the individual soul (jīva), and it is also stated in the Śruti: "having entered by means of the self, which is the individual soul" (jīvenā'tmanā'nupraviśya). Therefore, since both Śruti and Smṛti declare that the agency belongs to the individual soul, one might raise the doubt: regarding this creation of the individual (vyaṣṭi-sarga), what is intended is merely the sequence of performing a task by a servant who has been impelled by his master. To this, we reply: that is not so; such a doubt is incorrect, for—since there is one [Lord].

—“There was only one Person; He, the enterer—the agent of entry—made the triad, having made earth, water, and fire tripartite; and He differentiated, having joined names and forms specifically to the things to be created as was appropriate,” so it is studied—so it is heard—so it is recorded in the Śruti. Therefore, the Blessed One—the Primordial Creator, the Supreme Self alone—is the inner self of those various individual souls, and being the controller through His entry into the interior of Brahmā and all those various souls, He brought about such a collection of effects.

He creates—that is, he fashions—the multitude of effects established by the Śruti, Smṛti, and other authorities, as they are carried out by various individual souls; (the creation is not brought about by another as if by a servant). Therefore, everything has the Supreme Self alone as its agent. || 11 ||

This scriptural passage, "He who [entered] with the living self (jīva-ātman)," does not teach the identity of Brahman and the individual soul (jīva), because it has already been stated that there is a distinction between their abodes: "One is the inner self (antarātmā), while the other is the body. Therefore, the Lord (Īśa), being qualified by that [individual soul], is the agent even during the entry [into the body] by means of his own instrument [the soul].
If the soul were the agent [of that action], the scriptural statement "it was spoken" would not be tenable here, because of the difference between the agents.

Regarding the scriptural passage, "By means of this living self (jīva-ātman),"—namely, the scripture that says, "Entering by means of this very living self, let me manifest names and forms"—this [text], though explicitly stated, does not teach the identity of Brahman and the individual soul; it certainly does not declare the non-difference between the supreme Self (para) and the inner Self (pratyagātman). For previously, [it was established that] the one is the Supreme Self (paramātman), while the other—the inner Self (antarātman)—is the one devoid of adjuncts (nirupādhika) who exists as the inner controller of all; and "the rest" refers to everything else, the entire collection of sentient and insentient beings, which constitutes His body (vapuḥ).

Regarding the phrase "having the nature of each respective body": because of the mention of a distinction between the *sthāyin* (the permanent substrate), and because the eternally established, eternal separateness (*pṛthaktva*) is demonstrated with proof in the *Śārīraka*, for that reason—that aforementioned reason—the Lord (*īśa*), the Supreme Self, even though he is the agent (*kartṛ*), becomes the causal agent (*kartṛ-kāraka*) in the act of entering (*anupraveśa*)—that is, in the process of entering by means of His own instrument qualified by the individual soul (*jīva-viśiṣṭa-svātmakaraṇakatvena*). [This constitutes] agency [by way of a difference in form].

Since there is no contradiction in the coexistence of the two [states of] being an agent, [one may interpret] the construction as "the agent even upon entering" (*anupraveśe'pi kartā*). Regarding the soul's agency—that is, the acceptance of the soul's (*jīvātman*) agency in the manifestation of name and form—there is here a scriptural authority (*śruti*) consisting of the suffix *tvā* found in this context; for the suffix *tvā* is not properly connected with the act of entering alone, because the agents are different (since the suffix *tvā* is prescribed only when there is a single common agent), due to the mutual difference between the agent who enters and the agent who manifests name and form. || 12 ||

If it is argued that the threefold nature [of fire, water, and earth] is stated by way of their distinct forms as they abide within the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa*), even though they are described as being consumed as fire, water, and food—then this is clearly established; thus, the two [elements] are each made threefold. Do not say so. Let there be the creation of the cosmic egg; how could it be preceded by a threefold transformation?
For when one consumes food and the like, the threefold transformation is stated [in the case of digestion], while the other [transformation] is observed in what is closely related [to the body]. (13)

Within the cosmic egg (brahmāṇḍa) situated in the midst of the egg, which falls within the scope of the individual creation, there are three elements known as earth; by means of their distinct forms—specific qualities of form known as red, white, and black—there is the triadic nature of fire, water, and so forth, through the process of triplication (trivṛtkaraṇa).

It has been stated: "That which is eaten by fire," and so forth, as described in the Śruti. Even though it is said that fire, water, and food are consumed—as in the scriptural statements, "Fire is eaten," "Water is drunk," and "Food is eaten"—this is clear: the process of tripartition (*trivṛtkaraṇa*) is manifest. Therefore, for the reason stated, the Creator (*vedhāḥ*), namely the Four-faced One (*caturmukha*) himself, is the accomplisher of tripartition (*trivṛtkṛt*). (Thus one might object. This is not correct; such an objection is improper, because this creation of the cosmic egg (*brahmāṇḍa-sṛṣṭi*) [belongs to those within the cosmic egg].

This creation—how could it exist prior to its own creation without the process of triplication (*trivṛtkaraṇa*)? It is impossible even to conceive [of it] without triplication; [this applies] to food and so forth once they have been consumed.

Having introduced food, water, and so forth as consisting of yellow and other colors, the transformation described in the Śruti passage, "It is made threefold," refers only to the state of transformation occurring after eating, drinking, and so on, and not to the process of *trivṛtkaraṇa* (the tripartite mixing). The "other"—namely, the description of distinctions such as redness and so forth in fire and the rest—is something else entirely; it is merely a detailed demonstration of subtle portions by way of analysis (*pradṛṣṭi*) within each individual element when it is closely associated with another element.
Therefore, the tripartition is performed by the Supreme Self alone; it is not performed by the individual soul. || 13 ||

—0— Summary of the Topic of the Section on Name and Form (*Saṃjñāmūrtikḷptyadhikaraṇa*): Having raised the objection that, because the *Śruti* passage "Having entered with this living self (*jīva*)" indicates that the differentiation of names and forms has the individual soul (*jīva*) as its agent, the creation of individual beings (*vyaṣṭisṛṣṭi*) must have Hiraṇyagarbha as its agent; [the author] states:

Because the instruction regarding the differentiation of names and forms occurs precisely for one who performs the tripartition—through the statements "Let me differentiate name and form" and "Let me make each of these threefold"—it is untenable that the tripartition has Hiraṇyagarbha as its agent. Furthermore, since the word "jīva" in the phrase "by this living self" refers to the Supreme Self whose body is the individual soul (jīva), it is stated that the creation of individual beings (vyaṣṭi-sṛṣṭi) has both Hiraṇyagarbha and the Supreme Self as its agents.

In the collective creation (*samaṣṭi-sṛṣṭi*), the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) alone is the cause; however, in the individual creation (*vyaṣṭi*) consisting of the triad of names and forms (*nāmarūpa*), that [causality] is attributed to the individual soul (*jīva*). (110)
Thus ends the section concerning the creation of names and forms (saṃjñāmūrtiklṛptyadhikaraṇa).
This is the conclusion of the work,
a compendium of the principles of the Śārīraka [Mīmāṃsā],
consisting of an enumeration and a measurement of the causes according to their production.
And [the treatise discusses] the essential nature of the vital breath (prāṇa), its magnitude, its presiding deities, and its non-sensory character. || 43 ||

(The lack of sensory organs for this [Self])—[it is] the creator of all these individual beings, beginning with those to be created. Thus, all of this has been correctly considered by means of this quarter-verse. 44.

(Ā): By means of the production of the instruments—along with the determination that the sense organs (*indriya*) are effects of the Supreme Self; (in the second [section]) enumeration—the counting of the sense organs as established by scripture and other authorities; (in the third) measure—the establishment of the atomicity (*aṇutva*) of the sense organs through the refutation of their all-pervasiveness; (in the fourth) the nature of the vital breath (*prāṇa*)—the determination that the vital breath is a specific state of air, through the refutation of the views that it is either general air or its activity; (in the fifth) ...

Regarding size: the subtle dimension (*aṇu-parimāṇatva*) of the chief vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*); [in the sixth chapter] its subordination (*nighnatā*), that is, its dependence on the Supreme Self; being presided over (*adhiṣṭhita*) along with consciousness by the Supreme Self; and the presiding authority (*adhiṣṭhātṛtva*) of deities such as Agni over speech and the other organs; its non-sensory nature (*anindriyatā*)—[in the seventh chapter] the vital air (*prāṇa-vāyu*) not falling within the category of the senses; and [in the eighth chapter] that the Creator—the Supreme Self alone—is the maker of the individual creation, including the names and forms (*nāma-rūpa*) of the world that is the object of individual manifestation.

The final conclusion—all this has been stated; by means of this quarter—the second and fourth foot—it has been thoroughly reflected upon and firmly established through meticulous deliberation. || 43–44 ||

In the first [section], all five types have been considered as they occur; in the second and subsequent sections, they are likewise examined. Therefore, both the first and the last [types] are appropriately included in this chapter. 45.

The reflection on the nature of the vital breath (prāṇa) occurs through the sounding [of it] as the vital breath of the organs; and incidentally, there is also a reflection on its specific distinctions based on that context. || 46 ||
The creation of those beings outside the egg has been contemplated previously; however, the creation of those within the egg is also to be contemplated by means of this mind. (47)

In the first [section], the *Turīyādyadhikaraṇa*, those topics already introduced—which are by nature not to be neglected—are recorded; and the five [sections] beginning with the second—the meaning of the second *adhikaraṇa* and so forth—namely, all fivefold categories such as the number and measure of the sense organs (*indriya*), have been reflected upon and determined through inquiry. Therefore, for the reason stated, in this *pāda* (the second quarter), both the first and the last—the initial *Prāṇotpattyadhikaraṇa* and the final *Saṃjñāmūrtiklṛptyadhikaraṇa*—are directly connected. || 45 ||

By the mention of the "instruments"—the senses which serve as the instruments of the individual soul—through the term "breath" (prāṇa), and by the citation in the Śruti of the chief vital breath (mukhyaprāṇa) also under the form of "breath" as a common attribute, there arises an inquiry into the nature of the breath—an investigation concerning the essential character of the chief vital breath—which is established incidentally; and likewise, an inquiry into its specific qualities, such as its magnitude and so forth, also occurs by way of incidental connection alone.

46. By the first—the second and third, the *viyat-pāda*—there is the creation of those things outside the cosmic egg (*aṇḍa*): the collective creation (*samaṣṭi-sṛṣṭi*) of the principles (*tattva*) such as space (*ākāśa*), which precede the individual creation known as the Brahmāṇḍa; this has been "contemplated," meaning it was specifically reflected upon.

But by this—the second, the fourth, the *prāṇa-pāda*—there is the creation of those within the egg, that is, those contained inside the Brahmāṇḍa: the formation consisting of the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpa-vyākaraṇa*); this would be "contemplated," meaning it becomes the object of investigation. 47.

This commentary composed by Śrī Rāmabhadra concludes the second [section]. In the *Adhikaraṇasārāvali*, the following were explained in the section on the Prāṇa: the birth of the senses; their number; the dimensions of the vital air (prāṇavāyu) here; its essential nature and subtlety; the presiding deities and others; the governance over both [the body and the senses]; the dependence [of the senses] upon it; the non-sensory status of the prāṇa; the various individual names for the diverse sentient and insentient entities; and the fact that [the prāṇa] is enveloped by a protective armor arising from its own name, all proceeding from the Primordial Being who performs the quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*). // 14 //

Here, in the *Prāṇapāda*—in the second and fourth chapters known as the *Prāṇa-pāda*—there is the birth of the letters, their number and measures—the arising of the sense organs, the calculation intended by the scriptures, and such measurements—as well as the essential nature of the vital breath (*prāṇavāyu*). This is the primary [subject].

The appropriate nature of that which is denoted by the term *prāṇa*, its subtlety—the minute form of the principal vital breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*)—and the presiding over both [the subtle body and the gross elements] by the deities and others—that is, the dependence of the principal vital breath, the sense organs, and the individual selves (*jīvātman*) upon the will of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*) in their respective activities regarding their own functions; the non-sensory nature of the vital breath—the exclusion of the principal vital breath from the category of the senses—and [the state] prior to the fivefold differentiation (*pañcīkaraṇa*).

These points have been stated: that the quintuplication (*pañcīkaraṇa*) which constitutes the collective creation proceeds from the Supreme Brahman alone—from Him who exists as the embodied Hiraṇyagarbha produced from His own navel; and furthermore, that the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*) regarding the various individual sentient and non-sentient entities is likewise [His work];
and that eternality resides in space, in atoms such as air, and in the Person (*puruṣa*), while qualities such as ignorance are not inherent in them.

For those who claim that the Creator [bestows] the state of being an element upon the skin and so forth, omnipresence upon the mind, and the status of being a distinct eternal principle; who claim the nature of the Self and so on upon the vital breaths, and sovereign freedom in the restraint of their own words within their own group; even for them, there is a collapse at these two feet [of yours]. (15)

To those who assert the eternity of space (*vyoman*) and the ether, as well as of the atoms of air, fire, and earth—that is, to the Vaiśeṣikas who maintain that these are devoid of origination and so forth; and to those who attribute to the Person (*puruṣa*), even the individual self (*jīvātman*), non-sentience and other such meaningless qualities—that is, the absence of being a knower, and the absence of agency and enjoyership, which are contrary to the Vedas; and [those who attribute] the nature of the elements, such as being of the nature of ether and so forth, to the group of senses like hearing, which are products of egoism (*ahaṅkārika*); and [those who attribute them] to the mind (*manas*)— [The text continues: ...to those who thus describe these things, [the author] says: "In the sky, in the ether, and even in the atoms of air, fire, and earth, for those who speak of their eternity—the proponents of their lack of origination and so forth—and even in the Person, the individual self, for those who determine such meaningless things as non-sentience and the rest—the absence of being a knower, and the absence of agency and enjoyership—which are not based on the Śruti; and in the group of senses such as hearing, which are derived from egoism, the nature of the elements, such as having the form of ether and so forth; and in the mind—"

When the form of the mind (*manas*) has been experienced as a sense faculty (*indriya*), [the author] describes its sovereignty—its omnipresence (*sarvagatatva*) and its eternal nature as a distinct reality—as being of the nature of a separate, unproduced, and inseparable principle; its state as the self (*ātman*) and so forth, namely its nature as the experiencing subject (*bhoktṛ*) and its nature as the instrument (*upakaraṇa*) of the senses; and its sovereign freedom in governing its own station among the hosts of heaven—the assembly of gods who shine having attained their celestial abode—within the vital breaths (*prāṇa*), specifically the primary breath (*mukhyaprāṇa*) which serves to sustain the body.

Regarding the subject of the restraint of those who have attained their own state, there is absolute independence; for the four-faced Brahmā, appointed by the Lord to carry out the creation of the Creator’s emanation, [this independence exists]. For those various disputants who claim that once the mechanism is released, the Supreme Self lacks independence—just as the creator lacks independence once the machine has been set in motion—the refutation and rejection occurs within these two quarters (pādayugme). (The meaning may also be: "the defeat of the disputants' two feet," implying the destruction of their course. || 15 ||

If it is argued that no contradiction is established when one speaks of the non-sublation [of the Vedas] by means of fallacious reasonings (*tarka*) which appear true at first glance, then, insofar as the actual state of things is concerned, one's own cherished position would be undermined. Therefore, this chapter, which serves to pacify contradictions, is opposed to the Buddhist;
for the "unestablished nature of reasoning" (*tarkāpratiṣṭhā*) found in the Sūtras should be applied only to those arbitrary doctrines that turn away from the path of the Śruti.

By means of arguments (*tarka*) that appear to be true to those of superficial vision—arguments resorted to as proofs—the statement of non-contradiction (*avihatikathana*), which is the establishment of the absence of contradiction, would result in the very contradiction (*vyāhati*) being established—that is, the contradiction which is the counter-correlate (*pratiyogin*) of non-contradiction—would be rendered stable, provided that by "proper" (*samyak*) arguments resorted to as proofs, it is indeed [established] according to the actual nature of things (*vastuvṛttyā*). If it were indeed real...

If it is said that this is a statement of non-contradiction, then there follows the obstruction of one's own cherished view—the unavoidable repudiation of the truth of the attributeless pure consciousness (nirviśeṣa-cinmātra) which one holds dear. For this reason, this second chapter of the Śārīraka [Brahma-sūtra], which is intent on resolving contradictions—that is, engaged in removing the conflict between the meaning of the Vedānta and [the doctrines of] Logic (Tarka), Tantra, and so forth—is [addressed] to the Buddhist kinsman through his doctrine of the falsity of the world (jagan-mithyātva).

For the Advaitin who is closely associated with the Buddhists, there is a contradiction—that is, an opposition—consisting in the "unestablished nature of reasoning" (*tarkāpratiṣṭhāna*) as stated in the *Śārīraka-sūtra* ("Because of the non-establishment of reasoning"). This non-establishment of reasoning—meaning the incapacity of reasonings to prove their objects due to their instability—is to be applied to the independent doctrines that turn away from the path of the Śruti; it is to be applied to those arbitrary doctrines opposed to the Vedic path (it should be understood as referring to them), but it is not to be known as referring to reasoning that conforms to the Śruti, because such reasoning is well-established. || 16 ||
The verse beginning with "ātmā" is the subject under discussion;
because of the sense of the statement "living beings [are produced] by water," the living being (jīva) indeed arises from the initial proposition.

Thus, this [view] is indeed essence-less, because it entails the fallacy of the destruction of what has been done (*kṛtavipraṇāśa*), and because of the scriptural statement that [the self] is eternal. || 27 ||

Because of the existence [of scriptural evidence]: since there exists in the *Taittirīyaka* the statement—"From whom the origin of the world [proceeds], by water he emitted living beings upon the earth"—which establishes the creation of all living beings; and because of the indicative proof consisting of the formal proposition (pratijñā)—"Indeed, when that is known, all this becomes known"—which establishes the attainment of the knowledge of all through the knowledge of one; it is accepted that the living being (*jīva*), who is the inner self (*pratyagātman*) and conscious, is indeed born, that is, is produced.

"It is correct," [one might] suspect; however, this is without substance—the reflection on the reasoning stated to prove the self's origination is extremely weak. For, if the creation of the *jīva* were accepted, then while the *jīva* is being produced, it would experience a specific result [only after the cause of that result has already been established, leading to the fallacy of *akṛtābhyāgama*]; furthermore, because a produced entity is necessarily subject to destruction, when that [entity] perishes, the results of the actions performed during its lifetime would perish without having been experienced.

Furthermore, because it would entail the fault of the destruction of performed actions (*kṛtavipraṇāśa*), and because there exist scriptural texts such as "Unborn, eternal, everlasting" (*ajo nityaḥ śāśvataḥ*) and "The eternal among eternals" (*nityo nityānām*) which establish the eternity of the individual soul (*jīva*), and because the non-arising of the self is to be determined through both reasoning and authoritative means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*). || 27 ||
