"The wise one is neither born nor does he die" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 1.2.18); "He is neither born nor does he die" (Kaṭha Upaniṣad 2.18). 246.

This living being is worthy of the state of being wise (*vipaścit*), which consists in consciousness as the substratum of manifold cognitions; even while in the state of depending upon a body, its essential nature is incapable of birth and death (being of the singular form of knowledge).
"Neither his equal nor anyone superior to him is seen.
(100) "No effect or instrument of action exists for him; neither his equal nor anyone superior to him is seen."

The Blessed One, who possesses unconditioned lordship over all worlds, has no body, sense organs, or the like, unlike Brahmā and others. No one at all can be conceived as either equal to or superior to him, whose nature is that of the Supreme Brahman.
Serial number, page 101: "The seer does not see death, nor disease, nor even suffering. The seer sees everything; he attains everything in every way."
One who sees thus does not see death.

The wise man who perceives Brahman as described does not at all contemplate death, disease such as fever, or any adverse circumstance directed toward himself within this world, which is a manifestation of the Lord’s playful power (*līlā-vibhūti*). Being a direct witness of all things, he is capable of attaining his desired objects through mere volition (*saṅkalpa*) in all places, at all times, and in all conditions.
He becomes one in whom sinfulness and other such defects have ceased to manifest.
Inherently free from [the notion that] "after death there is no consciousness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.5.13).

After this living being has attained the supreme state (liberation), following death (having attained liberation after passing away), there exists no knowledge subject to contraction and expansion caused by physical birth, destruction, and so forth; (or rather, the delusion known as the identification of the body with the self does not remain).
103. "For one who possesses a body, there is indeed no removal of the pleasant and the unpleasant. Verily, the pleasant and the unpleasant do not touch one who dwells bodiless.
"For one who possesses a body...
(Chāndogya Upaniṣad 8.12.1)

For a person who is joined to a body initiated by karma known as merit and demerit, the avoidance of the experience of pleasure and pain based upon that [body] is simply not possible; (since the body is initiated precisely for the sake of experiencing pleasure and so forth,) pleasure and pain do not bind a person who is devoid of such a body.
"For there is no loss of the knowledge of the knower"—
that is, the knowledge which is an attribute of the individual self (jīvātman), the substratum of consciousness, never undergoes destruction at any time.
"There is no other seer than this":

apart from the Blessed Lord, the Inner Controller (antaryāmī), who possesses unconditioned omniscience, there is no other—the individual soul (jīva) whose knowledge depends upon instruments—that, while itself unseen by others, becomes possessed of the knowledge of forms and so forth.
Serial number, primary text:
"Nārāyaṇa is the supreme Brahman; Nārāyaṇa is the ultimate reality."
"Nārāyaṇa is the supreme light, the Self; Nārāyaṇa is the supreme.

In the Śrutis and other scriptures, the reality described as the Supreme Brahman, the Supreme Principle, the Supreme Light, and the Supreme Self—with the intent of establishing His absolute pre-eminence—is Nārāyaṇa alone. Just as the individual soul is with respect to the body, He alone is the pervasive, the sustainer, the controller, and the sovereign (śeṣin) with respect to the universe; He alone is "higher than the high" (parātpara).
[As it is said: "Verily, he does not now know himself thus: 'I am this'; nor indeed these beings."

This individual soul (jīva), having attained deep sleep (suṣupti), is then unable to perceive its own self or the objects of its experience as qualified by specific forms such as its own name, caste, family, country, and so forth, in the manner it does during waking and dreaming, thinking "I am such-and-such."
I. "The eternal among the non-eternal, the conscious among the conscious, the one who bestows desires upon the many" (Śvetāśvatara Upaniṣad 6.13). II.
"The eternal among the non-eternal" (Katha Upaniṣad 5.13).

For the Supreme Self, although being Himself eternal and conscious just like the individual soul (jīva), possesses a nature and essence that is non-dual and distinct from everything else; He bestows upon the countless, eternal, conscious beings the objects of their desires. Therefore, the meditation upon Him and the direct realization thereof are the causes of supreme peace.
"There is not the slightest diversity here;
he who perceives diversity here goes from death to death."

II. "There is not the slightest diversity here" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 4.4.19). In the Supreme Brahman—which was previously introduced as the object to be seen, which has all things as its body, is the support of all, and is the ruler of all—in whom there exists not even the slightest difference regarding His being the substratum and the Self for everyone; in such a Supreme Self, the Lord of all and the Remainder of all, whoever conceives even the slightest difference, even in thought, enters into the continuous great cycle of transmigration and does not attain liberation at all.
The meaning is that there is nothing whatsoever that does not have Brahman as its essence.
Krama number,
page: "Not remembering this body as something newly produced."
For a conscious being who has attained union with the Supreme Self consisting of bliss, it is simply not possible to remember its former connection with a body and so forth.
"His supreme power is heard to be indeed manifold, and His knowledge, strength, and action are innate.

Thus, in the Śrutis, it is proclaimed that the Lord’s power—which is suited for the creation of the diverse and wonderful universe and which excels all others—along with the accomplishment of various actions endowed with knowledge and strength, is inherent to His very nature.
"One foot of Him are all beings; His three feet are the immortal in heaven. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 3.12.6) 203, 213, 75, 97.

This entire universe, containing many millions of Brahmāṇḍas, is but a single portion of this all-pervading Lord who is complete everywhere. That divine abode known as the Supreme Sky (*paramavyoman*), which is imperishable and therefore designated as "Immortal" (*amṛta*), constitutes His three-quarters and is truly vast. (Therefore, that Blessed One is the Lord of both the *Līlāvibhūti* [the realm of divine play] and the *Tripādvibhūti* [the manifestation of the three-quarters]). "Having realized the Self and the Impeller as distinct, being favored by Him, one attains immortality.
"Having realized the Self and the Impeller as distinct..."

Having discerned and ascertained through hearing and other means both the individual soul (*jīvātman*) wandering in this wheel of *saṃsāra* and the Supreme Soul (*paramātman*), the Lord (*īśvara*), the one who causes it to wander, the individual soul—being made an object of love by the Supreme Soul who is well-pleased through worship dependent upon Him—becomes liberated.
Serial number:
Pūrvakhaṇḍa manuscript no. "The Lord of the primary matter (prakṛti) and the knower of the field (kṣetrajña), the master of the guṇas."

The Supreme Self is the Lord of both nature and the person (the insentient and the sentient), endowed with the sixfold divine attributes such as knowledge and sovereignty; or, He is the controller of the three qualities (sattva, rajas, and tamas) which serve as His own instruments.
"Having entered, I shall manifest name and form," [it says].
"Mounted by the conscious Self"—

the individual soul (*jīva*), which constitutes the self of the body and stands in the place of the chariot— having attained a specific relationship with the omniscient Supreme Self who stands in the place of the charioteer, [it departs, leaving behind this body].
"Embraced by the conscious Self"—

at the time of deep sleep, this individual soul (jīva), being firmly and completely embraced by the Supreme Self known as the "Conscious One" (prājña), who is its most beloved friend, does not perceive anything else whatsoever, whether external or internal.
"When the vital breath departs, all the vital breaths depart along with it";
"The vital breaths, indeed, are the seers"; "Everything is established in the vital breath."

Just as in the central region of a chariot wheel called the hub (*nābhi*), the wooden pieces called spokes (*ara*) situated between the hub and the rim are well-established and remain firmly fixed; even so, in this present *prāṇa*, all the Vedic words (known as Ṛk, Yajus, and Sāman) and the entire world—characterized by the Brahmin and Kṣatriya classes, consisting of both the moving and the stationary—remain firmly established. "Prāṇa, apāna, vyāna, udāna, and samāna—all this is indeed the mind."

Among speech, mind, and breath, it is none other than *prāṇa* itself; by means of its various fivefold functions known as *prāṇana*, *apānana*, *vyānana*, *udānana*, and *samānana*, it bears those respective names such as *prāṇa* and so forth. (Krama Saṃkhyā Pūrva Saṃhitā).

By means of its various functions, it assists the individual soul (jīva), which is the substratum [of those functions]; thus, because the term "mind" (manaḥ) is applied figuratively to the benefactor [the mind] by virtue of the beneficiary [the soul], it also possesses the general name "anaḥ."
"Every morning they speak untruth—those who offer the Agnihotra before sunrise.

Those ritualists devoted to the performance of the Agnihotra who perform the Agnihotra oblation even before the rising of the sun, rise every morning and perform an act equivalent to speaking falsehood, because they perform the oblation with the mantra "Svāhā to Sūrya" at a time when the sun has not yet risen—an act that is prohibited.
(Chāndogya Upaniṣad, Commentary on "May I be many," Prapāṭhaka 6, Section 2, Verse 3; and on "Then It thought," Prapāṭhaka 6, Section 2, Verse 3)

"O Brahman, the slaves, O Brahman, the servants, and even these gamblers (Atharva Veda)—the fishermen (those who live by catching fish), the dependents, and those who live by gambling—all of them, because they are born from Brahman, attain non-difference from Brahman; for the relationship of progenitor and progeny, as well as the relationship of the body and the embodied, serves as the basis for the designation of non-difference."

"Brahman was the forest, Brahman was that tree from which they fashioned heaven and earth. O wise ones, I declare to you with my mind: Brahman stood presiding over the worlds, upholding them. Regarding the three questions posed by the phrase "What was the forest?", the Teacher provides the answer: Brahman alone is the equivalent of the forest that served as the means for the creation of heaven and earth, the tree situated therein, and the timber and other materials derived from it; nothing else.

Because it is omnipotent, it itself assumes all states—such as being the agent, the efficient cause, the material cause, and the instrument—without depending on any other collection of factors. "Verily, in the beginning, this was Brahman alone, one only. Being one, it did not flourish. It created that which is the form of excellence, the *kṣatra*—namely, those who are the *kṣatras* among the gods: Indra, Varuṇa, Soma, Rudra, Parjanya, Yama, Mṛtyu, and Īśāna. This world, prior to creation, while existing with its names and forms undifferentiated, is designated by the term "Brahman" alone. Thus is the sequence and number.

It was appropriate to speak thus: since there was only one, it possessed an unmanifested majesty. (Having first created Agni in the form of the Brāhmaṇa caste,) it created its own singular form called ‘Kṣatra’ as the most preeminent, which manifested its own majesty. These are indeed those known as the Kṣatriyas within the assembly of gods, who are the very embodiments of the world-protectors (lokapālas).
TB Kramasaṃkhyā Pūrvasaṃkhyā (The sequential numbering of the Taittirīya Brāhmaṇa according to the older enumeration)

"Consisting of mind, having the vital breath as its body, whose form is light, whose resolve is true, whose self is space, possessing all works, possessing all desires, possessing all odors, possessing all tastes, pervading all this, without speech, and without concern."

The Supreme Self has been described: He is perceivable solely by a pure internal organ; He is the controller even of the chief vital breath (*mukhya-prāṇa*); He is endowed with a divine, auspicious form that is eternally and unsurpassedly radiant; His own volition is unimpeded; His nature is subtle and transparent like space—or rather, He is the controller even of the *pradhāna* known as the unmanifest space (*avyākṛtākāśa*); He is the creator of the entire universe; He is the one to be propitiated through all ritual actions; He is enriched with objects of enjoyment, instruments of enjoyment, and places of enjoyment consisting of the most excellent *sattva*; and He is non-material (*aprākṛta*).

Relying upon a multitude of auspicious qualities—such as divine fragrance, flavor, and so forth—which are common to all and fit to be experienced by both himself and others, and having attained all his desires, he remained with silence, treating everything as mere straw.
"It must be reflected upon": O Maitreyī, the Supreme Self alone is that which must be meditated upon; and for that purpose, it should be made firm through reflection preceded by hearing.
Pūrvamīmāṃsā-saṃkhyā-krama (The sequence of numbers in the Pūrvamīmāṃsā)
— Krama-saṃkhyā (The sequential numbering).
Pṛ.saṃ.

From Brahmā down to the lowest, He alone is the supreme one who created the entire multitude of living beings throughout all the worlds through the fourfold variety of bodies; there is no other higher than Him.

"That from which all these beings are born"—all moving and non-moving beings, established by means of valid cognition such as direct perception, are those whose very nature is obtained from that which serves as their own instrumental and material cause; (that alone is Brahman; that alone you should worship through hearing and other means).
"For where there is duality as it were, there one sees another. But when everything has become the Self alone, whom could one see, and by what means? Where, however, for this person...

"O Agni, that which is your red form is the form of fire; that which is white is [the form] of water; that which is black is [the form] of food."

The red color seen in the blazing fire is the form of unevolved light (*tejas*); the white color seen in that very same [fire] is the form belonging to unevolved water; and the dark color appearing therein should be known as belonging to unevolved earth.

"When the senses, together with the mind, stand still, and the intellect no longer stirs— that, they say, is the supreme goal. When the five senses, such as sight and the rest, which serve as the instruments of knowledge, attain a state of firm stability by withdrawing from their objects along with the internal organ (*antaḥkaraṇa*)— the cause of their own activity— and when even the intellect (which is the mind characterized by determination) reaches a state of inactivity, that very state is called the "supreme goal" (*paramā gati*) by those who know reality, because it is conducive to liberation.

"If this bliss did not exist in space [as the Supreme Self],"—the Supreme Self alone is the one who causes all beings to experience bliss; otherwise, no conscious being whatsoever would ever obtain the happiness arising from worldly existence, heaven, liberation, and so forth.
"Whatever Manu has spoken is indeed medicine.

Manu is so called because he is a thinker; he is both a seer (*ṛṣi*) and the Lord of Creatures (*prajāpati*). Whatever has been propounded by him, who desires the welfare of all the world, all that is undoubtedly like medicine, providing security and prosperity through the removal of mental anguish and disease and the granting of what is desired.
"He who dwells in the eye," and "He who dwells in fire"—
in the eye, which is the sense organ that serves as the instrument of seeing, and likewise in fire, which abides within— He who is there is the Supreme Self, your inner controller.

"Among you, when one has departed from this body, that by whose departure this body appears as if most wretched—incapable of its own functions in every way and perceived as disfigured [and, conversely, by whose remaining it remains sound]—he alone is the best among you.

This means: among you, speech and the others, when any one of you has departed from the body, if this body is known to be utterly incapable of its own functions and becomes deformed—as if most loathsome—and [when he remains, it stays] in good condition, he indeed is the most excellent among you.

page: "He whose body is the earth."
"He whose intellect is the body"— that is,

he with respect to whom the earth and the intellect exist as his body by way of being supported, being subject to his will, and being subordinate to him; that person who possesses the status of being the substratum and so forth, the inner self, the self-luminous Lord Nārāyaṇa.
"He whose body is the self," and "He by whom the self has been perceived and awakened"— referring to Him who,

for the sake of favoring the individual soul (*jīva*), entered this body which is full of misfortune and engaged in the experience of the fruits of karma, together with that *jīva*, and who is thus the object of worship and the goal to be attained by it.
He who exists is the wise Self; He is the Supreme Self, to be attained by the liberated.
"She whose body is the unmanifest," "She whose body is the ego."

The unmanifest (avyakta) and the ego (ahaṅkāra) consist of the principles (tattva); that which is their controller by virtue of being the substratum and so forth is the Person (puruṣa), the Lord Nārāyaṇa, the inner ruler of all.
"By which the unheard becomes heard. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.1.3) "Indeed, all those who depart from this world go to the moon. (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 6.2.15)

Whether they are the wise who have perfected the means to liberation, or the ignorant who are devoted to the performance of sacrifices and public works, all without exception, having departed from the body, ascend upwards (becoming partakers of heaven or liberation) and indeed reach the moon.
"Those two should be applied: He who, standing within the fire, is unknown to the fire, whose body the fire is, who controls the fire from within—he is your Self, the inner controller, the immortal.

(As heard at the beginning of the passage, "This indeed is the infant"): Although the vital breath (*prāṇa*) exists throughout the entire body,

the *prāṇa* residing in the central location of the body called the heart is like a newborn infant— because, unlike the *prāṇa* that moves to other locations, it does not produce any specific [external] activity.

"This person who consists of consciousness among the vital breaths, the light within the heart" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 2.3.5; 4.3.7)—he who has consciousness as his attribute and whose very nature is consciousness, who dwells in the midst of the senses and vital breaths denoted by the word *prāṇa*, and who resides in the center of the lotus of the heart; he who is the Person whose nature is the light denoted by the word *jyotis*—he alone is the Self known as the individual soul (*jīva*).
"He who dwells in the air... (190, 257, 167) "He who dwells in consciousness... whose body is consciousness."

II. "Abiding in consciousness" (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad 3.7.22) means "abiding in the Self which has the nature of knowledge and whose attributes are knowledge, and which exists in the form of the individual soul (jīva)," and so forth.

The sequential numbering begins here for the sake of the divine discourse: [the clay] is touched—that is, contacted—by the lump of clay. In reality, it is the very lump of clay that assumes various names and forms through its different states. All of that is indeed perceived through valid means of knowledge as "merely clay."
"Vāyu and the intermediate space (antarikṣa)—this is the immortal.
Vāyu and the intermediate space are the two formless forms of the Supreme Self that endure for a long time.
From wind, fire [arises]. 182, 187, 241. 182, 187.
From the supreme Self, which has air as its body, fire was produced.

"The individual soul (jīva) is to be known as a part of a hundredth part of the tip of a hair, which has itself been divided into a hundred parts; and that [soul] is capable of infinity. Even the tip of a hair is subtle by its very nature, and subtler than that is [the soul]. If one were to mentally conceive that even this [tip] possesses a hundredfold division, then one of those parts is to be contemplated as the measure of the soul.

Therefore, it must be determined that this [Self] is indeed atomic (*aṇu*). It is entirely beyond the range of gross perception. Although its essential nature (*svarūpa*) is thus [atomic], it becomes infinite by virtue of its own inherent attribute of knowledge (*dharmabhūtajñāna*), provided all obstructions have ceased. In the state of liberation (*mokṣa*), this [knowledge] becomes all-pervading (*vibhu*).
"By what means, O mortal, would one know the Knower?"—
by what other means, apart from the method known as meditation (*dhyāna*), could one know such an omniscient Supreme Self? What other sequence or number [of means] exists?
Pṛ.saṃ.

"The universe is Nārāyaṇa" (*Taittirīyopaniṣad*; the sequence is "the universe is Nārāyaṇa, Hari"). Because Nārāyaṇa exists as the cause through the sustaining, nourishing, and so forth of conscious beings—consisting of the bound, the liberated, and the eternal—as well as of unconscious things that serve as their objects of enjoyment, Nārāyaṇa is the self of the universe.
"All beings," and "I know this great Puruṣa,
resplendent like the sun, beyond the darkness."

I have directly perceived the Supreme Person, whose majesty is proclaimed in the Puruṣasūkta, whose nature pervades all things, whose splendor is like that of the sun, and who shines resplendent in the supreme ether that transcends all worlds.

"He becomes onefold.
The individual soul (jīva), liberated from all bonds and manifested in its own true nature, assumes various bodies through its own volition in accordance with the will of the Lord.

"He would not rejoice alone"; "this is one hundredfold the bliss of Prajāpati"— the bliss of the Supreme Brahman, which is the object of meditation, is infinite, its essential nature being characterized by a bliss that is a hundred times greater than the bliss of Prajāpati.
183. He is the cause, the lord of the lords of the senses; he has no progenitor, nor is there any lord over him.
He is the Supreme Self alone, the cause of all things, including all forms of knowledge. Not only that—[the number of verses in this section is] *krama-saṃkhyā*.

The soul (jīva), which is the presider and controller of the organs of action and knowledge, is itself the presider and controller of this [body].

(Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.6) "There he moves about, laughing, playing, and rejoicing. Having attained union with the Supreme Light, the individual soul (jīvātman) comes to possess its proximity and experience thereof as an inseparable concomitant. It becomes possessed of eating, play, and delight in accordance with the enjoyments of the Supreme Self. "Brahman is Truth, Knowledge, and Infinite. (Taittirīya Upaniṣad 2.1)

Brahman, which is the object of the meditative worship that serves as the means to liberation, is endowed with unconditioned existence (*nirupādhika-sattā*), has the single form of eternal and non-contracted knowledge, and is devoid of limitations by space, time, or substance. (He who worships that [Brahman] hidden in the cave of the heart, having experienced Brahman and its qualities, becomes blissful. "One whose desires are true, one whose resolves are true" (97, 203).
"In the beginning, my dear, this was indeed Being alone, one only, without a second. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1)
II. "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone, one only. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1) III. "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1)
IV. "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone" (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.2.1).

The universe, which is known through perception and other means as being manifold and characterized by differentiated names and forms, existed prior to creation as nothing but Brahman—being, devoid of any other cause, undifferentiated in name, and non-dual.

189. "My dear, all these creatures have Being as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support. All this has that as its self; that is the Truth, that is the Self; That art thou, Śvetaketu.
(Chāndogya Upaniṣad VI.8.4) "My dear, all these creatures have Being as their root, Being as their abode, and Being as their support. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad VI.8.6)

WZ... The sequence of manifestation is as follows: all this collection of sentient beings is conjoined with the insentient; that which is denoted by the word "Being" (sat) is Brahman, which possesses the capacity for thought, is the effect of Brahman, and dissolves back into that very same source. All this, established by valid means of knowledge, is pervaded by Brahman, who serves as both its material cause and its inner controller. And because He is the ruler of all, that Brahman is the Self (ātman) of everything. O Śvetaketu, you are of the nature of such a Brahman-Ātman!

"These seven worlds in which the vital breaths move—seven by seven, they are deposited in the secret cave. From the Supreme Brahman, known as the Imperishable (akṣara), [proceed] the principles beginning with the vital breaths (prāṇa) and ending with the oblation (homa), according to their sequential number.
(Pūrva-saṃhitā).
"If he becomes desirous of the world of the fathers"—

having meditated upon the Supreme Self known as the small ether (*daharākāśa*) and its inherent auspicious qualities, and having attained the supreme state, being freed from all dependence, if he should desire to behold his ancestral lineage of fathers belonging to many previous births, then his ancestral fathers, manifesting by his mere will, become objects of his experience.
"Indeed, all this is Brahman" (71, 176, 196).

Since this entire world has its origin dependent on Brahman, dissolves back into Brahman alone, and possesses its nature, existence, and activity dependent on Brahman, one should realize that "all this has Brahman as its self" or "Brahman indeed has everything as its self. Having known this, and without harboring envy, anger, or the like toward anything, one should worship Brahman while remaining tranquil.

"Everything would abandon him who knows everything as being other than the Self"—that is, if one were to perceive the entire world as existing independently of Brahman, as something established in itself, knowing it to be non-Brahman in nature, then even that entire world would overcome him. "All this is indeed enveloped by Prāṇa";
the entire range of activities of the sense organs, such as speech and the rest, is dependent solely upon Prāṇa.

"Indeed, all these deities, contending for preeminence, having come together and abiding in this body—the deities such as speech and the rest—entered into a rivalry with the vital breath (*prāṇa*) in order to proclaim their own respective superiority, and they departed from this body one after another. (In the end, they determined that the preeminence belongs to the vital breath alone.)"
"Indeed, all these beings enter into breath alone and emerge from breath alone.

All beings that have come into existence possess an origin dependent upon their connection with breath, and they dissolve back into breath alone. (*Abhisaṃviśanti* means they dissolve; *abhyujjihate* means they arise. "That indeed is this great, unborn Self—undecaying, undying, immortal Brahman. (The sequence number: 1.
"Verily, this great unborn Self... (Praśna Upaniṣad 2.5)

This Supreme Self, previously introduced, is free from birth, old age, and death, and is beyond the cycle of transmigration (*asaṃsārī*). "Together with the wise Brahman"—the worshipper of the Supreme Brahman, who is established in the cave of the heart and whose nature is truth, knowledge, and infinity, experiences that Supreme Brahman as the object of worship, as well as its innumerable auspicious qualities within the supreme ether (*parame vyoman*).
"One who performs good deeds becomes good; one who performs evil deeds becomes evil.
One becomes virtuous through virtuous action and wicked through wicked action.

Thus, one intent on performing the sattvic actions prescribed by the Vedas and other scriptures is born endowed with a beautiful body as a Brāhmaṇa or similar caste. Conversely, one habitually engaged in prohibited rajasic and tāmasic actions comes to possess a contemptible body such as that of a dog or a Caṇḍāla. These states of being a doer of good or evil are likewise caused solely by prior merit and demerit.

"The Creator fashioned the sun and the moon as they were before. The four-faced Lord, the ruler of the manifested world, just as in the previous *kalpa*, likewise in this present *kalpa*, ordained the sun and the moon for the establishment of day and night. "This very Deity thought: 'Come now, let me enter these three deities with this living self (the *jīva*) and differentiate names and forms. [He made] each of them threefold, threefold. (Chāndogya Upaniṣad 6.3.2–3) The sequence and number [of the elements].
Pūrva Saṃhitā: "This is the deity that never sets, namely Vāyu.

Deities such as Agni and Āditya sometimes cease from their own functions and thus reach "setting," which is to say invisibility. But the deity in the form of Vāyu, because its motion is constant, has an unceasing function; being a deity devoid of setting, it is the most excellent of all.

"If the slayer thinks he slays, or if the slain thinks he is slain, both of them do not understand; the Self neither slays nor is slain.

If some killer, aiming at someone, should think, "I shall kill this person," or if someone, having been struck by another and with a limb severed, should think, "I have been killed by him"—both of these are not knowers of reality. This is because the Self, which is devoid of birth, death, and the like, and whose sole form is knowledge, is incapable of being slain or the like (since it consists of nothing other than right knowledge).

The sense-faculties such as the eye, their auxiliary conditions such as light, the object of apprehension such as a jar, and the immediately preceding momentary cognition—these four are the causes for the arising of cognition in general. "The locus, likewise the agent, the various instruments, the diverse and distinct activities, and destiny as the fifth among these."

The body is the locus for the self's activity and so forth; the individual soul (jīva) is the presiding agent over the body; the sense organs, such as speech and the rest, together with the mind, are the instruments for its functions; the vital breath (prāṇa) is the cause of activities such as the closing and opening of the eyes and the sustainer of the body; and the Supreme Self (paramātman) is the controller of all—these five are the causes in all effects.

"This is the Great Upaniṣad, endowed with the four Vedas;
it is designated as Sāṅkhya-Yoga and also as Pañcarātra."

This Vaiṣṇava Tantra is indeed most exalted and worthy of being designated by the term "Upaniṣad," because it reveals the ultimate secret reality accessible only to yogis. Furthermore, it is integrated with the four Vedas—namely the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva—as it brings about the realization of the essential truths, benefits, and human goals taught therein. Likewise, because the doctrines of Sāṃkhya and Yoga are also merged within it, it bears the meaningful name "Pañcarātra," as it unites the five systems of scripture consisting of the four Vedas, Sāṃkhya, and Yoga, which bestow supreme knowledge.

This [work] has indeed been extracted from the extensive narrative of the Bhārata, consisting of one hundred thousand [verses], like clarified butter drawn from curds by churning with the intellect as the churning-stick. (In the second half of verse 174, there is also a variant reading: "having churned the unsurpassed ocean of knowledge with the churning-stick of the intellect.")

That which is presented here as the essential subject matter has been extracted—like butter churned from curds—by means of the churning-stick of a sharp intellect, from the extensive narrative named the *Mahābhārata*, which consists of a hundred thousand verses. (The *Nārāyaṇīya Pañcarātra*)

"This is the highest good; this is Brahman; this is the unsurpassed benefit. "It is honored by the Ṛg, Yajur, and Sāma Vedas, as well as by the Atharva-Āṅgirasas. "O gods, this instruction of mine shall indeed be authoritative."

The entire range of subjects taught in this scripture known as the Pāñcarātra is the supreme means for both types of human goals—worldly prosperity (*abhyudaya*) and liberation (*niḥśreyasa*). It is also perfectly connected with the four Vedas, namely the Ṛg, Yajur, Sāma, and Atharva; for [it contains] the sequence and enumeration of the principles (*tattva*), the beneficial, and the human goals. *Ta. That which is denoted by the word "Being" in the passage, "In the beginning, my dear, this was Being alone," cannot be the *pradhāna* (primordial matter) described by the Sāṃkhyas, which is understood solely through inference apart from scripture; for there is the use of the verbal root *īkṣ* ("to see") in the Śruti—"It thought: May I be many"—which indicates that the referent of the word "Being" possesses consciousness. Just as when fire is situated anywhere inside a house or similar structure, its light pervades every part of that house, so too this entire universe consists of the power of the formless supreme Brahman, which extends everywhere.
"In this way, Sāṃkhya, Yoga, the Vedas, and the Āraṇyaka—these are mutually limbs of one another; indeed, they are called the Pañcarātra."

Sāṃkhya is devoted to the instruction of the yoga of knowledge (*jñānayoga*), which serves as the means to liberation by means of analytically demonstrating the twenty-five principles whose essence is the Supreme Brahman; Yoga is devoted to the instruction of the yoga of action (*karmayoga*), which consists of the performance of rites prescribed for the various castes and stages of life—known as *śrauta* and *smārta*—as a form of procedure (*itikartavyatā*) toward the worship of Brahman endowed with the eight limbs beginning with restraint (*yama*) and observance (*niyama*); and the Vedas are devoted to the instruction of the specific nature of rituals consisting of the propitiation of deities, [as well as] of actions and meditations.

And since the Āraṇyakas are devoted to demonstrating that [the Pañcarātra] consists in the propitiation of the Blessed Lord, when one combines these fivefold scriptures—namely Sāṃkhya-yoga, the four Vedas, and the Āraṇyakas—they are described as the Pañcarātra, being unified by their mutual relationship of primary and subordinate members and their common purpose of propounding a single reality.

That portion of the scripture in which the established doctrine (*siddhānta*) is accepted as authoritative, and wherein twice-born practitioners—who have received the initiation for worship through hereditary lineage and are devoted to the meditation on Brahman—perform the worship of the fourfold manifestation (*vyūha*) consisting of Vāsudeva, Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha, that doctrine is called the *Āgama-siddhānta*, placing the fourfold principles beginning with Vāsudeva at its forefront. "The cause of this [soul]’s births in good and evil wombs is attachment to the qualities (*guṇas*)."

This conscious being, having obtained birth in specific wombs such as those of gods or humans through the transformation of primordial nature (prakṛti) dependent upon its prior karma, possesses a mind attached to the pleasures and other experiences consisting of the *guṇas* associated with those various births; thus, it engages in actions consisting of merit and demerit which serve as the means for attaining them.

And thereafter, for the sake of experiencing the fruits thereof, one is born again in various wombs—whether good or evil—in accordance with one's own karma. Thus, through the continuous succession of the wheel of birth, action, and so forth, one becomes helplessly attached to the cycle of transmigration (*saṃsāra*) with its unceasing activity. Therefore, attachment to the qualities (*guṇas*) such as *sattva* and the rest is itself the cause for obtaining diverse births. "Nature (*prakṛti*) is said to be the cause in the agency of the effect and the cause;
the person (*puruṣa*) is said to be the cause in the experience of pleasure and pain."

Regarding the maintenance of the life-force (*jīva*)—that is, the body which serves as the locus of experience—and the senses together with the mind which serve as the instruments of experience, when they perform their respective functions, the cause is *prakṛti* alone presided over by that specific *jīva*. However, when the experience of pleasure and pain is to be accomplished, the cause is consciousness (*cetana*) itself as conjoined with *prakṛti*. Therefore, the distinction is this: in the accomplishment of bodily and other such effects, the agency of the *puruṣa* consists in its nature as a presiding director (*adhiṣṭhātṛtva*); but in the production of experience, that agency consists in its nature as a substratum (*āśrayatva*).

"Brahman is that from which the birth and so forth of this [world] proceed"—

that is, that which is the cause of the creation, maintenance, dissolution, and ultimate absorption of this world of manifold and infinite forms, that alone is Brahman. "The living being, the non-living, influx, bondage, shedding, restraint, and liberation."

The soul (*jīva*) possesses the qualities of knowledge, vision, bliss, and energy; the non-soul (*ajīva*) consists of the various objects of experience for the soul; the influx (*āsrava*) takes the form of the sense organs and other instruments belonging to the soul; bondage (*bandha*) is eightfold, comprising the four destructive (*ghāti*) and four non-destructive (*aghāti*) karmas; shedding (*nirjarā*) consists of austerity as established by the teachings of the Arhats, serving as the means to liberation; restraint (*saṃvara*) is the cessation of the senses, designated by the term "samādhi"; and liberation (*mokṣa*) is the manifestation of the soul's innate nature once the afflictions such as passion have ceased—this is the summary of liberation.
The means to liberation consists of truth, knowledge, vision, and conduct; these are the principles accepted by the Jains.

And because of that absence of error, the witness-hood of this Puruṣa is established, as well as his isolation, neutrality, state of being a seer, and lack of agency.

From the statement "the three qualities are non-discriminative," etc., because of the dissimilarity between the Puruṣa and both the manifest (vyakta) and the unmanifest (avyakta), these attributes are established for the Puruṣa as appropriate. These are: isolation (*kaivalya*)—the state of being absolutely devoid of connection with suffering and so forth; witnesshood (*sākṣitva*)—non-agency despite possessing the capacity for cognition; observerhood (*draṣṭṛtva*)—the direct illuminator of the intellect; non-agency (*akartṛtva*)—the state of not exerting effort toward the attainment of one's own desired ends; and neutrality (*mādhyasthya*)—the absence of attachment, aversion, and the like caused by connection with pleasure, pain, and so forth.

"Therefore, through union with that [Puruṣa], the insentient *liṅga* appears as if it were sentient; and although the qualities (*guṇas*) are the agents, the indifferent [Puruṣa] likewise appears as if he were the agent. Since it has been established by the aforementioned reasoning that sentience and agency do not reside in a single locus, the *liṅga*—the principle of *buddhi*—though itself devoid of sentience, becomes, due to its proximity to the principle of *puruṣa* and the resulting failure to perceive their distinction, as if connected to the sentience residing in the *puruṣa*, and thus becomes the object of the empirical usage "I know."

In this very same way, qualities such as pleasure and so forth residing in the intellect (buddhi), as well as agency itself, appear as if they have passed over to the Puruṣa due to the mutual superimposition of their attributes; yet in reality, the Puruṣa remains strictly indifferent, because it is remote from attributes such as agency.

"How can the agency of creation and so forth be attributed to Brahman, who is devoid of qualities (nirguṇa), immeasurable (aprameya), pure (śuddha), and stainless-souled (amalātman)?"

How can agency— consisting in the accomplishment of effects such as creation— be attributed to the Supreme Self, who is untouched by qualities such as passion (*rāga*), who is beyond the scope of the means of valid cognition that grasp objects like sound, and who, though existing, is unsullied by limiting adjuncts (*upādhi*) such as karma, since He is distinct from the common agency found in worldly beings?

He is the cause of all causes, the first manifestation within the fourfold arrangement (*caturvyūha*), known as Vāsudeva. He alone is the Supreme Brahman, the goal to be attained by the liberated. From Him emerges the manifestation named Saṅkarṣaṇa, who presides over the egoity of all individual souls (*sakalajīvābhimāna*). (Saṅkarṣaṇa is so called because he performs a "drawing together" [saṅkaraṇa] properly joined to the Cause; thus, he is the withdrawer at the time of dissolution. From Him arises the manifestation named Pradyumna, who presides over the mind. And from him emerges the manifestation named Aniruddha, who presides over the ego-sense (*ahaṃkāra*).

"By way of transformation, like water, due to the specific nature of each respective substratum of the qualities. Just as water fallen from a mass of clouds upon the earth, having reached herbs, trees, and so forth, becomes the cause of a diversity of tastes in their bark, stems, leaves, and the like; so too, it is entirely logical that the Unmanifest, which is subject to transformation into effects beginning with the Mahat and ending with the Earth, brings about a variety of effects. The reason for this is "the specific nature of each respective substratum of the qualities."

An object that serves as the substratum for specific qualities is a "substratum of each quality" (*pratiguṇāśraya*). In every individual instance—which serves as the substratum for specific qualities—there exists a particularity corresponding to each respective quality. Just as there is a transformation of specific tastes such as sweet or sour due to the particularities existing in individual fruits like the *jambīra* (citron) or the coconut, so too, from the particularities residing in each respective principle beginning with *mahat*, arises the manifold diversity of the world, which is the effect culminating in the earth element.

300. For the sake of the Puruṣa's perception and for the sake of the isolation (kaivalya) of Pradhāna, there is a union of both, like that of a lame man and a blind man; from this union, creation proceeds.
II [The bondage of the Puruṣa and the Pradhāna; the creation is their connection.]

III. For the sake of accomplishing the manifestation of experience—consisting of the Puruṣa as the conscious agent and Pradhāna as the object of action—and for the sake of achieving liberation characterized by the discriminative discernment of the difference between Puruṣa and Sattva (Prakṛti), the process of creation of the principles beginning with Mahat proceeds from the union of both Puruṣa and Pradhāna, brought about by time and karma, serving as the means for both experience and liberation.

"The activity of Pradhāna proceeds for the sake of the liberation of the Puruṣa," just as the activity of even insentient milk occurs naturally for the growth of calves among cows, without depending on knowledge, desire, or other such factors; likewise, the sequence and number [of the constituents] of Pradhāna, though insentient, [proceed in this manner].

The activity of Prakṛti, being impelled [by Puruṣa], serves as the cause for the transformation of the body and so forth, in order to accomplish the purpose consisting in the liberation of the Puruṣa situated within it.
"The Person exists because there must be an enjoyer";
"All living beings are indeed cities for the one who dwells in the cave, who is unslain and free from blemish.

All embodied beings are the cities of the Supreme Self—who dwells in the cave of the heart, who is full, untouched by anything that is not the goal of man (apuruṣārtha), and unaffected by slaughter, bondage, and the like; they serve as His dwelling places for the purpose of His playful sport. "City" (pur) means a place of residence for the sake of His pastimes.

"Know that both Prakṛti and Puruṣa are indeed beginningless, O Kaunteya! Both the Pradhāna—which, by its nature, undergoes transformation into the form of the principles (tattvas) beginning with Mahat and ending with Earth—and the Puruṣa, who is non-transforming, are denoted by the word 'beginningless' as being devoid of origin. "All actions performed in every way are wrought by the qualities of Prakṛti.

‘One whose self is deluded by egoism thinks, “I am the doer. (II) The conscious being, possessing the delusion that the body is the self and not knowing its own self to be a non-doer, wanders about while regarding itself as the agent of actions whose accomplishment depends upon the qualities such as *sattva* belonging to *prakṛti*. Agency belongs to the qualities of *prakṛti*; it does not belong to the individual soul (*jīva*) who is of the nature of the Self—this is the meaning.
"It is my conviction that there is nothing more delicate than Prakṛti; for once she has been seen [by Puruṣa] with the thought, 'I have been seen,' she does not present herself to his sight again."

As I discern Prakṛti according to her own nature, this understanding arises in me: "She is of an exceedingly delicate nature"; for, like a woman of good family, she is possessed of extreme modesty, and imagining that she has been seen by a man, she conceals herself, distancing him from any further sight of her. Once the discriminative knowledge of the difference between the Puruṣa and Prakṛti has arisen, and through the attainment of liberation (kaivalya) for the Puruṣa, there will never again be any contact with Prakṛti.
Pṛ.saṃ.

"O best of ascetics, they exist just as heat exists in fire. "Because of the finite measure of individual manifestations, because of their commonality, because of their activity through power, because of the distinction between cause and effect, and because of the non-distinction of the manifold universe, there exists the Unmanifest Cause."

There must necessarily exist some cause designated as the "Unmanifest" (avyakta), which possesses a single nature consisting of a universal that is free from mutual opposition, for those manifest effects such as the Great Principle (mahat) and the rest, which possess various specific attributes that are mutually contradictory and whose individual natures are manifest; thus, everything manifest has the Unmanifest as its very root.

In this regard, five reasons are established: (1) because specific forms (*viśeṣa-rūpa*) are limited, they cannot be the cause since they lack the capacity to persist through all effects by virtue of being denotable by specific terms; (2) because general forms (*sāmānya-rūpa*) are pervasive, they can be the cause since they possess the "concordance" (*samanvaya*) consisting in persistence through all [effects] by virtue of being denotable by general terms; and (3) because it is observed that only that which possesses such [general] power engages in the production of an effect.

Because the effect exists in its cause as a subtle form within the universal [cause], and because it is only after attaining separation from that cause that it manifests as an effect—thereby justifying its designation by the term "effect"—and because the very nature of destruction is the concealment (tirobhāva) consisting in the attainment of non-separation from its own cause by the effect which has entered into various and diverse states.
Regarding the phrase "the senses with the mind as the sixth":

the individual soul (*jīva*), whose knowledge and sovereignty are extremely contracted, acts as the lord of the five senses and the mind-sense—the sixth sense—which reside within their respective bodies as transformations of *prakṛti* bound by its own beginningless succession of karma; drawing all six of these senses hither and thither, it sustains the journey of the body.

"An eternal portion of My very self, having become a living soul in the world of living beings... This individual soul (*jīvātman*) is beginningless; it belongs to Me, Lord Vāsudeva, who is the indweller of all bodies and thus the source of all attributes. Although it has attained the status of a "portion" (*aṃśa*)—in the sense of being a specific part of the qualified whole—it has nonetheless entered into the state of a transmigrating soul (*jīva*) because it is bound by beginningless ignorance in the form of karma. Abiding only in the world of living beings, it wanders about, conjoined with bodies, senses, and so forth, according to its own respective karma.

"Hating Me in their own bodies and in the bodies of others, these envious ones are indeed people of demonic nature (āsuraprakṛti). Dwelling while relying on self-destruction such as pride and egoism, they hate Me—who am situated everywhere within as the Inner Self—in their own and others' bodies by exposing faults; thus, they perform actions that cause Me displeasure."

"One who knows the reality of the six mudrās and is proficient in the supreme mudrā, having meditated upon himself as seated on the *bhaga*-throne, attains nirvāṇa. This means that the seeker of liberation who understands the ultimate truth of the six mudrās—such as the necklace (*kaṇṭhikā*), the breast-ornament (*rucaka*), and so forth—as taught in the Śaiva Āgamas, and who is likewise skilled in other superior mudrās, becomes established in absolute isolation (*kaivalya*) by contemplating his own essential nature as seated in the place called the *bhaga*.
"Root-nature is unevolved; the seven, beginning with the Great One (mahat), are both nature and evolved;
the group of sixteen is evolved only; and the Person (puruṣa) is neither nature nor evolved."

There are twenty-five principles (*tattvas*). Among them, the first principle is *mūlaprakṛti* (root-nature). Since it is not the effect of anything else, it is called "unmodified" (*avikṛti*). The principles that possess both causality and effectuality are seven in number: the Great One (*mahat*), ego-consciousness (*ahaṅkāra*), and the five subtle elements (*tanmātras*). The sixteen principles—consisting of the five organs of cognition, the five organs of action, the mind (*manas*), and those known as the five gross elements—are exclusively principles that are effects; they are not causes for further principles.
The Puruṣa, however, is the principle of consciousness; it is neither the effect of anything, nor is it the cause of anything.

"O Acyuta, you who consist of all the gods, you are eternally worshipped through sacrifices by those beyond thought; you alone are the consumer of the *havya* and *kavya* offerings, assuming the very forms of the ancestors and the gods."

O Blessed One, Nārāyaṇa, who has become the inner self of all deities! O You whose nature is changeless! You alone exist as the one eternally worshipped by the rites known as Śrauta and Smārta, which are to be performed by those of the three twice-born castes. You alone, having assumed the form of the ancestors (Pitṛs), are the receiver of the sacrificial offerings at the Śrāddha; and having assumed the form of the gods (Devas), You are the receiver of the divine oblations.

the human being."

Having properly propitiated Me—who am the one upon whom the maintenance, origination, and so forth of the four classes of embodied beings, beginning with the gods, depend, and who pervades this entire collection of elements both internally and externally—a qualified person attains perfection in the form of reaching Me.
"In all things, according to scripture and according to reason, the Lord Nārāyaṇa is the ultimate goal. 177

"Just as in the world a king, though residing in a region full of terrible scorpions and amidst a crisis of calamities, is not touched by defects because his body is fanned away by a whisk, and he protects the people according to their desires and maintains enjoyments such as perfumes that are for the common use of all; so too this Lord of the World, with the fly-whisk of His own sovereign power waving, is not touched by defects; He protects the worlds beginning with the realm of Brahmā and maintains enjoyments that are for the common use of all."

For a king seen in the world, engaged in the protection of his subjects, has gone out for the purpose of hunting those who cause harm to the virtuous; remaining in a region filled with insects and the like that cause distress, he dwells in comfort with his body unharmed by mosquitoes and other pests due to the abundance of equipment such as fans, which serve to brush them away; he protects his esteemed and loyal subjects without restraint, and he himself shines forth, endowed with the enjoyment of his own unique perfumes, garlands, and other luxuries.
In the same manner, this Supreme Lord [is described] in sequence.
Pṛ.saṃ.:

The Blessed One, having accepted the consecration for protecting the world, enters into all embodied beings as their inner controller (*antaryāmin*); by the power of his knowledge and other faculties which depend upon his own nature, he removes those obstacles to human goals caused by contact with the body, and—being filled with his own unique and unsurpassed knowledge and other qualities—he carries out the protection of the entire world.
"That which is water is indeed the body of Viṣṇu":
all that is created by the Supreme Self, characterized by water and so forth— the entire universe— is nothing other than the very body of the Blessed Lord Mahāviṣṇu.
"He who investigates by means of reasoning knows Dharma, and no other.
"Because from this scripture the supreme, imperishable Brahman known as Vāsudeva is properly attained through action preceded by knowledge."

Since the Supreme Brahman— which is designated as Vāsudeva, established in the Bhagavacchāstra, and transcending the threefold limitations— is correctly understood from this scripture known as the Sātvata through sacrificial rites accompanied by discriminative knowledge, therefore this scripture is the most excellent of all.

"Even those who, endowed with faith, worship other deities—they too, O Kaunteya, worship Me alone, though not according to the prescribed rule. O Kaunteya! Those people who, being possessed of faith, become worshippers of other deities and propitiate those deities in the form of Indra and others through prescribed rituals—even they worship Me, Vāsudeva, who am the indwelling Self of all those respective deities. However, because they do not recognize Me as the indwelling Self and instead mistakenly perceive those deities themselves as the Supreme, their worship is "not according to the prescribed rule" (avidhipūrvakam).
Therefore, the action of these people does not result in the attainment of Me as its fruit.

"O Lord, those men who, devoted to their own duty (*svadharma*), have propitiated you, they cross over this entire *māyā* for the sake of self-liberation. O refuge of all! Those men who, intent on the performance of the duties pertaining to their respective caste and stage of life (*varṇāśrama-dharma*), worship you—they, for the sake of liberation from all bonds, cross over the goddess *māyā*, composed of the qualities (*guṇamayi*) which causes the obstruction between the individual soul (*jīva*) and the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), and become partakers of natural bliss. (IS B III-58, IEC)
Just as a dancer, having displayed the sequence, number, and page of the performance, withdraws from the dance; so too does [the mind].
In the same way, having manifested herself to the Puruṣa, Prakṛti desists.

Just as a dancer, having reached the stage of the theater, displays her own form to the audience through her physical and verbal activities and then withdraws, even so does this primordial nature (prakṛti), consisting of intellect and the rest, withdraw from the stage of the intellect once its purpose has been fulfilled.

Having displayed her own nature— consisting of pleasure, pain, and delusion— to the person standing near her, and having also brought about his discriminative discernment (*viveka-khyāti*) between the *sattva* and the *puruṣa*, she, having become the means for liberation in the form of isolation (*kaivalya*) and considering her purpose accomplished, withdraws from the proximity of the *puruṣa* so as never to be seen again.

"A Rudrākṣa bracelet on the hand, a single lock of matted hair on the head, and bathing with ashes using a skull"— this is the vow of a man who has accepted the Śaiva initiation (dīkṣā): namely, the wearing on the arm of a bracelet strung with Rudrākṣa beads for the purpose of protection, a mass of hair fashioned into matted locks upon the crown of the head, the carrying of a human skull-bowl for the sake of begging alms, and the bathing of the entire body with charcoal and ashes.

The complete sūtra is: "For [the Lord] is indeed possessed of manifold forms" and "so too within the Self, for He is indeed possessed of manifold forms. "By worshipping the *vibhava* [manifestations], one attains the *vyūha*; by worshipping the *vyūha*, the subtle Supreme Brahman known as Vāsudeva is attained.

Through the worship of the divine manifestations of Rāma and Kṛṣṇa according to the Sātvata injunctions, and through the worship of the fourfold manifestation (caturvyūha) known as Aniruddha, Pradyumna, Saṅkarṣaṇa, and Vāsudeva—preceded by the attainment of that fourfold manifestation—the practitioner attains the supreme Brahman, the most subtle one called Paravāsudeva; such is the culmination of the worship taught in the Pāñcarātra.
"But in case of contradiction, it would be independent";
"in case of contradiction, it would be independent;

for when [the Smṛti] is absent, there is inference"—this is the remainder of the Sūtra. Among the means of valid knowledge that determine dharmas, such as Śruti, Smṛti, and so forth, when Smṛti and the like—which depend upon their own source, the Śruti—contradict a directly perceived Śruti, [the former is not authoritative].

Point 1: When a conflict arises, that which is contrary to the Śruti, such as Smṛti and the like, is simply not to be respected; it is not to be accepted. Indeed, the possibility of inferring [the existence of] Śruti from it occurs only when no contradiction exists.

"By a single fraction of Myself, I stand supporting this entire universe," O Arjuna! This whole world, comprising both the sentient and the insentient, existing in the states of cause and effect, is presided over by Me alone—Vāsudeva—and I abide as its controller through even a mere fraction of My own majesty.

Therefore, they are related exclusively to the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). Just as in the world, the potency consisting of heat resides only in fire and is not related to anything else, so it is here.

Since the aggregate of material objects—which, having attained a state of composition, assumes the form of the body and so forth—has as its sole nature the accomplishment of a purpose for another, there must necessarily exist someone who partakes in such a purpose; and this [person] must be distinct from *prakṛti*, which consists of the three *guṇas*.

The existence of the Puruṣa is established because [the Pradhāna] must have a supervisor; because, seeing that the Pradhāna—which serves as the substrate—is insentient and an object of enjoyment, it is inevitable that its supervisor possesses sentience and the status of an enjoyer; and because the activity of the Pradhāna (Prakṛti) is for the sake of liberation, it is the Puruṣa alone who must be postulated as that which attains liberation.

"Having come together in mutual conjunction and being mutually dependent, those [principles] beginning with Mahat and ending with the specific elements (viśeṣa) produce the cosmic egg. 7: Therefore, with respect to objects beyond the reach of the senses, scripture alone is the means of valid knowledge (*pramāṇa*). Reasoning (*tarka*) is to be employed solely for the purpose of corroborating that [scripture].

However, in the case of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*), who is free from all taint (*apahatapāpman*), even though He has the entire universe—both gross and subtle—as His body, there is not even a trace of connection with *karma*; therefore, the possibility of even a trace of that which is not a human goal (*apuruṣārtha*) does not arise. Just as in the world, although those who obey a king’s command and those who disobey it experience pleasure and pain brought about by the king’s favor or punishment, the ruler—the king himself—does not incur the status of being an enjoyer of the pleasure and pain caused by obedience or disobedience merely by virtue of possessing a body.

9. Herein lies the truth: Brahman alone, having the sentient and insentient entities as its body and thus being the mode (*prakāra*) of that [body], is always denoted by all words. At certain times, it possesses the sentient and insentient entities as its body in a subtle state, such that they are not yet fit for separate designation from itself; this is Brahman in its causal state (*kāraṇāvastha*). And at other times, it possesses the sentient and insentient entities as its body in a gross state, such that they are fit for the conventional usage of distinct names and forms.

And that [effect] is non-different from its cause; thus, the world, which is of the nature of an effect, is non-different from the Supreme Brahman, its cause. Regarding the body-like sentient and insentient entities and their embodied Lord, Brahman, there is a distinction between qualities and defects based on their respective natures as established by hundreds of scriptural texts, both in the causal state and in the effected state.

10. For indeed, all the Śrutis, along with the Smṛtis, Itihāsas, and Purāṇas, establish that the Supreme Cause, Brahman, is the Lord of All—eternally omniscient, omnipotent, of true resolve, faultless, and characterized by unsurpassed bliss that is unlimited by space or time and devoid of any further excellence. They do not, however, establish anything else as superior to the Lord, such as a mere "Being" (sanmātra) that is the Lord of the Lord. 11.

11. Just as the single air within the body, assuming various modes of activity, takes on different names, forms, and functions such as *prāṇa* (out-breath), *apāna* (in-breath), and so forth; even so, the one Brahman alone becomes the world in its diverse forms of the moving and the stationary. Thus, the non-difference of the world from the supreme Brahman, the ultimate cause, is established. 12. Brahman is an entity distinct from the individual self (*pratyagātman*), because the latter is subject to internal and other forms of suffering.
Indeed, the supreme Brahman is designated as distinct from the individual self in such passages as, "He who dwells in the self... (Bṛhadāraṇyaka Upaniṣad). 11. [Section] Number.

In that context, the sequence of numbers refers to Saṅkarṣaṇa, Pradyumna, and Aniruddha as the presiding deities of the principles (tattvas) of the individual soul (jīva), mind (manas), and ego (ahaṅkāra); thus, their designation by the terms "individual soul" and so forth is not contradictory,
just as [the term "breath"] is used for space (ākāśa) and the vital air (prāṇa).
The designation of Brahman.

Therefore, that Blessed One—Vāsudeva, who is known solely through the Vedas and designated as the Supreme Brahman—is an ocean of infinite, noble qualities such as knowledge and bliss, which consist exclusively of auspiciousness and are opposed to everything that is to be abandoned; He whose resolve is ever true, having beheld His devotees established in the system of the four castes and four stages of life and intent upon the human goals known as dharma, artha, kāma, and mokṣa, is a great ocean of boundless compassion, virtuous character, parental affection, and magnanimity, [revealing] His own essential nature...

Having ascertained the Vedas—divided into the categories of Ṛg, Yajus, Sāman, and Atharvan, possessing immeasurable branches, and consisting of injunctions, explanatory passages, and mantras—which reveal His own glory, the means of worshipping Him, and the true nature of their fruits, and which are difficult for all other gods and humans to fathom, He Himself composed the Pāñcarātra scripture that reveals the true nature of their meaning; thus, everything is beyond reproach.

Because human-authored treatises (*pauruṣeya-tantra*) propound mutually contradictory matters, and because the Vedas—being non-human-authored (*apauruṣeya*) and thus free from all taints of defects such as negligence—propound matters that are not contradicted [by other means of knowledge], it is difficult to find authoritative validity regarding the state of things as they truly are within those human treatises. Furthermore, the object known through the Vedas is Nārāyaṇa, who is the Supreme Brahman.

Therefore, the reality of the principles (tattvas) such as Pradhāna, Puruṣa, and Paśupati, which are taught in their respective Tantras, must be accepted as having their true nature solely in Nārāyaṇa, who is the Supreme Brahman known through the Vedānta. For one who contemplates the fact that everything has Brahman as its essence, it is understood that Nārāyaṇa alone is the ultimate ground (niṣṭhā) of all those principles taught in the various Tantras.

Therefore, since Nārāyaṇa—who is the supreme Brahman known through the Vedānta—is himself the speaker of the entire Pāñcarātra, and since that system (tantra) expounds His essential nature and His worship, no one can attribute to it any commonality with other systems.

38. By the supreme Brahmā Nārāyaṇa—in the Pañcarātra itself—it has been elucidated that the twenty-five principles taught in Sāṃkhya, the yoga consisting of the restraints (yama), observances (niyama), and so forth taught in Yoga, and the essential forms of the rituals prescribed in the Vedas are all accepted; furthermore, the fact that these principles have Brahman as their essence, that yoga is a mode of meditating upon Brahman, and that ritual acts are a form of propitiating Him has been clearly explained therein.

The impossibility of arising pertains to that which exists— the supreme cause, the highest Brahman itself— and to the phenomenal world distinct from it, consisting of the unmanifest, the great principle (mahat),
ego-consciousness (ahaṅkāra), the subtle elements (tanmātra), the sense organs, space, air, and so forth; [this is established] by the sequence and enumeration through the knowledge of the One.

Since the state of being an effect has been understood through the proposition that all cognition is [of Brahman] and other such arguments, non-origination is not tenable; therefore, it is stated that everything other than Brahman is an effect of Brahman.

Because Brahman, which is the substrate of all manifested objects, is not the object of means of valid cognition such as perception—which grasp only the manifested objects—and because prior to hearing the Vedāntas there is no cognition of the substrate, and the final determination [of Brahman] is preceded by the absence of cognition of the substrate; and because in the world those various words are applied to each respective object, which is but a single part of what is denoted, by breaking [the word] again and again.

Alternatively, one might raise the objection that the designation of Brahman by words such as "fire" (*tejas*) and so forth would be non-primary (*amukhya*), since these words are conventionally understood to denote only those specific objects. Anticipating this, [the author] states: A word denoting moving and non-moving things is indeed primary when applied to Brahman, because the denotative capacity of all words is permeated by the nature of Brahman. This is understood from the scriptural passage concerning the differentiation of names and forms (*nāmarūpavyākaraṇa*).

193, 194. 41. What is called "being an effect" (*kāryatva*) is indeed the attainment of another state by a single substance. That [status] belongs to the individual soul (*jīva*) as well. However, this is the distinction: the kind of transformation that occurs in non-conscious entities such as space (*viyat*) and so forth does not apply to the soul. The transformation of the soul consists in the contraction and expansion of knowledge (*jñāna*); whereas for space and the like, it consists in a change in their essential nature (*svarūpa*). This very kind of origination, characterized by a change in essential nature, is denied in the case of the soul.

Transformation, which consists in the attainment of another state by the causal state, is common to both types [the sentient and the insentient] as well as to the possessor of those types (the Supreme Self).
Serial number,
primary reference: Brahman, whose body consists of the sentient and insentient entities in their gross and subtle states.

Even while abiding in both the states of cause and effect, it remains free from even a trace of all defects, standing as an ocean of boundless and noble qualities such as the power of true resolve (*satyasaṅkalpatva*). The non-fulfillment of human goals and the transformations of essential nature (*svarūpānyathābhāva*) pertain only to the insentient and sentient entities that constitute its modes; thus, everything is consistent.

By the passage beginning with "197–200 vālā" and so forth, it is heard in scripture that a substance similar to an atom (*aṇu*) is extracted [as the measure], and thus the soul (*jīva*) possesses that same dimension; therefore, this self (*ātman*) is indeed atomic (*aṇu*). Just as a drop of yellow sandalwood (*haricandana*), though residing in only one part of the body, produces a refreshing sensation pervading the entire body, so too the self, though residing in only one part of the body, experiences a sensation (*vedanā*) that pervades the entire body.

Just as the light of objects such as the sun or a jewel, though residing in only one place, is seen to pervade many places; so too, the knowledge of the Self residing in the heart exists pervading the entire body. The existence of knowledge—which stands in the place of light—to the knower outside its own substrate is established by analogy with the light of a jewel.

Just as there is a distinction (difference) between odor, which is perceived as a quality of the earth, and that earth itself, so too is established the distinction of cognition from the self, since cognition is perceived as a quality of the knower in the form "I know."
208–209 Serial Number (Pr. Saṃ.)

The scriptures enjoin the very enjoyer of fruits such as heaven and liberation to act as the agent; therefore, the purposefulness of the scriptures is established only if the conscious enjoyer is indeed the agent. Even though the self is endowed with instruments such as speech and so forth, it acts when it desires and does not act when it does not desire. Just as a carpenter, despite the proximity of tools such as an axe, acts or refrains from acting according to his own will.

The agency of this individual soul arises solely from the Supreme Self. In all actions, depending upon the effort exerted by the person, the inner controller, the Supreme Self, impels him by granting His permission; without the permission of the Supreme Self, his activity is not possible.

However, for one who exerts themselves with extreme devotion toward what is favorable to the Supreme Person, the Blessed One, showing grace, personally generates an inclination toward the auspicious actions that are the means to attain Him. And for one who exerts themselves with extreme hostility, He, restraining them, generates an inclination toward those actions that lead to lower states and are opposed to attaining Him.

It is stated that "this individual soul (jīva) is a portion of Brahman," because it is designated both as manifold and as one. The designation of manifoldness is made through such attributes as: being the creator and the created, the controller and the controlled, omniscience and ignorance, self-dependence and dependence on another, purity and impurity, the possession of auspicious qualities and their opposite, lordship and subservience, and so forth. The designation of non-difference is made through such statements as "That thou art" and "This Self is Brahman."
Thus, in order to establish the primary validity of both designations, it must be accepted that "this individual soul (jīva) is a part (aṃśa) of Brahman."

Thus, when the plurality of eternal selves is established by valid means of knowledge (*pramāṇa*), even though they are all of a single nature by virtue of having consciousness as their essence, the distinguishing form is perceived only by those capable of knowing the true nature of the self. 231. Just as the luminous light of the sun, fire, and so forth constitutes a part (*aṃśa*) of them; and just as the qualifiers such as "cowness" constitute parts of entities characterized by those qualifiers, such as cows, horses, white, black, and so on.

Or, just as the body is a part (*aṃśa*) of an embodied being such as a god or a human, so too the individual soul (*jīva*) is a part of the Supreme Self (*paramātman*). For "part-hood" (*aṃśatva*) consists in being a portion of a single entity. In this way, the relationship of part and whole between the individual soul and the Supreme—the qualifier and the qualified—as well as their difference in essential nature, is logically established. Just as... (as in the previous section).

Just as [the sun] becomes otherwise through the power of its radiance, so too the Supreme, who is the possessor of parts, is a distinct entity from the individual soul (jīva), which is His own part corresponding to that radiance.

Thus, designations of difference proceed by relying on the distinction in essential nature (svabhāvavailakṣaṇya) created by the relationship of qualifier and qualified between the individual soul (jīva) and the Supreme (para). However, designations of non-difference are established as primary by relying on the fact that qualifiers which cannot exist independently terminate in the qualified entity. This is because, in such passages as "That thou art" (tat tvam asi) and "This Self is Brahman" (ayam ātmā brahma), the words "thou" (tvam) and "this Self" (ayam ātmā)—just like the words "that" (tat) and "Brahman" (brahma)—denote a single referent by virtue of expressing Brahman as having the individual soul as its body (jīvaśarīraka-brahma).

Thus, although all [individual souls] are equal in their non-difference from Brahman, in being impelled by Brahman, and in their nature as knowers—and although they are all of one form—nevertheless, due to their connection with bodies that are pure or impure according to whether they are Brāhmaṇas, Kṣatriyas, Vaiśyas, Śūdras, and so forth, it is logically consistent that for some there is permission to study the Vedas and perform their prescribed duties, while for others there is a prohibition thereof; and for some there is permission to see or touch [others], while for others there is a prohibition thereof.

Just as fire, although it possesses a single uniform nature by virtue of being fire, is brought forth from the house of a Vedic scholar (*śrotriya*) but avoided when coming from a cremation ground or similar places; and just as food and other such things are accepted from a Vedic scholar but rejected from one who is accused of a crime or otherwise censured.

Even though the individual souls (*jīvas*) are of a uniform nature by virtue of being portions of Brahman (*brahmāṃśa*) and so forth, there is no confusion of experiences because they are distinct from one another and, being atomic (*aṇu*), are separate in each body. The sense organs (*indriyas*) are not merely seven, but rather eleven; for while the soul resides in the body, the hands and other limbs also serve as instruments for its experience, and because their functions are distinct. Indeed, a difference in function is observed in the hands and other limbs, just as it is in the ears and other senses, such as grasping and so forth. Therefore, these too certainly exist.

The mind itself is designated by the terms *buddhi*, *ahaṅkāra*, and *citta* due to the distinctions in its functions of determination (*adhyavasāya*), self-conceit (*abhimāna*), and reflection (*cintā*). Thus, there are exactly eleven sense organs; those who maintain a higher number do so with the intention of referring to the different modifications of the mind. Conversely, the designations found in various places that suggest a lower number are prompted by specific intended functions, such as the act of walking and so forth. The vital breath (*prāṇa*) is preeminent; it is not merely air, nor is it simply the movement of air, because in the scripture (*śruti*) "vital breath" and "air" are taught as distinct entities.
Prāṇa is simply air that has reached a different state; it is not a distinct substance like fire and the rest.
This *prāṇa* exists in five forms as *prāṇa*, *apāna*, *vyāna*, *udāna*, and *samāna*;
it benefits the living being (*jīva*) through practices such as *dhāraṇā*, and its sequential enumeration is like that of the eyes and other sense organs.
